title: What does a verifier's silence tell you?
summary: When reporting costs c, a truthful verifier paid the score gain over an anchor α abstains exactly when |p−α| < √c (Brier) or KL(p‖α) < c (log), so silence is an interval of signals and carries evidence unless the anchor is a symmetric prior. At prior 0.1 the outcome rate among reporters is 0.57; an aggregator that drops silent verifiers has log-loss 0.62 against 0.02 for one that uses silence at n=12 (it worsens as verifiers are added); a stale anchor makes silence point at the wrong state. Quadrature and seeded Monte Carlo. Stylised.

title: Under a latency deadline, how much engine area does picking the most accurate model first cost, compared with choosing model and lane count together?
summary: Exhaustive joint search over the 40 measured accel-kws keyword-spotting models and six MAC lane counts (240 designs), against a model-first flow, at deadlines of 2,000–20,000 cycles. The most accurate model (validation 0.775, test 0.752) needs 16 lanes at 2,000 cycles and 7,667 generic cells; accepting 2 validation points less (test 0.738) cuts area by 31–42%, and 3 points by 35–56%. Stylised and only partly the milestone: models are a fixed measured table (the dataset was unreachable), cycles for more than one lane are analytic and not RTL-simulated, memory bandwidth is not counted, area is generic gates, and no NSGA-II or Bayesian search was run (the space is small enough to enumerate).

title: Which dataflow should a small keyword-spotting accelerator use, and does the answer survive allowing an input buffer?
summary: Four dataflows (output-, weight-, input-stationary and reduction-tree) of a P -lane MAC array, as schedules walked cycle by cycle on the 40 accel-kws models, with SRAM-access counts that match closed forms exactly and, at P = 1, the measured RTL cycles of accel-kws . At batch 1 output-stationary is best (input-stationary is a median 1.2× to 4.1× worse, falling with lanes); at batch 4 it wins every model while weight-stationary is a median 4.5–9.0× worse through partial-sum traffic. Allowing an activation buffer flips the batch-4 winner to the input-mapped flows at 32 lanes (1.37× better), so the ranking rests on a modelling choice. Stylised: assumed energy constants, a one-cycle register model, no RTL beyond one lane, Timeloop not tried.

title: How large must an activation buffer be before the best dataflow for a small keyword-spotting accelerator changes?
summary: A bounded LRU activation buffer of K 8-bit words added to the four accel-dataflow schedules and swept over the 40 accel-kws models at 8, 16 and 32 lanes. At batch 1 output-stationary wins every model at every K . At batch 4 input-stationary first ties or beats it at K = 32, 64 and 128 words (8, 16 and 32 lanes; 10 of 40 models at 8 and 16 lanes, 30 at 32), and no flip occurs for the 2-bit models. If a buffer read costs half an SRAM read instead of a tenth, the flips mostly disappear. Buffer-read energy is assumed and buffer area is not charged. Stylised.

title: How cheap must idle flops be, relative to a weight fetch, for register-file weight-stationary to beat output-stationary?
summary: Breakeven price ratios solved from the RTL-measured counts of accel-planebatch (P = 8, batch 1 to 16, two accel-kws layers). Register-file weight-stationary beats output-stationary on energy only if an extra flop costs under about 1% of a weight fetch per cycle at B = 4 (2.6×10 −3 at B = 16), a bar that falls roughly as 1/ B unless idle flops are clock-gated. Weight-stationary with partial sums in SRAM wins only if a 24-bit partial-sum access costs under 0.25 to 0.48 of a weight fetch, which looks implausible. Stylised: no energy constant is measured or sourced, so which side real technology falls on is left open.

title: Does the keyword-spotting engine fit a small open-toolchain FPGA, and how fast does it clock?
summary: The accel-kws serial-MAC engine, wrapped with on-chip weight ROMs and run through Yosys and nextpnr-ice40 for 15 geometries (hidden width 8–128, 2/4/8-bit weights) on the iCE40 UP5K and HX8K, 3 seeds each. All 15 fit: at most 1,138 of the UP5K’s 5,280 logic cells (22%) and 24 of its 30 block RAMs, because Yosys put the weights in block RAM, so logic grows with weight bits rather than width. Post-route Fmax is 15–22 MHz on UP5K and 37–54 MHz on HX8K, so one inference takes 0.04–0.70 ms. Stylised: the weights are random (Speech Commands was unreachable), accuracies are borrowed from accel-kws , and nothing was run on a board or measured for power.

title: Does the gated weight-stationary engine's verdict depend on how many lanes it has?
summary: Sweeps the lane count P (2 to 16, with a failed attempt at 32) of the four engine modes from accel-gatedrtl on the 64×70 keyword-spotting layer, in RTL simulation and Yosys synthesis to SKY130 HD. All 29 points are bit-exact and write the same accumulator bits in every mode. Accumulator clock-pin energy stays at B × OS for ungated WS and at 1.01 to 1.07× with a gate per set, independent of P ; gated WS stays 1.6 to 1.9× OS area at B = 4 (2.9 to 3.0× at B = 8), flat from P = 4. So the earlier conclusion (cheap to clock, not small) is a property of the batch, not the lane count. Stylised: synthesis only, clock-pin energy only; Yosys exceeded 7 GB at P = 32, so wider engines are not covered.

title: Why did the gated weight-stationary engine need so much synthesis memory, and does fixing it change its area verdict?
summary: The accumulator read in the engine of accel-gatedrtl indexed the whole accumulator bus with a variable, which Yosys builds as one wide shifter per lane and which stopped accel-gatedlanes at 16 lanes. An AND-OR read mux over the batch sets gives the same cycles, fetches, accumulator writes and flop count, bit-exact against NumPy at all 48 points (P = 2–64, B = 4 and 8), but weight-stationary engines come out 17–28% smaller in SKY130 HD synthesis (output-stationary unchanged). Gated weight-stationary is 1.45–1.50× the output-stationary area at B = 4 and 2.1–2.2× at B = 8, flat in P, against 1.6–1.9× and 2.9–3.0× before; every point now synthesises under the old 7 GB cap. Stylised: synthesis only, one layer shape, random data, clock-pin-only energy; the cause is inferred from the before-and-after effect.

title: Does clock-gating the extra accumulators make register-file weight-stationary scheduling beat output-stationary?
summary: Follows up accel-pdkprice , where idle flops made weight-stationary (WS) lose to output-stationary (OS) once weights are packed into SRAM words. Reads the idle clock energy of a flop and of an integrated clock gate (ICG) from the SKY130 HD and GF180MCU liberty files: an idle SKY130 dlclkp_1 costs 0.86 of an idle dfxtp_1 (39.7 against 46.4 fJ per cycle), and GF180 gates cost 0.99 to 1.02 of its flops at 3.3 and 5 V in both track heights. One gate shared by G accumulator flops therefore cuts the idle cost about G -fold. With one gate per 24-bit accumulator, WS needs a weight fetch of only 0.08 to 0.9 pJ (ungated: 2.2 to 26 pJ) and beats OS against every packed SKY130 macro in all 64 macro, layer and batch cells but one (an 80-bit macro on the 11×64 layer at B = 16 needs 27 flops per gate). Library characterisation values, a gate-per-group model with the enable logic, area and the register-file read mux unpriced; no RTL built or synthesised. Stylised.

title: Does the clock-gated weight-stationary engine hold up once it is written in RTL and synthesised?
summary: Writes the register-file weight-stationary (WS) engine of accel-planebatch with clock gates (one per 24-bit accumulator, or one per set of eight) and synthesises it to SKY130 HD with Yosys. All 32 points are bit-exact against NumPy and write exactly as many accumulator bits as the output-stationary engine, confirming the assumption of accel-gatedprice . A gate per set brings the accumulator clock-pin energy to 1.00–1.07× output-stationary (ungated WS: B ×), but area falls only 7–18 % against ungated WS, and gated WS is still 1.2× to 5.3× the output-stationary area at batch 2 to 16 because the extra accumulator sets are flops either way. Stylised: synthesis only, no place and route, clock tree or timing; energy is a liberty-based clock-pin model.

title: Does clock-gated weight-stationary scheduling still beat output-stationary on a second open process, with that process's own SRAM?
summary: Repeats the accel-gatedprice pricing with the IHP SG13G2 liberty files, which ship ten SRAM macros with separate read and write energies (GF180 has none). An idle IHP flop costs 34 fJ per cycle and an idle clock gate 0.75 of that (0.86 on SKY130, 0.95 on NanGate45); one gate per 24-bit accumulator makes register-file weight-stationary (WS) beat output-stationary (OS) in all 120 layer, batch, macro and packing cells, needing at most 6 flops per gate. Ungated WS also wins 33 of the 60 packed cells, where on SKY130 it lost nearly all of them: a packed IHP weight fetch costs 72 to 497 idle-flop-cycles against 18 to 62 for SKY130’s macros. A units trap (IHP declares 1 µA but its energies are pJ) is checked against C×V 2 . Library characterisation values, not measurements; clock gate priced for idle clock energy only, no RTL built for IHP. Stylised.

title: How small can a keyword-spotting accelerator get, and what does each bit of precision cost?
summary: A one-hidden-layer MLP on pooled MFCC features of Speech Commands v0.02 (10 keywords plus unknown), quantised to 2–8 bit weights, mapped to a serial-MAC RTL engine that matches an integer NumPy reference bit for bit on all 40 swept configurations. Test accuracy saturates near 75% (0.752 at 128 hidden units, 4 bits); 4-bit weights are within 0.4 points of 8-bit at 64 and 128 units, 2 bits collapses at small width, and a 64-unit 4-bit design (0.722) uses about 31% of the best design’s modelled energy. Modelled classifier energy is 0.0045–0.19 µW at 4 inferences per second, far below the 1.8 mW microphone floor in ambient-wearable . Stylised: assumed 45 nm energy constants not re-checked, generic-gate area without memories, no front end, a third-party dataset mirror, and a weak feature set.

title: Does the pruning and ternary-weight result from digits hold on real keyword-spotting features?
summary: accel-sparse 's 13 designs (pruned and quantised, ternary, binary) re-run on Speech Commands MFCC features of accel-kws (70-64-11 MLP, 5 seeds, same modelled energy). Negative: no multiplier-free design is within 5 points of float32 (ternary is 19 points down, where digits lost under 1); the cheapest design within 2 points is int8 pruned 50% at 69% of dense int8 energy. Stylised: untuned training, one hidden width, assumed 45 nm constants.

title: Does weight-sharing lookup-table inference beat a multiply-accumulate engine for a small accelerator?
summary: A k-means weight-sharing codebook with a per-input product table (no multiplier per weight) against int8 serial MAC engines, on the 64-32-10 digits MLP of accel-sparse , dense and 75% pruned, over 10 splits. Negative: within 2 points of float32 the table engine does not beat int8 (dense: 3.51 nJ for 8 shared values against 3.56 nJ for int8; pruned: 1.55 against 1.51 nJ), and it only looks better against a baseline that rereads activations per weight. An analytic sweep puts the break-even at layers of about 128 outputs or more, and then only if table reads cost a quarter of an array read. Stylised: assumed 45 nm constants, no retraining or RTL, substitute task.

title: Does fine-tuning the shared weight values rescue low-K lookup-table inference?
summary: accel-lut left its shared values untrained. Here the codebook is kept in the loop for 60 epochs (straight-through, k-means re-fit each step) on the same 64-32-10 digits MLP, dense and 75% pruned, over 10 splits. Mixed: in the pruned network 2 shared values go from a 6.5-point to a 1.7-point accuracy drop, and with an assumed cheap table read (0.04 pJ/bit) that is 1.30 nJ against 1.51 nJ for int8; at 0.16 pJ/bit it loses. In the dense network fine-tuning does not help (8 shared values: 3.2 points down against 1.6 without it). Stylised: assumed energy constants, one fine-tuning recipe, no RTL, substitute task.

title: What does a product-table inference engine cost in RTL, against a serial MAC engine?
summary: Both engines for a 64×N dense layer with 4-bit activations and int8 shared weights, written in Verilog, checked bit for bit against an integer NumPy reference, and synthesised with Yosys to generic gates (assumed gate-equivalent weights). Negative and stylised: the table engine keeps one accumulator per output, so its datapath is 2.4× (N=8) to 11.6× (N=128) the MAC engine's and it takes 1.1× to 3.0× the cycles, even though it stores half the weight bits. Random weights, area only, no energy measured.

title: Does a wider hidden layer make weight-sharing product-table inference beat an int8 MAC engine?
summary: Tests the break-even accel-lut predicted analytically, on trained 64-N-10 digits MLPs (N = 32, 128, 512, 10 splits), with the table engine on the wide layer and an int8 MAC on the 10-output layer. Mostly negative: the best table design is 14% below int8 modelled energy at width 512 only if a table read costs a quarter of an array read per bit (assumed), and 2× or worse at the array-cost read. Accuracy cost of sharing shrinks with width (K = 8: 1.6 points at 32, 0.4 at 512). Stylised, modelled energy, no synthesis.

title: Does NSGA-II find a keyword-spotting accelerator's Pareto front faster than random search at equal budgets?
summary: NSGA-II against random sampling, 30 seeds each, on a 3,840-design space (40 measured accel-kws models × 6 lane counts × 4 memory-bank counts × 4 supply levels) under a latency deadline, scored against the exact front from exhaustive search. At 20.8% of the space NSGA-II finds 54% and 89% of the exact front's designs (50 and 200 µs deadlines) against 19% and 21% for random search, yet hypervolume is 0.97–1.00 for both, so random search is already good enough if only a near-front is needed. Stylised: bank and supply models are assumptions and no multi-lane RTL was simulated.

title: Was accel-nsga's NSGA-II win a tuning accident? Does population size, mutation rate or crossover change how much of the exact front it finds?
summary: A sweep of NSGA-II population size (10–80), per-gene mutation rate (0.02–0.5) and crossover on the 3,840-design keyword-spotting accelerator space of accel-nsga , at 400 evaluated designs, 30 seeds, scored against the exact front. The earlier setting (population 20, mutation 0.25) was under-tuned: mutation 0.02–0.1 finds about 0.38 of the front at 50 µs (was 0.28) and 0.71–0.77 at 200 µs (was 0.59), against 0.13 and 0.12 for random search. Population 80 with mutation 0.5 is no better than random. Removing crossover changes little. Stylised: one budget, four genes, tuned on the score it is reported with.

title: At SKY130's own energy prices, does register-file weight-stationary scheduling beat output-stationary?
summary: Takes the breakeven price ratios of accel-fetchprice and prices them with the SKY130 HD liberty file (an idle dfxtp_1 flop costs 46 fJ per cycle, almost all clock-pin power) and the four OpenRAM SRAM macros shipped with OpenROAD-flow-scripts (10 to 90 pJ per access). If one 4-bit weight is fetched per access, weight-stationary wins at most batches; if weights are packed into the SRAM word (0.8 to 2.9 pJ per weight) output-stationary wins at nearly every batch, and weight-stationary with partial sums in SRAM loses in every case since a word holds fewer 24-bit sums than 4-bit weights. Library characterisation values, not measurements; the per-edge versus per-cycle reading of the OpenRAM figure is unresolved.

title: Does a loop-nest cycle model of a P-lane MAC array match RTL at more than one lane, tails included?
summary: Output-stationary and reduction-tree matrix-vector engines written in Verilog for the two accel-kws layer shapes (64×70 and 11×64), simulated in Icarus Verilog at 1 to 32 lanes. All 36 sweep points are bit-exact against NumPy, and RTL cycles equal the accel-dataflow schedule model plus a constant 2 (3 with a registered adder tree), including ragged last tiles: output-stationary needs 66 cycles against 46 for the reduction tree on the 11-output layer at 16 lanes, and 142 against 194 on the 70-input layer at 32 lanes. Yosys generic-gate area grows faster for the output-stationary engine (11,799 against 8,216 cells at 32 lanes), partly because of its registered output vector. Stylised: batch 1, generic gates not a library, no memories, no timing.

title: Does the weight-stationary advantage in the dataflow model survive RTL at batch above 1, and what does it cost in gates?
summary: One parameterised Verilog engine implements output- and weight-stationary batched matrix products (P = 8 lanes) for the two accel-kws layer shapes, simulated in Icarus Verilog at batch 1 to 16. All 20 points are bit-exact against NumPy, RTL cycles equal the accel-dataflow schedule model plus a constant 2, and RTL weight and activation fetch counts match the model exactly. Weight-stationary fetches the 4,480 weights of the 64×70 layer once instead of B times at identical cycles, but keeping its partial sums in registers grows the design from 3,024 to 12,284 generic cells (about 192 flops per extra batch element) against a flat ~3,000 for output-stationary. The model's ‘weight-stationary is worst’ ranking came from partial-sum SRAM traffic that this RTL trades for area. Stylised; generic gates, no memories, no energy figures.

title: How many MAC lanes of a keyword-spotting matrix engine fit on a small open-toolchain FPGA, and which dataflow is fastest there?
summary: The output-stationary (OS) and reduction-tree (RT, RTp) engines of accel-plane for the 64×70 layer, 4-bit weights, at 1 to 32 lanes, through Yosys and nextpnr-ice40 on an iCE40 UP5K (5,280 logic cells, 8 DSP blocks), 3 seeds, with and without DSP mapping. OS at 16 lanes is the fastest design that fits: 10.2 µs per product, 2,942 cells, 27 MHz, against 12.0 µs for RTp at 32 lanes (3,708 cells). Adder trees clock 1.5 to 2× slower than OS, and OS at 32 lanes does not fit. Letting Yosys use the DSP blocks cuts logic by 13 to 41 % but fails to place beyond 8 lanes, as it does not fall back to logic. Stylised: synthesis and place-and-route only, operands from a shift register (no weight memory), no power, no board.

title: Does the accumulator-read bug found in accel-gatedmux also inflate accel-planebatch's weight-stationary area?
summary: accel-gatedmux found that a variable-index accumulator read made the weight-stationary (WS) engines of accel-gatedrtl 17 to 28 % too large. The batched engine of accel-planebatch has the same index. Rewriting its read as an AND-OR over constant indices and its write as decoded enables, and re-running all 40 points (two accel-kws layers, batch 1 to 16, P = 8), gives bit-exact outputs and identical cycles and fetch counts, with WS area between −3 % and +12 % of the original and no trend in batch (WS/OS cells at B = 4: 1.66 before, 1.62 after). Negative: the earlier verdict stands, because here the accumulators are a Verilog array that Yosys already muxes per entry. Generic-gate cells from one mapper run per point, which moves about 3 % by itself.

title: Does a small control network need an accelerator to meet the control-rate deadline?
summary: Small MLP policies, cloned from a computed-torque controller for a two-link arm with DAgger and quantised to 8 and 4 bits, with inference latency modelled for microcontroller loops and P -lane accelerators (assumed constants) and the closed loop simulated with that latency. Preliminary and mostly negative: the int8 policies track at least 300× worse than the teacher, which itself barely notices a sample of delay, so policy accuracy rather than hardware speed limits control; the deadline model says hardware only matters above about 10 kHz or for larger networks. Stylised; hardware figures are not measured.

title: When does a task's accuracy tolerance let an accelerator drop its multipliers?
summary: Pruning, int4/int8, ternary and binary variants of a 64-32-10 MLP on scikit-learn's 8×8 digits (a substitute task: Speech Commands was unreachable), with a modelled energy per inference for a zero-skipping serial engine, over 10 splits. Pruning 75% of int8 weights costs 0.2 points and cuts modelled energy to 36% of dense int8; ternary costs 1.4 points and binary 3.0. Within 1–2 points of float32 the cheapest design still has multipliers, because operand reads dominate in the assumed model; multiplier energy must be about 10× the assumed value before dropping it clearly pays. Stylised: assumed 45 nm constants, no RTL or synthesis, no lookup-table variant, toy task.

title: Can a quantised MLP surrogate of a finite-element beam beat the beam's own model-form error, and when would an accelerator for it pay?
summary: A 8-32-32-1 MLP imitates an Euler-Bernoulli finite-element cantilever with eight section heights. Shear deformation (Timoshenko vs Euler-Bernoulli) moves the tip deflection by a median 0.09 %; the float surrogate's median error is 1.66 %, about 18× larger, and quantisation adds little at 6 bits with quantisation-aware training (1.95 %) but 21 points at 3 bits post-training. Modelled inference is 3.7 nJ at 8 bits against about 407 nJ for the CPU solve, but the break-even is ~1,600 simulator flops, which a closed-form beam does not reach. Stylised: one tiny network, assumed energy constants, no RTL.

title: When the beam simulator is a 2D finite-element model, does a quantised surrogate (and an accelerator for it) pay?
summary: The cantilever of accel-surrogate meshed as a 2D plane-stress continuum (bilinear quadrilaterals, 32×4 and 64×8 meshes). An 8-32-32-1 MLP imitates each solve and is quantised to 6 and 8 weight bits. With assumed energy constants the FE solve costs 34× (32×4) and 319× (64×8) the 8-bit MLP's energy, so the break-even that failed for the closed-form beam is met. Against a 128×16 reference mesh the 64×8 solve is itself off by a median 9.2 %, the float surrogate by 8.7 % and the 6-bit QAT surrogate by 9.2 %; the surrogate adds little beside the simulator's own error. Limitations: the locking Q4 elements make the simulator inaccurate, two meshes, three seeds, assumed energy model, no RTL. Stylised.

title: Does a keyword-spotting accelerator fit in a Tiny Tapeout tile, and how accurate can it be?
summary: A streaming serial-MAC engine with no weight memory (the host feeds one operand pair per clock over the 16 input pins; hidden activations sit in a rotating shift register), bit- and cycle-exact against an integer reference in Icarus on 32 geometries, synthesised to SKY130 HD with Yosys. Area is 6,300–24,500 µm 2 (661–2,090 cells) for 8–64 hidden units and 2–8 bit weights; flops are 33–53% of it, and 8-bit weights cost about 3,000 µm 2 more than 4-bit. Against an assumed 161×112 µm 1x1 tile (18,032 µm 2 ), the best model by accel-kws test accuracy that fits one tile at 70% utilisation is 16 hidden units, 8-bit weights, 120 inputs (0.616); two tiles take 64 units at 4 bits (0.738), a 1.7× area step for 12 points. Stylised: synthesis only (no placement, routing or timing), random weights in the RTL check, accuracies carried over from accel-kws models that were not re-run through this engine, and the tile area is from a search-result snippet of a Tiny Tapeout guide, not the tile table.

title: A radar twin with no Doppler folding certifies an ego-velocity estimator at every speed: what does the folding sensor do to it, and when can it be unfolded?
summary: Real radar radial speeds wrap modulo 2 v u ( v u =10 m/s); the twin’s do not. The twin-tuned least-squares ego-speed estimator has RMSE 0.022 m/s in the twin and on the real sensor up to 9.5 m/s, then 0.18 (9.8), 1.9 (10) and 14.9 m/s (12). Its large- n bias is exact in closed form (−14.94 at 12 m/s, simulated −14.92) and saturates at − D , D =2 v u Σ c /Σ c 2 , once every target is one fold off. A wrapped-cost grid search restores the twin’s accuracy to 60 m/s with no mode errors, provided the azimuths are diverse: the nearest wrong speed has residual energy 4 v u 2 ( n −(Σ c ) 2 /Σ c 2 ), independent of speed, and Φ(−√ E /2 σ ) matches Monte Carlo (0.061 vs 0.054 at ±8°); at ±5° the search picks the wrong fold in 120 of 300 scenes. Stylised: stationary scene, known azimuths and v u , Gaussian noise, no multi-PRF.

title: What does a radar twin with unlimited unambiguous velocity over-certify?
summary: A pulsed Doppler radar reports radial velocity modulo 2 V ; a twin that renders velocity as a real number never aliases. The real bias of a wrapped return is an exact Gaussian tail series (− V at speed V , −2 V beyond) and the real MSE has a bias 2 floor, so averaging widens the gap to the twin's claim s 2 / n : at V =10, s =1 and speed 8 the real/claimed MSE is 7.9× for one return and 2.1×10 3 for 10 4 . Speeds with |bias| ≤ 0.1 reach only 87%, 74% and 48% of V for noise 0.5, 1, 2. Unwrapping against a prior has exact failure probability 2Φ(− V /√( s 2 + s p 2 )) and stays within 10% of the twin's claim only for prior error ≤ 0.26 V . Stylised: one radial channel, Gaussian noise, simulated radar.

title: Which parts of an always-on Android listening service can be tested without a phone?
summary: A plain-Kotlin core (frame re-chunking, an energy-gate voice detector with hangover and pre-roll, an utterance segmenter that never emits silence, and a headset route policy that pauses rather than falling back to the phone mic) with 7 unit tests, which pass when compiled with Kotlin 2.0.21 and run through a test shim. The Android foreground-service shell is unbuilt : no SDK was usable, so no latency, battery or accuracy numbers exist. Synthetic square-wave frames only. Produced with AI assistance.

title: How much does speech-recognition error hurt an always-on assistant's trigger policies at equal annoyance?
summary: The ambient-interject world with an ASR word error rate (WER) entering each signal by assumption: a two-word wake phrase needs both words right, a keyword one, a transcript-reading intent score loses separation as (1−WER) k , an acoustic score is unaffected. At 2 false interruptions per hour, going from WER 0 to 0.5 cuts the wake phrase's recall from 0.151 to 0.039 (−74%) and the transcript threshold's from 0.365 to 0.089 (−76%), while the acoustic threshold falls from 0.189 to 0.087. With k = 1 the transcript policy stays marginally ahead at WER 0.5; with k = 2 the acoustic policy overtakes it at WER 0.25–0.4. Thresholds tuned at WER 0 stay under the false-interruption budget when deployed at higher WER. Stylised: the WER-to-signal mapping is assumed, not fitted to real recognition, and ASR confidence is not modelled.

title: How should a fixed audit budget be split between gold-labelled and noisy audits?
summary: Extending the stylised gold-audit model with a price: a gold audit costs 3, 10 or 30 noisy audits, with budgets of 200 and 1000. Spending everything on noisy audits read as truth is the worst or near-worst split in all 12 cells (0.387–0.388 at label accuracy 0.7). There is no single best share, but 25% of the budget on gold, fitted jointly with the noisy audits by EM, is within 0.0009 of the best in every cell and 50% within 0.0016. When gold is expensive, all-gold is worse (0.3843 at B = 200, cost 30). Stylised: uniform-error matrices, one auditor accuracy, round-number utilities.

title: Can an always-on assistant learn when to speak from accept/dismiss feedback alone, and what does it cost in dismissals?
summary: A simulated assistant learns an interruption policy online (greedy, ε-greedy or Thompson-sampled logistic model) from the user’s reaction only when it speaks. With an uninformed prior none of the three learns a useful policy in 100 h; with a prior that the intent score is informative, greedy reaches 90% of an offline oracle’s rate after a median 22.5 h and about 185 dismissals, and Thompson sampling takes 32.5 h. It still earns 10.4 against the oracle’s 12.7 per hour, and after a drop in classifier quality it does far worse than frozen offline weights (0.3 vs 4.4 per hour). Stylised: independent windows, instant noise-free feedback, picked costs.

title: Can the doubly robust cap be chosen by validation on an assistant’s own logs?
summary: A stylised follow-up to ambient-crossfit . The cap on the inverse-propensity correction is chosen from {2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, ∞} by 4-fold validation, scoring each candidate with an uncapped inverse-propensity estimate of its utility. With an informed prior the chosen cap matches the best fixed cap to within seed noise (12.23 against 12.19 utility/h at ε = 0.005; 11.45 against 11.84 at 0.002, with a wider spread). With an uninformed prior it does not rescue learning (between −21 and −1 utility/h with seed standard deviations of 24–51, against about 12 for a randomly sampled log), and the validation score is noisy enough that chosen caps scatter across the grid. Stylised, simulated only; 20 seeds, no significance tests.

title: When moments of need cluster in time, does a cooldown, a boost or a back-off help an always-on assistant at equal annoyance?
summary: Needs are made to cluster with a hidden episode/quiet chain (overall rate fixed at 3% of 10 s windows), and a plain score threshold is compared with three stateful rules at the same budget of false interruptions per hour, paired over 10 seeds. With strong clustering an episode-aware boost (lower the threshold after an accepted answer) raises recall by 0.039 at 1 false/h and 0.054 at 4 (0.467 to 0.521); a cooldown after speaking loses recall everywhere, up to 0.066; a back-off after a dismissal is within noise or slightly negative. Without clustering nothing helps. At the 1 false/h budget the boost also overshoots the budget slightly (1.19 vs 1.11). Stylised: false alarms are independent of the episode state, feedback is exact and immediate, every distribution is chosen, no real conversations.

title: How many audited messages does an always-on assistant need before it can trust a noisy urgency label?
summary: Extending the stylised urgency-label model, the assistant estimates the label’s class mix and confusion matrix from n audited messages and then acts by Bayes’ rule. With maximum-likelihood estimates, n = 10 is worse than ignoring the label (mean utility 0.363 against 0.382 at 70% label accuracy); n = 50 recovers 76% of the gain of knowing the true parameters and n = 200 recovers 92%. Add-one smoothing cuts the spread at tiny n but costs a little at high accuracy. Stylised: round-number utilities, uniform label errors, noise-free audit labels.

title: Does cross-fitting the outcome model help capped doubly robust learning from an assistant’s own feedback?
summary: A stylised follow-up to ambient-drclip . The outcome model behind the doubly robust pseudo-labels is fitted on the other half of the windows (2-fold cross-fitting) instead of on the same data, with the inverse-propensity correction capped at 5, 20, 100 or not at all. Negative result: with an informed prior the cross-fitted and in-sample fits are within about 0.1 utility/h of each other wherever the cap is finite, and the unclipped collapse at ε = 0.002 remains (1.53 vs 0.26 utility/h, against 12.71 for the oracle). With an uninformed prior the gaps are large but have no consistent sign (cross-fitting is better in some cells, worse in others) and both variants stay far below the biased fit. Simulated windows with costs chosen by me; no claim about a real user or device.

title: Does a doubly robust estimator fix learning from an assistant’s own self-selected feedback?
summary: A stylised follow-up to ambient-labelmatch . Doubly robust pseudo-labels (an outcome model plus an inverse-propensity correction on the windows where the assistant spoke) are fitted on every window and compared with biased, IPS, clipped and self-normalised fits on the same logged history. A negative result: with an uninformed prior all three variants are far worse than the biased fit (utility per hour below −15 against 12.71 for the oracle) and have huge variance, and with an informed prior they are level with or above the biased fit at they match the biased fit at ε = 0.005 and 0.02 butepsilon; = 0.005 and 0.02 but are not better than clipped IPS. Simulated windows chosen by me; nothing is claimed about real users.

title: Which of score, fold count and fold type made cap selection better in ambient-drvalid?
summary: A stylised, mostly negative ablation of ambient-drvalid : all 8 combinations of validation score (IPS or doubly robust), folds (4 or 8) and fold type (contiguous or random) choosing the doubly robust cap, 20 seeds. With an informed prior all eight are within 0.2 utility/h. With the uninformed prior, random folds are the most consistent help: at ε = 0.02 the 4-fold IPS selector gives −1.4 (std 24) against 5.6 (std 7.3) with random folds, and IPS on 8 random folds (6.3) matches DR on 8 random folds (5.9). At ε = 0.005 the DR score is worse than IPS on contiguous folds (−26.9 vs −17.7) and no selector is clearly best; seed standard deviations are 5–55. Every selector stays far below the label-matched control (about 12). Simulated, independent windows, no significance tests.

title: Does capping the inverse-propensity correction rescue doubly robust learning from an assistant’s own feedback?
summary: A stylised follow-up to ambient-dr , which left clipping untested. Capping the correction weight at 1, 5, 20 or 100 (instead of 1/ε up to 500) removes the collapse with an informed prior: at ε = 0.002 the unclipped fit scores 0.26 utility per hour and the capped ones 11.7–12.2, against 10.6 for the biased fit and 12.71 for the oracle. With an uninformed prior it does not help: capped fits that use the clipped-IPS outcome model stay between −17 and −50, and those that use the prior as outcome model score 4–8 at best, still below the random-subset control (about 12). Simulated windows chosen by me; one cap grid, 20 seeds, nothing claimed about real users.

title: How does the burstiness of an always-on trigger's false-wake counts grow with the counting window when the noise level drifts for hours?
summary: A stylised follow-up to ambient-wakeburst , which drew a fresh noise level per window. With a noise scale that drifts persistently (log-scale AR(1), 5% sd) the Fano factor of false-wake counts rises with the window instead of staying flat: about 1.9 at 100 s for any correlation time, then 14, 110 and 150 at 16, 256 and 1,024 blocks (28 h) for a 2.8 h correlation time, and 620 at 28 h for a 28 h correlation time, while the mean moves only 5%. A Poisson-given-scale (Cox) model, checked against a frame-level simulation (4.7 vs 4.7 and 44 vs 44), and a closed form (mean error 2% on the busy trigger, worst 11%) explain it. The drift is assumed, not measured, and the ‘rare’ trigger is one wake per 500 s, not one a day. Stylised.

title: Do repeated random fold assignments stabilise validation-based cap selection?
summary: A stylised, mixed follow-up to ambient-drablate : averaging the cap-selection score over 5 random fold assignments (instead of one) with an uninformed prior, 20 seeds. At ε = 0.02 it lifts the IPS-score selector from 3.5 to 5.3 utility/h and halves its seed spread; at smaller ε it changes nothing beyond noise. Single-assignment results differ from the earlier project's, showing how much one fold permutation can matter. Every selector stays far below the label-matched control (about 12). Simulated and stylised only.

title: Does a doubly robust validation score choose the doubly robust cap better than an IPS score?
summary: A stylised, mostly negative follow-up to ambient-capcv . Replacing the inverse-propensity validation score with a doubly robust one, on the same 4 folds, changes nothing with an informed prior and gives mixed results with the uninformed one (seed standard deviations of 20–51 utility/h). A doubly robust score on 8 random folds is the best selector in all three uninformed cells, but remains far below a label-matched control (about 12 utility/h against −11 to 6); score, fold count and fold type changed together, so the cause is untested. Simulated, independent windows only; preliminary.

title: Can an assistant learn its urgency label’s reliability from two noisy auditors, and what does a wrongly assumed auditor accuracy cost?
summary: Extending the noisy-audit model, a wrongly assumed accuracy for a 0.8-accuracy auditor costs 31% of a 0.9 label’s gain if the auditor is trusted fully, 17% if assumed 0.9 and 6% if assumed 0.6 (about 39–47% at either extreme for a 0.7 label). With two independent auditors on every message, Dawid–Skene EM learns all three confusion matrices with none supplied: it recovers the true-parameter value exactly in the population limit and at n = 1000 is within 0.0005 of the oracle given the same number of labels, 0.0009 to 0.0128 above taking one auditor as truth. At n = 50 with two 0.7 auditors it still falls below ignoring the label in 18% of audit sets. Stylised: uniform errors, independent auditors, round-number utilities; nothing measured on people.

title: What does Dawid–Skene do when the two auditors share their errors?
summary: Extending the two-auditor model, the second auditor copies the first with probability ρ (each stays 0.8 accurate). Dawid–Skene reads their agreement as correctness: the accuracy it assigns auditor 1 rises from 0.80 to 0.91 at ρ = 0.5 and 1.00 at ρ = 1. At label accuracy 0.9 its policy utility falls from 0.4066 (ρ = 0) to 0.4026 and 0.3992, where it equals taking one auditor as truth, and never goes below that in this model; an oracle told auditor 1’s accuracy is unaffected. Stylised: one shared-error model, uniform errors, round-number utilities; nothing measured on people.

title: What if the two auditors only share errors on hard messages, and can a hardness-aware EM fix Dawid–Skene?
summary: A fraction h of messages is hard for both auditors (accuracy 0.5 or chance) and the rest easy, with each auditor still 0.8 accurate overall. Dawid–Skene again over-trusts the auditors (0.84 for a true 0.8 at h = 0.3, hard accuracy 0.5), but the utility cost is far smaller than with copying: at label accuracy 0.9 its policy utility is 0.4060 against 0.4066 for the true parameters. Only in the extreme cell (30% of messages at chance, the rest perfectly easy) does it fall to the naive estimator’s 0.3992, and it never goes below it. A hardness-aware EM with an informed start recovers the classifier’s matrix and the policy utility at the population level, but the hard share itself is not identified: different starts fit the same joint distribution with P(hard) from 0.24 to 0.35. Stylised, simulated results only.

title: Does fitting only on the windows an assistant explored at random fix learning from its own feedback?
summary: A stylised follow-up to ambient-labelmatch and the reweighting and doubly robust fixes after it. The deployed learner already draws a random sample for free: the windows it spoke on only because its ε coin came up. Fitting on those windows alone, unweighted, reaches 11.99 utility/h at ε = 0.02 and 12.25 at 0.05 with an uninformed prior, against −13.08 and −71.85 for the fit on every spoken window (oracle 12.71; 20 seeds), and as a learner it earns 6.49/h online at ε = 0.005 against −2.04. Exploration costs dismissals (online utility falls at larger ε), and with an informed prior the plain fit is better at small ε. Stylised simulation only.

title: How many false wakes a day does an always-on trigger get when its frame scores are correlated, and what does requiring m frames in a row buy?
summary: A stylised new question for track 2. A trigger fires after m consecutive 10 ms frames at or above a threshold, on Gaussian AR(1) background scores. Setting the threshold so that P m = 1 per day (independent frames) is nearly right for m = 1 (0.78 wakes a day at φ = 0.9) but wrong and unsafe for m ≥ 2: at φ = 0.9 it gives 613, 4,793 and 20,993 wakes a day for m = 2, 3, 5. Exact rates from a grid Markov chain match Monte Carlo (largest |z| 1.69), and the threshold that really gives one a day is 2.0–2.5 sd higher. The score is a model, not a real wake-word detector, and no audio was used. Stylised.

title: Does selection bias actually hurt an always-on assistant that learns only from windows where it spoke?
summary: A stylised follow-up to ambient-ips : on the same logged history, a model fitted only on windows where the assistant spoke is compared with an inverse-propensity-weighted fit and with a full-information fit that sees every window’s label. The full-information fit reaches the oracle (12.72 against 12.71 utility per hour); the biased fit loses 1.3 to 2.1 per hour with an informed prior and fails with an uninformed one, so the bias is large, contrary to a guess in ambient-ips . Weighting recovers part of the loss only at ε = 0.02 with an informed prior. The comparison also mixes bias with data volume (no label-matched control). Stylised, simulated only.

title: Can a noise-adaptive voice gate fit in about 120 bytes of RAM on a pendant microcontroller, and does a cheaper noise floor cost battery life?
summary: A stylised follow-up to ambient-gateroc . Its adaptive energy gate (open when a 20 ms frame is at least 4× the minimum energy of the last 5 s) is ported to plain C99 and checked frame by frame against the Python reference. The exact 250-frame floor needs 1020 bytes of state and about 244 comparisons per frame. Keeping one minimum per block of 10 frames cuts that to 120 bytes and about 24 comparisons, flips 0.02–0.08% of gate decisions, and changes mean recall by at most 0.0002 and modelled battery life by at most 0.07 h (of about 82–90 h) on synthetic audio, 20 seeds × 4 rooms. Limitations: synthetic audio only; host gcc struct sizes and comparison counts, not measured cycles on an ARM core; battery hours inherit the ambient-wearable model.

title: What does the adaptive voice gate cost on a Cortex-M4, in flash and instructions per frame, and is the block-minimum floor worth it?
summary: A stylised follow-up to ambient-gatefw . Its C gate is built with clang for Cortex-M4 (Thumb-2, soft float) and run frame by frame in an emulator on ambient-gateroc ’s synthetic audio. It is bit-exact with the Python reference, takes 236–258 bytes of code at -Os, and its only library call is the 64-bit divide, once per frame. The exact gate executes 3237 instructions per 20 ms frame at -Os; the block-10 floor executes 2096, a 35% cut, because the 320-sample energy sum (about 1980 instructions) is the floor under the saving. Instructions are not cycles, the divide is not counted, and nothing ran on hardware. Stylised.

title: Does a fixed energy-gate threshold survive different rooms on an always-on audio pendant, and what does an adaptive one buy in battery life?
summary: A stylised follow-up to ambient-wearable . Synthetic harmonic ‘speech’ bursts (−36 to −20 dBFS) over pink-ish background noise at −60, −50, −40 and −30 dBFS plus short transients (20 seeds × 120 s per room) are passed through a Python port of the pendant’s energy gate (checked frame by frame against the compiled C), and the gate-open fraction is turned into battery hours with the same power model. Any fixed threshold that holds worst-room speech recall at 0.9 or more ((−30 dBFS or lower)minus;34 dBFS or lower on the grid I swept) stays open nearly all the time in the loudest room, giving 57.6 h, the always-streaming figure. One adaptive threshold (4× a 5 s running-minimum noise floor) gives 82–90 h at recall 0.89–1.00 in all four rooms. Within a single room the two trade-off curves are almost the same; the adaptive gate’s gain is that one setting transfers. Stylised: synthetic audio, uniform one-microphone model, assumed power parameters, nothing measured on hardware or real speech.

title: Do a dual-MAC energy loop and a divide-free threshold make the Cortex-M4 voice gate cheaper?
summary: A stylised follow-up to ambient-gatem4 . With the block-minimum floor the SMLALD energy loop cuts executed instructions per frame by 17% at -Os and 37% at -O2, but without it the gate gets slower (64-bit ring entries), RAM doubles and code grows by about 60%. A divide-free sum-domain threshold matched the original decision on all 36,000 frames per configuration and removes the only library call; the divide itself is not counted, so its saving is unmeasured. Emulator instruction counts on synthetic audio, not cycles and not hardware.

title: When is a glance better than speech for an always-on assistant?
summary: A stylised expected-utility model chooses between speech, a glanceable display and silence by noise, other talkers, free eyes and message length; a Monte Carlo check agrees with the closed form to 0.001. A glance wins in about half of 84 grid contexts, and the look rate, the number a simulator is least able to supply, drives the twin gap (up to 0.036 utility per message). Every parameter is a round figure of mine: nothing is fitted or measured.

title: How many gold-labelled audits replace noisy ones when the auditor’s accuracy is unknown?
summary: Extending the stylised noisy-audit model, 200 or 1000 audits from a 0.8-accuracy auditor read as truth give mean utility 0.387–0.388 (label accuracy 0.7) and do not improve with n, while 25 gold audits already match them and 10 do not. Pooling noisy with gold audits as truth is worse than gold alone. Fitting the mix, the label matrix and the auditor’s matrix jointly by EM, with 10 gold and 200 noisy audits, reaches 0.4054 against 0.4066 for the true parameters at label accuracy 0.9 (gold alone: 0.3955). The advantage vanishes by 200 gold audits. Stylised: uniform-error matrices, one auditor accuracy, EM started at the true value, round-number utilities.

title: Can a likelihood-ratio test tell “no hard messages” from “some”, and is the chi-square cutoff usable?
summary: Testing h = 0 in the three-auditor hardness-aware Dawid–Skene model. Under the null the likelihood-ratio statistic has median about 5 and 95th percentile about 13, so the chi-square cutoffs 3.84 and 5.99 reject 62–72% and 35–49% of null data sets. A parametric bootstrap (39 refits) rejects 7/60 and 0/60 under the null and detects h = 0.3 reliably at n = 1000 (100%) but only 37% at n = 200 with hard accuracy 0.5; h = 0.1 is undetectable. Stylised, 60 draws per cell.

title: Does the bootstrap likelihood-ratio test of “no hard messages” hold its level?
summary: A larger null-only check of the parametric-bootstrap test from ambient-hlrt (B = 39): 200 data sets with no hard messages at each of n = 100, 200 and 500. Rejection at nominal 5% is 11/200, 9/200 and 8/200 (exact 95% intervals all contain 0.05) and at 10% is 20, 16 and 19 of 200; mean p is about 0.5. The earlier 7/60 at n = 200 looks like noise. Stylised: one dependence model, level only, intervals about ±0.03.

title: Does the bootstrap test of “no hard messages” stay valid when the auditors differ in accuracy?
summary: Data with no hard messages but three auditors of unequal accuracy (equal, 0.9/0.8/0.7, 0.95/0.8/0.65; mean 0.8), tested against a null that forces one shared auditor matrix. With 100 draws per cell at n = 200 and 500, rejection at nominal 5% is 6–10/100 at 200 and 0–6/100 at 500; five of six exact intervals contain 0.05 and the sixth (0/100) is conservative. No inflation is seen, but intervals are about ±0.05 wide. Stylised: accuracy heterogeneity only, level only.

title: When should an always-on assistant speak, and does a policy tuned in a simulator keep its annoyance budget in a real room?
summary: Simulated 10 s listening windows (needs at 3%, an intent score with d ′ = 2, wake-phrase and keyword signals) compare interruption policies at equal annoyance. A wake word is precise (0.69) but catches 15% of needs; adding a keyword reaches 53% recall at 28.7 false interruptions per hour (0.72 for the wake word). At a budget of 1 false per hour a score threshold reaches recall 0.26 and a logistic policy that also uses the keyword and wake flag 0.33; recall at that budget climbs from 0.17 to 0.82 as d ′ goes from 1 to 4. Tuned to 1 false per hour, policies keep the budget when only the need side shifts (weaker detector, rarer needs) but run at 3.6–3.9 per hour when the no-need background shifts (noisier score, more wake false alarms); 16 labelled hours restore it for the noisier score, and no threshold can for a wake detector that alone causes 3.5 false per hour. Stylised: independent windows, Gaussian scores, chosen costs, no real conversations.

title: Does inverse-propensity weighting fix an always-on assistant learning from its own accept/dismiss feedback?
summary: A stylised follow-up to ambient-bandit : the assistant speaks with a known probability (ε-greedy) and refits its model with each labelled window weighted by 1/propensity. Mostly negative: exploration itself costs more utility than the learning gains at every ε tried, weights up to 500 make the weighted fit unstable at small ε (a standard deviation across seeds of tens of utility units per hour), and the weighting did not rescue the uninformed-prior or the drift scenarios. Only at ε = 0.02 with an informed prior is the weighted model slightly closer to the oracle (12.2 vs 11.4 per hour at 100 h, oracle 12.7). Stylised: every distribution is chosen by me.

title: Is the gap in an assistant that learns only from windows where it spoke caused by selection bias or by too few labels?
summary: A stylised follow-up to ambient-fullinfo . A control that fits on a uniformly random sample of windows, of the same size as the biased fit’s label set, gets 12.2–12.5 utility per hour against an oracle of 12.71, while the biased fit gets 10.6–11.4 with an informed prior and fails with an uninformed one: in this world the gap is mostly selection bias. Capping the inverse-propensity weights at 10 or 50 beats raw weights and the biased fit with the informed prior, but is worse than the biased fit with the uninformed prior; self-normalised weights are noisy. The control uses labels a real assistant never sees, so it locates the loss rather than recovering it. Stylised: chosen distributions, independent windows, noise-free feedback, simulated only.

title: Under a storage limit, which transcripts should an on-device assistant keep, and what survives?
summary: Seven simulated days of 1500 utterances each with 6 planted facts per day. BM25 finds every fact (hit@5 = 1.00) when the key words are rare, which is the easy case. With the store limited to 10% of the week, dropping oldest or random utterances keeps 0.11 and 0.10 of the facts; keeping the highest mean-IDF utterances keeps 0.93, because the facts are rare-word lines by construction. An importance-ranked extractive summary at 5% of a day holds 85% of its facts, against 3% for the first lines. Index build 0.04 s, query 1.9 ms on one container CPU. Stylised: synthetic words, lexical queries, no paraphrase, no speech errors. Produced with AI assistance.

title: How accurate must an always-on assistant's urgency label be before acting on it beats ignoring it?
summary: In the stylised urgency model, perfect urgency knowledge is worth 0.034 utility per message. Acting naively on a noisy label stops being worse than ignoring it at about 70% accuracy with uniform errors (about 53% if errors only hit neighbouring classes), and at 70% it loses in 18 of 48 contexts. A Bayesian reading of the label never loses to ignoring it when the prior and confusion matrix are known, but a prior that over-weights high urgency drops it below ignoring the label. Every parameter is a round figure of mine: nothing is fitted or measured.

title: Does a likelihood-ranked multi-start make the hardness-aware EM robust to a poor start?
summary: Fitting the three-auditor hardness-aware Dawid–Skene model from 8 grid starts (none near the truth) and keeping the highest-likelihood fit recovers the hard share at the population level (P(hard) 0.300), where a single poor start stays at 0.500 with a lower likelihood. At finite n it matches one informed start (P(hard) 0.290 vs 0.290 at n = 1000, hard accuracy 1/3) and avoids the poor start’s utility loss (0.3913 vs 0.3843). With no hardness at all the hard share is not identified, and fitted shares of 0.3–0.4 appear anyway. Stylised.

title: What does a noisy auditor do to an assistant that learns its urgency label’s reliability from audits?
summary: Extending the stylised urgency-label model, the audit labels are themselves wrong. Taking them as truth biases the estimated label accuracy (0.57 instead of 0.70 with a 0.8-accuracy auditor) and does not improve with more audits: the policy loses 47% of the label’s gain over ignoring it at label accuracy 0.7, and 31% at 0.9. A 0.9 auditor costs only 8–14%. Maximum likelihood over the unseen true class, given the auditor’s accuracy, recovers the true-parameter value, but it needs that accuracy known (not identifiable from one auditor) and is no better at 50 audits with a poor auditor. Stylised; both label and auditor are made-up uniform-error matrices.

title: How much latency and memory does an open-model voice pipeline cost on a CPU, and what reply time does it leave?
summary: A streaming Silero VAD, Whisper tiny.en (int8), Qwen2.5-0.5B (4-bit) and Piper chain on four CPU cores, on six synthetic sentences. VAD costs 0.15 ms per 32 ms frame, ASR 306 ms per segment (RTF 0.11), the first LLM sentence 267 ms, the first TTS chunk 88 ms, and the models add about 740 MB. End of speech to first audio is 0.94–1.55 s at 200–800 ms endpoint hangover, of which about 0.7 s is compute; a 200 ms hangover already cut one utterance in two, and a 0.5 s target is impossible once the hangover alone exceeds it. Stylised: synthetic clean speech, one server CPU not a phone, batch ASR, LLM answer quality not evaluated.

title: How much pre-roll buffer does an energy-gated audio pendant need to stop clipping the first word, and what does it cost in RAM and battery?
summary: A stylised follow-up to ambient-gateroc , which did not measure onset clipping. On synthetic speech over background noise at −60 to −30 dBFS (20 seeds × 120 s per room), a noise-adaptive gate opens on the first frame in quiet rooms, so a pre-roll ring buffer buys nothing and costs battery (82.4 h to 76.9 h at 5 frames). In the loudest room it opens 2.3 frames late on average, and onset recall (first 500 ms of each utterance) goes 0.866, 0.980, 0.999 for 0, 5 and 25 buffered 20 ms frames (0, 3.1, 15.6 KB), at 90.0, 81.1 and 69.7 modelled hours. A gate set too deaf (k = 8) is not rescued: 50 frames lift onset recall only from 0.610 to 0.877. Pre-roll and hangover cost the same per frame and protect different ends of an utterance. Synthetic audio, a stylised power model, no hardware.

title: When is a second or third earbud tone worth it before a glance?
summary: A stylised extension of the urgency model lets the assistant repeat a tone up to four times, 3 s apart, each noticed independently and cancelled once the wearer looks. Choosing the number of tones per context raises mean utility per message from 0.387 (plain glance or one tone) to 0.409; two tones give most of it, and the gain is nil for low urgency and 0.062 for high urgency (partly built in by the weights). Always repeating is barely better than one tone. A Monte Carlo check agrees with the closed form to 0.002. Tones are assumed independent and annoyance flat per tone, and every parameter is a round figure of mine: nothing is fitted or measured.

title: Can a sentence-completeness cue let an always-on assistant stop waiting so long before it replies?
summary: A stylised signal-detection model: the endpointer waits a short hangover Hs after a sentence the cue calls complete and a longer Hl otherwise. With medium pauses (2 per turn, median 250 ms, assumed) and a 10% cut-off budget, a fixed hangover is 913 ms; a cue of quality d = 2 cuts the mean wait to 574 ms if no pause sits at a complete point, but only to 837 ms if half of them do, because the cue is blind to those. With long or widely spread pauses, where a fixed hangover is 1.9 to 2.6 s at a 5% budget, d = 3 gives 571 to 873 ms. The cue, the pause model and the share of clause-boundary pauses are assumed , not measured; only the 682 ms reply chain is measured. Closed forms agree with a Monte Carlo check.

title: How much reply latency can an always-on assistant hide by starting its pipeline before the speaker has finished?
summary: Using the measured ASR, LLM and TTS times from ambient-pipeline (a 682 ms median chain on one server CPU, six synthetic utterances), the reply pipeline starts after S ms of silence instead of after the full end-of-speech hangover H and the reply is held until H confirms the turn is over. Holding saves exactly min(chain, H − S): at H = 1000 ms the median reply falls from 1744 to 1061 ms, at the price of 0.7 to 1.9 extra pipeline runs per turn depending on S, and the just-in-time start S = H − chain is the cheapest that hides everything. Pause durations inside a turn are assumed (five lognormal settings, not data); with median 400 ms pauses no hangover up to 1.2 s keeps cut-offs under 10%. Closed forms agree with a Monte Carlo check.

title: How many starts does the likelihood-ranked multi-start need, and are grid starts better than random ones?
summary: Fitting the three-auditor hardness-aware Dawid–Skene model from 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 nested grid starts versus the same number of random starts, keeping the highest-likelihood fit. When hardness is present and either strong or n With strong hardness or n = 1000 one start nearly always reaches the best optimum and 4 starts reach it in every such cell;nbsp;=With strong hardness or n = 1000 one start nearly always reaches the best optimum and 4 starts reach it in every such cell;nbsp;1000, one start usually reaches the best optimum (72With strong hardness or n = 1000 one start nearly always reaches the best optimum and 4 starts reach it in every such cell;ndash;100%) and 4 starts reach it in 82With strong hardness or n = 1000 one start nearly always reaches the best optimum and 4 starts reach it in every such cell;ndash;100% of draws; with mild hardness at n = 200 and under the null, more starts keep improving the likelihood (grid hit rate 72% at K = 1 to 97% at K = 16) but mean policy utility moves by at most about 0.0002. Grid versus random is mixed. Stylised: one dependence model, 40 draws per cell, optimum judged against the best of 32 fits.

title: Does a third auditor identify the hard-message share, and does it help plain Dawid–Skene?
summary: Extending the hard-message model to three auditors (each 0.8 accurate overall, a fraction h of messages hard for all). A hardness-aware EM now recovers the hard share at the population level (P(hard) 0.300 from four informed starts, where two auditors left 0.24–0.35), but only loosely from samples (sd 0.07 at n = 1000) and a poor start still lands on a degenerate fit. Plain Dawid–Skene gets worse with more auditors: in the extreme cell (30% of messages at chance) it reads them as 0.85 accurate and its policy utility falls to 0.3912 at label accuracy 0.9, below the naive estimator’s 0.3992; the hardness-aware EM stays at the true-parameter 0.4066. Stylised: one shared-hardness model, uniform errors, round-number utilities; nothing measured on people.

title: Does urgency, and a chime-plus-glance mode, change how an always-on assistant should deliver a message?
summary: A stylised expected-utility model adds three urgency classes (deadlines of 120, 20 and 6 s) and a chime-plus-glance mode to the speech, glance and silence choice. Chime-plus-glance is the best mode in 62% of normal and high-urgency contexts and raises mean utility per message from 0.351 to 0.417 (partly by construction, since high-urgency messages carry twice the weight); a Monte Carlo check agrees with the closed form to 0.002. The look and reaction rates drive the twin gap (up to 0.018 utility per message). Every parameter is a round figure of mine: nothing is fitted or measured.

title: How bursty are an always-on trigger's false-wake counts, and does a lockout help?
summary: A stylised follow-up to ambient-falsewake . On Gaussian AR(1) frame scores, wake counts per 1,000 s window are close to Poisson (Fano factor 1.05–1.5 at φ = 0.9–0.95). A window-to-window drift in the noise scale is what makes them bursty: a 5% lognormal drift lifts the Fano factor to about 9 for m = 3 while moving the mean only 4%, and 10% drift gives 38. A 10 s lockout cuts the Fano factor (9.8 to 2.5 with drift) but also cuts the mean by a third; a sub-second lockout changes little. The score is a model, not a real wake-word detector, and the drift is assumed. Stylised.

title: What limits the battery life of a pendant-style always-on audio wearable?
summary: A stylised average-current model for an nRF52840-class pendant with a 150 mAh cell, built from a few vendor figures read on 2026-10-13 plus labelled assumptions. The always-on microphone is the floor (about 170 h alone); gating codec and radio on speech at a 30% speech fraction gives about 105 h against 59 h for always streaming. A 74-byte energy-gate routine compiles for Cortex-M4. Nothing is measured on hardware, the datasheets were not read in full and there is no numeric comparison with Omi.

title: What does not knowing the horizon cost a market maker?
summary: An LMSR with liquidity b routes like Hedge with rate 1/b, but the tuned b needs the horizon T. A b t = c√t schedule with c* = 1/(2√ln N) pays exactly √2 over the horizon-aware bound (1.36 rising to 1.41 measured); the doubling trick is 1.70× worse than the continuous schedule against a price-reactive adversary; and self-tuning liquidity b t = Δ t−1 /ln N makes the subsidy equal the accumulated mixability gap (1.3 against 102 on easy data) with regret at most 2Δ.
