Code and white paper How should Shapley payments be sampled and audited? In a saturating contribution game v(S)=1−exp(−Σw i ) every estimator variance is exact. Permutation sampling always pays out exactly v(N) but is noisy; size-stratified sampling has 6–8× lower variance (exactly zero for equal contributors) yet misses the pot by up to 7% in a run; reversing each permutation cuts RMSE 1.6× at no cost; Hoeffding sample counts are 4–5× larger than needed, and stratification finds the top-3 payees with about 4× fewer samples. Stylised, n≤10. Pure-Python, 9 tests. Code and white paper Which proper score should verifiers face with K outcomes? For K-ary reports the Brier, spherical and log scores have exact regrets and exact worst cases (1−2p min +‖p‖² for Brier, ‖p‖−p min for spherical). Per unit of payment range the spherical score gives exactly √K times Brier’s incentive at a uniform truth, but both bounded scores nearly ignore a dropped rare class: at a 1% class the loss is 1.3×10 −4 (Brier) and 1.0×10 −4 (spherical) against 0.15 for log. Multiclass follow-up to tangent-log. Pure-Python, 6 tests. Code and white paper Can the multiclass log score be made payable? Extending x ln x below a cutoff ε by its second-order Taylor polynomial gives a strictly proper K-class score that equals −ln r y whenever every r j ≥ε and has payment range exactly 1−ln ε, the same for any K. Per unit of range it has 3× Brier’s rare-class incentive at a 5% class and 63× at 0.1%, the best cutoff is the rarest class’s mass, and a verifier that zeroes out a 1% class loses a closed-form 0.005 (Brier 1.3×10 −4 , log unbounded). Closes the gap left open in categorical-scores. Pure-Python, 7 tests. Code and white paper What does it cost to pay for a ranking instead of probabilities? A verifier who reports only the order of K classes can be paid with a score linear in the outcome indicator. It is strictly proper, and swapping two classes at adjacent ranks costs exactly (p i −p j )(w r −w r+1 ), linear in the gap. Per unit of payment range that beats a Brier-derived ranking whenever the gap is below 1/(K−1) (2.5× at gap 0.1, 250× at 0.001, K=5). Equal spacing maximises the smallest incentive, ranking everything costs K−1 times the mode, a top-k set costs the same as the mode, and the sample size to detect a swap is identical to Brier’s. Pure-Python, 7 tests. Code and white paper Should severity reports be scored with the order in mind? For ordered fault severities the ranked probability score is Brier on the cumulative distribution: strictly proper with exact regret Σ(R k −P k )², so moving mass ε a distance d costs exactly dε² where Brier charges 2ε² for every d. Pooling adjacent classes costs exactly half of Brier’s, and every threshold probability is within √regret of the truth. The price: per unit of payment range RPS gives Brier’s incentive only for a maximal-distance shift (1/(K−1) for adjacent ones). Extends categorical-scores. Pure-Python, 7 tests. Code and white paper Can we elicit the mode of a mixture of honest and cheating drift? When some workers cheat, drift is a mixture and the mean, which squared loss elicits, lands where almost no task lies (at a 30% cheater 6σ away, the mean’s window holds 0.15 of the mass versus 0.48 at the mode). The mode is not elicitable, but the centre of the width-2α window with the most mass is, with the bounded loss 1[|y−r|>α]. Regret is an exact window-mass difference; the best window is α=σ for normal drift and γ/√3 for Cauchy (no mean exists); an equal bimodal mixture has one α-mode iff α exceeds a closed-form root α*; and under 10–40% contamination the sample α-mode has ~0 bias while the mean is off by 5ε, at a 3.7× RMSE cost when clean. Pure-Python, 7 tests. Code and white paper Can a verifier be paid for a tolerance interval, not a point? The Winkler interval score is strictly proper for the pair of quantiles, with closed-form regret and an optimal expected score of exactly 4sφ(z)/α. Misreporting the width by the same factor costs more when narrow at 95% coverage but more when wide at 80%, so there is no universal rule that overconfidence is worse. Under Cauchy drift the scores have no mean, yet paired differences are bounded, so evaluate verifiers against a benchmark report. Code and white paper Should drift tolerances be per layer or on the total? Giving each of L layers its own tolerance lets a prover hide the sum of them: L·c(L,α)σ versus z α √Lσ for one test on the total, 6.6× more at L=16 and 23× at L=128. The sum test’s power depends only on the total shift; the exact (Šidák) max test’s depends on how it is spread, the prover’s best split is even (log Φ is concave), and the max test catches a 2.7σ one-layer shift half the time but lets 16σ through spread over all 16 layers. A union of both at α/2 caps the hidden budget at the sum test’s (7.8σ) while keeping one-layer sensitivity. Gaussian, independent layers, known σ. Pure-Python, 8 tests. Code and white paper How do you pay a verifier whose report decides the job? If a report of “fault” gets the job rejected and the outcome is seen only on acceptance, scoring observed jobs is improper: verifiers shade under the threshold to get scored, and every job is accepted (1.1–2.8× optimal decision loss at thresholds 0.7–0.2). A reserve payment for rejection makes truth optimal iff the score’s entropy minimum τ s is at least the threshold τ d , and then it is unique, 1+τ d ²−2τ d τ s . Plain Brier (τ s =½) therefore fails above τ d =½; recentring the score by a term linear in the outcome fixes every threshold, cheapest at τ s =τ d with rent τ 3 /3. Exploration with inverse-propensity payment is also proper but multiplies payment variance by about 1/ε. Stylised, single verifier. Pure-Python, 10 tests. Code and white paper How should a tolerance interval be paid for? The Winkler interval score is the sum of two pinball losses: proper for the equal-tailed quantile interval with exact regret (2/α)[PR(l,α/2)+PR(u,1−α/2)], finite even for Cauchy drift where the expected score does not exist, but its payment grows without bound in the miss distance. A width-plus-miss loss (u−l)+λ1[miss] is bounded by width+λ and elicits the density level set, the shortest interval for its coverage: 22–31% narrower than equal-tailed on lognormal(0,1) drift. The price is statistical: to detect a 20% understatement of a normal tolerance it needs 3–48× more tasks for α≥0.1 and about the same at α=0.01. Pure-Python, 9 tests. Code and white paper How well does Freivalds' check work in floating point? Checking a claimed matrix product by A(Br) ≈ Cr needs a tolerance t , so the error bound becomes size-dependent: a rank-one corruption of Frobenius norm F is missed by a Gaussian probe with probability exactly erf( t /(√2 F )), rank one is the worst case for fixed F , and m probes give erf m (4 probes for 1% at 3 t ). Rademacher probes miss a two-entry corruption with probability ½ at every size. Emulated float32 noise grows ≈ n 0.9 ; a hashed probe with free retries lets a cheater grind in 1/erf tries (125 at 100 t ). Stylised, additive corruption. Pure-Python, 7 tests. Code and white paper Who trades decides how liquid a verification market should be A Glosten–Milgrom market maker facing an informed share μ with accuracy q moves its posterior log-odds by exactly 2·atanh(μ(2q−1)) per net buy, so its price path is an LMSR with b* = 1/(2 atanh m) (verified to 2×10 −16 ). A wrong b costs log loss only in a transient whose peak is scale-free in m and 1.8–2.5× worse when overconfident; the LMSR subsidy tends to b* ln 2, exactly the spread the GM maker charges. Pure-Python, 10 tests, stylised. Code and white paper How many honest runs does a slashing tolerance need? A conformal tolerance (the k -th order statistic of n honest drift scores) has an exact, distribution-free false-slash rate ( n +1− k )/( n +1) — but only 51–56% of calibration sets deliver a rate ≤ α. A PAC-safe tolerance exists iff n ≥ ln δ/ln(1−α) (459 runs at 1%/1%), and its margin is hiding room for a cheater: the threshold sits 1.26× above the true quantile at n =2000 on Pareto-3 drift. Gaussian plug-in tolerances over-slash skewed drift up to 17×; pooling calibration across mixed hardware slashes the noisy class 4.8× too often and lets the quiet class hide 2.9× more. Pure-Python, 7 tests. Code and white paper What does a fee do to a prediction market’s price? A proportional fee f on an LMSR verification market gives every trader an exact no-trade band [ q /(1+ f ), ( q + f )/(1+ f )] of width f /(1+ f ), so an informed trader leaves the price at q /(1+ f ). At price ½ a signal of log-likelihood ratio λ moves the price iff f < tanh(λ/2) = 2 a −1, above which the market is dead; fee revenue on a monotone path is exactly fb ln((1− p 0 )/(1− p T )). With ten 0.65-accurate traders, the break-even fee (≈0.11) raises Brier error from 0.115 to about 0.16 and revenue is hump-shaped in f . Naive traders, synthetic signals. Pure-Python, 8 tests. Code and white paper How big should a random verifier committee be? Drawing m verifiers from a pool of N with B Byzantine, majority capture is exactly hypergeometric: zero once m ≥ 2 B +1 and up to 26× below the with-replacement binomial (N=100, B=30, m=41: 1.4×10 −4 vs 3.6×10 −3 ). For failure 2 −40 the exact size is a steady ≈0.90 of ln(1/ε)/KL(½‖β) while Hoeffding over-sizes it up to 2.2×. With stake-weighted draws only the Byzantine stake share counts: 20 of 100 nodes at 4× stake capture a 41-member committee half the time. A threshold- t rule trades wrong acceptance (2.7×10 −7 to 1.1×10 −16 ) against stalls (2.7×10 −7 to 3.3×10 −2 ). Static adversary, exact computation. Pure-Python, 11 tests. Code and white paper Can a calibration test certify a verifier? No. A hedger with no information at all keeps its expected calibration error below √( K +1)(1/(2 K )+1/√ T ) against any outcome sequence, even one that sees its forecast distribution: ECE 0.016 at T=2000 while its Brier score is 0.254 against 0 for a verifier who knows the rule. A lazy constant forecaster is slashed; the hedger passes every calibration threshold tried, but a Brier-gap test against an informed benchmark catches it in 100/100 runs. Code and white paper When should a paid verifier stop checking? A verifier who checks a claim one noisy check at a time and stops when it likes, paid a proper score, follows a symmetric threshold rule (confirmed against dynamic programming over all policies). Accuracy is p k = 1/(1+((1− a )/ a ) k ) and expected checks are k (2 p k −1)/(2 a −1), exactly. Participation needs a score scale κ ≥ 4 c /(2 a −1)² under Brier (log needs about half), Brier’s threshold is ln(κ(2 a −1)²/((1− a ) c ))/λ within one step, and adaptive stopping matches a fixed-sample verifier’s accuracy with 2–3× fewer checks. Binary state, known accuracy. Pure-Python, 8 tests. Code and white paper Why should the first verifiers be sealed? Verifiers who are paid for being right and see earlier verdicts herd: once two more revealed signals point one way than the other, everyone copies. With signal accuracy a the cascade is wrong with probability exactly (1− a )²/( a ²+(1− a )²) (0.155 at a =0.7) and forms after 2/( a ²+(1− a )²) revealed signals (3.4), so accuracy is capped at 0.845 however many verifiers join, versus ≈1 for an independent majority of 101. A sealed first batch of m ≥ 3 lifts the cap (0.875 at m =3, 0.949 at 11) and beats a majority of the same paid size. Recursion checked against fully Bayesian simulated agents. Stylised, symmetric signals. Pure-Python, 9 tests. Code and white paper How many verifiers does deterrence-by-audit need? Stake sets the audit rate a = G /( G + S ); the audits then form a queue with offered load R = λ as . Erlang-C waiting matches simulation (P(wait) 0.409 vs 0.407), and square-root staffing c = R + 1.06√ R is within 1.5 servers of the exact minimum for R ≥ 100, so the spare capacity needed falls from 60% at R =5 to 1.1% at 10 4 . Stake and headcount trade off with first-order optimum G + S = √( ws G /( rd 0 )): total cost 23.6 at the optimum versus 76.8 with too little stake and 65 with too much. Heavy-tailed audit times make Allen–Cunneen pessimistic (0.97 vs 0.63); batches of simultaneous audits make it optimistic (0.82 vs 1.45 at batch size 4). Stylised costs, FIFO, static outages. Pure-Python, 8 tests. Code and white paper When most verifiers miss a fault, who should be believed? If a fault is flagged by fewer than half of the verifiers (0.45 detection, 0.05 false alarms), majority vote is wrong on faulty jobs with probability 0.84 at n =101 and 0.96 at n =301. The surprisingly-popular rule (verdict plus predicted verdict fraction) reduces for truthful Bayesian verifiers to an exact fraction threshold θ = v /(1− u + v ) and errs 2.1×10 −5 on faulty jobs at n =101, needing 47 votes for 10 −3 total error against 36 for a Bayes rule that knows the detector. A wrong believed prior wrecks finite- n accuracy (0.51 error), a wrong believed detector quality breaks the limit, and Byzantines who vote clean and predict “everyone flags” break it at exactly 13.6%. Stylised, truthful reports assumed. Pure-Python, 7 tests. Code and white paper What is a seat in a prediction market worth? In a sequential LMSR verification market the verifier in position k earns in expectation b ·I( y ; s k | s < k ), a conditional mutual information, so seat rents telescope to the maker’s expected loss (at most b ln 2); an explicit cost-function simulation agrees to three decimals. Rents fall with position, the successive ratio approaching e −C (Chernoff information) from below; order only redistributes a fixed total (a 0.9-accurate verifier gets 0.368 of 0.407 first, 0.303 last). With entry cost c , accuracy improves roughly as 1/ b : 11 verifiers at b =0.25 (92%), 41 at b =5 (99.6%). Myopic traders, symmetric signals, monotonicity numerical. Pure-Python, 8 tests. Code and white paper How should a model be cut across devices of unequal speed? For a fixed pipeline order, greedy filling is an exact test of a target stage time (agreeing with an independent dynamic program, with and without memory caps), and every order satisfies W / V ≤ T * < W / V + m w max / V . A speed-blind equal split costs exactly v̄ / v min times the lower bound (2.40× at log-speed spread 0.5, 8.25× at 1.0) while speed-aware cutting stays within 1.4% at 240 layers. What is left is the device order: at 14 layers and 6 devices the worst order is 1.34× the best, fast-first and slow-first sorts do no better than an arbitrary order (all about 1.16× optimal), and pairwise-swap search gets within 1.1%; the penalty fades to 1.03× at 224 layers. Memory that shrinks as speed grows inflates the bottleneck 1.7×. No communication cost, static speeds. Pure-Python, 8 tests. Code and white paper What does it cost to skip the slowest workers? Waiting for the fastest k of n workers has exact round time s + ( H n − H n−k )/μ for exponential tails, and for Pareto tails the mean is finite iff n − k +1 > 1/α, so with α ≤ 1 waiting for everyone has infinite expected round time. For SGD on a quadratic the time to accuracy has a minimum k and an interior optimum (34× faster than waiting for all at zero fixed cost, 1.12× at large fixed cost). If speed correlates with data, the fastest- k average is biased by Σ(π i / k −1/ n )θ i ; Horvitz–Thompson reweighting removes it but only pays when the bias is large. Code and white paper Does a bigger swarm learn more from shared rollouts? Not without incentives. With diminishing returns and a peer-rollout discount θ, symmetric Nash play gives every agent exactly the learning level of a lone agent whatever the swarm size (total effort caps at ( a / c −1)/θ), while the efficient level grows linearly in N : welfare per agent is 4.5× higher at N =256. At θ=1 a single agent generates everything. A Pigouvian matching subsidy covering θ( N −1)/(1+θ( N −1)) of cost implements the optimum exactly, and junk rollouts beat honesty iff c −ε > p (τ+ F ). Code and white paper What does it cost to make workers race? If a round pays the first k of n finishers a prize R and workers buy speed at cost c per unit rate, the win probability’s slope at the symmetric point telescopes to (1− k / n )( H n − H n−k ), so equilibrium speed is R ( n − k )( H n − H n−k )/( nc ) and the round time is exactly nc /(( n − k ) R ). Paying every finisher buys no speed at all; for a fixed budget, speed alone wants winner-take-all (0.10 at k =1 versus 3.2 at k =16 for n =32), and only the statistical floor on k justifies more winners. Recruiting more workers barely helps: total speed bought saturates at kR / c . Exponential races, linear cost, symmetric risk-neutral workers; equilibrium checked on a grid. Pure-Python, 12 tests. Code and white paper Who drops out of a race when workers have unequal costs? If only the first k of n finishers are paid, a slow worker entering at a vanishing rate wins with probability rate × E X ( k ) of the fast workers, which gives an exact exit rule: workers with cost ratio c s / c f ≥ n f /( n f − k ) stay out entirely, and paying k ≥ n f never excludes anyone (checked by best-entry payoffs at thresholds 4/3, 2, 4). At cost ratio 4 with four fast workers, k ≤ 3 shuts the slow ones out and k =4..7 readmits them (share of prizes 0.21→0.46 against a fair 0.5). The note also proves the telescoping identity behind the symmetric race and shows that with convex speed cost, headcount does buy speed. Two cost types, exponential races, grid-checked equilibria. Code and white paper How should a router treat modules that are usually asleep? If only awake modules report and each awake module’s wealth is multiplied by 1+η(ℓ̂−ℓ i ), the ledger is exactly budget balanced, sleeping wealth never moves (each regime keeps a private ledger), and a module’s regret against the market on its awake rounds is at most ln(1/π i )/η + η n i in its own awake time (the exponential variant pays η T /8 and is not budget balanced). Admitting a module with wealth ε costs each incumbent ln(1/(1−ε))/η in its bound. With recurring regimes the ledger matches the per-round oracle (0.1004 vs 0.1000, regret about 2.7 whatever the number of specialists) while a forced-to-report Hedge sits at the generalist (0.30) and fixed share is worse (0.34–0.36). The bound is loose (measured regret 2.7 against a bound near 10 3 ); losses bounded, wake sets exogenous. Pure-Python, 8 tests. Code and white paper How stale can a shared rollout be before it is worthless? With Gaussian policies whose mean has moved by δ standard deviations, the importance weight has exact moments E w = 1 and E w ² = e δ² , so the effective-sample fraction is e −δ² (0.37 at δ=1) and a learner needing fraction ρ accepts a lag of √ln(1/ρ)/drift policy versions. Truncating weights has closed-form lost mass, bias and variance (matched by simulation); the best cap cuts the mean-shift estimator’s MSE 1.9× at δ=1, 12.8× at δ=2 and about 750× at δ=3, and finite-sample ESS is optimistic once weights are heavy-tailed. Equal-variance Gaussians, one statistic. Pure-Python, 7 tests. Code and white paper How should a verifier's vector report be scored? For a report of an expected drift r ∈ ℝ d with noise covariance Σ, every quadratic Bregman score −( y − r ) T A ( y − r ) is proper and charges a misreport D exactly D T AD . Against a trusted reference the per-task gap has exact mean D T AD and variance 4 D T A Σ AD for any noise law, and Cauchy–Schwarz shows A =Σ −1 has the best signal to noise for every deviation at once, needing 4 z ²/( D T Σ −1 D ) tasks. An isotropic score has efficiency at least 4κ/(1+κ)² (Kantorovich), attained by a deviation split between the extreme eigendirections: 25× more tasks at condition number 100, and power 0.29 against 0.80 at 48 tasks in simulation. Per-layer normalisation alone barely helps; with Σ estimated from m reference draws, efficiency is 0.61 at m =2 d and 0.95 at m =100. Quadratic scores, trusted reference, finite covariance. Pure-Python, 7 tests. Code and white paper Can a module game a ledger by choosing when to sleep? Yes, if it declares after seeing its loss. The wealth ledger pays each awake module exactly its leave-one-out saving, η W A (1− p i ) S i , but a module that sleeps whenever its own loss exceeds θ earns η p B θ(1−θ)/2 per unit wealth against an equal-skill honest rival (best 1/8 at θ=1/2) and takes the market from a 0.1 share in about 130 rounds, while the router’s realised loss stays at 0.5. Declared before the router serves, the same wealth is a real saving that falls from 0.125 to 0.011 as the module’s signal about its own loss gets noisier. A sleeping tax that stops the exploit must be at least η p B /2, a fixed-share rate that halves an honest specialist asleep 90% of the time in 6 rounds, so commitment, not taxation, is the fix. Two modules, uniform losses, threshold strategies; mean-field predictions 3–8% slow. Pure-Python, 9 tests. Code and white paper How should a router pick k distinct experts? Sparse mixture-of-experts routing as a capped Hedge market: expert prices are min(1, λ w i ) with a single shadow price λ and an exact KL projection. Regret against the best fixed k -set stayed within k ln( N / k )/η + η Tk /2 in every run (41–58% of it, not proved here); plain normalisation prices an expert above 1 in 282 of 300 rounds and understates loss 3.2×; systematic sampling realises exactly k distinct experts with 8–14× lower loss variance. Oblivious losses only. Pure-Python, 6 tests. Code and white paper How many skipped training steps hide in the loss noise? If a worker paid for T steps runs only (1− f ) T , the verifier’s log-loss test (null sd σ′, level α) hides exactly the compute at which the loss curve, inverted, crosses the noise band: L ((1− f *) T ) = L ( T )e σ′( z α + z P ) . For a power law with a loss floor this is closed form and grows as the reducible share r falls (6% at r =1 but 64% at r =0.05 for σ′=0.02). Run-to-run seed noise is a floor that no evaluation size removes: with 2% seed noise a 5% cap is unreachable for r ≥ 0.05, while without it 10 4 to 4×10 6 eval samples suffice. On exactly solvable quadratic GD the predicted detection probability matches simulation within 1.5 points, and the loss test is worth only about 4.4 random step audits at best (0.16 once training is floor-dominated). Stylised: one statistic, normal approximation, known curve family. Pure-Python, 14 tests. Code and white paper How much does an appeal ladder of juries buy, and what must appeals cost? A dispute goes to 3 jurors; the loser may pay a fee (proportional to panel size) to appeal to 11, then 27. If the fee lies in the window V (1− q ) ≤ j n < V q , only the wrongly ruled truthful side appeals and the final error is exactly the product of the tiers’ error rates; below the window both sides appeal and only the last tier counts, above it nobody appeals. With jurors 70% accurate and prize 100 the smallest deterring panel is 11 (23 at prize 1000, 41 at 10 4 ); the 3→11→27 ladder errs 2.4×10 −4 at 5.8 expected juror seats, against 12.6% for a single 7-seat panel, while a 9-juror middle tier leaks 0.78 wrong-side appeals per dispute. If jurors share a common bias with probability ρ, error cannot fall below ρ(1− a ) however many tiers are added. Independent jurors, myopic appeals, no juror incentives or bribery; exact results agree with 200,000-trial simulation.

title: How should a scarce audit budget be spread?
summary: Refereed verification with jobs of different gain and harm: a best-responding cheater is deterred iff the audit probability reaches g/(g+S), so allocation is a knapsack (deter a set exactly, spend the rest on one job). Density greedy with a partial-only candidate has a proved 1/3 guarantee and is within 1% of optimal on 91% of random instances; uniform auditing needs up to 1.9× the budget to deter everything and still leaves 26% of harm at that budget; gain heterogeneity lowers deterrence cost (Jensen); stake substitutes for audits via Σ g/(g+S) = B. Stylised.

title: Do verifiers and solvers learn the audit equilibrium?
summary: Hedge dynamics in the inspection game: a conserved potential, a closed-form cycle period (matched to simulation within 0.1%), time-averages that converge while per-round audit probability collapses, and optimistic Hedge that converges last-iterate. Stylised.

Erlang-C waiting matches simulation (P(wait) 0.409 vs 0.407), and square-root staffing c = R + 1.06√ R is within 1.5 servers of the exact minimum for R ≥ 100, so the spare capacity needed falls from 60% at R =5 to 1.1% at 10 4 . Stake and headcount trade off with first-order optimum G + S = √( ws G /( rd 0 )): total cost 23.6 at the optimum versus 76.8 with too little stake and 65 with too much. title: Can audits be predictable without corrupting scores?
summary: If truth arrives only on audited tasks and the audit rate depends on the report (say g(r)=a+br), “score when audited” is no longer proper: the verifier shades by about −bp(1−p)/(2(a+bp)) and, for steep b, hides at r=0 (Brier excess 0.25 at p=0.5). Weighting the audited loss by 1/g(r) is exactly proper for any audit rule, at variance E[B²]/g−L² and payout cap 1/g min ; the Neyman audit allocation minimises variance but gains only 3–11% over uniform. Stylised.

title: How much is one long digital-twin run worth when its output is serially correlated?
summary: Twin output such as queue waits is autocorrelated, but a run is usually summarised as mean ± 1.96 s /√ n . For AR(1) output the run-mean variance is exact (matched to simulation), so 1000 draws at φ =0.9 are worth 53. For an M/M/1 lab instrument the variance of the run mean is 9.7×, 33× and 363× the iid value at ρ =0.5, 0.7, 0.9: from 10 4 jobs the naive 95% interval covers the true mean wait 53%, 26% and 9% of the time, and a twin “certifies” an SLA of 8 against a true mean of 9 in 26% of runs. Higher load needs a longer run (470 jobs by the iid formula, 170,268 exactly at ρ =0.9). Batch means restore coverage (94–95%) only when batches outlast the correlation time; it is 53.5% at φ =0.99 and 82.5% at ρ =0.9, n =10 4 . Stylised (Gaussian AR(1) and M/M/1, simulated “real” system).

title: Does a twin with a rigid drivetrain miss the hunting cycle caused by gear backlash?
summary: On a discrete PI loop the rigid twin has spectral radius 0.71–0.89 and converges, yet the real loop with a gap of half-width h settles on a limit cycle of motor amplitude 1.30–2.94 h that scales exactly with h (1.302317 for h =0.01, 1, 100). The backlash describing function is an excitation-dependent gain (0.21 at A / h =1.2, 0.99 at 30) with a phase lag, and harmonic balance predicts the cycle but overestimates its amplitude by 6.7–10.1%. Negative result: the loop is bistable in some settings (hunting 1.165 h from small starts, converging from large steps), so a large-step validation can pass a configuration that hunts. Follow-up to the deadband twin. Stylised: scalar loop, symmetric known gap, noiseless.

title: Is load balancing a congestion price?
summary: Capacity-constrained expert routing is a softmax with a per-expert price, the Lagrange multiplier of its capacity, and the dual is smooth and concave. Any price vector gives a computable upper bound and, after repair toward the uniform assignment, a feasible lower bound, so a verifier certifies near-optimality from prices alone (gap below 10 −4 at the optimum, always above the true suboptimality). Sign-update balancing has a sampling floor of about 2.5/√B in max relative overload that no step size removes, plus a step-proportional limit cycle on a fixed batch (22.6% at γ=0.2, 1.2% at 0.01). Two-expert Gaussian price of balance is closed form with price shift equal to the median gap; a Hoeffding audit of ln(2N/δ)/(2ε 2 ) tokens covered 400 of 400 trials. Synthetic scores only. Stylised.

title: What approach speed can a lidar twin that returns every beam certify?
summary: Scanning-lidar detection of a thin obstacle has an exact random-phase beam-count law and a product-over-scans miss probability (matched to a beam-pattern Monte Carlo). A twin calibrated on the mean return rate but with independent beams has no whole-scan fades; the real miss probability cannot fall below s n for n scans. At level 10 −3 the twin certifies 13.3 and 12.9 m/s against the real 12.0 and 10.9 (fade rates 0.3, 0.5), with real miss probability 0.09–0.125, about 100× the level; the gap vanishes for early-visible obstacles and reverses sign when several returns are required. The probabilities are off by orders of magnitude but the speed by only 10–30%, because miss probability is a cliff in speed. A few hundred calibration scans repair it. Stylised.

title: Do the file sizes and line counts of this repository follow Benford’s law?
summary: First-digit frequencies of the byte sizes and line counts of the 35,648 git-tracked files at one commit, scored against Benford’s law by chi-square and Nigrini’s mean absolute deviation (MAD). All files together are nonconforming (byte MAD 0.0183, line MAD 0.0278), because a few sizes repeat thousands of times (1,071 bytes 1,297 times, 47 bytes 993 times, 4 lines 1,822 times). Counting each distinct size once, byte sizes conform acceptably (MAD 0.0068, n = 12,429). By extension, .json and .html stay nonconforming even deduplicated, and distinct Python line counts are acceptable (MAD 0.0103, n = 476). Descriptive: one commit of one generated, templated repository; an illustration of when the law fails, not a test of the law.

title: An instantaneous-exposure twin of a finite-exposure camera certifies detection at every speed: what is the real speed limit, and what does a blur-matched filter buy back?
summary: A bar of width w moving d = vT px during the exposure is imaged as an exact trapezoid (peak C ·min(1, w / d ), energy Cw conserved), matching a 2000-sub-exposure simulation to its quantisation. A single-pixel peak detector that the twin certifies at Pd = 1 everywhere loses power as soon as d > w (at w = 6, C /σ = 10: Pd 1.00 → 0.28 at d = 24), with speed limit d * = wC /(σ z ) (13.7 px). A box filter of length d collects all of Cw at noise cost √ d , output Cw /(σ√ d )·(1− w /4 d ), so the limit grows quadratically in SNR: 5–55× faster over 12 settings, but it needs the speed, and a filter tuned on the twin (length w ) still drops to Pd 0.26 at d = 60. Stylised: 1-D, known location, constant velocity, white Gaussian noise, no real footage.

title: For a fixed budget, how much should a fitted digital twin spend on real data and how much on simulation length?
summary: A twin fitted to n real observations and simulated for m jobs has relative variance a ( ρ )/ n + b ( ρ )/ m about the real wait (Whitt’s M/M/1 constant matched to simulation: 30.4 vs 29.0). One real interarrival–service pair carries the information of about two simulated jobs at any load (ratio 2.23 → 2.00), so the optimal real-data share of a budget is interior: 0.97 / 0.81 / 0.57 as a simulated job costs 0.001 / 0.05 / 0.5 of a real observation. In a full pipeline the optimal split has 2.5× lower RMSE than 20% real data. A simulation-only confidence interval is for the twin, not the system: its coverage of the real wait falls from 0.79 to 0.17 as the run grows from 200 to 50 000 jobs, while adding the input variance gives 0.92–0.95 for runs of 1000 or more. Stylised: M/M/1, simulated data, first-order variances.

title: Can a calibration test certify a verifier?
summary: No. A hedger with no information at all keeps its expected calibration error below √( K +1)(1/(2 K )+1/√ T ) against any outcome sequence, even one that sees its forecast distribution: ECE 0.016 at T=2000 while its Brier score is 0.254 against 0 for a verifier who knows the rule. A lazy constant forecaster is slashed; the hedger passes every calibration threshold tried, but a Brier-gap test against an informed benchmark catches it in 100/100 runs.

title: When does automatic blurring miss a bystander's face, and which filming platform is conspicuous?
summary: An assumed size-to-recall model of blurring strangers' faces while filming in public. A face detector that is 50% reliable at 20 px leaves a face-on face of at least 32 px unblurred 5% of the time per frame (8% at 5 m on an 8K 360 camera); blurring the head region of any detected body instead drops it under 0.1%, because a body is 11× taller than a face. A telephoto frame resolves about 10 identifiable people at once against 2.5 for an 8K 360 view. Per-frame blur is worse than it looks: with independent misses a person filmed for 5 s at the edge of range shows unblurred in some frame 100% of the time, 25% if misses last the whole shot, and an offline edit that blurs a whole track after one detection is left with 0–5%. Size alone does not separate the tall platforms. All detector curves, sizes and angles are assumptions; no real detector or footage; blurring is not legal compliance.

title: How long a lens can a 360 camera fake by cropping into a reel, and what perspective can no crop fake?
summary: Pixel and perspective geometry for the simplest multi-angle rig, a 360 camera on a pole reframed in software. An 8K (7,680 px) equirect cropped into a 1080×1920 vertical reel is native only up to about 24 mm full-frame-equivalent; 50 mm is upscaled 2.1× and 85 mm 3.5×, and a native 85 mm crop would need a ~27,000 px equirect. Perspective is set by distance: from a stick at 0.8 m a feature 10 cm nearer the lens images 14% larger, against 7.6% from the 1.4 m an 85 mm head-and-shoulders shot is taken at, with the background 1.7× larger. So portrait and compressed-background shots need a camera standing back, whatever the resolution. Upper bounds from pixel counts (real cameras resolve less); framing distances and depths are stated assumptions.

title: How much of a multi-camera shoot can an automatic edit recover, and what stops it?
summary: A synthetic model of four cameras whose true angle quality changes every 2–8 s, seen through a noisy detector. At noise 0.3 a fixed 3 s rotation shows mean true quality 0.546; an offline Viterbi edit that maximises detected quality minus a cost per cut reaches 0.802 against 0.815 for the same search on true scores, while picking the best score every frame gives 0.723 with 345 cuts a minute and every shot under 1.5 s. The cut cost matters more than detector accuracy (best near 1.0, about 14 cuts a minute). Clock sync from a shared loudness envelope fails first on short clips: a 5 s clip at noise 0.25 is off by over 40 ms in 25% of trials, 15 s in 5%. No real footage, reframing or film-look grade; quality is a made-up random process.

title: Which platform can follow a travel creator through a crowd and keep the shot?
summary: A 2-D crowd simulation of a tripod, a wheeled robot, a wheel-legged robot and a drone holding a camera 2.5 m behind a walking creator among pedestrians who do not react to it. A drone that ignores pedestrians frames the creator 99.9% of the time at any density, but steering around people drops it to 69% at 0.1 people/m 2 and 39% at 0.3; a ground robot on a plaza with curbs and one ramp is stopped 42–47% of the walk, and wheel-legs hold the frame 70% of the time in a thin crowd but 4.5% in a dense one. Avoidance and framing trade off: a flat-floor wheeled robot that ignores people frames 98% of the time while passing within 0.5 m of a pedestrian about 500 times an hour. All platform speeds, powers and masses are assumed; pedestrians do not avoid the platforms, and the drone is not limited by altitude, wind or regulation.

title: What should a travel creator pack to film from many angles under a weight budget and the 100 Wh battery limit?
summary: Exact search over 17,280 kits of cameras, lenses, mounts and battery packs (11,520 legal), scoring distinct focal-band × viewpoint shots (18 at most) and recording hours against carried weight. With a 4 h recording floor, exact search reaches 15 shots at 4 kg and all 18 at 5 kg, while a greedy best-gain-per-gram packer stalls at 12 from 3 kg because a lens is worthless without its body. Without a floor, variety-first search returns kits that record only ~2.2 h. Every device figure is assumed (round class-typical numbers, not datasheets); only the 100 Wh limit is sourced.

title: How many cameras, and where, to film a person from every angle?
summary: A 2-D geometric model of N cameras on a ring or a 90° front arc 3 m from a subject, scored on angle coverage and triangulation error. Cameras buy coverage, angle buys depth accuracy: a 30° gap between neighbours needs 13 cameras (15° needs 25), while centre depth error barely moves with count (0.52 mm for 3 on a ring, 0.23 mm for 16) but falls 11× as a pair’s convergence angle goes from 5° to 90° (7.3 mm to 0.64 mm). Four cameras on a front arc are within 11% of four on a ring. Idealised lower bounds with assumed noise (0.5 px) and no occlusion; novel-view quality is not modelled.

title: Which proper score should verifiers face with K outcomes?
summary: For K-ary reports the Brier, spherical and log scores have exact regrets and exact worst cases (1−2p min +‖p‖² for Brier, ‖p‖−p min for spherical). Per unit of payment range the spherical score gives exactly √K times Brier’s incentive at a uniform truth, but both bounded scores nearly ignore a dropped rare class: at a 1% class the loss is 1.3×10 −4 (Brier) and 1.0×10 −4 (spherical) against 0.15 for log. Multiclass follow-up to tangent-log.

title: Does a more robust CFAR detector survive a Gaussian-clutter radar simulator?
summary: Four window detectors (cell-averaging, order-statistic at ranks 3 N /4 and N /2, log-t) are calibrated in a Gaussian-clutter twin and deployed in gamma-textured clutter. None is meaningfully more robust: at design 1e−4 the false-alarm inflation is 30–44× at ν=2 and 8–9× at ν=5, and the ranking flips with ν and design rate. A known-scale oracle with no window noise inflates 2.88× at 1e−2, ν=2 against cell-averaging’s 3.02×, so most of the error is the test cell’s own texture, which reference cells cannot see. After repairing each threshold to the design rate, cell-averaging detects best everywhere (Rayleigh target, 20 dB, ν=2: 0.758 vs 0.744, 0.732, 0.703), and the twin’s promised detection probability is overstated (0.70 vs 0.43 at 15 dB). No interfering targets, so order-statistic detectors are tested away from their home ground. Stylised.

title: What does a constant-product pool concede to informed traders?
summary: A Uniswap-style pool with invariant ∏ r i = C 0 n is a cost-function prediction market: its worst-case loss is C 0 and is never attained, and a trader who moves the price to belief π earns exactly C 0 (1 − n ·GM(π)) with GM the geometric mean, against C 0 (1 − H (π)/ln n ) for LMSR at equal worst-case loss. Near uniform beliefs the ratio is exactly ln n , so the pool is cheaper than LMSR for two outcomes and dearer from three. Its price tails are polynomial, ( C 0 /gap) n , so pushing a binary price to 0.999 costs 3.4× LMSR. As an expert router it satisfies an exact regret identity (settlement term ≤ C 0 plus Bregman terms), but under regime switches it shows no advantage over Hedge (negative result). Symmetric pools, no fees. Pure-Python, 10 tests.

title: Can stake shorten a challenge window when proposers can be bribed?
summary: In optimistic verification a fraud pays G unless a challenge is included within w blocks; the attacker controls each proposer w.p. ρ and otherwise pays b to censor. The exact attacker recursion V(n) = ρV(n−1) + (1−ρ)max(−S, V(n−1)−b) gives a closed-form deterrence window (0 mismatches in 5000 instances; Monte Carlo agrees) with a gamble-first, bribe-last optimal attack. A luck-only analysis underestimates the window 100–170×; with an exogenous bribe price the window is 63 blocks for every stake from 10 to 1600; if the bounty is paid as a priority fee the price becomes θS and S·w ≈ G/((1−ρ)θ). Stylised.

title: Does the order or naming of equivalent Verilog change what Yosys and ABC synthesise?
summary: Provably equivalent rewrites of generated adder and multiplier RTL (random wire names, shuffled statements, shuffled order of added operands; 864 scored variants, every text proved equivalent to its reference) are scored under three ABC scripts. Names and statement order never change cells×depth. Operand order changes one carry-select adder by up to 1.43× within a script, and its best variant under dch is 17% better than the best adder chip-abc-sweep reported, so that earlier best was one draw from a distribution the text controls. Five other structures are unaffected. Stylised: two designs, one Yosys version, 12 seeds, generic-gate counts, cause not yet traced.

title: Which Yosys pass makes the operand order of a + b + constant change the synthesised adder?
summary: A follow-up to chip-abc-order . All 36 operand orders of a 16-bit carry-select adder's a + b + const chains (each proved equivalent to the reference) are run through synth one pass at a time. The cell counts first diverge in opt_merge : when a block's two sums both start with a and b , one shared a + b is kept (7 adders instead of 10), which happens in 4 of 36 orders. Cells×depth then takes only two values per ABC script, and the shared netlist is 1.20–1.28× larger under dch_map and resyn2_map but 0.92× under Yosys's default script. Removing opt_merge does not remove the dependence: the spread over orders widens to 1.44–3.17×. Stylised: one adder, Yosys 0.33, generic-gate cells×depth, no place and route.

title: Does the ABC synthesis script matter as much as the written RTL structure for adder and multiplier area and depth?
summary: A follow-up to chip-ppa-loop : five ABC scripts are applied to five written 16-bit adder structures and eight 6×6 multiplier structures, each proved equivalent to its reference by a Yosys miter. For the adder, cells×depth moves by up to 1.75× with the script for one structure and 1.18–1.94× across structures for a fixed script; the best pair is 0.48× the default-script plain adder. All eight multiplier structures score identically under each script, yet the script alone moves them by 1.17×. Stylised: two designs, one Yosys version, generic-gate counts rather than layout.

title: How do MAC-lane count and bit width trade area against latency in a tiny quantised-MLP accelerator?
summary: A generator for an 8-8-4 integer MLP engine with P multiply-accumulate lanes and 4-, 6- or 8-bit weights, simulated in Icarus Verilog and matched bit for bit and cycle for cycle against an integer NumPy reference in all 12 configurations. Synthesised with Yosys to generic gates, latency falls from 110 to 20 cycles as lanes go from 1 to 8 while area grows about 3× to 4×, so cells×cycles is smallest at 4 lanes for every width. 6 bits matched float accuracy on the toy task; 4 bits lost about 3 points. Stylised: one synthetic task and seed, weights baked into logic, gate counts rather than layout, nothing about a real chip.

title: Does writing a fixed-weight multiplier as shift-and-add with canonical signed digits beat Yosys's x * K?
summary: For every 8-bit constant K (1–255), an 8-bit input is multiplied three ways — the * operator, binary shift-add, and canonical-signed-digit (CSD) shift-add/subtract — and scored by Yosys 0.33 in generic gates; every variant is proved equivalent to the operator form by a miter. The operator tracks binary shift-add (cells correlate 0.97 with the number of set bits of K, 0.65 with CSD digits). CSD uses 75.7 mean cells against 112.9 for the operator (33.0% fewer; fewer cells for 230 of 255 constants, worse for 14) at similar mean depth (20.0 vs 19.6); K=255 drops from 222 to 30 cells. Preliminary: one tool version, one ABC script, generic gates rather than library area, one input width, no shared sub-sums across constants.

title: How many gates could an exact 4-input rewriter still remove from Yosys/ABC netlists?
summary: chip-exact4 found Yosys/ABC about 1.2 gates above the proven minimum on isolated 4-input functions. Here every gate of six small netlists (adder, multiplier, comparator, popcount, shifter, priority encoder) under five ABC flows is checked against that exact minimum over all its 4-leaf cuts, counting only logic a local replacement could delete. The disjoint headroom is 0 gates in 28 of 30 runs and 1 gate in the other two, even though the default script cuts 25–42% of the gates of plain mapping on add16 and prio16 : the flow’s gains are not local, so an exact small-cone rewrite proposer would find almost nothing. Stylised: six blocks, gate count with free inverters, one Yosys build; replacement circuits were not constructed.

title: How many gates above the proven minimum does Yosys/ABC use for 4-input logic?
summary: The exact minimum 2-input gate count of every 4-input Boolean function (222 NPN classes, by SAT) against what Yosys/ABC returns on 884 sampled functions. The default flow is exactly optimal on only 34% and averages 1.19 gates above the minimum (max 4); the best of seven scripts per function reaches 38%. A heavier resyn2 script is worse (1.72), and the count changes with which negated or permuted form of the same function is synthesised. One Yosys version, generic gates, 4 inputs only. Preliminary.

title: Does the rewrite-versus-sweep verdict for a 16-bit leading-zero count survive five ABC scripts?
summary: A follow-up to chip-ppa-logic : its 34 equivalent candidates for popcount, leading-zero count (clz16) and absolute difference are re-scored under five ABC scripts, and every mapped netlist is proved equivalent to the reference (none of 170 failed). On clz16 the verdict flips with the script: the no-model sweep wins under the default and dc2 scripts (344, 405), while a session-written nibble-combine file wins under three others (216–336 against the sweep’s 344–462); the overall best is 0.35× the reference’s default score. Popcount’s winner holds under all five scripts; absolute difference’s under three. Stylised: three tiny blocks, one Yosys version, hand-written proposer files, generic-gate cells×depth rather than layout.

title: Which MAC-lane count is best for a tiny quantised MLP if every P from 1 to 20 is built and checked?
summary: Every MAC-lane count P = 1–20 of chip-accel 's engine on an F-16-4 quantised network (F = 16, 32), all 40 designs simulated in Icarus Verilog bit for bit against an integer NumPy reference with measured cycles equal to the formula, then scored with Yosys. The best P is 8 at F = 16 and 16 at F = 32, so the earlier hand-picked sweep already contained the optimum; P > 16 only adds cells at equal cycles, and no non-power-of-two P wins (best is 44–62% behind). Cell count is far from monotone in P (F = 32: P = 15 has 2.4× the cells of P = 16), a possible generator artefact left untested. One network family, one seed, gate counts only; no layout or power.

title: Is P = 32 being smaller than P = 16 at equal cycles a real effect or a synthesis artefact?
summary: chip-systolic-p32 found the 32-lane MAC engine smaller than the 16-lane one although both take the same cycles. Re-synthesised with three model seeds and three Yosys/abc flows at F = 16 and 32, the sign depends on the flow: P = 32 is smaller in all 6 cases under two flows and larger in all 6 under a four-gate library, by 47 to 699 cells (1–10%). That swing is far above the 0.7% margin used to rank the best design earlier, so that ranking should be discarded. Three seeds, one tool version, generic-gate counts only; the mechanism is not traced.

title: Does sharing sub-sums across a bank of fixed-weight multipliers cut gates beyond per-constant shift-and-add?
summary: A follow-up to chip-constmul : one 8-bit input feeds a bank of M random 8-bit constants (M = 2, 4, 8, 16; 40 banks each), written three ways — the * operator, per-constant canonical-signed-digit (CSD) shift-add, and a greedy shared-sub-sum (MCM) form — scored by Yosys 0.33 in generic gates, every variant proved equivalent to the operator form. Sharing uses 9% fewer cells than per-constant CSD at M = 2 and about 20% fewer at M = 8 and 16 (690 vs 866 at M = 16; 43% fewer than the operator), fewer in 130 of 160 banks and more in 2. Adders removed in the source predict cells saved (Pearson 0.875, about 15 cells per adder). Sharing also recovers the depth CSD loses on large banks (28.2 vs 33.2 at M = 16). Preliminary: random rather than trained weights, one greedy heuristic, one tool version, generic gates rather than library area.

title: At which Yosys stage does the P = 32 versus P = 16 cell gap appear?
summary: Follow-up to chip-macp32cells . Counting cells of the 16- and 32-lane MAC engines (identical cycles, F = 16, three seeds) after the word-level, bit-level and abc stages of one Yosys script: the 32-lane engine is 640–770 cells larger at the word level but about 500 cells smaller after techmap, and abc only trims the gap to 270–410. The sign is therefore set before abc runs. Which pass removes the extra lanes was not identified. Preliminary; one Yosys version, generic-gate counts.

title: Which Yosys pass flips the P = 32 versus P = 16 cell gap?
summary: Follow-up to chip-p32netlist . Running the fine passes of Yosys 0.33 one at a time on the 16- and 32-lane MAC engines (identical cycles, F = 16, three seeds): the 32-lane engine is still about 2,100 cells larger after techmap and 114–125 cells smaller after the next opt -fast , before any abc; abc -fast adds about 400 more. It also corrects the earlier project: Yosys 0.33’s -run :abc runs abc -fast , so its “pre-abc” column was post-abc. Localised to a pass, not explained; one Yosys version, generic cell counts. Stylised.

title: How far do synthesis-only area and delay sit from placed-and-routed numbers on SKY130?
summary: Thirteen small designs (adders, multipliers, FIFOs) pushed through generic gate counting, Yosys/ABC mapping onto the SKY130 HD library, and an OpenROAD flow with placement, clock tree, global routing and timing repair. Generic gate count stays within 5.1–5.8 um² per gate for combinational logic but is about 3× higher per gate for FIFOs, whose flops dominate; mapping makes a ripple and a + adder identical. Layout adds 0–28% area (most where timing needs repair), and wires add 3–19% to delay before repair. The ABC clock target did not change the netlist at all. Stylised: tiny designs, one corner, global-route parasitics only, no detailed route or DRC, nothing about a fabricated chip.

title: Does an equivalence-gated rewrite loop beat a parameter sweep on popcount, leading-zero count and absolute difference?
summary: A follow-up to chip-ppa-loop on three small blocks where written structure matters. Every candidate is proved equivalent to its reference by a Yosys miter before its generic-gate cells×depth counts. Popcount: no real gain (0.98×). Absolute difference: 0.86×, a structure the sweep also contains. Leading-zero count: the session-written rewrites reach 0.80× but a no-model sweep reaches 0.56× (depth 8 against 11) and beats the proposer in 168 of 200 equal-budget draws. Also fixes a gate bug that rejected correct ROM-style tables. Fifteen attempts by one author, one tool version, gate counts only.

title: Does a rewrite proposer beat a parameter sweep on area and depth when every rewrite must be proved equivalent?
summary: A loop in which rewrites of a 16-bit adder and a 6×6 multiplier must be proved equivalent to the reference by a Yosys miter before a generic-gate ABC script scores cells and depth. With nine attempts written by the session agent (not an LLM benchmark; two were seeded faults the gate rejected), the best adder is a 4-bit carry-select at 0.85× the reference cells×depth, the same circuit family as the best config of a no-model parameter sweep, so a random sweep of the same budget never beats it (ties in 63 of 200 seeds). No multiplier rewrite beat a * b . Stylised: gate counts, not layout; one tool version; two designs.

title: Does fusing the accumulate into the partial-product tree beat multiply-then-add once the ABC script varies?
summary: A follow-up to chip-ppa-script on a 4×4 unsigned multiply-accumulate ( a × b + c ): three hand-written proposer files and a 12-config sweep (chain, tree or carry-save summation, c first or last) are scored under five ABC scripts, and every mapped netlist is proved equivalent to the reference (none failed; one seeded fault is rejected by the gate). Under the default script nothing beats the reference (1.06× its cells×depth), and under three of five scripts the best rewrite is 1.04–1.10×. Only carry-save forms win, under dch (0.91×) and a resyn2 -style script (0.94×); the overall best is 0.93× the reference under its own best script. Stylised: one tiny design, one Yosys version, a generic-gate library, proposer files written by the session agent.

title: Does a rewritten adder or multiplier still beat the reference once the ABC script is allowed to vary?
summary: A follow-up to chip-abc-sweep and chip-ppa-loop : the earlier proposer files and a 16-adder and 8-multiplier sweep are scored under five ABC scripts, and every mapped netlist is proved equivalent to its reference (none failed). For the adder the best rewrite is 0.80–0.86× the reference under the same script, but the reference under its best script is already 0.61× its default score, so much of the headline gain was the script. For the multiplier no rewrite beats a * b under any script; the only gain (0.90×) is from the script. Stylised: two designs, one Yosys version, a session-written proposer, generic-gate counts rather than layout.

title: Do the carry-save multiply-accumulate rewrites still win once mapped to real SKY130 cells, and does the generic-gate score predict that?
summary: A follow-up to chip-ppa-mac : the same 17 candidates for a 4×4 unsigned multiply-accumulate are mapped to SkyWater SKY130 HD cells with ABC under four scripts, and every mapped netlist is proved equal to the reference (none failed). Carry-save forms are 3–17% better in area×delay under three scripts and 6–11% worse under a resyn2 -style script; the plain a*b+c under that script is the best design overall. The generic cells×depth score agrees only weakly with cell-level area×delay (Spearman 0.20 over 64 pairs; 0.74 for cells against area, 0.26 for depth against delay). Stylised: one tiny design, one tool version and corner, ABC's load-free delay estimate, no place and route, session-written proposer files rather than an API model.

title: What does a no-model baseline repair when a scripted RTL checker is the only feedback?
summary: A companion to chip-rtl-loop : a four-stage checker (compile, lint, simulation, SAT miter) over ten small Verilog tasks, with a random-mutation hill-climbing baseline that uses no model. Given 1, 2 or 3 injected faults and 60 checker evaluations, the baseline repairs 9/20, 4/20 and 4/20 cases. The session agent (Claude) passed all ten tasks on its first attempt, so the feedback rounds were never exercised and no pass-rate-versus-rounds curve is reported. Preliminary: tiny tasks, one attempt, mutation faults unlike a language model's mistakes, and the optional API proposer is untested.

title: How much does simulation and formal feedback help a proposer repair small Verilog designs?
summary: A checker (Verilator lint, Icarus lockstep simulation against a golden model, Yosys SAT proof for combinational tasks) scores nine small tasks. With the session itself as proposer, 6 of 9 pass from the spec alone and all 9 after one round of mismatch feedback; the three failures were a Gray encoder written as a decoder, a logical shift on a signed value and a combinational pulse that should be registered. Anecdotal: one attempt per round, one proposer who also wrote the tasks, no resampling baseline, simulation only for sequential tasks. Not an LLM benchmark.

title: Which check catches an RTL bug: lint, random simulation or a formal equivalence proof?
summary: A harness (a proposer writes Verilog; lint, random-vector simulation and a Yosys equivalence proof score it) with 12 small tasks. One attempt per task written by the session agent (not an LLM benchmark) passed every stage at round 0, so the loop never had a failure to use. Of 414 single-point mutants of those designs, lint rejects 56, simulation 303 and only the formal proof 30 (7.7% of the 389 rejected), while 25 pass everything. A no-LLM random-mutation repair baseline fixes 11/36 broken designs within 4 proposals and 22/36 within 16. Toy: tiny modules, bounded 10-cycle proof for sequential tasks, syntactic mutants.

title: How does generic-gate area grow with bit width for adders, shifters, popcount and multipliers?
summary: Seven behavioural blocks synthesised by Yosys 0.33 to generic gates at widths 4–64. Cell counts for the adder, comparator, equality and 4:1 mux are close to linear in width (fitted exponent 1.00–1.13); the multiplier is quadratic (2.19 overall, 2.06 on the largest widths); the barrel shifter sits at 1.27–1.35. Logic depth scales differently from cells: the default-script adder's depth grows about 2×W (7 to 125) while the comparator's grows slowly (5 to 16). Preliminary: five widths, one tool version, generic gates rather than library area, no confidence intervals.

title: How rugged is the landscape of SKY130 area×delay over ABC pass sequences for a multiply-accumulate, and do simple searches beat random at 10–40 evaluations?
summary: A follow-up to chip-ppa-sky130mac : every one of 800 (design, ABC pass sequence of length ≤3) points is evaluated, so the optimum is known: 1062 µm 2 ·ns for the carry-save MAC, 11% below the best earlier script, and its netlist is proved equal to the reference. The landscape is needle-like (0.1% of points within 1% of the optimum; 108 sequences make ABC abort). At equal budgets of 10, 20 and 40 evaluations over 200 seeds, random search and hill climbing reach a median 1.135, 1.117/1.095 and 1.095/1.088 times the optimum, differences within noise at two of three budgets. One attempt of 40 session-written proposals reaches 1.088. Stylised: one 4×4 design pair, ABC's static delay estimate, no placement, not a language-model benchmark.

title: Does an output-stationary systolic array beat a MAC-lane engine for a tiny quantised MLP?
summary: An R×C systolic-array generator for the 8-8-4 integer MLP, simulated in Icarus Verilog and matched bit for bit and cycle for cycle against an integer NumPy reference in all 12 configurations (batch of 4). Against the MAC-lane engine of chip-accel at 4, 6 and 8 bits, synthesised with the same Yosys generic-gate script, the array has 1.6× to 1.8× more cells×cycles at its best shape (a negative result), but lower latency: 40 cycles for 4×8 against 80 for 8 MAC lanes, at about 3.9× the cells at 4 bits. Stylised: fan-in 8, one network, gate counts rather than area, no clock, power or layout.

title: Does the MAC engine beat a systolic array under every ABC script, not just Yosys's default?
summary: The 20 designs of chip-systolic-p32 (six output-stationary arrays and four MAC-lane engines on an F-16-4 quantised network, F = 16, 32), each simulated against an integer NumPy reference and then scored with Yosys under five ABC scripts. A negative result for arrays: the best MAC engine wins in all ten F × script cases, by 1.28× to 1.60× in cells × cycles per vector, so the size of the lead depends on the script but the ranking does not. Stylised: one network, one seed, generic-gate counts, no layout.

title: Does a larger batch let a systolic array catch a MAC-lane engine on a tiny quantised MLP?
summary: A batch-size sweep (R = 4, 8, 16, 4-bit weights) of the output-stationary systolic generator from chip-systolic , simulated in Icarus Verilog and matched to an integer NumPy reference and the cycle formula in all 6 configurations, then scored with Yosys against the MAC-lane engine of chip-accel . A negative result: the best array has 1.6×, 2.1× and 2.9× the cells×cycles of 4 MAC lanes at R = 4, 8 and 16, because array area grows with the batch while MAC-lane area does not, even though it needs far fewer cycles (83 against 464 at R = 16). Stylised: fan-in 8, one network, an array that grows a row per vector, gate counts rather than area, no clock, power or layout.

title: Do the optima of the fan-in sweep move when columns and MAC lanes go past 8?
summary: The F-F-4 quantised-MLP comparison of chip-systolic-fanin with wider grids (C up to 16, P up to 32, F = 16 and 32), all 12 array configurations matched to an integer NumPy reference in Icarus Verilog and scored with Yosys. A negative result: the earlier optima were at the sweep edge and move inward (best array 2×8, best MAC engine P = 16 at F = 32), but the best array still costs 1.25× (F = 16) and 1.20× (F = 32) the cells×cycles per vector of the best MAC engine. Stylised: one network family, one seed, generic-gate counts, no layout.

title: Does a wider fan-in let a small systolic array catch a MAC-lane engine on a tiny quantised MLP?
summary: The small output-stationary arrays of chip-systolic-small on an F-F-4 quantised MLP with F = 8, 16 and 32 (4-bit weights), all 12 array configurations matched to an integer NumPy reference and the cycle formula in Icarus Verilog, scored with Yosys against MAC-lane engines. A negative result: the best array costs 1.36×, 1.25× and 1.26× the cells×cycles per vector of the best MAC engine at F = 8, 16 and 32, so the gap narrows but does not close. Stylised: one seed, gate counts rather than area, no clock, power or layout, and some optima at the edge of the sweep.

title: Does the array/MAC-engine gap change when the hidden width is fixed at 8 and only the input fan-in grows?
summary: The quantised-MLP comparison of chip-systolic-fanin on an F-8-4 network (F = 8, 16, 32; 4-bit weights), all 12 array configurations matched to an integer NumPy reference in Icarus Verilog and scored with Yosys against MAC-lane engines. A negative result: the best MAC engine wins at every F, by 1.35×, 1.22× and 1.20× in cells×cycles per vector, so the gap narrows but does not close. One network family, one seed, gate counts only; no layout or power.

title: Does the MAC-engine lead survive a wider hidden layer (H = 16) and more MAC lanes?
summary: The chip-systolic-hidden comparison repeated on an F-16-4 quantised network (F = 16, 32; 4-bit weights), all 8 array configurations matched to an integer NumPy reference in Icarus Verilog and scored with Yosys against MAC-lane engines up to P = 16. A negative result: the best MAC engine wins at both F, by 1.30× and 1.27× in cells×cycles per vector. At F = 32 the best lane count (P = 16, 3% ahead of P = 8) is again the largest tried, so its optimum may lie further out. One network family, one seed, gate counts only; no layout or power.

title: Does the MAC-engine lead survive MAC lanes up to P = 32 and arrays up to R = 4?
summary: The chip-systolic-hidewide comparison (F-16-4 quantised network, F = 16, 32) extended to MAC engines with P up to 32 lanes and arrays up to 4×8 and 2×16, every design simulated in Icarus Verilog against an integer NumPy reference and scored with Yosys. A negative result: the best MAC engine still wins, by 1.30× and 1.28× in cells×cycles per vector. P = 32 adds no cycles over P = 16 (only 16 hidden outputs) and a 0.7% cell-count difference at F = 32; 4×8 does not beat 2×8. One network family, one seed, gate counts only; no layout or power.

title: Does a small systolic array reused over a stream of vectors beat a MAC-lane engine on a tiny quantised MLP?
summary: Output-stationary arrays with R = 1, 2 and 4 rows, each reused for 32 vectors, simulated in Icarus Verilog and matched to an integer NumPy reference and the cycle formula in all 6 configurations, then scored with Yosys against the MAC-lane engine of chip-accel . A negative result: the best array (1×4) has 1.35× the cells×cycles per vector of 4 MAC lanes (65702 against 48546), and per-vector cost rises with the number of rows. Stylised: fan-in 8, one network, gate counts rather than area, no clock, power or layout.

title: What does an all-open RTL flow report for small designs, and can it prove them equivalent?
summary: Installs Yosys, Icarus Verilog and Verilator, records versions, and synthesises adders, a multiplier and a FIFO to a generic gate library: a ripple-carry adder is 5 W −3 gates deep 2 W −1, and the operator form + gets the same depth with a few more gates. A SAT miter proves the two adders equivalent and rejects a deliberately broken one. Stylised: gate counts, not silicon area; OpenROAD and a PDK are not yet part of the flow.

title: What does an FMCW radar twin without range–Doppler coupling get wrong about a moving target?
summary: A sawtooth chirp radar reads a moving target’s range as R + κ v , κ = f c T / B ; the twin reads R . A signal-level beat-tone simulation matches the formula to ≤ 10 −4 range cells, and the bias is f D T cells independent of bandwidth: 0.6, 3.1 and 4.8 cells (9 cm, 46 cm, 2.9 m) at 30 m/s for fast 77 GHz, mid 77 GHz and slow 24 GHz ramps. Within the unambiguous speed it is under half a cell, but compensating with the radar’s own wrapped Doppler is worse than doing nothing on exactly half of the over-range speeds. For a stationary scene (±60°) a centroid fit absorbs 0.71κ v of along-track position error and leaves 0.46κ v rms distortion. Stylised: single up ramp, noise-free tone, no radar data.

title: How often should preemptible workers checkpoint?
summary: Exact checkpoint interval under Poisson churn: w* = (1+W 0 (−e −1−λC ))/λ, independent of restart cost, with Young/Daly overshooting by 5–25%; intervals within 2× cost under 3.5%; a synchronous job on n workers restarts at rate nλ so efficiency falls to 50% near n≈700, and admitting flaky workers cut throughput five-fold. Stylised.

title: Can a twin identified from logs of the deployed controller tell you whether a different controller is stable?
summary: A twin fitted to closed-loop logs predicts the pole under a new gain k ′ with sd ( σ /√ n )√(( k − k ′) 2 / τ 2 +1/ v ), set by the dither τ : held-out one-step error is 1.00–1.005 σ 2 at every τ , while the predicted pole's sd goes 0.037 to 0.82 (matching the formula to a few percent). With no dither the minimum-norm fit gets b ̂=−0.22 (true +1) and certifies a real-unstable gain in 100% of fits. Point-rule false certification is 3–48%; the OLS upper bound cuts it to 0.1–4.7% but rarely certifies a good gain at low dither (5–9%). A predicted-pole sd of 0.05 needs τ =1.23 / 0.40 / 0.16 at n =200 / 1000 / 5000. Stylised: scalar linear plant, simulated data.

title: How much of a best-of-40 gripper design's score is selection noise when every design gets its own trained grasp force?
summary: Companion to codesign-gripper with a different objective and a searched grasp force. Five parameters of a 3D-printable two-finger gripper (width, thickness, length, V-groove depth, TPU pad) are searched under a print-time cap; for each design a grasp force is tuned in MuJoCo and the design is scored on 40 held-out scenes (cylinders, spheres, boxes of 100–900 g). With 40 designs each, the best seeds of all three baselines reach 0.93–0.95 test success (medians 0.875, 0.887, 0.900 over 8 seeds) and one session-agent trajectory (n = 1, hand-written proposals) reaches 0.95 after 20 designs. On 100 fresh scenes every method’s best design drops 0.06–0.07 on average and the agent’s falls to 0.81, level with the baseline median: the task is nearly saturated and the ranking is within noise (standard error about 0.05). Stylised: assumed costs and strengths, rigid fingers, grid-plus-refine policy search rather than deep RL, nothing printed.

title: Which printable two-finger gripper holds eight different objects for the least plastic, and can an agent beat CMA-ES and Bayesian optimisation at 40 simulations?
summary: A parametric 3D-printable gripper finger (length, thickness, pad width, V angle) scored in MuJoCo on eight objects with a per-design grip force. At 40 evaluations the median best objective is 0.991 for Bayesian optimisation, 0.979 for CMA-ES, 0.965 for random search and 0.963 for a session agent’s hand-written proposals (one run; Bayesian optimisation matched or beat it in 10 of 10 seeds). The best designs are tiny flat fingers (0.5 g), but re-scored with object offsets tripled they hold 5 of 8 objects against 6 of 8 for the agent’s wide V. Rigid, stylised, no learned policy, nothing printed.

title: Can a protocol pay workers to report how often honest replicas agree?
summary: Yes, from two runs and no more: the squared error against the agreement indicator is proper for the collision probability Γ=Σ p i 2 with exact regret ( r −Γ) 2 , and one run provably cannot (the level sets are not convex). The all-pairs U-statistic has exact variance and needs about a quarter of the runs of disjoint pairs (variance ratio 0.27 at n =100). A fleet of H equal hardware classes has Γ=1/ H , so strict equality over k honest replicas false-slashes with probability 1− H 1− k . Colluders returning one common wrong value leave agreement unchanged at ε=2Γ/(1+Γ), so Γ cannot be used alone. Runs are i.i.d. and float32 fleets are simulated summation orders.

title: How big should a random verifier committee be?
summary: Drawing m verifiers from a pool of N with B Byzantine, majority capture is exactly hypergeometric: zero once m ≥ 2 B +1 and up to 26× below the with-replacement binomial (N=100, B=30, m=41: 1.4×10 −4 vs 3.6×10 −3 ). For failure 2 −40 the exact size is a steady ≈0.90 of ln(1/ε)/KL(½‖β) while Hoeffding over-sizes it up to 2.2×. With stake-weighted draws only the Byzantine stake share counts: 20 of 100 nodes at 4× stake capture a 41-member committee half the time. A threshold- t rule trades wrong acceptance (2.7×10 −7 to 1.1×10 −16 ) against stalls (2.7×10 −7 to 3.3×10 −2 ). Static adversary, exact computation.

title: A twin with an ideal magnetometer returns the true heading: how large is the hard-iron and soft-iron error, what does it do to a compass-held path, and how much of a turn does a swing calibration need?
summary: A hard-iron offset β (relative to the field B ) gives a peak heading error of exactly asin(β/ B ) (11.5° at 0.20, 53.1° at 0.80); soft-iron axis scaling r gives asin(|1− r |/(1+ r )) (6.4° at r = 0.8), unchanged by removing the offset. A compass-held 100 m square misses its start by 2 L β/ B (2, 6, 20, 60 m at 0.01–0.3) for every offset direction tried, while the ideal twin closes to 10 −14 m; a straight leg stays within 1 m cross-track for only 10–50 m at β/ B = 0.02–0.10. A circle-fit swing calibration over a full turn has offset error ≈ 2σ/√ n (0.0040 at n = 100), growing ×1.8 at 180°, ×12 at 90° and ×45 at 60° of turn (median heading residual 0.18° → 2.2° → 10.7°). Stylised: level 2-D sensor, simulated data, no gyro fusion, no ellipse fit; the 2 L β/ B closure law is verified numerically, not proved beyond first order.

title: How far can DiLoCo reports be compressed?
summary: Unbiased compression of each worker’s pseudo-gradient (noise proportional to the signal, ω) has exact stationary variance α V w (1+ω)/( Ms (2−α sc )), c = 1+ω/ M : it caps the outer step at 2/( sc ) and the contraction at 1−1/ c (keeping 10% of coordinates with 8 workers: 0.53, 22 rounds to 10 −6 against 1), and random participation is the special case ω = 1/ p −1. Dithered quantisation only adds Δ 2 /12 to the variance and leaves stability alone. At fixed bandwidth, sparsifying favours few full reports, while quantising has an interior optimum near 1.3 bits per coordinate with many workers, about 4× below 8-bit reports (the textbook high-resolution law understates the noise 2.9× at 1 bit). Matched to simulation within 3%. Stylised.

title: What does compressing the pseudo-gradient cost local SGD, and is it better than syncing less often?
summary: Unbiased compression of each worker's displacement (rand-k, relative variance ω) gives an exact stationary variance α V w (1+ω)/( N s ((2−α s )−α s ω/ N )) and shrinks the stable outer step to 2/( s (1+ω/ N )): more workers restore the step (0.47 → 2.44 for ω=99, N =16 → 256) but never the floor, which stays (1+ω)×. Norm-scaled (QSGD-style) quantisation has a closed form through one scalar T = E | d | 2 ; at equal error energy its loss equals coordinate-wise at H =1 and is about 10% worse at H =16, with the stiff mode's variance doubling. For equal bytes, syncing 1/ρ times less often leaves the floor unchanged at α=1 while keeping a fraction ρ multiplies it by 1/ρ. Matched to simulation within 2%. Stylised: quadratic, shared curvature (no client drift), unbiased compressors only.

title: What does it cost to buy decentralised compute?
summary: Reverse auction for k compute units from n devices with private costs: the truthful threshold auction pays exactly k(k+1)/(n+1), twice the winners’ true cost for every n and k (also with a reserve), the buyer-optimal reserve is exactly v/2 (worth up to +1.03 utility in thin markets, nothing once v≥2), and the pay-as-bid equilibrium has closed form and matches revenue (1.3334 vs 1.3333). Stylised.

title: How many skipped training steps hide in the loss noise?
summary: If a worker paid for T steps runs only (1− f ) T , the verifier’s log-loss test (null sd σ′, level α) hides exactly the compute at which the loss curve, inverted, crosses the noise band: L ((1− f *) T ) = L ( T )e σ′( z α + z P ) . For a power law with a loss floor this is closed form and grows as the reducible share r falls (6% at r =1 but 64% at r =0.05 for σ′=0.02). Run-to-run seed noise is a floor that no evaluation size removes: with 2% seed noise a 5% cap is unreachable for r ≥ 0.05, while without it 10 4 to 4×10 6 eval samples suffice. On exactly solvable quadratic GD the predicted detection probability matches simulation within 1.5 points, and the loss test is worth only about 4.4 random step audits at best (0.16 once training is floor-dominated). Stylised: one statistic, normal approximation, known curve family.

title: How many honest runs does a slashing tolerance need?
summary: A conformal tolerance (the k -th order statistic of n honest drift scores) has an exact, distribution-free false-slash rate ( n +1− k )/( n +1) — but only 51–56% of calibration sets deliver a rate ≤ α. A PAC-safe tolerance exists iff n ≥ ln δ/ln(1−α) (459 runs at 1%/1%), and its margin is hiding room for a cheater: the threshold sits 1.26× above the true quantile at n =2000 on Pareto-3 drift. Gaussian plug-in tolerances over-slash skewed drift up to 17×; pooling calibration across mixed hardware slashes the noisy class 4.8× too often and lets the quiet class hide 2.9× more.

title: How precise should a training-contest leaderboard be?
summary: In a winner-take-all contest ranked on a noisy holdout of m samples, equilibrium effort is V·a n √m/s with a 2 =a 3 =1/(2√π) exactly, but the formula stops being an equilibrium once V/σ² passes a ceiling (12.35, 7.78, 6.11, 5.60, 5.80 for n=2, 3, 5, 10, 20) that sits below the zero-rent limit and falls to half of it at n=20. The organiser's optimal holdout is min(m cap , (wVa n /2sκ)²): when evaluation is cheap the ceiling, not cost, binds. Quadrature checked against Monte Carlo and brute-force best replies. Stylised.

title: What does a controller designed in a twin with the wrong actuator gain cost in the real world?
summary: For a scalar LQR controller (plant x ′= ax + bu + w ) the real cost under the twin’s gain K is exactly ( q + rK 2 ) W /(1−( a − bK ) 2 ). With a =0.9, a twin that believes the actuator is half as strong claims 1.245 but costs 1.508 (+40%); at 0.2× the real loop is unstable while the twin claims a finite cost. Unlike an estimator, a controller has an instability cliff ( m < a /( a +1) as r →0), which is a band when control is penalised, and a too-strong twin is the safer error (+20% vs +40% at a factor of 2). Negative result: running the twin’s controller on the real system identifies only the closed-loop pole, not a and b ; with dither the least-squares covariance is closed-form and the retune regret matches a delta-method law (∝1/ n ), while dither costs performance and its optimum shrinks with the data budget. Stylised: scalar linear-Gaussian, stationary, known a .

title: Does a well-featured twin overstate scan-matching accuracy in a corridor, where the scan cannot see the along-track direction?
summary: In a bare corridor the point-to-line information matrix is exactly singular along the track and the matcher returns its initial guess; door-frame stubs every 20/10/5/2 m give an exact along-track sd of 8.1/6.3/3.9/2.2 mm (MC 7.3/6.2/4.3/2.4), 1.6–6× a well-featured room's 1.35 mm, while lateral accuracy (≈ 0.8 mm) is unchanged. A Kalman filter fed the room twin's 1.9 mm covariance across a 20 m blind span has NEES 432 (1 cm/step odometry) and 1535 (2 cm/step) against 0.75 for the exact-covariance filter; the exact covariance is valid only inside a matcher basin of ≈ 0.2 m, and the covariance-aware filter is still overconfident at re-entry (NEES 2–8). Stylised: simulated 2D lidar, one-dimensional filter.

title: Does a twin that models each axis alone certify gains that actuator coupling destabilises?
summary: For a two-axis loop x ’ = x − kGx with cross-gain c , the stable-gain limit is 2/(1+√ p ) ( p = c 12 c 21 ≥0) or 2/(1+| p |) ( p <0) instead of the twin’s 2, so a twin-certified 10% margin ( k =1.8) fails at c =1/9, and no positive gain is stable once √ p ≥1. The twin-deadbeat gain has real rate √| p |, not 0 (6–270 steps to 10 −6 for c =0.1–0.95 vs 1). A diagonal gain fitted from logs is 1+ cρ for input correlation ρ (Monte Carlo matches to four digits), giving real rate c (1+ρ)/(1+ cρ ) (0.300 at ρ=0, 0.461 at ρ=1); the unbiased full fit has variance ∝ 1/(1−ρ 2 ) (verified within 5%), so near-collinear logs make coupling unidentifiable while the per-axis fit returns a confident wrong gain. Follow-up to the control twin. Stylised: linear constant coupling, two axes, noiseless plant.

title: Does giving two policies the same seed in a digital twin actually pair them?
summary: Common random numbers pair two policies only while their read pointers into the random stream stay aligned. If one policy consumes an extra draw with probability q per step, the paired correlation is exactly ρ = ∑ t ∑ d Bin(t,q)(d) w t w t+d /∑w t ² (matched to simulation within 0.012). A flat 20-step score keeps ρ=0.95/0.77 at q =0.05/0.3, but a terminal-only score has ρ=(1− q ) T (0.36/0.001). Sizing a comparison as if seeds stayed synchronised (n=12) gives power 0.85 to 0.11 against a nominal 0.90; keying each draw by (episode, step) restores ρ=1. Stylised: Gaussian per-step noise, policies differing only in draw consumption, no robot data.

title: Should a verifier's continuous drift report be scored by CRPS or log score?
summary: For Gaussian reports N(m,s²) both rules have exact expected scores. Overconfidence costs at most σ(√2−1)/√π = 0.234σ under CRPS but is unbounded under log (4995 nats at s=0.01σ); mean errors cost linearly versus quadratically; CRPS is 1-Lipschitz in the realised outcome (log slope 75/σ in our example); a plug-in fit from n samples costs 5σ/(8√πn) versus 1/n; and per-round score variance is finite for Student-t tails ν>2 (CRPS) versus ν>4 (log), which matters for sequential tests. Gaussian family, one verifier. Stylised.

title: What does submitting copies earn under Shapley payments?
summary: Paying contributors of data or gradients by Shapley value rewards replication even when copies add zero information: in a Bayesian mean-estimation game the replicator's payment rises with every copy to its stand-alone value, exactly (n+2)/2 times the honest payment against n unit-precision others (5.5× at n=9).
