If the evaluator treats copies as independent the replicator's pot share tends to 100%; leave-one-out pays true copies exactly zero but distributes only 1/(n+1) of the pot; collapsing duplicates fixes it but underpays independent look-alikes by 45%. Exact computation checked against permutation brute force. Stylised.

title: Does measurement noise, or dither, hide an actuator deadband the twin lacks?
summary: At K =0.5, d =0.1 the linear twin’s exact stationary rms is s √( K /(2− K )); the real deadband loop is 27× worse at s =0.01 (0.1591 vs 0.0058) but 0.37× at s =0.05 (0.0107 vs 0.0289), because noise dithers the actuator, so a validation in the high-noise regime would call the deadband harmless. Deliberate dither removes the noise-free stall (rms 0.2000 to 0.0001 at a = d ) but only hurts at s =0.05 (0.0103 to 0.0226), and under noise mild under-compensation of the width beats the exact width (0.0053 vs 0.0116 at s =0.02). Follow-up to the deadband twin. Stylised: scalar integrator, single-seed simulations without confidence intervals.

title: What does a twin with no actuator deadband promise a proportional loop, and what does the real one do?
summary: With a deadband d the real servo loop rests at exactly | x | = d / k (0.500 at d =0.2, k =0.4) while the twin converges to zero, so the twin certifies tolerances the real loop never meets and needs k ≥ d / ε , which fails beyond k = 1. A linear twin fitted from Gaussian excitation of std s recovers 2 Q ( d / s ) (Stein’s lemma; 0.0457 vs 0.0455 at s =0.5), an excitation-dependent gain, while the small-signal gain is 0. Bisection needs about 8 real probes to cut the stall 0.784 → 0.0005, with exact residuals ( d − d̂ )/ k under-compensated and a period-2 chatter ( d̂ − d )/(2− k ) over-compensated. Stylised: scalar integrator, noiseless, k ≤ 1.

title: What does a linear photon-counter twin of a SPAD lidar miss about dead time?
summary: An ideal counter twin reads flux linearly; a real detector with dead time τ reports half the flux at nτ=1 (non-paralyzable) or 36.8% (paralyzable), and the paralyzable curve peaks at 1/ e , so one reading has two fluxes (0.259 or 2.543 at mτ=0.2; a twin is 12.7× too low on the high branch). First-photon timing of a Gaussian pulse is biased early by − N /(2√π)σ at small N (exact) and saturating near −2σ: −0.28σ at N =1 and −1.50σ at N =10 (−22.6 cm for σ=1 ns) while the spread shrinks to 0.62σ, so it is bias, not averaging noise. A Coates correction of the first-photon histogram restores the mean to within 0.02σ. Stylised: one pulse, no background light, afterpulsing or crosstalk.

title: Peer-prediction markets for decentralized ML training verification
summary: Proper scoring rules, Peer Truth Serum, Correlated Agreement and LMSR aggregation, with eight follow-ups on mechanism-aware adversaries (trust farming, whitewashing, closed-loop attackers) and defences. Pure-Python, dependency-free.

title: What does it cost to route between models with conditional markets, and what does a stake do to the answer?
summary: Markets that forecast each model’s loss if chosen only ever see the chosen arm. An inverse-propensity Brier payment is exactly proper even when the router reads the report (without the weight a trader shades its forecast, or hides), and its price is exact: E[1/π] = 1+(K−1)e ω 2 /2τ 2 , so payment variance blows up as the router cools (a probit router has infinite variance for τ ≤ ω; Monte Carlo at τ=0.3 sees 29 against the exact 195). Exploration regret is at most 0.2785τ. Equal owner stakes cancel in the decision, a stake gap shifts the reported gap by a closed-form fixed point, and the loss it causes is second order, ∝(ΔB/k) 2 . Gaussian, one-shot, stylised.

title: What does a verifier's score gap cost in decisions?
summary: Exact calibration functions turning a proper-score gap into a certified cap on accept/audit/slash regret: Brier transfers as ε², log as a KL, polyhedral hinge linearly but without proper elicitation, and an audit action tightens the guarantee; the certificate is never violated in simulation and is attained by a two-point verifier. Stylised.

title: How do you pay a verifier whose report decides the job?
summary: If a report of “fault” gets the job rejected and the outcome is seen only on acceptance, scoring observed jobs is improper: verifiers shade under the threshold to get scored, and every job is accepted (1.1–2.8× optimal decision loss at thresholds 0.7–0.2). A reserve payment for rejection makes truth optimal iff the score’s entropy minimum τ s is at least the threshold τ d , and then it is unique, 1+τ d ²−2τ d τ s . Plain Brier (τ s =½) therefore fails above τ d =½; recentring the score by a term linear in the outcome fixes every threshold, cheapest at τ s =τ d with rent τ 3 /3. Exploration with inverse-propensity payment is also proper but multiplies payment variance by about 1/ε. Stylised, single verifier.

title: How much outer step does overlapping communication with compute cost, and how many rounds should be in flight?
summary: Applying the averaged displacement τ rounds late obeys z τ+1 − z τ + c = 0 with c = α s , so the stable step is exactly c < 2 sin(π/(4τ+2)) ≈ π/(2τ+1): 2, 1, 0.62, 0.45 for τ = 0…3, shrinking like 1/τ. The fastest single-mode rate is the double root τ/(τ+1), and the stationary noise floor is an exact Yule–Walker solve (closed form (1+ c )/((1− c ) c (2+ c )) at τ = 1) that matches literal delayed-DiLoCo simulation to 0.3%. Delay is free at small steps (+1% at α = 10 −3 , τ = 4) but multiplies the floor by 3.9× at c = 0.8. At an equal floor each delay round costs only about 6% more rounds, so the wall-clock-optimal delay is exactly ⌈latency / compute time⌉ (1.9–7.5× faster than no overlap). Stylised: constant delay, identical workers, quadratics, no momentum.

title: What does late feedback cost a market router?
summary: Hedge/LMSR routing of modular experts when losses arrive after device-dependent delays: regret ≤ ln N/η + ηT/8 + ηD/2 with D the total outstanding rounds, so mean delay d̄ inflates the horizon by 1+4d̄; ignoring delay costs 12× regret against a reactive adversary at delay 100, the worst-case tuned rate is too cautious on oblivious data, an observable-count adaptive rate recovers most of it, and LMSR subsidy grows about 20× at mean delay 5. Stylised.

title: Does cloning an expert from logs recorded in a digital twin recover the expert?
summary: Demonstrations logged as applied (actuator-clipped) actions bias a linear clone even in a perfect twin: at an actuator limit of 1 the clone gain is 0.58 against the expert’s 0.96 and its real cost is 9.8% higher, with the exact Gaussian-state gain k 0 P(| k 0 x |< U ) from Stein’s lemma. Twin errors act through the states they visit and can help: 0.25× noise cuts the gap to 0.002, 2× raises it to 0.75, and a loose twin limit of 3 nearly removes it. Log-state coverage narrower than half the saturation width recovers the expert, while DAgger with applied-action labels converges to a worse gain (0.5575, gap 0.169 vs 0.141). Stylised: scalar plant, population-level fit, no real logs.

title: How wide should a dispute bisect?
summary: Arity and leaf size of k-ary bisection dispute games for refereed verification: the optimal arity solves k ln k − k + 1 = a/b (binary only if a/b ≤ 2ln2−1), arity 10 is 1.9× cheaper than binary at a million steps and 6× at a/b=1000, exact adaptive schedules gain at most about 1%, early-stopping with referee re-execution saves 9–56%, and latency just widens arity. Verified on an executable SHA-256 dispute. Stylised.

title: Which ego-velocity estimator should a radar twin choose when the real scene has moving targets?
summary: Radar ego-velocity from n Doppler returns. In a static-world twin least squares beats the median by exactly π/2, so the twin picks the mean; in a scene where a fraction ε of returns come from moving targets (extra offset sd τσ) the mean’s variance is exactly 1 + ετ 2 times the twin’s claim and the median’s exact variance is a one-dimensional integral, both matched to simulation. The twin’s choice is wrong on a band of ε (τ=10: 0.006–0.97; τ=3: 0.086–0.83; τ=1: never); at ε=0.1, τ=10 the mean has 5.8× the median’s variance and the twin’s 95% interval covers 48.7% of the time. 2-D least squares scales the same way. A residual-kurtosis test needs about 50 returns to detect it at ε=0.1, τ=10, and hundreds at ε=0.02, τ=3. Stylised: zero-mean Gaussian contamination, no RANSAC, no radar data.

title: A linear-drag twin of a quadratic-drag vehicle: what does it get wrong about braking, terminal speed and the safe speed under a stopping limit?
summary: Real drag c v|v|, twin k v with k matched at one speed. Coast-down time to fall to v 0 /10 is 9/( c v 0 ) for the truth and independent of v 0 in the twin (0.05×, 0.51×, 1.02× the truth at v 0 =1, 10, 20 for a fit at 5); terminal speed is off by v term / v fit ; a least-squares fit over [0, v max ] has k =3 c v max /4, exact only at 0.75 v max . The safe speed under a 10 m stopping limit is mis-stated by −20.8%, −8.9%, +7.0%, +41.1% for fits at 1, 5, 10, 20 m/s, so the error changes sign with the fit speed, and trace-fitted k falls from 0.382 to 0.223 as the coast-down lengthens because the slow tail dominates. Stylised: one dimension, pure quadratic drag, closed-form noiseless truth.

title: How wrong is the thinnest obstacle a lidar twin certifies as detectable when real beam dropout is clustered?
summary: A thin obstacle covers m adjacent lidar beams and is detected if at least k return. The twin drops beams independently at 10%; the real sensor drops them in bursts (a Markov chain with the same rate and lag-1 correlation λ). The exact miss law is a small DP, and for k = 1 the real/twin ratio is (1 + λ(1− p )/ p ) m −1 . At the width certified for miss 10 −3 ( m = 3) the real miss is 0.041 (λ = 0.6) to 0.067 (λ = 0.8), and the claimed detection range is 4× to 8.3× too long. Inflating the drop rate to match one width is wrong at the others. Fitting the chain from a flat-target log recovers the median width but 40% of repeats still miss the target at 5,000 beams; two extra beams cut that to 1%. Stylised: one scan, a simulated ‘real’ sensor, no lidar data.

title: How many synthesised designs from a new family does a cell-count surrogate need before it is usable, and is it better to pool them with old families or train on them alone?
summary: A follow-up to eda-surrogate on its 133 designs in four generator families: when a word-level cell-count surrogate meets a family it has not seen, how many Yosys syntheses of that family restore it? Over 30 random draws per cell, one synthesised design pooled with the other families cuts the linear model’s median error from 48.6% to 18.4% (median over the four families), and training on the new family alone overtakes pooling from about three designs (4.8% against 10.4% at five). Boosted trees need far more (about 12 designs to get under 20%) and pooled boosting is worse than zero-shot on one family for up to five designs. Ranking is good throughout. Stylised: small clean families, random rather than chosen adaptation designs, a synthesis-only target, no place and route.

title: Which few designs of a new family should you synthesise to adapt a cell-count surrogate, and should they count for more?
summary: A follow-up to eda-adapt on the same 133 designs in four generator families. Choosing the k adaptation designs by farthest-point spread in feature space, instead of at random, roughly halves the linear model’s held-out median error at k = 5 (5.3% against 8.5%, new-family weight 5); picking the smallest designs is worst (15.2%). Upweighting the new family’s points helps the linear and ridge models from k = 5 but hurt boosted trees. Stylised: four small clean families, a synthesis-only cell-count target, deterministic choosers scored on different remaining sets, no confidence intervals.

title: How much of a surrogate screen’s lead over random search comes from the free objectives?
summary: A follow-up to eda-screen on the same 80-design accelerator table. A random search that uses the free cycles and error objectives (no cell-count model) finds 0.901 of the true front’s hypervolume at 12 syntheses, against 0.860 for plain random, 0.878 for TPE and 0.990 for the 4-fit screen (100 seeds). So +0.041 of the screen’s +0.130 lead comes from the free objectives and +0.089 from the surrogate. The baseline stalls once the free-objective layer is spent and falls below random and TPE by 30 syntheses. Stylised: one 80-design space, generic-gate cell counts, no place and route.

title: In what order should an automated design loop run random, directed and formal checks?
summary: Replay of the eda-verify mutation log (91 mutants, 20 seeds), costing each check cascade in CPU seconds. Formal alone takes 16,354 s for 47 kills and 16 equivalence proofs; random simulation first and formal only on the survivors takes about 7,500 s and finds 66 of 66 killable mutants, a 54% saving. The order among the cheap stages changes the total by under 2%; the remaining cost is formal working on equivalent or timed-out mutants, which no ordering removes. Stylised: a re-analysis of one design, one solver and its timeouts; nothing new was simulated.

title: Do synthesized-netlist features predict which simulation survivors Yosys can prove equivalent?
summary: Follow-up to eda-equivpredict on the same 27 survivors, now with Yosys installed. Position-free features (cell-count change after synthesis, miter size, identical cell histogram) are scored under leave-one-line-out. None beats guessing the majority class (16 of 27, 59.3%); the source-line rule gets 25 of 27. The nine solver timeouts barely change the netlist (|Δcells| 0 for six), but equivalent mutants span 0 to 178, and miter size is nearly constant (1,188–1,199). A negative result on one design; cone depth and fan-in were not tried (see eda-conehash ).

title: Do fan-in cone features of a mutant predict which simulation survivors Yosys can prove equivalent?
summary: The next step eda-conefeat named. Golden and mutant are lowered to gate level without ABC, and each flip-flop and output is compared by a Merkle hash of its fan-in cone. Features of the changed cones (count, gates, depth, leaves, registers reached downstream) are scored under leave-one-line-out on the same 27 survivors. None beats the 59.3% majority class (best 13 of 27). One observation, found after looking at the table: all seven survivors that change exactly one sink are literal edits on two lines, and none is provably equivalent (six of the nine solver timeouts are among them). One design, one solver, stylised.

title: When can a check cascade stop formal verification early without losing kills?
summary: Replay of the eda-verify mutation log with a time cap on the formal stage. Every formal kill in the log finished within 164 s, while equivalence proofs take about 222 s, so a 170 s cap loses no kill (66 of 66 killable mutants still found) and saves 41% of the cascade's CPU, but gives up all 16 equivalence proofs; a 230 s cap keeps 15 of them and saves 23%. Caps of 30 s or less start losing kills. A cap learned from half the mutants worked on the other half when the training half contained formal kills and failed (1.6 of 29 kills lost) when it contained none. Stylised: one design, one solver, 91 mutants; nothing new was simulated.

title: How sure is the 93% nearest-line equivalence predictor?
summary: Uncertainty for eda-equivpredict , replayed from the same eda-verify log. The 27 survivors sit on only 11 distinct source lines, so a line-cluster bootstrap gives a 95% interval of 76.5–100% around the observed 25 of 27 (92.6%), against a 59.3% majority-class baseline, and a permutation test that shuffles line groups gives p = 0.012. One design, one solver, predictors chosen with the log in view. Stylised.

title: Can cheap features say which simulation survivors formal can prove equivalent?
summary: Replay of the eda-verify log on the 27 mutants that 16 directed vectors do not kill (16 provably equivalent, 9 timeouts, 2 formal kills). Predicting from the mutated source line and running formal only on predicted-equivalent survivors costs 3,298 CPU-s against 7,414 s for always running formal (−55%) and still finds 14 of 16 proofs, 93% accurate under leave-one-line-out; smoother rules (3-NN, a one-split rule) find 12 of 16 and operator kind is no better than guessing. The signal is the design region the solver finds hard, not a transferable rule. Stylised: 27 mutants, one design, one solver; nothing new was simulated.

title: Does "the mutant synthesises to the golden netlist" predict formal equivalence on a second design family?
summary: Follow-up to eda-conefeat on a design the idea was not fit on: a 2×4 systolic array from chip-systolic is mutated, 32 of 143 compiling mutants survive random simulation, and Yosys tries to prove them equivalent (12 proved, 20 timeouts at 60 s/120 s, none killed). An identical post-synthesis cell histogram is always right (3 of 3 across this design and the MAC engine) but finds only 3 of the 28 proved equivalents, so it saves about 3% of formal CPU; equivalent mutants usually change the netlist by −75 to +131 cells, and a zero change is as common among timeouts as among proofs. Two designs, short timeouts on the new one. Stylised.

title: Do cheap rungs of the chip-design tool ladder rank designs like synthesis, and how much synthesis time does screening save?
summary: A three-rung ladder over 40 logged MAC-engine designs: a free analytic model (cells ≈ lanes×bits 2 ), cycle-accurate simulation, and Yosys synthesis. The analytic rung ranks the cells×cycles objective with Spearman 0.74 against synthesis (0.95 for cells alone) and finds 2 of the 5 best designs. Successive halving that screens on the cheap rungs reaches the optimum with certainty at 20 s of tool time, against 0.10 for random search at the same budget and 205 s for synthesising everything. Stylised: one toy design family with its optimum at a corner, no place-and-route rung, and the search is a replay over the committed log.

title: Does the best ABC recipe for one design transfer to another?
summary: All 400 ABC pass sequences (up to three passes of seven) mapped to SKY130 on eight small datapath designs, so every optimum is known. The best recipe differs per design and transfers badly: one design’s best recipe scores a mean 1.31× (worst 2.06×) the other’s optimum, and score rankings of recipes correlate only weakly across designs (Spearman −0.51 to 0.46). A leave-one-out consensus recipe is only slightly better than a median sequence (1.22× against 1.26×), and warm-starting a hill climber with it helps one design ( mac4 ) but is within noise of random search on average at budgets 10 to 40. Stylised: eight hand-picked toy designs, ABC’s static delay, no place and route; the OpenROAD-settings half of the milestone is not done.

title: Does the order a grid proposer walks a chip-design space change how quickly it finds the Pareto front?
summary: The lexicographic grid that the harness ships is replayed against Halton, farthest-point and Latin orders and random shuffles on the 80-design table from eda-proposers (stdlib only, nothing new simulated). Lexicographic scores worse than all 300 random orders up to 30 evaluations and needs 75 evaluations for the whole front; a Halton order reaches 90% of the front's hypervolume in 7 evaluations against a median 17 for random, while random-start farthest-point and Latin orders gain only +0.010 to +0.042 over random from 8 to 20 evaluations and nothing by 40. Stylised: one small table, and the deterministic orders are single draws with no interval.

title: Does a space-filling grid order beat the harness's lexicographic order on other chip-design families, or was that luck of one table?
summary: The grid orders from eda-gridorder are replayed on the MAC and FIR design families of eda-surrogate (36 designs each, Yosys cell count against analytic cycles; nothing new synthesised). Lexicographic is not reliably bad but arbitrary: worst on MAC (90% of the front’s hypervolume after 25 evaluations against 3–4 for the others), best on FIR (4 against 5–9), because it wins exactly when the front sits at the first corner of the leading axis. Farthest-point beat random from about 6 evaluations on every table and found FIR’s full front in 16 evaluations against 28 for random; Halton was mixed. The harness gains an order option on its grid proposer. Stylised: two small families, two objectives, deterministic orders are single draws.

title: Can one harness check, score, cache and log candidate chip designs for any proposer?
summary: A loop that takes a parameterised generator and a search space and runs each candidate through lint, bit- and cycle-exact RTL simulation, a gate-netlist simulation check and Yosys synthesis, caching by design hash and logging every evaluation as JSON. On chip-accel ’s MAC engine (40 designs) all candidates pass; synthesis and the gate-level check take 99% of the 424 s of wall time and RTL simulation under 1%. The Pareto front matches chip-accel ’s. Stylised: one design family, generic-gate counts, simulation-based (not formal) equivalence, no place and route.

title: Which search method finds a chip design's Pareto front with the fewest evaluations?
summary: Random search, a grid, simulated annealing, a genetic algorithm, NSGA-II and a TPE-style Bayesian method are compared at equal evaluation budgets on an 80-design space (MAC lanes × bit width × ABC script) of a toy quantised-MLP accelerator, using Pareto hypervolume over 100 seeds. TPE reaches 0.917 of the true-front hypervolume at 16 evaluations against 0.891 for random, and 0.980 against 0.943 at 30; annealing trails random throughout. Stylised: the space is tiny (random search at 40 evaluations already scores 0.965), hyperparameters are untuned, objectives are generic-gate counts, and nothing is said about real chips.

title: Does the ranking of design-search proposers survive a change of hypervolume reference point or quality indicator?
summary: The 100-seed proposer runs of eda-proposers re-scored under five hypervolume reference points, front recall, IGD+, an epsilon indicator and log-scaled cell counts. The winner (TPE at budgets 16 and 30) is the same under all of them, but its lead over random at budget 30 shrinks from +0.045 (reference 1.01) to +0.002 (reference 5.0), while recall shows +0.279. At budget 8 the order is decided by annealing and flips with the indicator. Stylised: one 80-design space, generic-gate counts, no place and route.

title: Does a cell-count surrogate used as a screen find a chip design’s Pareto front with fewer syntheses than random search or TPE?
summary: On the 80-design accelerator table from eda-proposers , a screen that synthesises 4 spread designs, fits a log-linear cell-count model, and then synthesises designs in order of predicted Pareto rank finds 0.990 of the true front’s hypervolume at 12 syntheses (random 0.860, TPE 0.878; 100 seeds) and the whole front on 87% of seeds by 20. The screen reads cycles and error for free, which the baselines do not: with no cell-count model that alone gives 0.908, so the surrogate adds the rest. Stylised: one small smooth space, the surrogate fitted inside one family, no place and route.

title: Can cheap word-level RTL features predict synthesised cell counts well enough to screen a design search, and does that survive a new design family?
summary: A surrogate for Yosys generic-gate cell counts, trained on 24 word-level features (multiplier, adder, mux and register sizes read after proc; opt , about 30× cheaper than synthesis) over 133 designs in four generator families I wrote: MAC engines, FIR filters, ALUs and sorting networks. On families it saw, a non-negative linear cost model has a 3.9% median error and within-family Spearman 0.995, beating boosted trees (8.5%). When a whole family is held out, median errors run from 10.5% to 210.7% and the best model changes with the family, but rank agreement stays at Spearman 0.75–1.00. Ordering a 36-design pool by predicted cells×cycles found a design within 2% of the best after 1–5 syntheses against 12.4 (MAC) and 18.6 (FIR) for random order, both optima sitting at an edge of the space, so the test is weak. Stylised: synthesis-only target, no place and route, small designs.

title: How many injected RTL bugs do random, coverage-directed and formal checks catch, and at what cost?
summary: Mutation study on the MAC accelerator: 91 compilable mutants (operator, literal, deletion and ROM edits), of which 66 are killable and 16 are proved equivalent by induction. 64 random vectors kill 99% of the killable ones, 16 coverage-directed vectors 97% (16 random: 95%), and bounded Yosys formal checking 71% because 19 SAT runs timed out. Cost per kill: about 1 s for simulation against 52 s for a formal kill. Stylised: one design, one bound, one solver.

title: What does a proper score buy when effort is private?
summary: Scoring-rule payments as moral-hazard contracts for costly inference: a closed-form shirking threshold (matched to 1%), first-best effort at scale equal to marginal value with a fee, and under limited liability only 48–65% of first-best surplus, with log score cheaper than Brier at high effort. Stylised.

title: What does it cost to pay a verifier to check?
summary: Effort elicitation with proper scoring rules in an exact beta-binomial model: implementable efforts are the concave envelope of the value curve, Brier information rent is exactly (n−1)/(a+b) times effort cost, and the log score needs half Brier's payout spread on rare-fault priors. Stylised.

title: What does a twin get wrong when its gain is fitted from a noisy logged input, and does more data fix it?
summary: Regressing the plant output on a logged input that carries sensor noise attenuates the fitted gain by the reliability ratio λ = σ u 2 /(σ u 2 +σ v 2 ) exactly (0.800 vs 0.802 simulated at λ =0.8). It is bias, not variance, so more data makes it worse: the twin's own 95% interval covers the true gain 53% / 15% / 0% at n =20 / 50 / 200 while covering the attenuated value 94–97%, and the twin's fit residuals are exactly uncorrelated with its regressor, so nothing warns. A feedforward controller built on it overshoots the real plant by exactly 1/ λ (1.25× at λ =0.8, 2× at 0.5). A known-noise correction or a second independent measurement as instrument removes the bias (RMSE 0.20 to 0.02–0.05 at n =200–1000), but a 20% misjudged noise variance leaves a ±5% bias and at n =20 with λ =0.5 the repairs are far worse than the biased fit. Stylised: scalar Gaussian plant, simulated “real” system.

title: How much energy can each storage technology hold per kilogram, at the most?
summary: Theoretical ceilings from first principles for batteries, hydrogen, flywheels, pumped hydro and heat, reproducing five published values to within 0.3% (lead-acid 170, Zn-air 1,086, Li-S 2,567, Li-O 2 3,458 Wh/kg; Al-air 8,100 on Al). No battery couple releases more than 1.65 eV per reactant atom, so the spread comes from atomic mass: Wh/kg = 26,801 × eV per atom / mean g/mol. A carbon-fibre flywheel holds at most 756 Wh/kg (0.34 eV per atom), sand at 500 °C 107 Wh/kg of heat (41% recoverable as electricity) and water lifted 300 m 0.82 Wh/kg. Ceilings for the active material only, with some voltages and material properties assumed.

title: How big should a home's solar array and battery be, and at what installed price does the battery pay?
summary: An hourly simulation of rooftop solar plus a battery on an 8,000 kWh/yr home, over 20 seeded synthetic weather years (Haurwitz clear sky, a three-state cloud chain, an invented load) with assumed round-number prices. A 6 kW array alone meets 35% of the load; 5, 10 and 15 kWh of battery lift that to 49%, 59% and 62%, then returns diminish fast. With import at $0.30 and export at $0.05 per kWh a 10 kWh battery pays only below about $451/kWh installed (assumed $800), $143 at $0.20 export, and never when export is paid at the import price. Stylised: synthetic weather, flat tariff, no incentives or degradation; not installation advice.

title: Which energy-storage technology is cheapest per MWh delivered at 1 hour, 1 day and 3 weeks?
summary: Levelised cost of storage for lithium-ion, vanadium flow, pumped hydro, cavern compressed air and cavern hydrogen, from capital cost, round-trip efficiency, life, fade and charging power. With round assumed inputs Li-ion is cheapest to about 4 hours ($116/MWh at 4 h) and costs about 3× a cavern store at 24 hours ($337 vs $109); cavern hydrogen beats Li-ion above 11 hours but cavern compressed air only above 308 hours. Li-ion would need an energy cost of $43/kWh instead of $200 to win at 24 hours. The 8–10 hour winner flips with the discount rate and charging price. Stylised: every input is assumed and unsourced, caverns need geology, one fixed use pattern.

title: Can a house-sized sand heat store carry summer heat into winter, and how does its electricity use compare with a heat pump?
summary: A transient finite-volume model of a spherical sand store in mineral wool (a hot-water tank run through the same code), checked against analytic cases. A store sized to still give 10 MWh after 120 days needs 222 m 3 (against 70 if lossless) and returns only 26% of the electricity put in as heat, so a COP-4 heat pump wins unless its electricity costs 15× more, before capital cost. After a day or a week the same store returns 79% and 73%: a days-scale store at house size, seasonal only near 1,000 m 3 (43% left after 180 days). Stylised: assumed properties, a sphere, instant uniform charging, no pipes or ground.

title: Does error feedback rescue the noise floor that compressed local SGD loses?
summary: Workers keep the unsent part of their displacement and add it to the next message. On a quadratic with random sparsification the second moments close exactly: stability requires αs < 2(2− ρ ) Nρ /( Nρ 2 +4(1− ρ )) — half the unbiased limit for a single worker, above the uncompressed limit for large cohorts — and the floor has a closed form that returns to the uncompressed one at small steps (1.08× at ρ =¼ where unbiased compression pays 4×) while the mean keeps its speed. What the residual buys is unbiasedness: dropping converges to the send-rate-weighted mean, feedback to the true mean, but at a variance that only pays off for very small steps. Top-k is simulation only; stylised quadratics.

title: Escalating bonds: cheap challenges, fixed deterrence, a γ-fold capital asymmetry
summary: Bond-escalation dispute games with a fallible oracle, solved exactly: the opening bond that deters false challenges is εV/((1−ε)C−εD) and shrinks geometrically in rounds (20.4 to 10 −5 ) while the attacker's total outlay barely moves (20.41 to 20.62); against a capital-limited attacker the honest defender needs exactly γ·max{C(r)≤B C } ≤ γB C , so the responder pays γ per exchange. Stylised.

title: How much should a router extremize?
summary: Pooling calibrated experts with shared training data: the Bayes-optimal logit exponent a* = n/(1+(n−1)ρ) (matched to a numerical argmin), extra experts saturating at 1/ρ effective experts, naive independence pooling doing worse than chance at ρ=0.9, and an online learner that finds a*. Stylised.

title: How optimistic is the cost a planner quotes from its own twin rollouts?
summary: A planner picks the cheapest of K plans by n twin rollouts each and explains the choice by quoting that simulated cost. With equal true costs the quote is low by exactly e K · s ( e K = expected maximum of K standard normals: 0.56 at K =2, 1.16 at 5, 1.87 at 20; Monte-Carlo within 0.5%), a nominal 95% interval around it covers the true cost 88%, 78% and 60% of the time at K =5, 10, 20, and two identical plans are quoted a gap of 1.13 s . Reporting from fresh rollouts removes the bias exactly but costs selection quality (regret 0.069 to 0.104, best-plan rate 0.76 to 0.68 when 8 of 20 rollouts are diverted). It does not remove the twin’s own model error b k ~ N (0,τ 2 ): the quoted-minus-real bias is − e K τ 2 /√(τ 2 + s 2 ) (formula −0.531, simulated −0.530 at τ=0.5), so only real trials of the chosen plan give an honest real-cost quote. Stylised: independent Gaussian sample means (one skewed check: formula 7% high), no human study, no robot.

title: Do free retries break hash-derived spot checks?
summary: When an audit challenge is the hash of the prover's own commitment, a cheater simply re-rolls until the challenge misses its corrupted steps, so expected profit is exactly G−c/p (p = C(T−k,q)/C(T,q)) and the stake plays no role. Deterrence needs q ≈ ln(G/c)·T/k opened steps against ln2·T/k for a post-commitment beacon: 10×–60× more for G/c = 2 10 …2 60 . Proof-of-work on the challenge has a closed-form optimum x* = v/λ p − c 0 . Real SHA-256 grinding matches the geometric law. Stylised.

title: What does a state estimator tuned in a twin with the wrong noise levels cost in the real world?
summary: For a scalar Kalman filter (plant x ′= ax + w , sensor y = x + v ) the real error under the twin’s gain K is exactly ((1− K ) 2 Q + K 2 R )/(1−(1− K ) 2 a 2 ). With a =0.9 and Q = R =1, a twin 10× too quiet claims MSE 0.215 but the real MSE is 1.32 (+121%), while one 10× too noisy is slightly pessimistic (+42%); at 100× the quiet twin costs 5.0 against 0.64, and for a random walk quiet-twin regret grows as m −1/2 . Regret is locally c (ln m ) 2 . Negative result: for an unstable plant the twin’s gain never destabilises the filter. The lag-1 innovation covariance is zero iff the gain is optimal, and a one-shot moment retune from real innovations cut regret from 2.15 to 0.026 at n =200 and 0.0002 at n =25,000 (simulation, ∼1/ n ). Stylised: scalar linear-Gaussian system, stationary, known dynamics.

title: How many real steps does a twin-pretrained policy save, and which twin errors does fine-tuning inherit?
summary: On a quadratic real loss with SGD noise, the expected loss after k real steps from a twin start is exact (matched to Monte Carlo within 0.3%). A twin start with 0.6× the cold-start error saves 64–67% of the steps to every target from 8× to 1.2× the SGD floor; at equal error it saves nothing and at 1.5× it costs 138 extra steps (negative transfer). For any curvature spectrum the loss left by a twin error of norm b is at most b 2 /(4 eηk ), attained by the direction λ * =1/(2η k ), so twin error decays as 1/ k , not geometrically. At the same initial loss, an error in the stiffest direction needs 13 steps to reach 2× the floor and one in the flattest 1,541. Stylised: fixed offset, isotropic noise, no robot data.

title: How high a bandwidth does a rigid-body twin let you push when the real joint is flexible?
summary: A twin with one rigid inertia says the PD loop is stable at every bandwidth. With load-side sensing the real two-mass loop is unstable above ε c = w / w s , the smallest root of a cubic in modal damping δ and twin damping ratio ζ : exactly independent of the mass ratio, ≈ δ / ζ for small δ (0.0143, 0.0714, 0.286 for δ = 0.01, 0.05, 0.2 at ζ = 0.7), and unstable at every gain with no modal damping. Motor-side (collocated) sensing was stable at all 7 320 grid points, so the twin is right about one sensor placement and wrong about the other. Twin and real step responses differ by under 1% at 0.9 ε c , so ordinary validation gives no warning; a twin that overstates δ by a factor f certifies ε c high by the same factor, and a design at fraction m of the certified bandwidth tolerates f ≈ 1/ m . Stylised: one flexible mode, linear, PD only, continuous-time, noiseless.

title: What ghost ranges does a single-ray lidar twin never produce at a depth edge?
summary: A one-ray twin returns the near or the far surface at a depth edge; a real beam with a Gaussian footprint and merged return pulses reports an energy-weighted range in free space. The ghost band is exactly 2Φ −1 (1−ε/ D ) beam standard deviations wide for equal energies (2.56 at ε/ D = 0.1, 4.65 at 0.01, none once ε ≥ D /2), checked against a direct scan to 10 −4 , and shifts toward the near side and narrows when the far wall is brighter (1.67 at a 100× energy ratio). A scan with an edge every ≈ 100 beams has a ghost fraction equal to the prediction to within 0.3%, and a 3-of-5 persistence filter on a static robot passes 80–99% of ghosts because they come from geometry, not noise. Stylised: hard merge threshold, 1-D footprint, centroid detector, no real scans.

title: Does agreement pay reward shared laziness?
summary: Multi-task peer prediction pays 2G·Cov of two reports. If lazy verifiers copy a shared per-task default (the same public model’s guess) pay becomes 2G[a i a j pq + (1−a i )(1−a j )d(1−d)], effort is a coordination game with threshold a* = (k/2G + s)/(pq + s), and the all-lazy profile is always an equilibrium paying 2G·d(1−d): equal to honest pay when the default matches the prior, 1.19× it at p=0.3, d=0.5. Closing it with gold checks needs payment mass (2Gs+k)/(1−acc D ), larger than the honest pay itself. Stylised.

title: A lidar twin without atmospheric loss overstates range in fog: by how much, how sensitive is it to a mis-set extinction, and what does it do to a driving policy?
summary: Detection range solves r e α r = r 0 , i.e. r = W (α r 0 )/α; the clear-air twin overstates it by exactly e α r (×2.32 at 200 m visibility) and a relative extinction error moves range by the elasticity W /(1+ W ) < 1. With lognormal episode-to-episode fog a policy sized on the median fog is violated 50% of the time (mean fog 34%), the 5%-quantile range gives exactly 5% at a 43.5% speed cost, and in patchy fog one extinction calibrated on a bright target underestimates dark targets by up to 29% (calibrated on a dark one, bright targets are overestimated 61–168%). Stylised: hard threshold, Beer–Lambert medium, no lidar data.

title: Can a fixed inflation radius stand in for a rectangular robot's footprint in a narrow gap?
summary: A 1.0×0.5 m robot with Gaussian heading error crossing a gap: pass probability is exactly 2Φ(θ*/σ)−1 with θ* = asin( g / R )−atan( W / L ) (matches a corner-geometry Monte Carlo within 0.0013). Inscribed- and circumscribed-circle twins are step functions (always pass / always fail below 1.118 m); an inflation calibrated to 95% at σ = 0.05 is 0.17 m too small at σ = 0.15 (real pass 0.49), and ten-gap missions succeed only 0.60 of the time where the twin says 1. Stylised: simulated robot, Gaussian heading error, no sensing error.

title: Can two verifiers be compared while the data streams in?
summary: For fixed reports r A , r B and binary outcomes with frequency q, the Brier difference is a two-point gamble and A is better exactly when q is on A’s side of the midpoint π=(r A +r B )/2. Betting a fraction λ of wealth on it gives an anytime-valid e-process whose best bet grows at exactly KL(q‖π), so the expected decision time is ln(1/α)/KL. A z-test checked after every task falsely declares a winner in 19–38% of null runs at nominal 5%; a uniform mixture over bets stays at or below 3.8% and costs 15–41% extra tasks; a bet twice too large has negative growth. Fixed reports, i.i.d. outcomes. Stylised.

title: Can a verifier tell from old-task losses that a continual-learning job skipped or shortchanged tasks?
summary: Extends the forgetting law to a trainer that skips each task with probability s or takes a step fraction a : the final-checkpoint loss on the task at position t is exactly ρ t −1 [(1−2 m 1 + m 2 )( r / d )λ k + ( r / d )ρ(ρ k −λ k )], matching exact quadrature and simulation. A skipped task is at least d /( d − r ) times worse than a trained one at every lag but clearly so only in a window (ratio ≥2 for lags ≤6.7 at d =16, r =2). Catching a skipping trainer is lag-free: about 17–20 jobs for 20% skipping at any audit lag, scaling as 0.7/ s 2 and falling with job length, while a 10% step shortfall needs about 9,600 jobs. Stylised: linear regression, Haar-random tasks, known initial error.

title: How fast does a shared model forget a task, and does splitting it into modules help?
summary: Training to convergence on random rank- r tasks in R d is a projection, and the expected loss on a task learned k tasks ago is exactly ( r / d )(1− r / d )(ρ k −λ k ): zero when learned, a peak (0.044 at d =12, r =3, lag 2.5) at a lag near 0.7 d / r , then decay because the tasks agree; matched by simulation to the third decimal. Routing tasks to m modules dilutes both rates by m and cuts short-horizon forgetting (5.9× at T =4, m =8) but a single shared model minimises seen-plus-fresh loss at every horizon tried, and two modules forget more than one at T =12. With conflicting tasks forgetting has a floor 2 r τ²/ d that only task-specific modules remove. Stylised: linear regression, exact convergence, isotropic tasks.

title: Which significance rule gives a classifier two-sample test the right false-rejection rate on a digital twin?
summary: Follow-up to free-c2stpower , whose empirical null was noisy. On the exact pendulum twin (200 replicates per cell, boosted trees, nominal 0.05) a naive rank-sum test on cross-validated scores and a t-test on per-fold AUROCs falsely reject 0.060–0.130 of the time, never below 0.060, while a half-and-half holdout split with an exact-null rank-sum test stays at 0.040–0.060 as the theory requires. The price is power: for a 10% Coulomb error holdout rejects 0.20 at n = 200 and 0.92 at 400, against 0.62 and 1.00 for the over-sized cross-validated rule, so it needs roughly twice the data. A permutation-calibrated cross-validated statistic is untried. Stylised, simulated, one classifier.

title: Does a permutation test on the cross-validated statistic keep its size and beat the holdout rule's power on a digital twin?
summary: Follow-up to free-c2stexact on the stylised pendulum twin. A permutation test on the pooled cross-validated AUROC (39 label permutations, p ≤ 0.05) falsely rejects 0.040 of the time at n = 100 and 0.020 at 200 (100 replicates), while for a 10% Coulomb error at n = 200 it rejects 0.367 against 0.183 for the half-and-half holdout rule (60 replicates, intervals just overlapping). The unadjusted cross-validated rule rejects 0.600 but is not a valid test. Costs about 40 times the training. A first run using p < 0.05 on the k/40 grid had an effective level of 0.025 and was rerun. Stylised, simulated, one classifier, few replicates.

title: How many real trajectories does a classifier two-sample test need to reject a wrong digital twin, compared with a paired error test?
summary: Follow-up to mimic-twinc2st on a stylised pendulum (Coulomb friction, Student-t sensor noise). The rejection threshold is the 95th percentile of the exact twin’s own null, and power is the share of replicates above it. For a Coulomb error of 20% the paired error test (same start angles, noisy real vs noise-free twin) has power 0.76 at 50 trajectories and 0.98 at 100, while the boosted-tree C2ST has 0.04 and 0.25 and needs about 200 to reach 1.00. For a 10% error the paired test stalls at 0.09–0.20 for every n up to 800 (a plausible but untested cause: the squared heavy-tailed noise has infinite variance), while the C2ST reaches 0.62 at 200 and 1.00 at 400. For Gaussian instead of Student-t noise of the same sd the paired test has power 0.04–0.07 at every n , the C2ST with second-difference features 0.92 at 50. Caveat: the null threshold comes from 60 replicates, and a check on fresh null replicates falsely rejected 0–29% of the time (nominal 5%), so power at small n is approximate. Stylised, simulated, 24 replicates per cell.

title: How many research READMEs admit their citations are unchecked, and which works need checking first?
summary: A stdlib scan of all 550 project READMEs for lines that flag a citation or figure as written from memory or not re-checked: 94 (17.1%) have at least one, 137 flagged lines in all, naming 41 distinct author-year works. Four recur most: Dawid & Skene (1979) in 10 projects, Zhang et al. (2019) in 9, Horowitz (2014) and Horvitz (1999) in 6 each, so checking those once from a networked session clears many flags. A flag is the README's own admission, not a verdict; nothing was verified in this run (Crossref was unreachable).

title: Which test input should you use to calibrate a mass-spring-damper twin?
summary: Fitting mass, damping and stiffness of a lightly damped oscillator (ζ = 0.1) from one 10 s noisy trace under four equal-energy inputs, with Cramér-Rao bounds and 100 Gauss-Newton fits each. A sine at the natural frequency gives the lowest held-out prediction error (mean RMSE 3.1×10 −4 against 1.1×10 −3 for a step and 2.8×10 −3 for an off-resonance sine) although it has the worst Fisher condition number (527 against 56 to 114), so conditioning ranks the inputs backwards. The step estimates damping 4.5× less precisely. Fitted spreads are within 0.83 to 1.09 of the bounds. Stylised: one plant, one noise level, truth inside the model class. Preliminary.

title: Do documentation complaints in agent run records repeat more than chance?
summary: A permutation null for the repeat rate in swe-friction . Of 418 classified doc_friction entries (1 to 18 October 2026), 171 name a (file, theme) pair reported on an earlier day, against a null median of 238 (95% interval 224 to 250; none of 2,000 shuffles reached 171). Complaints repeat less than chance on 16 and 17 October and match it on the 18th, so the rising repeat rate is mostly arithmetic of a growing history. Consistent with fixes landing, but the commits are not linked. Keyword themes, self-reported, 18 days. Preliminary.

title: How much does a wrong process-noise guess cost a Kalman filter?
summary: Exact steady-state MSE of a scalar Kalman filter run at the wrong process noise q a = λ q , matched to simulation within 1%. Underestimating costs far more than overestimating: at λ = 1/100 the excess is ×7.4 against ×1.6 at λ = 100; the over-estimate is bounded (MSE → r ) and the under-estimate is not. The filter’s claimed variance is 5× too small at λ = 1/10. The gap closes at high signal-to-noise. Textbook-level and stylised: scalar, steady state, Gaussian.

title: Do low-discrepancy scenarios make a twin evaluate a policy more accurately than iid domain randomisation?
summary: Averaging a policy’s return over n randomised scenarios, compared across iid, Latin hypercube, randomly shifted Halton and shifted R d lattice samplers, against exact means. Latin hypercubes keep the n −0.5 rate (MSE cut 1.6–12×). Shifted Halton improves the rate for smooth returns (slope −0.92 at d = 2, MSE 149× lower at n = 1024) and keeps a 4–24× gain on a discontinuous success-rate return, shrinking as the number of randomised parameters grows. The R d lattice is erratic (no better than iid at d = 5). 95% intervals from 8 independent randomisations cover 94–97%. Stylised: analytic returns on a uniform cube, no simulator.

title: Why does the R<sub>d</sub> low-discrepancy lattice lose its advantage at d = 5 when evaluating a twin policy?
summary: Follow-up to free-qmcdr . The shifted R d lattice’s error exponent at d = 5 is −0.45 ± 0.01 over six seed strings, no better than iid, so it is not a seed fluke; across d = 2…8 it dips at 5 between −0.72 and −0.61 neighbours, so it is not a smooth dimension effect; a generator built from √ p j reaches −0.66 at d = 5. A resonance score against small integer relations scores both generators alike, so the mechanism is not identified. Stylised analytic returns, not a simulator.

title: Which paired test of a digital twin survives both heavy-tailed cells and whole bad runs?
summary: Follow-up to free-robusttails , which found no single robust statistic won against both Student-t(2) cells and 10%-of-runs-10×-noisier bad runs. Here each trajectory’s squared residuals are summarised robustly (median or 20%-trimmed mean), then the per-run values are summarised robustly across runs. On the same stylised pendulum (10% Coulomb error, n = 50–200, 400 null replicates) the trimmed-then-trimmed statistic has power 0.99–1.00 under t(2) cells and when t(2) cells sit inside bad runs, 0.86 / 0.95 / 1.00 under bad runs alone, and 0.84 / 0.99 / 1.00 under Gaussian noise, against 0.91 / 0.99 / 1.00 for the per-run mean-squared median; the best single-level statistics reach only 0.10–0.28 or 0.15–0.38 in the case they fail. Size is 0.02–0.08 against a nominal 0.05. One toy pendulum, one twin error, one contamination design; stylised and simulated only.

title: Was the paired digital-twin test weak, or was its statistic?
summary: Follow-up to free-c2stpower , where a paired error test stalled at 0.09–0.20 power for a 10% Coulomb-friction error under Student-t(3) sensor noise. On the same stylised pendulum, the mean squared residual again has power 0.06–0.10 at every n up to 400, while a median, a 20%-trimmed mean, a mean absolute or a Huber statistic reaches 0.94–1.00 from n = 50 (400 null and 400 test replicates per cell). Under Gaussian noise the choice barely matters. Stylised; one seed per noise kind; not a claim about a physical system.

title: Which robust paired test still catches a wrong digital twin when noise has infinite variance or whole runs go bad?
summary: Follow-up to free-robustpaired on the same stylised pendulum (10% Coulomb-friction error, n = 50–200 matched trajectories, 400 null replicates). With Student-t(2) cells (infinite variance) the mean squared residual has power about 0.05 at every n, while median and trimmed squared residuals reach 1.00 and a Huber loss with a MAD-estimated scale reaches 0.70–1.00 (0.20–0.53 with the scale fixed at 0.02). When 10% of runs are 10× noisier, every cell-level statistic stalls (0.04–0.40) while the median over runs of per-run mean squares reaches 0.89–1.00; that statistic is nearly the worst under t(2) cells (0.11–0.19). No statistic wins both, and under Gaussian noise the median pays at n = 50 (0.72 against 0.98). Stylised.

title: With noisy scores, does a "beat the record by a margin" rule pick the best candidate more often than the best cutoff?
summary: Simulation ( n = 50 candidates, parameters tuned on 8,000 training trials, scored on 60,000 fresh paired trials) of a two-parameter margin rule: skip r −1 candidates, then take the first whose noisy score beats the earlier maximum by at least d . P(pick the true best) rises from 0.2334 to 0.2444 at noise 0.5 (+0.0111, se 0.0014) and from 0.1429 to 0.1491 at noise 1 (+0.0062, se 0.0015); at noise 2 the gain (+0.0018, se 0.0011) is not distinguishable from zero, and with no noise the tuning picks the plain cutoff. One setting, one seed pair, a coarse grid; the Bayes-optimal policy is not computed.

title: How much does noisy scoring cost the secretary problem, and should the 1/e cutoff move?
summary: Simulation of the classical cutoff rule for hiring the best of n = 50 candidates when only a noisy score is seen (noise sd 0 to 4 times the quality sd, 40,000 trials per cell, checked against the exact noiseless formula). The best cutoff barely moves, 19 with no noise and 16–17 at every noise level; the chance of picking the true best falls from 0.373 to 0.145 at noise 1 and 0.043 at noise 4 (lottery: 0.02). Keeping the classical cutoff costs at most 0.006. A high mean true rank wants a much earlier cutoff (7–9). Cutoff rules only, Gaussian, one setting; the optimal noisy policy is not computed.

title: How many simulator rollouts does a sequential test save when certifying a failure rate?
summary: Exact dynamic-programming comparison (no sampling) of Wald’s sequential probability ratio test with the smallest fixed-size binomial test, both at 5% error, for deciding between an acceptable and an unacceptable failure rate. At either rate the sequential test uses about half the rollouts (for 1% vs 5%: 79 and 113 on average against 181). Between the two rates the saving shrinks to 6–17% at its worst point in the four cases tried. Assumes iid rollouts that match reality, so it says nothing about the sim-to-real gap.

title: How well does Freivalds' check work in floating point?
summary: Checking a claimed matrix product by A(Br) ≈ Cr needs a tolerance t , so the error bound becomes size-dependent: a rank-one corruption of Frobenius norm F is missed by a Gaussian probe with probability exactly erf( t /(√2 F )), rank one is the worst case for fixed F , and m probes give erf m (4 probes for 1% at 3 t ). Rademacher probes miss a two-entry corruption with probability ½ at every size. Emulated float32 noise grows ≈ n 0.9 ; a hashed probe with free retries lets a cheater grind in 1/erf tries (125 at 100 t ). Stylised, additive corruption.

title: How wrong is the stopping distance of a twin that models friction as purely viscous?
summary: With Coulomb friction c the real coast-down stops in finite time with exact distance ( m / b )[ v 0 −( c / b )ln(1+ b v 0 / c )] (RK4 agreement 9×10 −9 ), while the viscous twin only decays exponentially (6.5 s to reach 10 −3 vs 1.95 s real). The least-squares gain b + c E[ v ]/E[ v 2 ] depends on the logged speed range (1.23 on [1,3], 3.44 on [0.05,0.3]); fitted on [1,3] the twin overestimates stopping distance ×1.8 at v 0 =1 and ×17 at 0.05, is exact at 7.34 and underestimates above. Negative result: no single viscous gain does better than 0.87 worst relative error over [0.05,3], while an affine fit recovers ( b , c ) exactly. Stylised: one mass, noiseless logs.

title: How many redundant sensors does a twin with independent errors say a robot needs?
summary: Redundant sensors that share an error source have pairwise correlation ρ ; the equal-weight fused variance is exactly σ 2 (1+( n −1) ρ )/ n , so a twin with independent errors understates the fused std by √(1+( n −1) ρ ), n sensors are worth fewer than 1/ ρ independent ones, and no fleet beats σ√ρ . For a target std of 0.25 σ the twin says 16 sensors; the real fleet needs 30 at ρ =0.03, 77 at 0.05, 376 at 0.06 and none at 0.0625 or above. A 3- σ gate sized from the twin false-alarms 8.6× too often at ρ =0.05 ( n =16). Repair from calibration logs is mixed: the estimated ρ is unbiased, but a plug-in fleet size misses the target in about half of repeats; a 90% bootstrap upper bound misses in 8.5% (T=400) at almost twice the sensors, and short logs cannot support the target. Stylised: equal-variance Gaussian errors with one common factor, simulated fleet, no sensor data.

title: Does an assistive garment pay for its own mass?
summary: A one-joint ankle model of an exosuit-style garment: a suit adding a fraction of the biological push-off torque cuts modelled whole-body metabolic cost by 3.1, 8.8 and 14.1% at gains 0.1, 0.3 and 0.5, but a delay of 0.25 of the gait cycle removes the benefit and a stiff passive spring raises ankle cost 17%. Added mass erases the saving at 8.9 kg if each kg costs 1% of whole-body power and at 1.8 kg if it costs 5%; the break-even scales as 1/sensitivity, a number the project does not supply. Stylised: lumped muscle, prescribed gait, assumed constants; not OpenSim or MyoSuite.

title: Does it pay to move an exosuit's motor and battery from the shank to the waist?
summary: Extends the exosuit power-train model with where the mass sits: a kg at the shank costs an assumed multiple of a kg at the waist, and a waist layout pays a Bowden-cable loss (efficiency 0.6–1.0) and keeps 0.3 kg of cable at the ankle. At gain 0.3 with a 4 h battery the waist layout wins once the shank penalty exceeds 1.03–1.39× the waist one; at ratio 3 and 8 N m/kg the shank suit is +20.7% against +3.3% for the waist suit. The ratio is assumed, not sourced, so the result is the break-even, not a prediction. Stylised.

title: Is it the motor or the battery that decides whether an exosuit pays for its own mass?
summary: Extends the ankle exosuit model with a power train: motor mass from peak torque and a torque density, battery mass from electrical energy and hours of use, and the resulting mass fed back into metabolic cost. With an assumed 8 N m/kg motor the gain-0.3 suit weighs about 9 kg, 8.4 of it motor, and raises whole-body cost 0.2–1.9%; the sign flips between 8 and 20 N m/kg, while eight hours of battery add under 2 kg. Stylised: every power-train constant is assumed, not sourced.

title: How much cable bend can a waist-mounted exosuit power train tolerate before the shank layout wins?
summary: Replaces the assumed Bowden-cable efficiency in the shank-versus-waist model with the capstan law exp(−μθ) for friction μ and total bend θ. At gain 0.3, a 4 h battery, 8 N m/kg and an assumed penalty ratio of 3, the waist layout stays ahead until about 31 rad of bend at μ = 0.1 (about 15 rad at 0.2), far beyond a hip-to-ankle route, so energy lost to friction does not decide the layout. Hysteresis, backlash and pretension are not modelled, and μ and the ratio are assumed. Stylised.

title: What does a degree of comfort cost in fabric?
summary: Joins the thermal comfort model to the garment cost chain for five fabric levers (infrared transmittance, low emissivity, white, thinner, thicker cloth). Levers combine sub-additively (infrared-transparent plus thin: +2.58 °C jointly, +3.25 summed), and in each scenario only one treatment helps, so a price premium sets cost, not ranking. At assumed premiums the treatments cost $0.5 to $19 per °C on a $20–50 replica trench and $3 to $114 on a designer one, because the retail chain multiplies the premium about 6×. Stylised: every premium and the thickness pricing are assumed, not quoted, and the comfort model has no reference for its optical extension.

title: Does contact resistance at yarn crossings matter for an RF-shielding fabric?
summary: A two-layer resistor network of a conductive weave: warp and weft touch only through a contact resistor at each crossing, and yarn segments break at random. On an intact fabric the contacts carry no current, so they have no effect at all. Once yarns break they carry the bypass currents: with 20% of segments broken, the median sheet resistance is 1.74 segment-resistances with perfect contacts, 2.11 with contacts equal to one segment, 4.07 at ten and 16.7 at a hundred. For a stylised stainless weave that is 59.6 dB against 52.3 dB at ten segments (thin-sheet only, aperture limit excluded). Stylised: contact values are a sweep, not measurements; one lattice size, 20 draws, independent breaks.

title: How much longer must a $2,850 coat last to beat a $56 replica on cost per wear?
summary: Combines the modelled replica costs and reported prices of garment-teardown with an assumed durability layer. With no resale and equal care the $2,850 trench must outlast a $56 replica by about 46× (52× for the $3,850 coat). With lognormal lifetimes (log-sd 0.5) and a 60-wear replica, the designer coat needs a median life near 3,100 wears to win half the time and wins about 6% of the time at 1,000; designer care of $1 per wear pushes the needed median to about 73,000. Lifetimes, care and resale are all assumed, not measured. Stylised.

title: How much cloth does a cutting plan save by mixing sizes in one marker, and is the saving real?
summary: Cutting-order planning as an exact integer program (marker mixes and plies) over 34 nested markers of a stylised three-size shirt. Laying several garments per marker saves 9–11% of cloth against one garment per marker on 20 random orders. Mixing sizes adds a further 0.4–3.7% in sample, but re-nesting the markers the plan picked with fresh seeds leaves a +0.09% difference: the gain is within annealing noise (about 5%) and partly selection of luckily short markers. Stylised: invented shirt, linear size grading, small annealing budget, mixes of at most four garments, free setup cost.

title: Does it matter where an RF-shielding fabric is damaged, and whether worn contacts go with the breaks?
summary: Follow-up to the contact-resistance model, on a 24×24 conductive weave with 60 draws per cell and bootstrap intervals. When contacts next to a broken yarn are worn (contact resistance × k ), the median sheet resistance at 20% broken and a base contact of one segment rises from 2.05 segment-resistances ( k = 1) to 3.03 ( k = 10). Clustering matters more: a fold band across the current that holds the mean break fraction fixed but breaks 4× as often inside the band leaves the weave open in 57 of 60 draws at 20% broken, while the same band along the current direction lowers the resistance to 1.43. Stylised: square lattice, one lattice size, a rule-of-thumb wear multiplier rather than a measured one, no flexing physics, and no measurement.

title: How many home-sewn coats before the labour cost per coat settles?
summary: Applies a Wright learning curve (unit time falls by a fixed share per doubling of output) to the replica trench coat of garment-teardown ($43 materials, 76 experienced-operator minutes). With an assumed first coat 4× experienced time and an 85% rate it takes 20 coats to get within 2× of experienced time; with 8× and 90% it takes about 9,100, so the answer is set by the two assumed parameters. The first coat stays under $50 only if the sewer’s time is valued at $1.45/h or less ($4.28/h for the 100th). In a factory run the learning surcharge is under 8% after 200 coats. Stylised: learning rates are assumed, not measured.

title: What do seam allowance and mixed sizes do to marker efficiency, and what does that do to a garment's cloth cost?
summary: Follow-up to the nesting and cost-teardown projects. Adding a 1 cm seam allowance to stylised pieces lowered marker efficiency from 0.69 to 0.63 for a shirt and from 0.71 to 0.51 for a four-gore skirt (the skirt mostly loses its interlocking gores); nesting three shirt sizes in one marker was 9% shorter than three separate markers. Swapping the measured efficiencies into the teardown formula moves a $7/m 2 trench’s cloth cost from $26 (assumed 0.80) to $33–41. Stylised: invented outlines, one ply, small annealing budget (differences of a few cm are noise), and the coats were not nested, so the cost step is a sensitivity, not a measurement.

title: How far is a fixed 0.80 marker efficiency from a nested coat, and what does the difference do to the cost model?
summary: Follow-up to the nesting and cost-teardown projects (stylised, preliminary). A coat drawn as 10 shell and 5 lining polygons, grown by a 1.5 cm seam allowance and nested by annealing at cloth widths of 110, 140 and 150 cm, gives marker efficiencies of 0.68–0.73 for the shell and 0.59–0.68 for the lining, against the fixed 0.80 assumed earlier (0.77–0.82 without allowance). Transplanted into the teardown trench model, the efficiency alone raises factory cost by about $20–30; the larger uncertainty is the pattern area, which these invented pieces do not settle. One ply, one size, my own shapes, no exact reference.

title: How much cloth does marker making waste, and do annealing and exact methods beat greedy nesting?
summary: Marker making as strip packing. On 20 random 8-box markers an exact MILP proves optimality on 19; shelf heuristics (NFDH, FFDH) are on average 20% and 17% longer than optimal, bottom-left 7.3%, and simulated annealing over placement order 0.5%. On two stylised garments (a shirt and a four-gore skirt, no seam allowance, one ply) true-polygon nesting with 180° turns beats bounding-box packing at the same annealing budget in every case, by about 5–9% for the shirt and 9–43% for the skirt. Stylised: the shapes are invented, polygon results have no exact reference, and the raster is conservative.

title: How much conductive yarn does an RF-shielding fabric need, and how fast does breakage ruin it?
summary: A thin-sheet shielding model of a conductive square weave (sheet resistance, aperture bound, metal mass) plus a Monte Carlo of random yarn breakage. Every design tried has a sheet shielding of 54–87 dB, but the aperture bound limits it: 36 dB at 2.4 GHz for a 1 mm pitch, about 15 dB at 28 GHz. Breakage raises resistance as the effective-medium estimate 1/(1−2 f ) up to 30% broken segments and the weave stops conducting near 50% (bond percolation). Stylised: plane wave, ideal crossings, recalled constants, no measurement; covers only the RF part of the optics milestone.

title: Can a cheap cloth drape score how well a flat pattern fits a body, and is a fitted pattern body-specific?
summary: A flat skirt-tube pattern is draped by position-based-dynamics cloth on two synthetic elliptical-section bodies and scored by circumferential strain and waist ease. The best waist is close to the body’s waist perimeter (×1.01 and ×1.03); tighter patterns strain, looser ones leave ease. A pattern optimised for one body costs 2.1–2.9 on the other against own optima of 0.15–0.75 (arbitrary cost units). Stylised: the body is a stack of ellipses, the cost weights are assumptions, the hem optimum sits at the edge of the search range, and the optimum cost moves from 0.75 to 1.34 on a finer mesh.

title: What would a suit-like protective garment weigh and cost, and what limits it?
summary: A Cunniff-style specific-toughness scaling (U*) for nylon, aramid and UHMWPE with a 0.5 m 2 torso-panel mass, cost, thickness and stiffness model. At equal weight UHMWPE gives 1.49× aramid's V50 in this scaling, and needs 0.20–0.67× the areal density depending on an unknown exponent. Under a 3 mm, 1 kg suit-like limit the panel falls short of a 4 kg/m 2 aramid reference except for UHMWPE with an optimistic exponent. Stylised: recalled formula, assumed properties and unsourced prices, no ballistic physics and no protection claim.

title: How many clothing sizes does it take to fit a population, and does a regular S-M-L grid waste them?
summary: Stylised and preliminary: a synthetic bust and hip population (assumed means 95 and 100 cm, sd 8 cm, no survey data) with a fit tolerance of ±4 cm. Choosing k sizes to fit the most people is maximum coverage; solved exactly (integer program), greedily and as a regular grid on 300 people, 3 seeds. At bust–hip correlation 0.9, exact sizes fit 12–25 points more people than the best grid and 6 sizes reach 80%; greedy is within 3.7 points of exact. At correlation 0 the gap is small, and on 20,000 fresh people the exact set is no better than the grid, so the optimiser overfits small samples. Limits: Gaussian two-measurement population, pass/fail box fit, no cost of extra sizes.

title: How many clothing sizes does a stretch fabric save?
summary: Stylised and preliminary: follow-up to the size-set project on a synthetic bust and hip population (assumed means 95 and 100 cm, sd 8 cm, no survey data). A body fits a garment if it is at most 8 cm smaller and no more than stretch larger than the nominal size, in both measurements; the best k sizes are found exactly (integer program). Sizes needed to fit 80% fall from 6 to more than 8 with no stretch to 2–3 at 10% and 1 at 20%, and the loss on fresh people shrinks too. The stretch model is idealised: usable stretch is far below rated stretch, so these are upper bounds.

title: Which sensors in a smart garment recognise what you are doing, and how fragile is that to garment slip?
summary: Synthetic chest, thigh and wrist accelerometers and knee and elbow strain channels, six activities, a softmax classifier on spectral features and unseen simulated people. Two sensors reach about 99% and all five 99.9%, because the invented classes are easy to separate. A model trained on clean data falls to 81, 61 and 45% when the IMUs rotate by 0.3, 0.6 and 1.0 rad (a garment slipping), while training with 0.6 rad of slip holds 94–99%. Strain-only stays at 97% under slip by construction. Stylised: sinusoidal signals, no real dataset, no drift or hysteresis.

title: Does a tail-risk objective, or a correlated-error model, rescue the angle-stable structural-colour stack?
summary: Follow-up to garment-stackrobust . The 8-layer stacks are trained on a CVaR objective (mean of the worst quarter of 8 sampled thickness errors) or on errors with a shared rate-drift component (ρ = 0.5), then cross-evaluated on 200 held-out draws under both error models (5% error, 8 seeds, 3000 evaluations). Negative result: no optimised design beats the plain quarter-wave stack (red, independent error: mean cost 14.1 against 16.5 for the best optimised one). CVaR trims Nelder–Mead's 90th-percentile cost (47.1 to 43.1) while raising its mean, and correlated-error training did worse. Stylised thin-film model; nothing was coated or measured.

title: Does adding layers cut the angle shift of a structural-colour coating at fixed chroma and oxide mass?
summary: The constrained problem of garment-stackpareto with the layer count varied from 2 to 12 (Nelder–Mead restarts, 3000 calls, 8 seeds per cell). For the red target at C* ≥ 40 and 4 g/m 2 , 2 and 4 layers reach a best mean ΔE of about 3.4, while 6, 8 and 10 layers reach 0.5–0.8; medians are several times higher, so the ranking among 6–10 is within noise. At 12 layers few runs were feasible, probably a search limit at equal budget rather than a property of the stack. Stylised: flat substrate, three angles, no thickness tolerance; no coating was made.

title: Can an optimiser cut the angle shift of a structural-colour coating, and what does it give up?
summary: Eight-layer thin-film stacks on a flat nylon-like substrate, optimised to minimise the colour shift between 0 and 15–45° incidence while keeping chroma C* ≥ 40 and hue near a quarter-wave target. At an equal budget of 3000 evaluations (10 seeds), Nelder–Mead with restarts cuts the median mean ΔE 76 shift from 12.4 to 1.4 (red target) and from 25.9 to 5.6 (blue), beating random search and differential evolution, but chroma falls toward the floor and oxide mass rises about 1.8–2.5×. Stylised: flat substrate, three sample angles, recalled indices, no fabrication tolerance; no LLM involved.

title: How much angle shift can a structural-colour coating shed at a given chroma and oxide mass?
summary: The 8-layer stacks of garment-stackopt re-optimised on a grid of chroma floors and oxide-mass caps (Nelder–Mead restarts, 3000 calls, 5 seeds per cell). For the red target at a chroma floor of C* 40 the best mean angle shift is 0.68 ΔE 76 at a 4.0 g/m 2 cap, 2.71 at 3.0, and no run is feasible at 2.0 or below; raising the floor to 60 costs more (2.84 at a 4.0 cap). Mass binds before chroma. Stylised: flat substrate, three sample angles, untuned penalties, a coarse grid and a single optimiser, so cell values are noisy and the front is not smooth.

title: Does an angle-stable structural-colour stack survive layer-thickness error?
summary: The 8-layer stacks optimised in garment-stackopt are fabricated virtually with independent Gaussian thickness error (3 and 5%) and scored on 200 held-out draws. The nominal optimum (angle shift 1.4 ΔE 76 ) degrades to a mean cost of 24.9 at 3% error, worse than the plain quarter-wave stack (13.2), and only about half of draws keep an acceptable colour. A robust objective averaged over six error draws, at equal total cost, recovers part of this (red target, 3%: 11.7 against 13.2) but not the colour drift, and at 5% error or the blue target the quarter-wave stack is hard to beat. Stylised: flat substrate, no dispersion, uncorrelated errors, 10 seeds, no significance tests, two optimisers.

title: Where does a designer coat's price go, and what does a $20 to $50 replica keep?
summary: A bottom-up cost model for a lined woven coat (fabric from pattern area and marker efficiency, trims, sewing minutes times wage, overhead, brand and retail multipliers) applied to two reported designer prices. Under assumed inputs the factory cost is $186–248 for a $2,850 trench and $469–551 for a $3,850 coat, under 15% of the price in every wage scenario, and the assumed multipliers do not close the gap. A cheap-cloth replica costs $46–100 to make; only a very lean case reaches $29–34. Stylised: every cost input is assumed, prices are from search snippets, and fit and durability are not scored.

title: How much comfort can an infrared-transparent or gating textile buy, and which fabric properties matter?
summary: A Fanger/ISO 7730 PMV model and a Gagge-style two-node model extended with fabric infrared emissivity and transmittance, solar absorptance and vapour permeability. The no-optics PMV matches an open-source ISO implementation to 0.006 over 144 cases. Indoors without sun, infrared transmittance (0 to 0.8) is worth about 2.4 °C of comfort at 28 °C, more than cutting insulation from 0.7 to 0.3 clo (1.8 °C), but makes a 16 °C room feel 7.3 °C colder; in sun, solar absorptance (7.7 °C span) dominates the infrared properties. Stylised: assumed fabric properties, a parallel-path radiation model with no reference data, and recalled two-node constants.

title: How thin must a coating be to colour a fibre without dye, and how fragile is that colour?
summary: A transfer-matrix model of dielectric quarter-wave stacks on a flat nylon-like substrate, with colour computed under an equal-energy illuminant. Six-pair stacks reach 99% reflectance with 2–3 g/m 2 of oxide and saturated colour, but the peak blue-shifts from 620 to 540 nm by 60° incidence (ΔE 76 48), and 10% layer-thickness error moves hue by ΔE≈10 while roughly preserving chroma. Stylised: flat substrate, constant indices, no fibre scattering.

title: Which design choices explain the gap between the repository's two-node model and an open-source Gagge implementation?
summary: Rebuilds the two-node model with nine switchable choices (body area, constants, convection, clothing radiation, skin mass fraction, vasodilation gain, sweat caps, update order, step count), each set to the repository's version or to the pythermalcomfort version read from its source. With all nine set to the reference's, the model matches it to 0.008 in every output over 108 conditions. Switching one at a time, the skin-temperature gap (mean 0.58 °C) falls most with the variable skin mass fraction (to 0.36), the convection coefficient (0.43) and the vasodilation gain (0.44); body area, constants, update order and step count each change it by under 0.01 °C. A comparison of two implementations, not of either against people; the effects interact, so the attribution depends on the order.

title: How far is the repository's two-node thermal model from an open-source implementation of the Gagge model?
summary: Runs the two-node model from the thermal-comfort project against pythermalcomfort over 108 conditions (18–36 °C, 30–80% humidity, 1–2 met, 0.3–1 clo). Core temperature agrees within 0.25 °C everywhere; skin temperature differs by 0.58 °C on average and up to 2.1 °C, mostly in cool air; evaporative loss differs by up to 14 W/m 2 in hot humid air. The direction of change with insulation and humidity agrees in 23 of 24 cases. This compares two implementations, not either against people; causes of the skin-temperature gap are untested and the optical extension is not covered.

title: Do the closed and open bounds of an infrared-gating textile survive other two-node design choices and steady state?
summary: Re-runs the two fixed states of a gated textile (infrared transmittance 0.15 closed, 0.8 open) from an earlier model in the switchable two-node comparison, under two sets of design choices and at 3 h and steady state (stylised, preliminary). Opening the gate lowers skin temperature by 0.20–0.25 C in a 31 C room and 1.4–1.5 C in a 16 C room, and moves 5.5–6.2 W/m 2 from evaporation to dry loss at 31 C; the choice sets differ by about 0.05 C there. Limits: two fixed states with no switching dynamics, evaporative heat loss rather than sweat mass, no validation against people.

title: If a thermostat infrared-gating band is tuned on some rooms, does it still help in rooms it never saw?
summary: A stylised, preliminary follow-up to garment-twonodemet . A skin-temperature gate band is tuned by exhaustive grid search on rest-to-walk and walk-to-rest steps in 22, 24 and 26 C rooms, then scored unchanged on held-out rooms (23, 25, 20 and 28 C). The tuned band (a narrow 33.6–33.7 C) beats the untuned 33.2–34.2 C band and both fixed states on both held-out sets under both choice sets, by 0.01 to 0.06 C against the untuned band. It also beats the four-schedule oracle on training scenarios, because the oracle is restricted, and it chatters (up to 24 switches in 180 min) with instant, free switching, so the gain may not survive actuation lag or cost. Six training and eight held-out scenarios from one model; no real fabric or person.

title: Does a tuned infrared-gating thermostat survive an actuation lag and a cost per switch?
summary: A stylised, preliminary follow-up to garment-twonodeheld . The skin-temperature gate band is retuned by exhaustive grid search for each actuation lag (0, 2, 5, 10 min) and each cost per switch (0, 0.01, 0.03 C), then scored on held-out rooms. A 10 min lag cuts the tuned gate’s gain over never switching from 0.23 to 0.15 C (“between” rooms, this repository’s choice set). A switch penalty widens the band and removes the chatter. The tuned band is not always better: under the reference choice set it loses to the untuned band by up to 0.035 C in 3 of 24 cells, and once to never switching (0.052 C). Six training and eight held-out scenarios, assumed lags and penalties, one model; no real fabric or person.

title: When the metabolic rate steps from rest to walking, does a thermostat-driven infrared-gating textile beat its fixed states?
summary: A stylised, preliminary follow-up to garment-twonodestep . One step in metabolic rate (1 to 2 met, or back) at minute 90 of 180 in the switchable two-node model, scored by mean |skin temperature − 33.7 °C|. In a 20 °C room the gate never opens; at 24 °C it beats both fixed states under this repository’s choice set and ties fixed closed under the reference’s; at 28 °C staying open is as good as any policy; after walking stops a 10 min actuation lag erases most of the gate’s gain. Bands were not tuned and results depend on the choice set. Not a claim about any real textile.

title: How far is the thermostat-driven infrared-gating textile from the best possible switching schedule when the room temperature steps?
summary: A stylised, preliminary follow-up to garment-twonodestep . Exhaustive search over open/closed schedules (at most 3 toggles on a 10 min grid, instant actuation) in the switchable two-node model, scored by mean |skin temperature − 33.7 C| (a proxy, not a comfort index). One toggle is enough (more improve the score by at most 0.001 C). The best toggle is not always at the step: it is early or late after a step down. The gate is within 0.02 C of the optimum after a step up but 0.06–0.11 C away after a step down (0.18 with 10 min lag in one case). One person, two assumed transmittances, a coarse grid; not a claim about any real garment.

title: Do the fabric-optics conclusions of the thermal-comfort model survive a different two-node implementation?
summary: Adds infrared transmittance, outer emissivity, solar absorptance, radiant temperature and solar load to the switchable two-node model and compares each property’s effect under the repository’s design choices and under those of pythermalcomfort . Over four stylised scenarios the properties rank identically by dry-heat-loss effect; sizes agree within 3% in a 28 °C room but differ by up to about 2× in cool air (traced mostly to the variable skin mass fraction) and in sun (convection coefficient); the one sign change is under 0.1 °C. The reference has no optics, so its optical terms are my own linearised construction without an external check. A comparison of implementations, not of people or measured fabrics.
