title: At what switching penalty does a proportional infrared gate beat the on/off thermostat gate?
summary: A stylised, preliminary follow-up to garment-twonodeprop . Both gates are retuned on training rooms for each actuation lag and a per-swing penalty (one full close-to-open swing = 1 for either gate; the penalty scale is an assumption), then scored on held-out rooms. The proportional gate has the lower cost in 52 of 80 cells, by at most 0.096 C on a proxy of order 0.3–1.5 C; at the highest penalty the gain holds in the between rooms (8 of 8) but mostly reverses in the outside rooms (2 of 8). Simulated comfort, not a claim about any real garment.

title: Does an infrared-gating band tuned for one person and clothing level still work for other clothing and body sizes?
summary: A stylised, preliminary follow-up to garment-twonodewide . Both gates are tuned on one person (0.5 clo, 70 kg) and scored unchanged on other clothing levels and body sizes. Body size barely matters (retuning gains at most 0.002 C), clothing does: retuning an on/off band for 1.2 clo gains up to 0.375 C, while the proportional gate's gap stays at most 0.075 C. Proportional wins every cell except three at 0.3 clo and penalty 0.1. Mass and height enter the model only through body area and heat capacity; simulated comfort, not a claim about any real garment.

title: Does a proportional infrared-gating textile beat the on/off thermostat gate?
summary: A stylised, preliminary, negative follow-up to garment-twonodelag . A transmittance that ramps linearly with skin temperature is tuned by exhaustive search (72 bands) for each actuation lag (0 to 10 min) and scored on held-out rooms against the tuned on/off gate. Proportional wins in 5 of 16 cells and every difference is within 0.010 C: the search picks bands only 0.1 to 0.2 C wide, i.e. nearly on/off. Forcing a softer ramp (at least 1.4 C wide) costs 0.02 to 0.07 C. Switching is free in this run, so a switch penalty could change the answer. Six training and eight held-out scenarios; no real fabric or person.

title: Do the fabric-optics effects on thermal comfort change once the two-node model reaches steady state?
summary: Re-runs the switchable two-node comparison of fabric optics (infrared transmittance, emissivity, solar absorptance, insulation) for 24 h of model time instead of one hour (stylised, preliminary). In the 28 C room, with hot walls and in sun the one-hour effects are already steady. In the 16 C room the one-hour disagreement between the repository’s design choices and those of pythermalcomfort (ratio 1.9–2.7) shrinks to 0.89–0.98 at steady state, so it was mostly a transient-speed difference. A model fixed point, not a claim about people; no fabric or person was measured.

title: When the room temperature steps, does a thermostat-driven infrared-gating textile beat its fixed states and approach an oracle?
summary: A stylised, preliminary follow-up to garment-twonodeswitch . One step in room temperature at minute 90 of 180 in the switchable two-node model, scored by mean |skin temperature − 33.7 C| (a proxy, not a comfort index). After a step to a hotter room the gate beats both fixed states and lies within about 0.02within about 0.02–0.07 C of an oraclenbsp;C of an oracle that knows the schedule; after a step to a cooler room it gains little, and a 10 min actuation lag can make it worse than staying closed. Transmittances are assumptions; no fabric or person was measured.

title: What does a thermostat-driven infrared-gating textile do that its fixed closed and open states do not?
summary: Adds a skin-temperature-triggered gate (hysteresis band, first-order actuation lag) to the switchable two-node comfort model (stylised, preliminary). In constant 31, 24 and 16 C rooms over 3 h the gate settles into one of the two fixed states with at most one change, so it cannot beat the best fixed state; a 10 min lag only delays the start (open 94% vs 98% of minutes at 31 C). Threshold placement matters more: a 32–35 C band opens under one set of design choices and never under the other. A mostly null result; it needs changing conditions to show value. No fabric or person was measured.

title: Is the outside-room reversal of the proportional infrared gate a training-range artefact?
summary: A stylised, preliminary follow-up to garment-twonodepen . Both gates are retuned on a wider set of rooms (20–28 C instead of 22–26 C) and scored on rooms held out of both. At the highest penalty, proportional wins 7 of 8 cases at 21 and 27 C when tuned wide, against 4 of 8 when tuned narrow, so the reversal is partly an artefact of the training range. At 18 and 30 C the gates differ by at most 0.007 C, which this model cannot resolve. Two penalties only; simulated comfort, not a claim about any real garment.

title: Does a fabric lever still pay once you weight it by where the garment is worn?
summary: Weights the comfort benefit of fabric levers by wearing time across a warm room, sunny outdoors and a cool room, and adds an idealised gated infrared lever. A fixed infrared-transparent shell has positive expected benefit only if the warm room takes more than 75.5% of wearing time (against the cool room); white never harms and has the best benefit per dollar in all four mixes tried. Across 66 wearing mixes the best garment changes with the mix, and the gate is chosen in 65 of 66 mixes at the fixed shell's premium but in 18 of 66 at twice it and none at four times. Stylised: premiums, gate cost and wearing shares are assumed, and the gate is an upper bound.

title: Is a second garment better than a dearer single one?
summary: Lets the wearer own two garments (a shell and a layer) and wear whichever is most comfortable in each of three scenarios, searching all lever pairs under one total added-retail budget on the replica trench. With thin cloth allowed the pair beats the best single garment in 58 of 66 wearing mixes at $50, but the apparent $20 gain is an artefact: thin cloth has a negative assumed cost that funds the second garment. With thin cloth removed the gain is 0 at $20, +0.49 °C (54 of 66 mixes) at $50 and +1.02 °C at $100, usually a warm-weather infrared-transparent shell plus a cold-weather thick low-emissivity coat. Stylised: premiums, wearing shares and fabric properties are assumed, garments are not stacked, and no real garment was measured.

title: How often can a wearer pick the wrong garment before a second garment stops paying?
summary: Re-runs the two-garment wardrobe search of garment-wearpair with a wearer who picks a wrong option in a share e of scenarios, re-optimising each purchase at each e (replica trench, 66 wearing mixes, thin cloth removed). If a wrong pick is a random wrong option the pair’s edge holds (+0.55 C at e = 0, +0.57 C at 0.3, $100 budget), because errors hurt a single garment’s all-or-nothing choice more than an overlapping pair. If every mistake is the worst owned option the $100 edge falls to +0.09 C at e = 0.3, with a break-even e of median 0.72 and as low as 0.04. At $50 the edge is negligible either way. Stylised: error rates and premiums are assumed, no wearer behaviour was observed, and the conclusion flips between the two error models.

title: A twin whose sensor never produces outliers: does an innovation gate help or hurt the real estimator, and what does it do after a jump?
summary: With a Gaussian-sensor twin an innovation gate ( z = 2.58) costs 8.5% of the update MSE, since every gated measurement is good data; with 5% real outliers at 10× the noise scale the same gate cuts the MSE 1.74 → 0.58 (3.0×) while still passing 28% of the outliers. The ungated error grows like κ 2 in the outlier scale, the gated error is bounded and worst at a finite κ * ≈ 4, and a better-tuned gate width gains only 0–6%. After a jump D in a random-walk state the gate rejects the correct measurements and re-convergence takes ≈ 76 D 2 steps (30,512 at D = 20) against 30 with no gate. Exact post-update MSE checked by quadrature and Monte Carlo. Stylised: scalar update, simulated outliers, simplified covariance rule in the jump experiment.

title: A point-target radar twin of two unresolved scatterers: it has the right median, so what does it get wrong, and does averaging looks converge where it says?
summary: Ideal monopulse on two unresolved scatterers (strong 1, weak r , random phase) gives Y =(1− r 2 )/(1+ r 2 +2 r cosφ): the mean is exactly the strong scatterer and the median exactly the power centroid, variance 2 r 2 /(1− r 2 ), and the estimate lies outside the target span with probability arccos( r )/π. A variance-matched Gaussian centroid twin gets the median right and the mean wrong by 2 r 2 /(1+ r 2 ), is 27× too optimistic at a 3σ gate at r =0.9, and predicts √(var/ N ) for averaged looks where the real mean floors at that bias (0.90 vs 0.09 at N =1024); the median converges and beats the mean on variance for r ≥0.477. Stylised: noise-free ideal monopulse, two scatterers, no radar data.

title: A satellite-positioning twin with white range noise certifies an error radius the real receiver does not meet: how wrong is it once multipath is correlated, and does averaging fix it?
summary: Real receiver: 2-D position and clock from n pseudoranges with multipath; twin: white noise σ only. For an evenly spread constellation HDOP is exactly √(4/ n ) (simulated to 0.3%) and collapses to 4.25 over a 90° arc; one biased satellite of size b moves the fix by exactly 2 b / n toward that satellite, which no amount of averaging removes. With AR(1) multipath ( ρ = 0.99) the twin predicts a 1/√ T gain but the simulated error only falls from 1.58 to 0.80 m over 500 epochs (exact 0.80), and a 95% radius calibrated on single epochs covers 33% of fixes at T = 10 and 5% at T = 100 (exact 31% and 5%). A residual integrity test tuned to 1% false alarms on the twin alarms 21% of the time when multipath equals the noise (exact closed form), and the statistic rises by only b ²(1−3/ n ) while the position bias is 2 b / n . Stylised: 2-D, linearised, evenly spread or arc constellations, stationary AR(1) multipath.

title: What can one stubborn node do to gossip training?
summary: Pairwise gossip averaging as a stand-in for all-reduce: disagreement contracts by exactly (n−2)/(2(n−1)) ≈ ½ per matching round (about 20 rounds at any n), the noise floor is (n−1)(n−2)s²/n (matched to 0.3%), a single stubborn node captures the honest mean at exact rate 1−1/(n(n−1)), and a trust-region clip turns capture into linear creep of at most τ/(n(n−1)) per step. Stylised.

title: How firmly should a robot grip when its friction twin is too clean?
summary: A pinch grasp slips if μ F < w 0 and crushes if F exceeds a fragility limit; with log-normal friction and crush force the expected loss is a sum of two normal CDFs in ln F and its optimum solves a quadratic. A twin whose friction spread is 0.1 instead of 0.3 grips softer, claims a risk of 1.1×10 −5 and delivers 0.069 (4.0× the optimum; 11.6× at spread 0.05). A near-zero-spread twin has a flat zero-risk plateau, so its ‘optimal’ force is a tie-break: real slip 0.50 at the lower edge, 0.015 at the upper. Biased friction costs ≈ ½ J ″Δ x ² (85% of the optimum at −0.3 in log-friction), and a widened randomisation width can cancel a known bias but costs 1.5× the optimum if the bias is of opposite sign. A plug-in from n real friction measurements has regret matched by the delta method within 5% for n ≥ 50. Stylised: static friction threshold, chosen parameters, no contact dynamics or reactive re-grasp.

title: Does a twin with no gravity certify PD gains that sag, or cannot hold a pose at all?
summary: A pendulum under PD control u = k p (θ*−θ)− k d ω; the twin omits gravity and promises zero error at every gain. The real hold sags to the root of k p (θ*−θ)= g sinθ nearest the target (RK4 agrees to six digits; 0.182 rad at k p =4, θ*=1), falling only as ≈1/ k p . Holding upright is stable iff k p > g : below it the arm settles 0.2–1.9 rad away, and just above it the basin is tiny (0.116 rad at 1.02 g , 0.519 at 1.05 g , none below 3 rad from 1.1 g ; numerical scan). A gravity feedforward with calibration error leaves a sag linear in ( g ( g − g ff )minus; g ff ) (±0.0185 rad at ±10%). Companion to the lag and flex twins. Stylised: one rigid joint, noiseless, no friction.

title: A grid twin over-states every route by a heading-dependent factor: does a finer grid fix it, and can it rank two routes the wrong way round?
summary: Real route: a straight line of length L ; twin: shortest path on a k -connected lattice. The grid/Euclid ratio depends on heading and connectivity, not cell size: 8-connected it is cos φ +(√2−1)sin φ , mean 8(√2−1)/ π =1.0548 and worst 1.0824 at 22.5° (4-connected mean 1.2732, worst 1.4142; 16-connected 1.0144, 1.0275), matched by Dijkstra; refining the cell from 8 m to 0.1 m leaves a 100 m route at 22.5° at 1.0824. Calibrating by the mean leaves −5.2% to +2.6% (8-connected). For two routes of Euclidean length 1 and 1.03 at random headings the twin ranks the longer one shorter with probability 0.194 (0 at ratio ≥ 1.0824), and for a fixed pair 22.5° apart rotating the map flips the ranking for 31% of orientations. Stylised: free space only, no obstacles, length as a proxy for time or energy.

title: A twin without ground effect: where does a landing altitude loop go wrong?
summary: With the constant-power ground-effect multiplier G ( z ) = 1/(1−( R /4 z ) 2 ) a gravity-feedforward altitude hold sits above its target by 2.7, 17.7 and 30.2 mm at 3, 1 and 0.6 rotor radii (twin: 0), 0.9% to 50% of the height. A sampled loop with one-sample delay that the twin gives 27.6% gain headroom at every height loses it as the vehicle descends: the real margin is 1.19 at one radius and reaches the stability boundary at 0.54 radii, confirmed by a nonlinear simulation; the undelayed thrust-gradient stiffness matters, since scaling the gain alone misses the instability. Negligible above about two radii. Stylised: point mass, closed-form ground-effect model, no rotor lag.

title: A twin whose wind gusts are matched to the logged variance each step: how wrong is the position variance of a PD-held vehicle, and does matching the spectrum instead fix it?
summary: Real gust: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck with rate a and variance s 2 ; exact real variance s 2 ( a + k d )/( k d k p ( a 2 + ak d + k p )). A twin drawing iid gusts per step has variance s 2 dt /(2 k d k p ): 141× too small at a =1, dt =0.01 (270× at a =0.05), a standard deviation scaling as √ dt , and a 10 −3 margin that the real system exceeds 78% of the time. A spectrum-matched white twin is always conservative, real/twin = a ( a + k d )/( a 2 + ak d + k p ) < 1 (0.71 at a =1). Fitting the OU rate from logged wind recovers the real variance (within 1% at 10 5 samples). Stylised: linear loop, Gaussian gusts, no wind data.

title: A gyro twin calibrated on white noise hides the bias random walk: how wrong are its heading error, re-alignment interval and dead-reckoning budget, and does a single-point Allan fit help?
summary: Real rate = white noise N plus a random-walking bias K ; the twin keeps only N . Heading variance is N 2 t + K 2 t 3 /3, so the real/twin ratio is exactly 1 + ( t / t *) 2 with t * = √3 N / K = 86.6 s (2.33 at 100 s, 134 at 1000 s), confirmed by Monte Carlo and a simulated Allan deviation (within 3% for short averaging times, noisy at 1000 s). Re-aligning to keep 2σ heading within 1° is needed every 416 s; the twin allows 10 000 s (24×), where the real error exceeds 1° with probability 0.986. An Allan fit at 1–10 s changes nothing; a fit at τ 0 = 100 s is exact only there (variance ratio 2.3 at 1 s, 0.18 at 300 s) and one at 1000 s is 5.6× too conservative. For 2σ cross-track error within 1 m the twin reports 1.74× (1 m/s) and 1.25× (5 m/s) too much usable distance. Stylised: linear-Gaussian, one axis, parameters chosen by me, no aiding, no real IMU data.

title: What does a light-tailed simulated human do to a collaborative robot's timeout?
summary: A robot that waits for a human and aborts after τ has cost J (τ) = w E[min( T ,τ)] + c P( T >τ), with slope S (τ)( w − c · h (τ)). Simulated humans with constant or increasing hazard (exponential, Weibull) therefore have only corner-optimal timeouts and, when aborting costs more than the mean wait, never give up. Against a lognormal human (σ=1.2, an assumed model) the interior optimum is 9.4 s and the light-tailed twin’s regret is 3.7% of the optimum, rising to 37% (σ=1.6) and 81% (σ=2) for heavier tails and cheap aborts. A lognormal twin with the right mean and σ off by 0.2 recovers all but 0.5%. Fitting the correct family from n real trials costs regret ∝ 1/ n , matched by the delta method to within 11% (0.0323 at n =10, 0.00034 at n =1000). Stylised: scalar i.i.d. response time, one fixed timeout, no real human data.

title: How should a model be cut across devices of unequal speed?
summary: For a fixed pipeline order, greedy filling is an exact test of a target stage time (agreeing with an independent dynamic program, with and without memory caps), and every order satisfies W / V ≤ T * < W / V + m w max / V . A speed-blind equal split costs exactly v̄ / v min times the lower bound (2.40× at log-speed spread 0.5, 8.25× at 1.0) while speed-aware cutting stays within 1.4% at 240 layers. What is left is the device order: at 14 layers and 6 devices the worst order is 1.34× the best, fast-first and slow-first sorts do no better than an arbitrary order (all about 1.16× optimal), and pairwise-swap search gets within 1.1%; the penalty fades to 1.03× at 224 layers. Memory that shrinks as speed grows inflates the bottleneck 1.7×. No communication cost, static speeds.

title: How should a server weight workers that ran different numbers of inner steps?
summary: With worker i running H i steps, weighted averaging has exact floor α 2 Σ w i 2 V i /( r (2− r )), r = αΣ w i s i . One worker's information is I ∞ tanh(λ H /2): H =8 carries 20% of the ceiling and H =64 93%, so a fast device is worth far less than its step count. Information-optimal weights span at most 2×, hence equal weights lose at most 9/8 (measured ≤1.09), whereas step-proportional (FedAvg-style) weights lose up to 1.76× per mode and 10.5× on three modes when one worker in eight is 256× faster. Matched to simulation within 1%. Stylised: quadratic, shared optimum (no client drift), fixed H i .

title: Paying for improvements, not for overfitting
summary: A model-improvement market paying holdout-loss decreases: the budget telescopes, but naive payment feedback lets a data-less adversary be paid while the published model's true loss worsens; a Ladder-style threshold removes the attack at a measured cost to honest small contributors. Stylised.

title: How far ahead should a controller planned in a twin with the wrong plant pole look?
summary: A receding-horizon controller uses the H -step gain of a twin whose pole is m × the real one; the real cost of that fixed gain is exact (matched to simulation within 0.3%). When the twin overstates the pole the gain rises with H past the real optimum, so cost is not monotone in the horizon: at m =2 ( a =0.9, r =1) the real cost is 1.81 at H =2 and 3.97 at H =60 against an optimum of 1.48, and the saving rises from 12% to 91% as control cost goes from 0.1 to 20. The twin cannot see this (its own claim falls from 9.5 to 3.5 as H grows, ranking horizons backwards); the two-step controller stays stable up to m =(1+ a )( r + b 2 q )/( abq ) (4.22 vs 2.51 for H =60 at r =1). A terminal cost equal to the twin’s Riccati solution removes the effect. Stylised: scalar linear-Gaussian, only the pole wrong, best horizon chosen with the real cost known.

title: How much extra can a tight envelope cost before it stops paying back on a 480 sq ft backyard cottage?
summary: Inverts the question house-energy asks: instead of the lowest-cost package, the largest extra first cost each upgrade can carry before its 30-year energy saving no longer covers it, on the house-open-design ADU (24 × 20 ft). The whole tight package (advanced 2x6 wall with R-5 foam, R-49 attic, U-0.27 windows, 3 ACH50, R-30 floor) saves $72 to $158 a year with a heat pump, so at a 3% real rate it can carry $1,409 (Houston) to $3,104 (Minneapolis) of extra cost, and $892 to $1,965 at 7%. Energy is linear in heat loss, so the one-at-a-time savings add up exactly to the package. At house-energy 's unsourced unit prices the attic ($319 extra) only breaks even in Minneapolis, air sealing ($500) needs energy 1.3 to 2.6 times as dear, and the windows ($1,392) 2.7 to 5.5 times; the wall switch is the best of the five upgrades. Stylised: degree-day climates from memory, every price assumed, no first-cost data for the wall or floor, not a design anyone should build from without a licensed review.

title: At what climate does each envelope upgrade start to pay, when climate is a continuous axis?
summary: Makes heating and cooling degree-days the axis of house-energy ’s 640-package net-present-cost search and finds each upgrade’s exact switch-on point. With a gas furnace and 500 cooling degree-days, slab-edge R-10 pays from 3,271 heating degree-days, an R-30 attic from 4,029, 5 ACH50 from 4,485, 3 ACH50 from 5,769 and an R-38 attic from 8,368; a heat pump lowers each of the first four by about 27% (2,386 to 4,209). Cooling switches on only the attic and air sealing, above about 3,000 cooling degree-days; windows never leave U 0.50. The slab-edge threshold falls exactly in proportion to the energy price. Stylised: house-energy ’s unsourced prices, degree-day loads and no solar gain.

title: How much of a floor-vibration penalty does the subfloor's T-beam action recover?
summary: The subfloor modelled as a partial flange of a T-beam by the gamma method (rederived from the parallel-axis theorem and tested against an independent transformed-section calculation), added to the frequency check of house-vibration for a 2x10 SPF No. 2 joist at 16 in. The result depends on two assumed, unsourced inputs, the connection efficiency γ and the panel modulus. At a panel modulus of 0.5 million psi the 15 ft first-mode frequency rises from 10.5 Hz to 12.6 Hz at γ 0.5 and 14.0 Hz at γ 1, and under a 15 Hz limit the span grows from 12 ft 6 in to 13 ft 2 in–14 ft 6 in. Strength checks stay joist-alone; live-load mass is left out, so gains are optimistic. Stylised, not validated against a measured floor, not a design.

title: Does a joist lapped over a middle support span farther than a simple-span joist?
summary: A pure-Python finite-element beam with pattern loading and the NDS bending, shear, bearing and deflection checks of house-spans , for two- and three-span continuous sawn-lumber joists (SPF No. 2). Under full uniform load a two-span joist's peak moment, w L 2 /8 at the middle support, equals a simple span's, so members whose simple span is governed by bending (most floor joists, all snow rafters) gain nothing from two spans (0.0% in 16 floor cells; three spans add about 5%), while deflection-governed ceiling joists gain 0.6% to 18.5%. With only 1.5 in of bearing on the middle support, the 1.25 wL reaction limits a 2x10 floor joist at 16 in to 11 ft 4 in, against 15 ft 3 in with 3.5 in. Stylised: equal spans, no vibration, not compared with published span tables. Not a structural design.

title: Where does a new home's price go, and which levers move it most?
summary: A driver-based price model anchored on NAHB's 2024 cost shares (construction 64.4% of the price, framing 16.6% of construction, lot 13.7%, profit 11.0%). Each construction stage scales with floor area, footprint or wall area, and the model reproduces every NAHB share at its 2,000 sq ft reference house. In a sweep, size moves the price most (index 87.8 to 112.0 for 1,600 to 2,400 sq ft), then one against three storeys (111.6 to 97.6), finish level, lot price and foundation type. A 14% cut in framing lumber, the gap between house-plan 's default and best plans, is worth only 0.85% of the price, or 2.4% if it also cuts framing labour by 20%. Stylised : a price index, not dollars; the stage-driver splits and lever ranges are my assumptions; the Census reconciliation and a priced takeoff are not done.

title: Does the house-cost lever ranking survive its assumed driver splits?
summary: A Monte Carlo over house-cost 's assumed splits of each construction stage over floor area, footprint and wall area (Dirichlet, concentration 5, 20 and 80; 2,000 draws each). Floor area stays the largest lever in 96–100% of draws. Storeys is the soft claim: one versus three storeys swings the price index 9.0–19.9 points at concentration 20 (baseline 14.0), 5.1–24.1 at 5. The framing-lumber result does not move. Seven of ten levers cannot move under this test by construction. Stylised: tests only the splits, not the lever ranges or the NAHB shares.

title: Where in a wall does water vapor condense, and does a vapor retarder or exterior foam fix it, by climate?
summary: A steady-state Glaser check of a 2x6 batt wall (gypsum, optional retarder, OSB, optional 1 or 2 in XPS, housewrap, siding) in four assumed climates. In winter nothing condenses in Miami or Atlanta. In Chicago painted drywall gives about 6 g/m 2 /day at the sheathing; 2 in of exterior XPS removes it and a kraft facing cuts it to 0.05. In Duluth only polyethylene reaches zero (painted drywall about 11 g/m 2 /day). The summer case shows no condensation because the model has no wet-cladding reservoir. Stylised: steady state, unsourced permeances and climate values, no moisture storage, not WUFI.

title: Does the half-and-half load split understate the demand on a garage-front wall?
summary: Re-asks house-structure experiment G with a rigid roof diaphragm: a four-spring sway-and-twist model splits the 115 mph gable load by wall stiffness. In a toy stiffness model the garage line carries less than half (at a centred 22 ft door, demand over capacity at 6 in nailing falls from 1.05 to 0.18–0.63) and the partner wall stays under 0.35, so the flexible split is the governing case. Stylised: the stiffness is an assumption, and torsion, collectors and seismic are not modelled.

title: Which envelope upgrades pay for themselves over 30 years, by climate, and does advanced framing belong in the answer?
summary: A degree-day net-present-cost search (not EnergyPlus) over 640 envelope packages of the house-framing house in eight US climates and two heating systems. The advanced 2x6 wall builds for $42 less than a conventional 2x4 and loses 40% less heat through the opaque wall, and is in every cost-optimal package: 13–15% lower 30-year cost than the baseline ($2,100–4,600). Past the wall the optimum is modest (attic R-30–38, 3 ACH50 air sealing, slab-edge insulation from about 3,000 degree-days); R-49 attics and better windows pay back in 23–190 years. At the assumed window prices the optimum picks U 0.50 windows, which a code floor of U 0.35 costs $440–1,270 to avoid; that result does not survive 4× energy prices. Stylised: every price is an assumption, climates are rounded from memory, and there is no solar gain.

title: Which foundation is cheapest for a small house as the frost line gets deeper?
summary: Sizes and prices four foundations for the house-framing house: slab on grade, frost-protected shallow, crawlspace and full basement, from roof and floor loads, soil bearing and frost depth. At 48 in frost the midpoint first costs are $13.2k (frost-protected shallow), $20.6k (slab), $24.1k (crawlspace) and $54.9k (basement); the frost-protected shallow foundation is cheapest in all 5,000 price draws from about 18 in of frost down, a basement adds $25–36 per sq ft over a crawlspace, and soil matters only below about 1,500 psf. Stylised: prices from memory, an invented insulation-wing rule, no soil-pressure, drainage or energy checks, and not a design.

title: How much lumber, labour and heat does advanced framing save in a house's exterior walls, and does it still carry the roof?
summary: An open takeoff of a stylised 28 × 40 ft one-storey house: every stud, plate, header, cripple and block under conventional and advanced (OVE) framing, with the NDS stud and header checks and a parallel-path whole-wall R-value. Advanced 2x6 framing at 24 in used 42% less exterior-wall lumber than conventional 2x6 and 27% fewer pieces, and raised the whole-wall R-value from 16.2 to 18.6. It still used 16% less lumber than conventional 2x4. At 30 psf of roof snow its studs work at 39% of capacity. The biggest single savings were 24 in spacing, the single top plate and header hangers. At assumed lumber prices the wall saving is only $450 to $900 a house, so the case for advanced framing rests on labour, which the model counts as pieces but does not price. Stylised : one house, exterior walls only, no lateral design, no labour rates, and not a code check or a design anyone should build from without a licensed review.

title: Does the rigid-diaphragm relief for a garage-front wall survive a nailed-wall stiffness model?
summary: Replaces the toy pier stiffness of house-diaphragm with a four-term deflection (chord bending, panel shear, nail slip, hold-down slip) and reruns the rigid roof-diaphragm split. The sign holds: a centred 22 ft garage door leaves the wall at 0.05–0.19 of its partner's stiffness, and its demand over capacity at 6 in nailing falls from 1.05 (flexible split) to 0.36, 0.48 and 0.59 at 100, 250 and 500 plf. Stylised: every constant is from memory and unchecked, stiffness is a secant at a fixed shear, and the flexible split still governs.

title: When does building a house's wall shell in a factory beat building it on site?
summary: Splits the exterior walls of the house-framing house into panels, nests the sheathing, loads the trailers and runs a Monte Carlo of the shell crew's days with weather. Panelised took 2.17 calendar days against 1.96 on site and cost 38% more at assumed rates; factory productivity does not change the days because the factory runs behind the foundation, and panelised is faster only from about 58 ft long (78 with no weather, 44 at 30% loss). Factory nesting saved 1 sheet in 33 (bound 26): a 97 in wall on a 108 in sheet wastes the same strip either way. Stylised: wall shell only, every labour rate and price is my assumption.

title: What does an open, reproducible plan set for a 480 sq ft backyard cottage look like when it is generated from code?
summary: Composes the track's six earlier models on one concrete design, a 24 × 20 ft one-bedroom accessory dwelling unit, and writes a floor plan and south elevation (SVG), a framing bill of materials (CSV), an IFC4 model and a report. The plan passes every layout rule and member check and needs 2,614 board feet of framing (5.45 per sq ft). A truss roof option (from house-truss ) uses 38% less roof lumber than the stick roof (667 against 1,070 board feet, lumber only). Under house-structure 's assumed coefficients the short walls carry 1,164 lb of wind per line at 6 in nailing; a tighter envelope cuts modelled heating and cooling cost 36–37% in every climate tested ($72–158 a year at assumed prices). The composition exposed rough edges (the lateral and energy models were built around a different house), the cost index is extrapolated far below its data, and nothing here is a buildable design: it needs a licensed review and a permit.

title: When should a builder order long-lead materials once holding them costs money?
summary: Extends the house-schedule Monte Carlo (3,000 builds per row) with the cost of material that arrives before it is used: a financed deposit, storage and handling, and damage or theft. Ordering each material about two lead times before its planned start cuts the build from 214 to 182 working days and interest plus holding cost from 3.34% to 2.91% of price. Ordering everything on day 0 saves more days (151) but costs 4.00%, worse than the baseline. The cheapest order time moves from three lead times (free to hold) to 1.5 (expensive to hold). Stylised: every cost is assumed and the order plan is fixed from the baseline schedule.

title: Does a roof overhang over south windows pay for itself, and in which climates does it cost energy instead of saving it?
summary: Adds overhang shading (profile angle, shadow depth on the glass, beam radiation only) to house-solar ’s south windows and searches projection from 0 to 4 ft with the 640 envelope packages. At an assumed $12 per foot of width per foot of projection no overhang is cost-optimal in any of 8 climates or 2 systems. Its gross energy value is at most $280 of 30-year net present cost (Miami, 4 ft); in cold and mixed climates anything deeper than about 1 ft loses more winter gain than it saves in summer. It would be chosen only below roughly $0.60 to $4.20 per foot per foot. Stylised degree-day model; height, gap and price are assumptions; not EnergyPlus.

title: Can a house plan be data, and which plan needs the least framing lumber per square foot?
summary: A single-storey house plan as a few parameters: rooms, walls and openings, a framing takeoff with members sized by the open NDS tools of house-spans and house-framing , a bill of materials, IRC-style room-size, light and egress checks, and an IFC4 export through IfcOpenShell. A search over 182,520 plans finds the least lumber per square foot: with two or more bedrooms the best plans use 4.8–5.2 board feet per sq ft at 640–1,024 sq ft and 5.9 at 1,216, and no stick-framed plan in the grid reaches 1,400 sq ft because joists and rafters run out of 2x12. Only 1.3% of the grid passes every check at 1,000–1,150 sq ft. At equal budgets a (1+1) local search found the exact optimum in 36 of 40 runs at 2,000 evaluations and random search in none. Stylised : one rectangular layout, stick framing only, board feet rather than prices, room rules paraphrased from memory, and not a design anyone should build from without a licensed review.

title: How much do fewer handoffs, parallel trades, early ordering and a factory shell cut the time to build a house?
summary: A Monte Carlo discrete-event model of one house build (20 tasks, a crew per trade, failing inspections, weather, material lead times; 4,000 builds per scenario with common random numbers). The zero-noise critical path is 100 working days but the baseline takes 214: the schedule is driven by waiting. Ordering long-lead materials at day 0 saves 63 days, fewer handoffs 21, parallel rough-in 12.5, faster inspections 11. A factory wall-and-roof shell saves only 6 days if ordered when the foundation starts and 78 if ordered at day 0. All levers together: 96 days, about 1.7% of the price in interest at 8%. Stylised : every duration and rate is my assumption and nothing is calibrated; the 63-day figure rests on a late-ordering baseline.

title: Does an independent second schedule model agree with house-schedule on what shortens a house build?
summary: A second, separately built Monte Carlo schedule (13 tasks, one crew per trade, weather, inspections, long-lead items; 4,000 builds per scenario). It agrees on the ranking: ordering long-lead items on day 0 is the biggest lever (205 to 181 calendar days, −11%, against −29% in house-schedule ), prefabricated panels alone save 1.5%, and the handoff gap moves the baseline by 35%. Merging crews does nothing. The disagreement in size shows the magnitudes are set by assumed baselines and lead times. Stylised; every input is an assumption.

title: Does the month a house build starts change how long it takes and the interest paid?
summary: Reruns the house-schedule Monte Carlo (3,000 builds per cell) with a monthly weather calendar and a slower concrete cure in the cold, starting in each month. In an assumed cold-winter climate a December start takes 231 working days against 211 for July (about 20 days, 0.3 points of the price in interest); in an assumed mild climate the swing is 4 days. Ordering all materials at day 0 saves about 63 days in every month, so the two levers add. A flat climate reproduces house-schedule exactly (tested). Stylised : the monthly loss fractions are my assumptions, not weather data, and seasonal prices are ignored.

title: Does a factory-built shell pay once the interest on the days it saves is counted?
summary: Joins house-offsite 's extra cost of panelising the walls ($1,373 at assumed rates) to house-schedule 's interest on working days saved, comparing a factory shell with a site-built house ordered on the same day. The shell alone saves 15.5 days (0.22% of price at 8%) when ordered at day 0 and only 6.4 days when ordered at the foundation start with a 25-day lead; it breaks even at a house price of about $629,000 at a $1,500 crane day and pays throughout at $750. Most of house-schedule 's 78-day saving is the ordering date, not the shell. Stylised: house prices are parameters and every rate is assumed.

title: Which uncertain input of the house-cost model drives the uncertainty in a house's price?
summary: A variance-based (Sobol) global sensitivity analysis of house-cost , treating the ten lever ranges, the framing materials share and the assumed driver splits as random at once (4,096 base samples, bootstrap intervals). Floor area explains 53% of the price-index variance and storeys 19%; finish level, lot price and foundation type 6–9% each. The three framing inputs together explain under 1%, so the lumber saving optimised in house-plan barely moves the price of a whole house, and the assumed splits explain none alone and 1.7% through interactions. Per square foot, storeys matters more (25–27%). Stylised: the answer is relative to the assumed uniform ranges and ignores correlations.

title: Does solar gain through windows change which envelope is cheapest over 30 years, and is the direction the windows face worth money?
summary: Adds window solar gain, computed from solar geometry by orientation, to house-energy ’s 640-package net-present-cost search. U 0.50 windows stay the optimum in 15 of 16 climate and system cases (Miami moves to U 0.35), and forcing U 0.20 glass costs $5,300 to $5,700 whatever its solar heat gain coefficient, so the earlier window result was not an artifact of the missing solar term. Which way the windows face is free and worth $420 to $1,740 of 30-year cost per house, south-heavy glazing best except in Miami. Stylised : degree-day model, assumed prices, latitudes and clearness, trigonometry written from memory and not validated against weather data.

title: How far can a 2x joist, rafter, header or beam span, and which check limits it?
summary: An open sizing tool for simple-span sawn-lumber members, derived from beam formulas and NDS base design values with no span table copied: bending, shear, deflection and bearing checks, a command line, and the governing check named for every result. For SPF No. 2 floor joists at 16 in the longest clear spans are 9 ft 2 in (2x6), 12 ft 1 in (2x8), 15 ft 3 in (2x10) and 17 ft 8 in (2x12). Bending governs 22 of 32 floor cells and live-load deflection the other 10; total-load deflection governs 31 of 32 ceiling cells; bending governs snow-loaded rafters in 29 of 32. The lightest passing floor joist is the deepest at 24 in, which uses 20–50% less lumber than 2x10 at 16 in, but floor vibration is not checked. A cross-check with house-framing found its header bearing area too generous for a single jack under a 2-ply header. Not validated against published span tables , no engineered lumber, no continuous spans, and not a design anyone should build from without a licensed review.

title: Does a small wood-frame house have enough shear wall for wind and earthquakes once the windows and doors are cut out?
summary: Wind and seismic base shear on the house-framing house (28 × 40 ft, one storey) against the segmented shear-wall length its openings leave. At 115 mph and SDS 0.50 the worst case uses 19% of a gable-wall line's capacity at the loosest (6 in) nailing; wind must reach 264 mph before that nailing runs out. Lateral load does not govern this plan, but glazing does: four windows per gable wall cut the usable wall from 24 ft to 11 ft, six leave none. A 16 ft garage door in the gable wall raises the load share to 41% at 6 in nailing, and a centred 22 ft door needs tighter nailing. Advanced and conventional framing carry the same shear. Stylised : the nailing table and load coefficients are from memory and unchecked, and diaphragms, uplift and overturning are not modelled.

title: How much does accidental torsion add to the garage-front wall's demand in a rigid-diaphragm wind split?
summary: Offsets the wind load by up to 15% of the house length in house-nailedwall 's rigid roof-diaphragm split. The relief survives but shrinks: for a centred 22 ft garage door, demand over capacity at 6 in nailing rises from 0.36–0.59 (load at the centre) to 0.44–0.71 at a 15% offset, still below the flexible split's 1.05, while the partner wall moves only from 0.27–0.31 to 0.29–0.33. Stylised: placeholder offset, unverified stiffness constants, along-ridge wind only, not a code check.

title: How much lumber does a prefabricated roof truss save over rafters and ceiling joists?
summary: A pin-jointed W-type truss solved by a small stiffness solver, with NDS chord and web checks and a search for the lightest passing 2x4 to 2x8 truss at 24 in o.c., against stick-built 16 in rafters and ceiling joists from house-spans . At 30 psf snow and 4/12 pitch the truss uses 40–55% less nominal lumber per sq ft of plan over 12–30 ft spans (45% at 24 ft: 1.26 against 2.30 board feet). Stylised: no connector plates, bracing or heel details, an unchecked tension value, and no comparison with a commercial truss design program.

title: How far can the beam under a two-span joist sit from the middle of the house?
summary: Two-span sawn-lumber joists (SPF No. 2) with unequal spans, reusing the finite-element beam of house-continuous and the NDS checks of house-spans with pattern loading and per-span deflection. For a 2x10 floor joist at 16 in, moving the beam off-centre costs 0.4% of total clear width at a short/long span ratio of 0.9, 4.3% at 0.7 and 13.3% at 0.5, because the short span relieves the long one (the long span grows from 15 ft 3 in to 17 ft 7 in); a 2x8 ceiling joist, which deflection governs, loses 5.1% at 0.9 and 24.1% at 0.5. A 28 ft wide house tolerates a beam 3.5 ft off the middle. Stylised. Not validated against published span tables, two spans only, no vibration, and not a design anyone should build from without a licensed review. The short span's end lifts off its support whenever live load is on the long span only (−103 lb per joist at a 10 ft short span, −271 lb at 6 ft; 2x10 floor).

title: Does a floor-vibration frequency limit erase the lumber saved by deep, widely spaced joists?
summary: A first-mode natural-frequency check ( f 1 = (π/2 L 2 )√( EIg / w ), derived and tested against the static-deflection form) added to the NDS strength and deflection checks of house-spans , for SPF No. 2 floor joists under 10 + 40 psf. The joist alone is modelled, with no subfloor composite action. Any limit up to 10 Hz changes nothing: the longest strength-passing 2x10 at 16 in (15 ft 3 in) already vibrates at 10.1 Hz. At 12 Hz it shortens to 13 ft 11 in, and at 15 Hz the least-lumber joist at a 12 ft span moves from 2x10 at 24 in (0.83 board feet per sq ft) to 2x12 at 24 in (1.00), while at 14 ft the 2x12 at 24 in no longer passes and 2x12 at 16 in (1.50) is needed. The limit in Hz is a policy choice swept here, not a code-book criterion, and the model is conservative by ignoring the subfloor and optimistic by ignoring live-load mass. Stylised.

title: Does any alternative to a wood-framed wall beat it on cost, carbon or heat loss for a small house?
summary: Prices six exterior wall systems (wood 2x6, steel stud, ICF, SIPs, CLT, 3D-printed concrete) on the 927 sq ft of net wall of the house-framing house, then runs 20,000 Monte Carlo draws over stylised cost, carbon and R-value ranges. Wood is cheapest in 96.8% of draws, lowest in product-stage carbon in 100% and lowest in first cost plus 30-year heat-loss cost in 99.9%; ICF and SIP save only about $500 of heat-loss present value against $5,500–8,300 more first cost, and SIP would need a 39% price cut to tie. SIPs and CLT take about half the crew hours. Stylised : every input is a range from memory, the result largely follows from them, biogenic carbon, avoided trades and strength are not credited or compared.

title: A fixed-step twin of a bouncing ball: how wrong are its restitution and time to rest, and does calibrating on the first bounce fix it?
summary: Truth is closed form: infinitely many impacts in the finite Zeno time T =( v 1 / g )(1+ e )/(1− e ), with d ln T /d e =2/(1− e 2 ) (10.5 at e =0.9, 100 at 0.99). A semi-implicit-Euler twin with a penetration test has an apparent restitution biased by the step with scheme-dependent sign (true 0.9: 0.886, 0.895, 0.879 at dt =10 −2 ) and its time to come to rest is off by −19.6%, +4.0%, −30.8% ( e =0.9; up to 47% at e =0.95), first-order in dt and 0.1–0.3% at 10 −4 . The restitution bias explains most of the clamp error (predicted −14.9%, measured −19.6%), but fitting e on the first rebound is not a reliable repair: it helps the clamp twin at dt =10 −2 (−19.6% to −4.8%), does nothing at finer steps and makes the mirror twin worse (+4.0% to +53%). Twin impact counts (238–688) are mostly floor chatter against 43–87 resolvable bounces. Stylised: one dimension, constant restitution, rigid contact, closed-form real system; the crude interpolated-contact variant is the worst here.

title: A point-mass twin of a rolling body ignores rotational inertia: how wrong are acceleration, slip and coast distance, and what does one calibration fix?
summary: A frictionless point mass overstates down-ramp acceleration by exactly 1+ k ( k = I / mr 2 : 1.4, 1.5, 2.0 for sphere, disc, hoop), so a 2 m descent takes 0.90 s instead of 1.07–1.28 s; a stick/slip simulation matches the closed forms to 3×10 −4 m/s 2 . The slip threshold μ * = k tanα/(1+ k ) is invisible to the twin, and a launch speed picked in the twin to coast 1 m carries a rolling body 40–100% farther. A gain fitted on one shape removes its own error but leaves −16% to +20% fall-time error on the others (pooled fit +6.7% to −10.7%), and the twin cannot rank the shapes. Stylised: planar incline, Coulomb friction, no rolling resistance or drag, no hardware data.

title: How much can a provider steal by serving a cheaper model?
summary: A decentralised inference provider substitutes a cheaper model on a random fraction p of queries; a verifier re-scores a fraction f under an anytime-valid mixture e-process. Detection delay scales as 1/(f p² χ²), so the profitable attack is a slow leak: undetected savings grow as √N rather than N (measured ×7.75 for ×64 queries). Closed-form audit rate to cap theft, cost-optimal check rate (hK/2Nc) 2/3 , and a substitute close enough to the claimed model that even checking every response cannot cap the theft. Seeded Monte Carlo. Stylised.

title: How much of a digital twin's error is that it was fitted to finite real data, however long it is simulated?
summary: A twin fitted to n real interarrival and service times has a steady-state wait that is one fixed number, so its error is input error that more simulation cannot remove. The relative sd is √(1+(2− ρ ) 2 )/((1− ρ )√ n ) (0.255 vs 0.257 simulated), so a 10% sd needs 1300 / 22 100 observations per stream at ρ =0.5 / 0.9. The fitted twin is unstable with exact probability P[F(2 n ,2 n ) ≥ 1/ ρ ] (0.370 at ρ =0.9, n =20). Used as truth, the point twin certifies a 10%-violated SLA in 36–46% of fits; the delta-method bound under-covers at high load (0.87–0.89), while bootstrap and posterior bounds reach 0.94 and cut false certification to 2–5% at a large power cost. Stylised: M/M/1, simulated data.

title: How safe is a robot's goal inference when its commit threshold was tuned against a simulated human?
summary: A robot commits to one of two goals when the evidence lead reaches h (a sequential test on binary motion cues); against a human of cue accuracy p the wrong-goal probability is exactly 1/(1+ r h ), r = p /(1− p ), matched to simulation. A threshold set for error 10 −3 in a twin with p s =0.9 gives real error 3.9× / 33× / 165× the target at p =0.8 / 0.7 / 0.6, while a too-irrational twin ( p s =0.6) is safe but 2.0–4.5× slower. A heterogeneous population (sd 0.08–0.10) doubles the error of the mean-human threshold, and humans with p <½ put a floor under any threshold. Calibrating p s from n real cues misses the target with probability 0.38 / 0.42 / 0.33 / 0.30 / 0.14 at n =10 / 20 / 50 / 200 / 1000; a lower-confidence-bound design cuts that to ≤4% at the cost of time. Stylised: two goals, i.i.d. binary cues, simulated humans.

title: Is an interference-free or mean-noise-rise radar twin right when robots' radars interfere with each other?
summary: Mutual radar interference between robots, with heavy-tailed c / d 2 interferer power hitting each frame intermittently. Per-frame detection probability has a closed form (matches Monte Carlo within 0.003); real Pd plateaus at the probability that no interferer hits the frame (0.656) rather than shrinking in range. A mean-noise-rise twin is 9% optimistic at Pd ≥ 0.9 (63.7 vs 58.4 m) but badly pessimistic for missions that tolerate hit frames (Brier 0.690 vs 0.003 for 3-of-10); for 9-of-10 missions knowing the interferer geometry helps (0.089 vs 0.101). Stylised: simulated interference, illustrative parameters, no radar data.

title: A link twin with independent packet loss says to send repeats back to back: what does burstiness do to repetition coding for shared maps, and what does spacing buy?
summary: An update is sent as r copies g slots apart and is lost only if all are. Against a two-state loss chain with the same marginal rate p = 0.2 and lag-1 correlation λ, the exact residual is p ( p + λ g (1− p )) r −1 against the twin’s p r . The twin’s 5 back-to-back copies for 10 −3 give a real residual of 0.026 at λ = 0.5 and 0.10 at 0.8 (81× and 311× the claim); two copies need spacing of 6 to 36 slots to come within 10% of the twin. With at most 8 copies the minimum-latency design is 12 to 154 slots (λ = 0.5 to 0.95) against the twin’s 4, and with at most 4 copies no spacing reaches 10 −3 . A counter-case: with no copy budget and a long deadline, back-to-back copies still beat a few spaced ones. Stylised: simulated link, known stationary parameters, no radio traces.

title: How should a tolerance interval be paid for?
summary: The Winkler interval score is the sum of two pinball losses: proper for the equal-tailed quantile interval with exact regret (2/α)[PR(l,α/2)+PR(u,1−α/2)], finite even for Cauchy drift where the expected score does not exist, but its payment grows without bound in the miss distance. A width-plus-miss loss (u−l)+λ1[miss] is bounded by width+λ and elicits the density level set, the shortest interval for its coverage: 22–31% narrower than equal-tailed on lognormal(0,1) drift. The price is statistical: to detect a 20% understatement of a normal tolerance it needs 3–48× more tasks for α≥0.1 and about the same at α=0.01.

title: Can a verifier be paid for a tolerance interval, not a point?
summary: The Winkler interval score is strictly proper for the pair of quantiles, with closed-form regret and an optimal expected score of exactly 4sφ(z)/α. Misreporting the width by the same factor costs more when narrow at 95% coverage but more when wide at 80%, so there is no universal rule that overconfidence is worse. Under Cauchy drift the scores have no mean, yet paired differences are bounded, so evaluate verifiers against a benchmark report.

title: Does inverting a quadratic thrust curve exactly fix the error a linear-thrust twin makes, and what if the thrust exponent is also wrong?
summary: Follow-up to thrust-twin . With the right model, the exact square-root throttle inverse realises the commanded acceleration inside the throttle limits and shrinks the up/down overshoot gap at ζ=0.7, p =2 from 3.00 to 0.09 points. With the thrust exponent misidentified (2.5 instead of 2) the exact inverse flips the asymmetry and halves the gap (3.67 to 1.65 points) but overshoot stays at 0.071–0.088 against the twin’s 0.046, and settling time is unchanged. Stylised: 1-D, noiseless, static thrust map, assumed throttle limits, exponent error only.

title: Does a twin fitted to the sensor-delay histogram certify gains that bursty delay makes unstable?
summary: Scalar loop x [ n +1]= x [ n ]− k x [ n − d n ]+ w [ n ] with random delay; the twin has the same marginal delay law (constant mean: stable iff k <2 sin(π/(2(2 d +1)))). Independent jitter moves the mean-square limit little and in either direction (1.000 for {0,2}, 0.952 for {0,1,2}, 0.668 vs the twin’s 0.618 for {0,1,2,3,4}); for {0,2} with P ( d =2)= p it fits k ( k +1)=1/ p . Persistence, invisible in the histogram, is the large effect: at fixed marginal the limit falls 1.000→0.875→0.672→0.624 at lag-1 autocorrelation ρ=0, 0.5, 0.9, 0.99 (towards the worst-case constant delay’s 0.618); a twin-certified k =0.9 is unstable from ρ=0.435, and below the limit the variance at k =0.6 inflates from 2.56 to 6.26 (ρ=0.9) and 15.2 (ρ=0.99). Almost-sure stability (simulated limit ≈1.84) is insensitive to ρ, so which stability the safety claim needs decides whether persistence matters. Companion to the latency twin. Stylised: scalar plant, sticky-redraw delay, Monte-Carlo almost-sure limits (one seed).

title: Is risk tolerance the learning rate of a wealth market?
summary: When agents bet a fraction λ of wealth Kelly-style, the clearing price is the λ·wealth-weighted mean belief, total wealth is conserved, and λ=1 is exactly the Bayes mixture. Market log-loss exceeds expert i’s by at most ln(1/s i )/λ i on any sequence (loose on i.i.d. data), the growth-optimal fraction is (π−p)/(q−p), and moving the price against calibrated others costs Vχ²(p 0 ‖p): equal to LMSR b·KL at b=2V for small shifts but 7.5× stiffer at p=0.99. On a truth that switches regimes, full Kelly is wrong about half of every segment (regret about 1630 at T=4000) while λ of 0.1–0.2 cuts it 3–7×. Binary events, static experts. Stylised.

title: How should a simulation budget be split across twin fidelities?
summary: A twin runs at several fixed-step fidelities (n=2 l+1 Euler steps). Multilevel Monte Carlo telescopes the finest-level answer over coupled pairs sharing scenario draws, with allocation N l ∝ √(V l /C l ). For a smooth terminal state (bias rate α=1.000, variance rate β=2.001, cost rate 1) it needs 3.6× fewer steps than one fine twin at RMSE 10 −2 and 897× fewer at 3×10 −5 . For a failure probability the variance only halves per level (β=1.000), so multilevel loses at loose targets (0.4× at 3×10 −2 ), breaks even near 10 −3 and reaches 7.7× at 10 −4 . Equal samples per level cost 156× (smooth) and 3.9× (failure) the optimum; a coarse twin alone is off by 10–48% however many runs. Stylised: one scalar linear system, exact level moments.

title: How much bandwidth can a controller tuned in a twin with an instantaneous actuator really have?
summary: Unit mass under PD control with a first-order actuator lag τ the twin omits. The twin’s loop is stable for every gain; the real loop is stable iff τ<τ*= k d / k p =2ζ/ω n (Routh, agreeing with the roots in 168 of 168 cases), hunts at exactly the twin’s own ω n , and grows at ω n 2 /(2(1+4ζ 2 )) per unit excess lag (formula, numeric slope and simulation agree). “Faster is better” fails: at τ=0.05, ζ=0.7 the real decay rate peaks at 4.8 (ω n ≈8) and is zero at ω n =28 where the twin promises 19.6; the poles sum to −1/τ, so no gains decay faster than 1/(3τ). Mild lag is nearly invisible in a step test (twin RMS error ≈0.04 ε). Companion to the slew, deadband and backlash twins. Stylised: linear, one lag, noiseless.

title: What does a digital twin without sensor latency do to a tuned controller?
summary: A scalar unstable plant is controlled by the LQR gain designed in a twin with no measurement delay. The exact stable-gain interval shrinks with the real delay (upper edge 1 at one step, 0.59 at two), so the twin-tuned gain (0.70) tolerates one step at 1.6× the delay-aware cost and is unstable from two; a retuned static gain costs 1.1–2.6× for delays 1–5, and a predictor built for the wrong delay is unstable in nearly every off-diagonal case tested. Identifying the delay from an i.i.d. probe takes about 2 z 2 (1+1/snr) samples. Stylised: scalar plant, integer delay, known dynamics.

title: Should drift tolerances be per layer or on the total?
summary: Giving each of L layers its own tolerance lets a prover hide the sum of them: L·c(L,α)σ versus z α √Lσ for one test on the total, 6.6× more at L=16 and 23× at L=128. The sum test’s power depends only on the total shift; the exact (Šidák) max test’s depends on how it is spread, the prover’s best split is even (log Φ is concave), and the max test catches a 2.7σ one-layer shift half the time but lets 16σ through spread over all 16 layers. A union of both at α/2 caps the hidden budget at the sum test’s (7.8σ) while keeping one-layer sensitivity. Gaussian, independent layers, known σ.

title: A pinhole twin of a radially distorted camera mis-ranges the near field: how far off does a twin-trained braking policy stop, and does focal calibration fix it?
summary: With Brown distortion x d = x (1+ k 1 r 2 ) and a camera at height h , the pinhole twin reads floor range off by exactly 1/(1+ k 1 h 2 / R 2 ): for k 1 =−0.3, h =0.5 m that is +15.4% at 0.75 m, +8.1% at 1 m and +0.5% at 4 m. A policy trained to stop at 1.0 m stops at 0.909 m (16.4 cm short at 0.75 m; the first-order formula understates this at large ρ). Least-squares focal calibration ( s =1+3 k 1 ρ max 2 /5) moves the error rather than removing it: near-field 8.1% → 3.2% but a new 4.4% far-field under-read, and a 4 m stop lands 17 cm long. One image of a known grid identifies k 1 (RMS 0.001 at 0.002 normalised-pixel noise). Stylised: one distortion term, axis-column floor points, known grid pose, no real lens.

title: What does a fee do to a prediction market’s price?
summary: A proportional fee f on an LMSR verification market gives every trader an exact no-trade band [ q /(1+ f ), ( q + f )/(1+ f )] of width f /(1+ f ), so an informed trader leaves the price at q /(1+ f ). At price ½ a signal of log-likelihood ratio λ moves the price iff f < tanh(λ/2) = 2 a −1, above which the market is dead; fee revenue on a monotone path is exactly fb ln((1− p 0 )/(1− p T )). With ten 0.65-accurate traders, the break-even fee (≈0.11) raises Brier error from 0.115 to about 0.16 and revenue is hump-shaped in f . Naive traders, synthetic signals.

title: What does infrequent averaging do to the answer?
summary: Local-SGD / DiLoCo-style averaging of heterogeneous quadratic workers has a closed-form fixed point: a weighted mean of the workers' optima with weights 1−(1−ηa i ) H that saturate, so it is exactly unbiased at H=1, forgets curvature as H grows (converging to the unweighted mean), and is non-monotone in between. Weighting by a i /w i removes the bias exactly; if the server trusts claimed step counts, a low-curvature worker moves the fixed point from 0.50 to 0.91 by claiming 100 steps instead of 5, tying communication savings to verified work. Wall-clock-optimal H under a bias tolerance is 5.7× faster than H=1 at moderate comm cost, with a non-interval feasible set. Noise formulas match Monte Carlo. Stylised.

title: What does an odometry twin that is too clean do to a loop-closure gate?
summary: A scalar position filter is tuned in a twin with drift variance T and gates loop closures by a chi-square test on its own covariance. With every closure accepted the real posterior variance is exact (1.47×, 2.14×, 4.03× the twin’s claim for real/twin drift-sd ratios 1.5, 2, 3; simulation within 1%), and genuine closures fail the 99% design gate 5% of the time at ratio 2. With the gate on, rejection compounds into lock-out: real error is 9–16× the ungated value at ratio 2 and 56–182× at ratio 3, growing with horizon. The gate halves error against aliased closures when the twin is right (0.52 vs 1.27) but is 8× worse than no gate at ratio 2 (13.9 vs 1.72), and a gate retuned with the real drift beats no gate only up to ratio 2. Fitting drift from measured ground truth fixes the median by 10 cycles but the lock-out tail needs about 30 (28% of trials lock out at 3). Stylised: scalar error, Gaussian drift, simulated not measured.

title: What does a too-clean odometry twin do to a SLAM loop-closure gate?
summary: A back end accepts a loop closure when its squared residual is below a gate; true closures are N (0, s 2 I ), aliased ones are wider, and the cost is a weighted sum of two chi-square probabilities with a closed-form optimal gate in 2-D. A twin whose odometry noise is half the real value picks a gate that claims a cost of 0.094 and 2.1% of true closures rejected; in reality it rejects 38.2% (checked against simulation), costs 4.4× the claim and has 62% regret; a conventional α = 1% gate rejects α 1/ρ 2 = 32%. A too-pessimistic twin (ρ = 0.5) is not safe either (145% regret), regret depends strongly on how costly a false closure is, a fixed inflation factor is a bet on the true noise, and re-fitting the variance from about 59 ground-truthed closures brings regret under 1% of the twin’s. Stylised: isotropic Gaussian 2-D residuals, hard gate, known costs, no real odometry data.

title: Who pays for the information in a manipulated market?
summary: An uninformed manipulator pushing an LMSR verification market from q to τ loses exactly b·KL(q‖τ), which equals to the digit the extra rent it hands to informed traders; the accuracy change is μ[e 1 (1−q) − e 0 q − (1−2q)], positive only in a liquidity band (0.107, 0.413 in the baseline): below it nobody enters and manipulation costs 1−2q accuracy, above b = Nc/(H(q)−ln(1/(1−ε))) entry is certain and manipulation is neutral. Matches an executable LMSR Monte Carlo. Stylised.

title: Markets as routers: LMSR = Hedge, quadratic potential = sparsemax
summary: Cost-function markets as online learners for modular, continual-learning expert routing: verified equivalence and loss/regret bounds, and a switching-environment simulation where the quadratic market stays sparse and low-regret at liquidity levels where LMSR degrades. Small-scale; limitations stated.

title: What does a slippage limit give away in a prediction market?
summary: A searcher who buys before and sells after a victim's LMSR trade extracts exactly the victim's slippage tolerance times its fair cost (εC 0 , error 1.4×10 −14 over 216 instances), with a closed-form front-run of about εb/(1−p) shares, so return on capital falls as 1/b. A proportional fee of about v(1−p)/(2b) makes it unprofitable at any tolerance; the victim's optimal tolerance grows only like √log of the stakes; pro-rata batching keeps 0.989–0.999 of the extraction and uniformly random ordering cuts it exactly 3×. Stylised.

title: How fast does a prediction market converge when traders only understand part of it?
summary: Traders who each move prices within a subspace of securities make a cost-function market a randomized subspace descent. The market maker’s expected loss telescopes to ½( e 0 ′ Ae 0 − e T ′ Ae T ) whoever trades, so accuracy is bought once. Correlated securities slow single-security traders in closed form (5 securities: 31 rounds to reach 10 −3 of the error uncorrelated, 356 at correlation 0.95), while offering A-conjugate bundles restores the exact rate 1−1/ d at any correlation. With noisy beliefs the fraction κ a trader moves acts as an SGD step size: floor d κσ 2 /(2−κ), and a per-security running-mean step beats the best constant step (error 0.26 vs 0.47 at 100 rounds; full steps stay at 5). A simulated 4-outcome LMSR matches the local rate predictions to within 0.01 for two of three bundle designs and is faster than predicted for the third, for a reason not isolated. Quadratic-cost theory with i.i.d. trader arrival and Gaussian belief noise.

title: Can interpretable models predict annual divorce incidence?
summary: Original ACS, NSFG and NLSY79 microdata analyses separate annual incidence from prevalence. A respondent-held-out enriched additive couple model reduces Poisson loss by about 3.4%; more flexible trees do not improve on it. Includes schooling/earnings pairings, direct contrasts, duration and first-birth checks, trained models and a portable report. A browser app runs the five models on two profiles to give year-by-year divorce odds with explanations, model disagreement and out-of-range flags. Older cohort; observational, not a personal or causal forecast.

title: How should independently trained modules be merged, and how much does parallel training buy?
summary: Averaging m modules trained to convergence on random rank- r tasks has an exact residual error 1−2 amp + a 2 ( mp + m ( m −1) p 2 ) with p = r / d , needing only isotropy. The optimal scale is 1/(1+( m −1) p ) and leaves (1− p )/(1+( m −1) p ): plain averaging stalls at (1− p ) 2 (0.78 vs 0.47 at m =8, d / r =8) and unscaled task arithmetic diverges (56 at m =64). The decay is harmonic, not geometric, so m parallel workers give a wall-clock speedup that grows only logarithmically (8.9× at m =16, 17× at m =64) and halves in efficiency near m ≈ d / r ×2.5. Seen and fresh losses are closed forms matched by simulation. Stylised: linear regression, exact convergence, consistent isotropic tasks.

title: How many milestones does an unenforced job need?
summary: A requester and an anonymous worker split a job into milestones, each a stage of pre-payment, work and late payment, with a grim trigger that forfeits the remaining surplus and a relationship value W . A milestone is self-enforcing under some pre-payment split iff its cost is at most the pooled continuation value, so pay-after-delivery needs P / W r equal milestones, pay-before C / W w , and the best split C /( W r + W w ) (110, 25 and 20 in the example), whoever holds the value. Because early defection also forfeits the remaining work, the largest milestone shrinks geometrically and the minimum count is ⌈ln(1+( V − C )/ W )/ln( V / C )⌉: 17 instead of 100 at C =100, V =120, W =1, with the first milestone 1−( C − W )/ V of the job. Cheap re-entry caps W and costs ln(1/ e ) milestones. Matched on 2000 random instances. Stylised: complete information, pro-rata value.

title: Does a prompt-free human-vs-machine detector hold up on context families it never saw?
summary: Detector side of mimic-anycontext , run without an LLM because the model download was blocked. A TF-IDF n-gram logistic-regression detector is fitted on seven of eight RAID-derived families and scored on the eighth: mean AUROC 0.934 against 0.985 when fitted inside the family, worst on recipes (0.843), abstracts and wiki. Forty labelled target items close most of the gap on recipes. Held-out generators cost little (AUROC 0.90–1.00) and length does not explain it. Stylised: plain-prompt machine text only, one detector type; the prompt-optimising imitator is not tested.

title: Can a prompt make a 0.5B model detect machine text, and does the prompt carry to families it never saw?
summary: Prompted-detector half of mimic-anycontext . Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct answers Yes/No to “was this written by a person?” for RAID human and LLM texts in eight families, with 16 candidate prompts (the plain instruction plus random subsets of a ten-fragment bank). Negative result: the detector is inverted, with mean AUROC 0.278 for the plain prompt and 0.293 for a universal prompt picked on six families and scored on the other two (0.5 is chance; no prompt reaches 0.5 on any family, best 0.424). Picking prompts on selection texts adds +0.015 to +0.033, within selection noise, so the seen/held-out gap (about 0.01) says nothing about transfer. The prompt-free n-gram detector in mimic-anycontext-detect gets 0.93 on the same kind of text. Stylised: one small model, shallow random search, plain-prompt machine text, 30+30 test texts per family.

title: How many texts from one source does a weak human-vs-machine text detector need before a batch verdict is reliable?
summary: The mimic-contexts n-gram detector scores a held-out RAID family; a batch is k independent texts and its statistic is their mean score. One text separates people from a plainly prompted LLM at AUROC 0.935 (mean of 8 families); four all-machine texts reach 0.997 and eight reach 1.00. If only half the batch is machine, k = 8 gives 0.98; a quarter needs about 32 (0.985); at 10% machine 32 texts give only 0.82. The catch is calibration: with a threshold set on 150 human texts, the share of human batches flagged drifts from 7.4% at k = 1 to 15% on average at k = 32 (books 60%), because the batch mean's spread shrinks while the calibration error does not. Preliminary: plain-prompt text, i.i.d. batches, one detector, no LLM run.

title: How many detector queries does an imitator need to evade a human-vs-machine text detector it cannot read?
summary: The word 1-2 gram detector of mimic-whitebox (held-out AUROC 0.948) is attacked by an imitator that sees only the score of each text it submits. It deletes each of Q candidate word types in turn, reads the score drop and removes the k largest. With k=20, 25 queries per text give AUROC 0.873, 50 give 0.722 and about 95 give 0.520, against 0.487 for the white-box attack that reads the weights; blind deletion (0 queries) changes nothing. Stylised and preliminary: a linear detector, one seed, no fluency check on the edited text, and no retraining of the detector against the attack.

title: How well do prompt-free detectors tell people from a plainly prompted LLM, and do they carry over to unseen kinds of text?
summary: Eight text families from RAID (300 human and 300 plain-prompt chat-LLM texts each), split by family: train on five, hold out poetry, reviews and wiki. Prompt-free detectors on the held-out families: character/word n-gram logistic regression AUROC 0.93 (95% interval 0.91–0.94), a Binoculars-style zero-shot score from Qwen2.5-0.5B 0.80 (0.77–0.83), perplexity alone 0.76; a length-only detector is at chance (0.52). Zero-shot scores are weak on mpt-chat text (0.65) while n-grams are not (0.95). Limits: the ‘imitator’ is RAID’s own chat generations, not a prompted or optimised one; three chat models; no author-group labels for fairness checks. Preliminary: first step of track 11, no game yet.

title: Does the prompt-only imitation game settle or cycle, and does beating the latest detector mean beating the others?
summary: Follow-up to mimic-loop . Every imitator prompt any of its eight runs produced is scored against every detector prompt (Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on both sides, 48 titles per cell, detector paired accuracy, 0.50 = chance), giving a 10×7 matrix on reddit and 9×10 on reviews. Both zero-sum games have a pure equilibrium with value below chance (reddit 0.396, 95% title-bootstrap 0.28 to 0.47; reviews 0.292, 0.17 to 0.34): no detector prompt guarantees chance, and no cell exceeds 0.56. On reviews the unadapted plain imitator prompt is the equilibrium imitator. Mean text length correlates with detector accuracy (Spearman 0.76 on reddit, 0.30 on reviews). No cycles at a 0.15 noise margin; overfitting to the latest opponent is small and not established. Stylised: one loop seed, a 0.5B detector that starts below chance. The model-size question is left open.

title: Can an imitator fool a prompt-free human-vs-machine text detector with cheap surface edits, such as typos, contractions or dropping the chat preamble?
summary: The mimic-contexts n-gram detector (held-out AUROC 0.927) is scored on poetry, reviews and wiki after scripted edits to the machine texts only. Markdown stripping, preamble removal and contractions move it by at most 0.005; 2% typos cost 0.012 (interval −0.014 to −0.010); keeping the first half costs 0.051, the largest drop, and no edit approaches chance. A detector refit on edited training text recovers and exceeds the baseline (0.956 to 0.969), partly by learning text length. Lowercasing and whitespace edits are null by construction. Preliminary: scripted rules, not LLM-chosen edits; one seed.

title: Does a prompt-free human-vs-machine detector carry over to a generator or decoding it never saw?
summary: The mimic-contexts n-gram detector fit on all eight RAID families, scored on text from a chat model or decoding left out of the fit (items split in two halves by source_id , halves swapped). AUROC falls from 0.991 to 0.978 (llama-chat), 0.983 to 0.971 (mistral-chat) and 0.981 to 0.959 (mpt-chat); leaving out sampling decoding costs 0.984 → 0.936 and greedy 0.989 → 0.964, with held-out wiki the weak spot (0.83 on sampling). Averaging the score over k same-source texts lifts AUROC from 0.971 (k=1) to 0.999 (k=4). Human batches are more varied than model batches (recipes distinct-2 0.589 against 0.373 for llama and 0.399 for mistral), but mpt-chat matches or exceeds human variety on poetry and reddit. Preliminary: plain-prompt RAID text, three chat models each present in only some families (generator and family partly confounded), one detector type, no LLM run.

title: Can prompt search alone move a frozen 0.5B imitator past a prompted 0.5B detector, and which proposer does it best at equal budget?
summary: A first, stylised run of the imitation game: Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct as imitator and detector, only prompts change, alternating rounds on two families (reddit, reviews) with four proposers (random, GA, GrIPS-style, local-LLM) at 4 evaluations per side per round. The plain detector starts below chance (paired accuracy 0.12), the final detectors reach 0.12–0.58 on 24 test pairs with intervals of about ±0.2, and the proposers cannot be ranked. Length is a major confound: imitators that wrote longer texts fooled the detector more. One seed; a harness and a first look, not a detection result.

title: Does MAUVE, a distribution-level score, rank human-vs-machine gaps the way a text detector does?
summary: MAUVE between human and RAID chat-model text in 20 family × model cells (TF-IDF/SVD embedding, 5 draws of 48–100 texts), against a cross-fit n-gram detector on the same texts. Human-vs-human MAUVE is 0.92–0.99; every human-vs-model cell is at most 0.83. MAUVE and AUROC rank cells loosely alike (Spearman −0.60, p = 0.005; wiki/mistral-chat is hardest for both), but disagree on recipes (AUROC 0.999, MAUVE 0.32) and news (0.97, 0.75), and MAUVE does not track the distinct-2 ratio (ρ = 0.24, n.s.). Preliminary: the embedding is lexical, not MAUVE’s usual GPT-2 features, so values are not comparable with the literature; plain-prompt text only, no LLM run.

title: Does a kernel MMD test catch the same wrong digital twins as a classifier two-sample test?
summary: A kernel two-sample test (unbiased RBF MMD, median-heuristic bandwidth) is compared with a gradient-boosted classifier two-sample test on the stylised pendulum of mimic-twinc2st . Rejection uses the 95th percentile of the exact twin’s own statistic. Raw-trajectory MMD has essentially no power against a Coulomb-friction error at n = 100–400 per class (0.05–0.06 at the median bandwidth, 0.37 at 0.03× for −20% friction), where the classifier reaches 1.00 at −20% from n = 200. MMD on second differences detects a +25% noise-level error at 0.97 from n = 100, where the raw-feature classifier is at 0.08–0.25. Stylised; 24 classifier replicates per cell, so those intervals are wide.

title: Does a kernel MMD test catch the same wrong MuJoCo digital twins as a classifier two-sample test?
summary: A MuJoCo hinge pendulum with Student-t sensor noise is the ‘real’ system; twins change the integrator, friction or noise. Rejection uses the 95th percentile of the exact twin’s own statistic. Boosted-tree C2ST power is 1.00 at n = 200 for semi-implicit Euler at 0.02 s and 0.90 at 0.01 s, and 1.00 for a Gaussian-vs-Student-t noise-shape error, where MMD (raw or on second differences) stays at 0.00–0.07. MMD on second differences does catch a +25% noise-level error (0.95 at n = 100). A 10–20% friction error is invisible to all three at n ≤ 200. Limitations: one toy system, 20 C2ST replicates, two sample sizes. Stylised.

title: Does a classifier two-sample test see the integrator, timestep and friction gaps of a MuJoCo digital twin?
summary: A MuJoCo hinge pendulum (RK4, 0.002 s, dry friction, Student-t sensor noise) is the ‘real’ system; twins change the integrator, timestep or friction. A boosted-tree classifier two-sample test (800 trajectories per class, 3 seeds) has AUROC 0.98 for semi-implicit Euler at 0.02 s (paired RMSE 0.028 rad), 0.90 at 0.01 s, 0.67 at 0.005 s (0.007 rad) and 0.53 at 0.002 s (0.003 rad), which is not separable from the null 0.51. A friction error of 10% gives 0.52 and 20% gives 0.61. Gaussian instead of Student-t noise of the same sd has zero paired error but AUROC 0.92. Limits: one toy system, one classifier, 3 seeds; the ‘real’ system is itself simulated. Stylised, preliminary.

title: How many human texts does it take to re-set a detector's threshold for a 5% false-positive rate on a new kind of text?
summary: Follow-up to mimic-threshold . The n-gram detector is fit on seven RAID families; k human texts of the eighth set its cut-off, 500 random draws per cell. Taking the empirical 95th percentile, k = 20 gives a mean false-positive rate of 9% and a 36% chance of exceeding 10%; k = 80 gives 6.1% and 10%; k = 160 gives 5.5%. A conformal rank rule holds the mean at 4.7–4.9% from k = 20 but gives up recall (0.66 against 0.79 at k = 20) and cannot flag anything below 19 calibration texts. Even at k = 80 one draw lands anywhere from 1.7% to 8.8% (10th–90th percentile). Recalibration fixes the false-accusation rate, not the detector: recipes still catches under half of machine text. Preliminary: plain-prompt RAID text, one detector, calibration from the same population as the test, no LLM run.

title: Does refitting a human-vs-machine text detector on attacked text stop a black-box evader?
summary: A black-box attacker with 50 score queries per text takes the mimic-whitebox word 1-2 gram detector from held-out AUROC 0.948 to 0.719. Refitting the detector on attacked training texts and letting the attacker re-attack settles after one round: AUROC on freshly attacked text stays near 0.81 over four rounds, while clean-text AUROC falls to about 0.90. Edits made against the original detector transfer to the refit ones at 0.85. Stylised: linear detector, one seed, no fluency check, no LLM run.

title: Does adding a zero-shot perplexity score to the n-gram detector help it catch machine text in families it never saw?
summary: The mimic-contexts n-gram detector and its Binoculars-style score (Qwen2.5-0.5B) are uncorrelated within each class (−0.02 human, 0.02 machine), yet combining them barely helps on the held-out families poetry, reviews and wiki: n-gram AUROC 0.926, mean of z-scores 0.935 (paired gain +0.009, 95% interval −0.010 to +0.026), fitted logistic stacks −0.003 and −0.019. It helps on wiki (0.892 to 0.935) and hurts on poetry and mpt-chat, where the zero-shot score is weak. Preliminary: 720 held-out texts, three chat models, a small scorer, one split; no LLM was run.

title: How much text does a prompt-free human-vs-machine detector need, and what does it key on?
