summary: The mimic-contexts n-gram detector (TF-IDF character and word n-grams, fitted on five families) is scored on poetry, reviews and wiki after cutting each text to its first N characters: AUROC 0.65 at 50, 0.75 at 100, 0.84 at 400 (the length the imitation-game loop shows its detector) and 0.93 at 1,500; refitting on the short text recovers only 0.02–0.07. Stripping punctuation changes AUROC by +0.003 and shuffling words by −0.014, so the detector reads vocabulary, not syntax or formatting (lowercasing and whitespace views are no-ops for this vectoriser). Preliminary: plain-prompt RAID text only, one detector, one split, no LLM involved.

title: If a human-vs-machine detector's threshold is set for a 5% false-positive rate, does that rate hold on a kind of text it never saw?
summary: The mimic-contexts n-gram detector is fit on seven RAID families and its threshold set so 5% of human text is flagged (out-of-fold), then applied to the eighth. Realised false-positive rates run from 0.00 to 0.54: abstracts 0.54, books 0.18, while news, poetry, recipes, reddit, reviews and wiki sit at 0.00–0.06. On recipes the cut-off is too strict instead: it catches 1.7% of machine text where a threshold set on recipes would catch 46%. AUROC does not show this (books has the best, 0.993, and the second-worst rate). Preliminary: plain-prompt RAID text, one detector type, one split, no LLM run.

title: Does a classifier two-sample test catch digital-twin errors that a paired trajectory error misses?
summary: A stylised pendulum with Coulomb friction and heavy-tailed (Student-t) sensor noise is the ‘real’ system; twins differ in friction, noise shape or noise level. A classifier two-sample test (5-fold CV AUROC, 800 vs 800 trajectories, 3 seeds) separates real from twin trajectories with boosted trees: a friction error of 0.03 (10%) that moves the noise-free trajectory by only 0.006 rad RMSE — a quarter of the 0.02 rad noise sd — gives AUROC 0.72, and 0.91 at 20%. A twin with the right dynamics but Gaussian instead of Student-t noise of the same sd has paired error exactly 0 yet AUROC 0.92 once second-difference features are added (0.59 on raw angles). A logistic regression on raw angles stays at chance (0.51) throughout, because the start angles are symmetric. Limits: one toy system, two noise models, three seeds, a handful of classifier settings; simulated only, nothing about real hardware. Preliminary, no LLM involved: a side piece of track 11.

title: Does randomizing only the sensor-noise level of a wrong digital twin keep domain randomization's rescue without its blow-up?
summary: Follow-up to mimic-twinrand on the same stylised pendulum PD task. Only the twin's noise sd is spread (uniform on nominal ± w ×0.02); friction and g/L stay nominal. A no-noise twin's regret falls from 0.0098 to 0 at w =2 and stays at 0.00035 (worst seed 0.0015) at w =4, where randomizing all four parameters has a worst seed of 0.042. A doubled-noise twin improves monotonically (0.0038 to 0.0012), which all-four did not. Friction and gravity errors are untouched (0.00138 at every width). 24 seeds, 48-point grid; preliminary, one toy system, no LLM.

title: How many real trajectories does a classifier test need to flag a wrong digital twin, and are the twins it flags the ones that cost a controller?
summary: On the stylised pendulum of mimic-twinregret , a boosted-tree C2ST with n real and n twin trajectories flags a twin when its AUROC beats the 95th percentile of the exact-twin null at the same n (20 replicates per cell, n = 10 to 160). The six twins whose controller regret is at least 0.001 are all flagged in at least 80% of replicates by n = 80 (by 40 for the four noise-level and noise-shape twins), so the test does not miss costly twins at that size. It also flags three twins that cost nothing (g/L −20%, noise ×0.5, noise ×0.75) by n = 40–80, while Coulomb −10% and −20% stay unflagged at 160. Spearman correlation of power at 80 with regret is 0.52 (p = 0.048, 15 twins). A flag is a cheap alarm, not a verdict on usefulness. Limits: one system, one task, 20 replicates, a null threshold that is degenerate at n ≤ 20. Stylised, simulated, no LLM.

title: Does domain randomization over a wrong digital twin cut the controller regret of tuning on one wrong twin?
summary: Follow-up to mimic-twinregret on the same stylised pendulum and noisy-feedback PD task. Gains are tuned on 200 start angles spread over 8 randomized twins (noise level, Coulomb and viscous friction, g/L each uniform on nominal ± w × the real value) and scored on 2,000 held-out real start angles, over 24 tuning seeds. For the no-noise twin, whose single-twin regret is 0.0098, randomization with w = 0.5 brings it to 0.00006, the same as the exact twin. No-Coulomb and g/L +20% twins fall from 0.0014 to 0.00012 at w = 1–2. It does not always help: for a doubled-noise twin regret stays about 0.003 for w ≤ 1 and at w = 2 the mean rises to 0.0057 with a worst seed 7.5× the single-twin worst. Limits: one system and task, a 48-point grid that quantises regret, one randomization family with a shared width. Stylised, simulated, no LLM.

title: Does a digital twin that a classifier can tell apart from the real system also make a worse controller?
summary: In the stylised pendulum of mimic-twinc2st with a torque input, a PD controller on noisy feedback is tuned on each wrong twin (48-point gain grid, 200 twin start angles) and scored on 2,000 held-out start angles on the ‘real’ system. Regret is its real cost minus the best grid point’s (0.259). Six of 15 wrong twins have regret exactly 0 in all 12 tuning seeds although the classifier two-sample test separates them from the real system with AUROC 0.58–0.999, among them g/L −20%, whose paired error is the largest (0.25 rad). The largest regret, 0.0099 (3.8%), comes from a twin with no sensor noise at all, whose paired error is 0. Across the 15 twins AUROC and regret correlate only loosely (Spearman 0.46, p = 0.08) and paired RMSE not at all (−0.28). Detecting a twin is not the same as the twin mattering for the task. Limits: one system, one task, a coarse grid that quantises regret, 12 tuning seeds. Stylised, simulated, no LLM: a side piece of track 11.

title: How many words must an imitator change to evade a word n-gram human-vs-machine detector that it can read?
summary: A word 1-2 gram logistic-regression detector (held-out AUROC 0.948 on poetry, reviews and wiki) is attacked by an imitator that knows its weights and deletes or swaps the k most machine-ward word types in each of its own texts. Deleting 10 word types drops AUROC to 0.738, 20 to 0.487 (chance) and 40 to 0.150; swapping 20 gives 0.317. A detector refit on text attacked the same way recovers to 0.94–1.00. Stylised: scripted edits with no fluency check, one seed, one detector family, no LLM run.

title: How should cheap biased twin samples be weighted against scarce real ones?
summary: For a mean estimated from n real and m twin samples with twin bias δ, the optimal weight and MSE are exact and the twin is worth at most σ 2 /δ 2 real samples however large m is (e.g. 157.5 of a 160 cap at m =10 4 ). Equal-weight pooling beats real-only iff δ 2 < σ 2 / n + σ 2 / m , so more twin data narrows the safe range (3.99× worse than real-only at δ=2√a). Estimating the bias from the data is costly: the plug-in weight is worse than real-only for large bias (peak 1.24×), and a 5% pretest peaks at 2.41×. Stylised: scalar Gaussian, constant bias, no robot data.

title: Can we elicit the mode of a mixture of honest and cheating drift?
summary: When some workers cheat, drift is a mixture and the mean, which squared loss elicits, lands where almost no task lies (at a 30% cheater 6σ away, the mean’s window holds 0.15 of the mass versus 0.48 at the mode). The mode is not elicitable, but the centre of the width-2α window with the most mass is, with the bounded loss 1[|y−r|>α]. Regret is an exact window-mass difference; the best window is α=σ for normal drift and γ/√3 for Cauchy (no mean exists); an equal bimodal mixture has one α-mode iff α exceeds a closed-form root α*; and under 10–40% contamination the sample α-mode has ~0 bias while the mean is off by 5ε, at a 3.7× RMSE cost when clean.

title: What share of the mass should a new module get?
summary: When a modular system adds an expert to a Hedge/LMSR router, the regret certificate to every expert is c i /η + η T /8 with c i = ln(1/π i ) + Σ j>i ln(1/(1−π j )), and for any share sequence Σ i e − c i = 1 (a Kraft identity). So uniform entry π = 1/( n +1) is the unique minimax rule (every c i = ln N , against 4.1–9.7 for constant shares at 4+12 modules), and against a prior on which module will be best the optimal shares are P j / S j with expected coefficient equal to the entropy of the prior. The price of entry is exactly ln(1/π)/η for a better arrival and ln(1/(1−π))/η for a worse one, independent of the quality gap; a recency prior cuts simulated regret from 3.11 to 2.70 nats. Known arrival rounds, fixed η. Pure-Python, 6 tests.

title: What does a twin that assumes the radar is aligned with the body get wrong about dead reckoning, and can loop-closure validation see it?
summary: With a planar mount-yaw error e , radar ego-velocity dead reckoning is exactly the true path rotated by e : error 2 sin( e /2)·|displacement|, bounded by the path diameter and zero after any closed loop, so loop and out-and-back validations pass while a straight 157 m run is off by 27 m at 10°. A closed-form rotation fit recovers e with standard deviation σ/√Σ|p i | 2 (matched by simulation, 95% coverage). Stylised: the result is planar; a pitched mount drifts vertically by exactly laps·2πR sin e despite perfect x-y closure.

title: What can be elicited from several independent draws of benign drift?
summary: The pair score (r−(y 1 −y 2 )²/2)² has excess loss exactly (r−σ²)², and kernels for mean², the third central moment and σ 4 need 2, 3 and 4 draws. Detecting a variance under-report takes ((z α +z β )/ρ)²(κ+1)/2 pairs (Monte Carlo power 0.70–0.79 against a nominal 0.8); scoring |y 1 −y 2 | beats the variance score for Laplace and t 5 ; all-pairs pooling cuts payment variance by (κ+1)/(κ−1); correlated draws make the score elicit σ²(1−ρ). Stylised distributions, no measured drift.

title: Many verifiers, one solver: the volunteer's dilemma in refereed verification
summary: Closed-form m-verifier audit equilibrium (detection pinned at s/(s+S), redundancy bounded by ln(1/(1-q))/q, cheating rising with m under split rewards), a saddle-point stability result, Hedge dynamics that concentrate audit burden on a subset, and bandit learners that need an exploration floor. Stylised.

title: Can the multiclass log score be made payable?
summary: Extending x ln x below a cutoff ε by its second-order Taylor polynomial gives a strictly proper K-class score that equals −ln r y whenever every r j ≥ε and has payment range exactly 1−ln ε, the same for any K. Per unit of range it has 3× Brier’s rare-class incentive at a 5% class and 63× at 0.1%, the best cutoff is the rarest class’s mass, and a verifier that zeroes out a 1% class loses a closed-form 0.005 (Brier 1.3×10 −4 , log unbounded). Closes the gap left open in categorical-scores.

title: A free-space radar twin ignores ground-bounce lobing: how wrong is it, and can a two-ray twin with a slightly wrong target height be worse?
summary: Two-ray detection 16 sin 4 u , u =2π h r h t /(λ r ): lobe-mean gain exactly 6 and a detected phase fraction 1−(2/π)asin(( c /16) 1/4 ), exactly 2/3 at the free-space range edge. The real system misses 20% of ranges inside the free-space range and detects 44% of those beyond it. A deterministic two-ray twin with height error δ h disagrees ≈4 h r δ h /(λ r ) (0.200 at 0.5 m, matching simulation) and is worse than free space at short range; a height-jitter ensemble scores Brier 0.119 against 0.197 deterministic and 0.533 free space. Stylised: perfect reflection, flat earth, hard threshold, no radar data.

title: How wrong is a twin's localisation error when real ranges have non-line-of-sight bias?
summary: A twin draws anchor ranges as true distance plus Gaussian noise; real sites also have long-biased NLOS ranges. On a ring of anchors the rms position error is exactly GDOP·√( σ 2 + p (2− p ) m 2 ) (1.105 vs law 1.095 m at p =0.1, n =6), 4.5× and 7.3× the twin's at p =0.1 and 0.3, with zero mean. A blocked side is a bias the linear formula predicts to about 0.02 m per coordinate (0.924 vs 0.930 m) while the twin predicts none. Sized on the twin, a 1 m / 95% corridor needs 4 anchors; the NLOS site needs about 28 ( p =0.1) or 46 ( p =0.2), and the 4-anchor ring leaves the corridor 34.7% of the time instead of 5%. Dropping the largest-residual anchor cuts rms error 0.947→0.414 m at p =0.1 but costs 24% with no NLOS. Stylised: 2-D ring, iid exponential NLOS, simulated site, no sensor data.

title: How much gradient noise survives in DiLoCo-style local SGD, and how should the outer step, momentum, worker count and sync interval be set against it?
summary: On a quadratic with M workers, H noisy inner steps and a heavy-ball outer step, the stationary variance per mode is exactly α V (1+β)/((1−β) s (2(1+β)−α s )) with V the averaged inner noise and s = 1 − (1 − η a ) H , matching literal simulation to 0.2%. At α = 1 the floor is independent of H ; for small α more local steps shrink it by less than a factor of 2. Momentum costs no extra floor at equal effective step (and lowers it at large steps), workers give near-linear speedup (331× at M = 256, α still below 1), and unlike the noise-free case the best sync interval grows as the noise-floor target falls ( H * = 5, 11, 38 at C = 10), up to 41× faster than syncing every step. Stylised: quadratic, Gaussian noise, shared Hessian, fixed α.

title: What if the referee itself is noisy?
summary: When verifiers are paid against a judge whose label flips with rates e 0 , e 1 , any proper score elicits the noisy probability e 0 +γp (γ=1−e 0 −e 1 ), the Brier incentive shrinks by γ², and rankings of truthful verifiers reverse at η*=0.25. The backward-corrected surrogate score is exactly unbiased for the true loss, at a 1/γ payment spread and (balanced case) 1/γ² more evidence; misestimated rates produce a closed-form affine bias whose cost falls as 1/m in gold checks. Stylised.

title: Can a lidar twin give each beam an independent visibility probability, or do neighbouring beams share occluders?
summary: For a Poisson field of occluders of radius ρ, beams a distance s apart are both clear with probability exp(−μ(2ρ+min( s ,2ρ))), which equals p 2 exactly when s ≥ 2ρ; any set of beams has the closed form exp(−μ·union length). An independent-beam twin therefore matches the mean number of clear beams but understates the variance and the blind probability: with 8 beams at 25 cm and single-beam visibility 0.5 (occluder diameter 1 m) the exact blind probability is 0.0815 against the twin’s 0.0039 (20.9×, 97× at 5 cm), and reaching a blind probability of 0.01 needs 16 beams instead of 7 (not reachable with 16 at 10 cm). The twin is exact once the spacing exceeds the occluder diameter, and an ensemble twin that samples occluder fields reproduces the exact value (0.0815 vs 0.0815 ± 0.0006). Stylised: one-dimensional lateral projection, binary opaque occluders, no lidar data.

title: What does a too-clean sensor twin do to a mapper's commit error?
summary: A grid cell committed when log-odds built with a twin's sensor model reach ± A has, under the real sensor, an exact error set by the Lundberg exponent θ* (equal to 1 for a correct twin) with a rigorous optional-stopping sandwich. A twin whose free-space false-hit rate is 0.05 against a real 0.15 turns a 10 −3 design into 1.45×10 −2 (14.5×, matched by simulation; 260× at 0.30), and an optimistic occupied hit rate (0.8 vs 0.6) gives 26×. Committing at ln(1/ε)/θ* restores the target at 1.4–16× the latency, and the real-data estimate of θ* needs several hundred known-free observations before the tempered mapper stops exceeding target in over a quarter of maps. Stylised: one independent-beam cell.

title: What does a simulator tuned on one-step odometry noise get wrong about drift, relocalisation and loop closure?
summary: A traversal has a persistent bias plus white noise, so real error after T steps has variance σ 1 2 (ρ T 2 +(1−ρ) T ); a twin fitted to one-step increments, identical for every ρ, predicts σ 1 2 T and is off by exactly 1+( T −1)ρ. With 5% of step variance persistent, the twin’s relocalisation interval is 3.4× too long (real miss probability 51.6% against a claimed 5%), and a 3σ loop-closure gate tuned in it accepts true closures with probability 0.64 at T = 200 instead of 0.997; in a closed loop the rejections let error run away (RMS 8.8 m against 0.17 m calibrated). A calibrated gate accepts 97–99% of aliased closures once drift uncertainty exceeds the alias offset, and a variance ratio fitted at one loop length does not transfer to others. Stylised: 1-D Gaussian, assumed one-step-fitted twin, no real odometry data.

title: Who trades decides how liquid a verification market should be
summary: A Glosten–Milgrom market maker facing an informed share μ with accuracy q moves its posterior log-odds by exactly 2·atanh(μ(2q−1)) per net buy, so its price path is an LMSR with b* = 1/(2 atanh m) (verified to 2×10 −16 ). A wrong b costs log loss only in a transient whose peak is scale-free in m and 1.8–2.5× worse when overconfident; the LMSR subsidy tends to b* ln 2, exactly the spread the GM maker charges. Stylised.

title: Should severity reports be scored with the order in mind?
summary: For ordered fault severities the ranked probability score is Brier on the cumulative distribution: strictly proper with exact regret Σ(R k −P k )², so moving mass ε a distance d costs exactly dε² where Brier charges 2ε² for every d. Pooling adjacent classes costs exactly half of Brier’s, and every threshold probability is within √regret of the truth. The price: per unit of payment range RPS gives Brier’s incentive only for a maximal-distance shift (1/(K−1) for adjacent ones). Extends categorical-scores.

title: When a spoon-feeding arm meets a moving mouth, what sets the force on the lips: the sensor, the approach speed or a force cap?
summary: A stdlib planar point-mass twin of a feeding arm and a swaying mouth, with 200 paired trials per row. With a 0.05 s forward lead the push on a blocked tip is 20 N·s/m × speed, so peak lip force tracks approach speed (1.0 N at 0.05 m/s, 4.0 N at 0.20). A camera lowers the share of trials that touch the lips (0.40 against 0.72 at 30 mm sway) without lowering the peak, and its advantage fades with latency (touch share 0.07 at no delay, 0.71 at 0.4 s). A 1 N force cap trims the worst peak but not the share of comfortable feeds. Stylised: all constants are assumed, the peak-force result is largely an identity of the chosen controller, and no human model or Assistive Gym was used.

title: Does searching an arm’s joint count, link lengths and mount, with its controller tuned in the loop, beat a fixed three-link body at the same cost?
summary: A stdlib model searches link lengths, joint count and mount position of a planar arm, with its inverse-kinematics controller tuned in the loop, against a fixed three-link body at an equal cost budget (300 evaluations, 10 seeds, held-out targets). On a shelf task that needs the tool pointing down, the search reaches 0.95 success against 0.26 for the fixed body with a tuned controller and 0.50 with the mount also tuned; on a long position-only reach the fixed body already succeeds and the search adds nothing. Random search beat a (1+4) evolution strategy here, weakly. Stylised: kinematics and static torque only (no MuJoCo dynamics), and every cost, mass and limit is assumed.

title: When a pest window sets a deadline, is a scout-and-treater fleet or a fleet of inline weeding robots cheaper?
summary: A stdlib extension of osrobot-pipeline that adds a hard finish deadline for 16 equal fields and searches up to four scouts, up to 16 treaters and up to 32 inline robots (no new simulation; every price an assumed round number). One scout cannot finish 16 fields faster than 5.3, 15.9 and 32.5 h (0.18, 0.72, 1.62 ha fields) however many treaters it feeds, against 0.7, 2.8 and 6.2 h for 32 inline robots. Cheapest pipeline over cheapest inline: 1.06 to 1.12 at 0.72 ha, rising as the deadline tightens, and 1.49 at 0.18 ha; at 1.62 ha the pipeline is cheaper (0.87 to 0.93) at every deadline it can meet but cannot meet 8 h, where only inline robots can. Stylised: equal fields, hard cut-off, no late-yield curve.

title: Does a spoon-feeding arm need more than two joints? Tip mass, lip force and servo cost of 2 to 6 joint arms
summary: A stdlib planar model gives 2 to 6 joint feeding arms an operational-space tip mass (servo, link and spoon masses plus each servo's rotor inertia reflected through a 345:1 gearbox) and feeds it to osrobot-assist 's lip-contact trials (200 paired trials per row, 30 mm sway, camera arm). The tip mass falls only from 0.63 to 0.50 kg from 2 to 6 joints; the worst peak lip force is identical (2.0 N at 0.10 m/s, 4.0 N at 0.20) and the safe share at 0.20 m/s is 0.60 to 0.65, within sampling error. Servo cost alone triples, from $52–98 to $156–295 (two retailers' listings, 2026-10-19). Most of the mass is the geared-up rotor. Stylised: planar, one pose, position-only task, assumed constants, so the real reasons for more joints (spoon orientation, 3-D motion) are not tested.

title: For a weeding robot with a cheap camera, is it better to treat weeds as it drives or to scout first and come back, and what does a weak sensor cost?
summary: A stdlib simulation of a lane-following weeding robot on a 60×30 m field with clustered weeds, a motion-blurred noisy detector and muddy squares. Scouting then touring the targets kills the same share of weeds as treating inline (0.399 against 0.401 at 1 m/s) and is slower in all 23 paired rows, by 2.8 to 7.8 min. Lane overlap repays a weak sensor at a steep price: 0 to 0.75 overlap raises the kill share from 0.40 to 0.86 and the time from 52 to 178 min; no grid configuration reaches a 0.9 kill share at a 0.5 hit rate. Stylised: every constant is assumed, the speed results move with the blur assumption, and the planner comparison is a statement about this cost model.

title: Does a better tour rescue scout-then-treat weeding?
summary: A stdlib follow-up to osrobot-field that swaps nearest neighbour for 2-opt as the second stage of scout-then-treat. 2-opt cuts the straight-line tour over about 232 detections from 539 m to 468 m (random order: 5,403 m), but a field still takes 56.1 min against 51.7 min treating inline (nearest neighbour: 57.0), and scouting is slower at every weed density from 0.05 to 1.2 per m². Stylised: assumed constants, a mud-blind planner, 30 fields per row; no robot was built.

title: Can a small twin of a liquid-handling bench catch protocol errors before they run, and how much pipetting error does a serial dilution tolerate?
summary: A stdlib deck-and-pipette twin tracks tips, well volumes, liquid labels and straight-line travel over labware, and checks protocols before they run. On 522 injected faults across three reference protocols it flags 366 (355 with the intended code) where a syntax-only baseline flags 100; the misses are mostly equivalent mutants. Collisions appear only where a move crosses taller labware (a tube rack in one protocol; forced travel heights up to 70 mm collide, 90 mm and above do not). With an assumed pipetting-error curve, a 12-well two-fold serial dilution has a final-well CV of 0.187 at 10 µL transfers, 0.100 at 20 and 0.035 at 100 µL. Stylised and circular by construction: the faults match the checks, and every geometry, timing and error value is assumed.

title: Does the real Opentrons simulator catch the protocol faults a small stdlib liquid-handling twin catches?
summary: The 522 seeded faults of osrobot-lab (three protocols, 11 fault kinds) were translated into Opentrons Python API scripts and run through the real simulator ( opentrons==8.0.0 , OT-2, p300). It raises on 270 of them against the twin's 366, and every one it catches the twin also catches. It catches scripting errors (unknown labware or well, missing or doubled tip pick-up, 350 µL or 5000 µL aspirate) and accepts tip reuse, a 5 µL dispense, a tip left on and a half-empty source, even with starting liquids declared. Those are mostly policy differences, not simulator misses. Stylised: the fault set was written for the twin.

title: If the person being fed leans toward the spoon, can a blind feeding arm do without a camera?
summary: A stdlib extension of osrobot-assist 's planar feeding-arm twin in which the user shifts the mouth toward the spoon tip at a swept lean speed (200 paired trials per row). At 30 mm sway and 0.20 m/s the blind arm's share of feeds with peak lip force at most 2 N rises from 0.21 (passive user) to 0.69 at 50 mm/s and 1.00 at 100 mm/s, against 0.71 to 0.97 for the camera arm; at 50 mm sway even 100 mm/s gives only 0.62 for the blind arm. Leaning removes contacts but not the peak force of the ones that remain (4.0 N at 0.20 m/s). Stylised: every constant, including the lean speed, is assumed; no person was modelled or tested.

title: If the person being fed misjudges the spoon, or sees it late, can a blind feeding arm still do without a camera?
summary: A stdlib extension of osrobot-lean 's planar feeding-arm twin in which the user leans toward a perceived spoon position that is delayed and offset by a per-feed misjudgement (200 paired trials per row, 30 mm sway, 0.20 m/s, 100 mm/s lean). A blind arm's share of feeds with peak lip force at most 2 N falls from 1.00 with a perfect leaner to 0.83, 0.60 and 0.47 at 10, 20 and 40 mm of misjudgement, and only 0.50 of feeds reach the mouth at 40 mm; the camera arm falls from 0.97 to 0.69 and always feeds. A perception delay of up to 0.2 s changes little; 1.0 s drops the blind arm to 0.46. Stylised: constant offset, assumed constants, no safety case.

title: If the person being fed judges the spoon better as it nears the mouth, how much of a camera's value does a blind feeding arm get back?
summary: A stdlib extension of osrobot-leannoise 's planar feeding-arm twin in which the user's misjudgement of the spoon position shrinks, linearly over the last 40 mm, by a swept fraction (200 paired trials per row, 30 mm sway, 0.20 m/s, 100 mm/s lean). A blind arm's share of feeds with peak lip force at most 2 N is 0.83, 0.60, 0.47 and 0.41 for a constant misjudgement of 10, 20, 40 and 80 mm, and 0.99, 0.95, 0.84 and 0.70 when the error falls to zero at the lips; feeds that never reach the mouth (0.50 fed at 40 mm) disappear. With the error shrinking, the blind arm is within 0.02 of the camera arm up to 20 mm; the camera keeps its lead at 40 and 80 mm. Stylised: an assumed linear shrink law, assumed constants, a point mass and no real person.

title: Is the peak force of a feeding arm on the lips set by the lips' stiffness, the arm's force loop, or its approach lead?
summary: A stdlib sweep of osrobot-assist 's feeding-arm twin over lip stiffness, loop stiffness and forward lead (200 paired trials per row, 30 mm sway, camera arm at 0.20 m/s). Mean peak lip force rises from 0.32 N at 100 N/m to 1.15 N at 800 and 2.02 N at 6400; the worst trial reaches 6.7 N, above the controller's 4.0 N stall push, so that push is a ceiling only for soft and medium lips. At 0.05 m/s every stiffness stays under 2 N. Stylised: assumed constants, a point mass and a passive user.

title: Does co-designing an arm's link lengths and controller beat tuning the controller on a fixed body?
summary: A stdlib planar two-link arm model searches the split of a fixed 0.50 m reach together with PD gains, against an equal-link body with tuned gains, at equal search budget. The tray is reachable only for splits of 0.40 to 0.60. Co-design gained 1.9% in held-out move time (0.283 against 0.289 s), within three-seed noise, while tuning the controller cut hand-set gains' 0.460 s by about 37%. Stylised, preliminary and mostly negative: one body parameter and an assumed torque limit.

title: Is a scout drone plus a camera-less ground treater cheaper per hectare than one weeding robot, and from what field size?
summary: A stdlib follow-up to osrobot-scoutpair that prices its matched-kill pair (scout at 1 m/s, 3 m swath, 0.343 killed) against one inline robot, with every price an assumed round number. Simulated time is linear in area (R² ≥ 0.9999 over 0.045 to 1.62 ha), so cost per field is a fixed set-up part plus a per-hectare part. Charging each machine only for the minutes it works, the pair costs about 2.5 times the inline robot on a 0.045 ha field, breaks even near 0.5 ha (0.8 ha at a 4,000 USD scout, 1.3 at 6,000) and is about 0.7 times as much per hectare at 5 ha (extrapolated). If the two machines are held for the whole job, as one dedicated pair would be, it never wins at the reference prices (1.08 times at 20 ha). The verdict flips with utilisation (2,000 occupied hours a year gives 2.09 times at 0.72 ha) and with labour and battery life. Stylised: assumed prices and constants, a straight-line extrapolation beyond 1.62 ha, no registration error or wind; nothing was built or flown.

title: If one scout drone feeds ground treaters in a pipeline, can a held fleet beat inline weeding robots?
summary: A stdlib scheduling follow-up to osrobot-pairprice using its fitted per-field minutes (no new simulation; every price an assumed round number). Set-up and battery swaps make the scout nearly as slow as the treater, so one scout keeps only 0.99 to 1.33 treaters busy and the cheapest pipeline is always one scout with one treater. Overlapping the stages cuts the held-pair penalty to 1.04 times the inline fleet at 0.72 ha fields (32 fields) and 0.86 at 1.62 ha, from 1.34 and 1.16; at 0.18 ha it stays 1.48 to 1.81 times. Extra treaters finish sooner but raise cost per hectare (13.92 to 24.56 USD for 1 to 5). Stylised: deterministic, equal fields, no weather or failures.

title: When does one shared robot beat a dedicated robot per job in a pick-and-place shop?
summary: A stdlib extension of osrobot-specialise equips a shop of 2 to 8 pick-and-place trays three ways: a robot per job, one shared gantry spanning all trays, or one shared arm, on capital cost over 200 random job mixes per row. Sharing wins only while the total load fits one machine (4 jobs at scatter 0.4 m: shared cheapest in every mix at demand 0.2 of a gantry per job, a robot per job from 0.3) and only while changeover is short (a robot per job in 99% of mixes at 1,800 s). Trays spread beyond about 0.6 m erode the saving. The shared arm can hold 1 to 2 mm in only 13% of default mixes, but is cheapest in about half of mixes with loose (5 and 10 mm) tolerances. Stylised: every cost, speed, demand and changeover figure is assumed.

title: Does a fast scout platform plus a ground treater beat one weeding robot, and does a mud-aware tour matter?
summary: A stdlib follow-up to osrobot-fieldtour that makes the scout a second platform with its own swath and detector, then compares at matched kill because both platforms lose detections as they speed up. With a 3 m scout swath at 1 m/s the pair kills 0.343 in 26.6 min against about 42 min for one inline robot interpolated to the same kill; with the scout's swath cut to the ground robot's 1 m the same kill takes 47.3 min and the pair loses by about 13%. The saving is the swath ratio, not the second vehicle. A mud-aware tour changes the total by 0.1 min or less at 0 to 80% mud. Assumed constants, no registration error and no pipelining or capital cost: stylised, simulation only.

title: When does a purpose-built gantry beat a general two-link arm at tray pick-and-place?
summary: A stdlib model compares an XY gantry with an equal-link planar arm over a square work area, on cost per good pick per hour. At 2 mm tolerance the gantry wins up to 0.35 m and above about 1.0 m; the arm wins between 0.36 and 0.99 m. Tolerance below 1 mm removes the arm’s band, and the band depends heavily on the assumed cost coefficients (halving the gantry’s removes it). Stylised: every cost, mass, speed and accuracy figure is assumed, and only one task is modelled.

title: How heavy must a purpose-built UAV for targeted observation be, and when does a hover-capable airframe stop being worth its weight?
summary: A stdlib mass-closure sizing model closes a quadrotor, a fixed wing and a fixed wing with a vertical-lift system for the same mission, choosing rotor diameter or wing area for least mass. For 3 km out, 20 min on station and a 0.5 kg payload the plain fixed wing is lightest (1.27 kg), against 2.14 kg for the quadrotor and 2.08 kg for the VTOL wing. The quadrotor does not close at 45 min on station; the VTOL wing is lighter than it from 30 min or beyond about 10 km. Stylised: every technology constant is assumed, no flight stack was run, and a fixed wing cannot hover or launch unaided.

title: How much heavier must an observation UAV be if the wind is uncertain, and is designing to a wind quantile cheaper than a bigger battery reserve?
summary: A stdlib extension of osrobot-uavwind draws one along-track wind per mission from a normal distribution (exact discretisation, no sampling noise) and sizes the airframe for a quantile of it. For a 3 km, 20 min, 0.5 kg mission with wind ~ N(8, 3) m/s, designing to the 95th-percentile wind (12.9 m/s) costs the fixed wing +3.7% mass (1.333 against 1.286 kg) and the multirotor +11.7% (2.518 against 2.254 kg). The standard 20% reserve, if it may be spent, already lifts a mean-wind design to 0.95 (fixed wing) and 0.99 (multirotor) success, and a larger reserve and a quantile design cost within a few percent of each other. At a 1 min stay the 95th-percentile design flips the lightest airframe from multirotor to fixed wing. Stylised: one steady wind per mission, assumed constants, no turbulence, no launch limit, and no flight.

title: If an observation UAV only launches when the forecast wind is below a limit, how much does forecast error bring failures back, and what does it cost in scrubbed missions?
summary: A stdlib extension of osrobot-uavgust sizes the airframe for a launch limit wind and launches only if the forecast of the wind is at most that limit, with a normal forecast error (exact discretisation, no sampling noise). With a perfect forecast every failure becomes a scrub (fixed wing, wind ~ N(5, 4) m/s: 48% scrubbed at the median limit, 4.6% at the 95th percentile, 1.274 to 1.313 kg). A 2 m/s forecast error brings the failure rate to 6.8% at the median limit but only 1.1% at the 95th-percentile limit. Stylised: one steady wind per mission, assumed constants, normal forecast error, no cost put on a scrub.

title: If a scrubbed observation-UAV launch can be retried later the same day, how much does persistent wind limit what retrying buys, and does retrying bring failures back?
summary: A stdlib extension of osrobot-uavnogo lets the crew look again at the forecast in up to 8 slots a day, with wind following a Markov chain of persistence ρ (exact probabilities, no sampling noise). Fixed wing, wind ~ |N(5, 4)| m/s, limit at the median wind, perfect forecast: one slot completes 52.0% of days, and eight slots complete 99.7% with independent wind but 97.0%, 87.2% and 71.5% at ρ = 0.5, 0.8 and 0.95. With a 2 m/s forecast error each retry is another draw of the error, so eight slots raise the failure share from 6.8% to 13.6% of days (23.7% at ρ = 0.95). Stylised: assumed constants, one steady wind per slot, forecast errors independent between slots, no abort, no value on a mission. Nothing was flown.

title: What is a UAV launch wind limit worth in money, and should the launch threshold sit below the design limit when the forecast is wrong?
summary: A stdlib extension of osrobot-uavnogo puts a money value on a completed observation, the loss of an aircraft on a failure and a scrubbed day, then searches the design wind limit L and the launch threshold T together (exact probabilities, no sampling noise). With a cheap airframe ($1,500/kg, assumed) the best design is for nearly every wind (L at 14 m/s or more in 17 of 18 cases, 11 on the grid edge) and the rule barely matters. With an expensive one ($30,000/kg, assumed) the optimum is interior, and with a 2 m/s forecast error the best T sits 1 to 6 m/s below L in all 9 cases, worth up to $284 per attempt over tying T to L, with failures at or below 0.1%. Money figures are assumptions, many optima sit on the grid edge, and a failure is assumed to lose the whole airframe. Stylised, no aircraft designed or flown.

title: Does a steady wind change which purpose-built observation UAV is lightest, and what is wind worth to a multirotor?
summary: A stdlib extension of the osrobot-uav mass-closure sizing adds a steady wind: headwind out, tailwind back, airspeed re-optimised, and station-keeping at airspeed equal to the wind. For 3 km out, 20 min on station and 0.5 kg the plain fixed wing stays lightest at every wind from 0 to 18 m/s (1.27 kg at 0, 1.30 at 10, 1.50 at 18); the quadrotor goes 2.14 → 2.33 → 2.86 → 7.0 kg at 0, 10, 15 and 18 m/s and the VTOL wing 2.08 → 2.54. The multirotor’s one win in still air (1 min on station) lasts to about 8 m/s. Designs sized for still air keep 17.2 (fixed wing) and 18.5 min (multirotor) of 20 at 9 m/s and 8.8 and 13.8 at 15 m/s; building for 15 m/s costs 34% (multirotor) and 9% (fixed wing) in mass. Crediting the multirotor with translational lift makes its mass fall to 1.71 kg at 10 m/s, an optimistic artefact of a steady known wind. Stylised: assumed coefficients, no gusts, crosswind or launch limits, nothing flown.

title: What does a shared pick-and-place robot cost once it has to stay up, and do spares change when sharing beats a robot per job?
summary: A stdlib extension of osrobot-reconfig adds independent unit failures (availability A) and buys the fewest spares that meet a service target, either per job or for every job at once (200 random job mixes per row, seed 7). While the shared robot's load fits one machine, spares change nothing in the per-job comparison: the shared fleet costs 0.68 of a robot per job at 4 jobs, A = 0.95, target 0.99, with or without spares. Asking every job to be up at once favours sharing (0.34 to 0.51 at 4 jobs, A 0.90 to 0.99; 0.41 at 8 jobs, A = 0.95), because a shared robot fails every job together while four independent jobs each need a spare. At demand 0.3 per job spares close the gap load opened (1.34 bare, 1.01 with spares). Limits: “served in full” is all or nothing, failures are independent with unlimited repair crews, and one assumed availability covers every machine. Stylised; no price or MTBF is sourced.

title: Can a DiLoCo-style run hide its synchronisation by applying the outer update rounds late?
summary: Applying the outer step τ rounds late gives a mode the recursion x t +1 = x t − α s x t − τ , stable iff α s < 2 sin(π/(4τ+2)) ≈ π/(2τ+1). The best step sits at that edge, so the rate is 1 − 2 sin(π/(4τ+2))/κ H (exactly κ H /(κ H +1) at τ=1), and outer momentum stops helping the moment τ ≥ 1 (69 rounds at τ=0 become 1388 at κ H =100). Even with the sync fully hidden the gain over blocking averaging is at most (τ+1) sin(π/(4τ+2)) ≤ 1, and an exact search over ( H , τ) finds overlapped training 1.5–4.9× slower than blocking averaging and 2.3–31× slower than blocking with tuned momentum. Giving the fresh pseudo-gradient weight above ½ removes the penalty entirely (stable for every τ; at weight 0.75 and τ=1 the stale term acts as negative momentum, 2× faster than no delay). Stylised: noiseless quadratic, shared Hessian, one common delay.

title: How should the outer optimiser and sync interval be set when workers run H local steps per round?
summary: On a quadratic, H inner steps make the outer optimiser see curvatures 1 − (1 − η a ) H , which saturate at 1: the outer condition number shrinks from κ to about κ/ H (1000 → 16.1 at H =64). Per-round rates are exact 2×2 spectral radii (matching literal simulation), the tuned heavy-ball outer step puts every mode at exactly √β*, and the best momentum falls from 0.88 at H =1 to 0.01 at H =1024, so a fixed Nesterov 0.7/0.9 needs 4–8× more rounds. With a sync costing C inner steps, the wallclock-optimal interval is H * ≈ C , worth about √ C /2 over syncing every step (16× at C =1000), while plain averaging has no interior optimum. Stylised: noiseless quadratic with a shared Hessian.

title: What happens to local SGD when workers drop in and out?
summary: Each of N workers joins a round with probability p . Averaging the participants has exact stationary variance α V w m /( s (2−α s )) with m = E [1/ K | K ≥1]; dividing by the expected count instead is stable only for α s < 2/ c , c = 1+(1− p )/( Np ), and cannot contract faster than 1−1/ c per round (0.22 at N =32, p =0.1). At matched speed the fixed normaliser is quieter at small steps by E [ K | K ≥1]· E [1/ K | K ≥1] (1.34×), and averaging wins only at fast rates. Reliable workers bias the fixed point (0.467 instead of 1.000 in our example) unless displacements are inverse-propensity weighted. Matched to simulation within 0.5%. Stylised.

title: A twin whose sensor never produces outliers: how many particles does a bootstrap filter need, and is the average effective sample size the right thing to size on?
summary: For a bootstrap particle filter the large- N effective-sample-size fraction is exactly c 0 e − ay ² in the measurement y ( c 0 = 0.866, a = 1/6 at P = R = 1). With 5% real outliers at 10× the noise scale the mean ESS fraction barely moves (0.671 in the twin, 0.645 real, at every dimension), but P(ESS < 1% of N ) goes from 2.5×10 −4 to 3.1×10 −2 (120×). Sizing N = 528 for ESS ≥ 50 at 1% failure in the twin fails 4.4% of real steps, and the particle posterior mean's error against the exact Kalman update is 45× to 421× the twin's for N = 50 to 1000, falling barely at all with N . The large- N formula is checked against quadrature and simulation and fails once Nρ is small (reported). Stylised: scalar update, simulated outliers, no resampling dynamics.

title: How noisy is peer-prediction pay with finitely many tasks?
summary: The plug-in multi-task payment (agreement minus the agreement implied by empirical frequencies) is exactly twice the sample covariance of two verifiers’ reports, so its variance is available in closed form and matches full enumeration; it is √2 less noisy than drawing fresh penalty tasks and pays a constant reporter exactly 0. Under limited liability a verifier who does no work still collects a noise rent ≈ σ/√(2π) (0.020 against 0.208 honest at n=100). A deductible removes it in closed form, but killing 99% of the rent costs the honest verifier 54% of its pay. Detection needs 56–329 tasks for g=0.7–0.3 (simulated power 0.94–0.95), and ranking two close verifiers takes ~870. Binary conditionally independent reports. Stylised.

title: How do you pay for effort when nobody knows the truth?
summary: Peer prediction for unverifiable labelling and judging work: output agreement pays 1.0 for always answering the majority label versus 0.68 for honesty, the Dasgupta–Ghosh payoff is exactly 2p(1−p)g i g j , effort becomes a coordination game with a closed-form threshold (12.8× higher for rare-positive tasks), and a cost-optimal gold-check rate √(c·g H /G) removes the shirking equilibrium. Stylised.

title: Should a pipeline replicate stages or skip them?
summary: A microbatch crosses L stages held by workers that come and go. The drop probability is the exact binomial tail P(Bin(L,q)>s) with stage outage q = ρ + (1−ρ)(1−a) r , so replicas cannot lift success above the shared-domain floor (1−ρ) L : at L=48, ρ=10 −3 no r reaches a 1% drop rate, but allowing one skipped stage makes r=3 enough. At a=0.9 a four-stage skip budget cuts the workers for a 10 −3 drop rate from 240 to 96; under a per-skip quality loss κ the cost-optimal design is skip-heavy for cheap skips and moves to replication as κ grows (gain over no-skip 2.9× down to 1.08×). Independent outages, multiplicative skip penalty. Stylised.

title: What is a seat in a prediction market worth?
summary: In a sequential LMSR verification market the verifier in position k earns in expectation b ·I( y ; s k | s < k ), a conditional mutual information, so seat rents telescope to the maker’s expected loss (at most b ln 2); an explicit cost-function simulation agrees to three decimals. Rents fall with position, the successive ratio approaching e −C (Chernoff information) from below; order only redistributes a fixed total (a 0.9-accurate verifier gets 0.368 of 0.407 first, 0.303 last). With entry cost c , accuracy improves roughly as 1/ b : 11 verifiers at b =0.25 (92%), 41 at b =5 (99.6%). Myopic traders, symmetric signals, monotonicity numerical.

title: How should a verifier's vector report be scored?
summary: For a report of an expected drift r ∈ ℝ d with noise covariance Σ, every quadratic Bregman score −( y − r ) T A ( y − r ) is proper and charges a misreport D exactly D T AD . Against a trusted reference the per-task gap has exact mean D T AD and variance 4 D T A Σ AD for any noise law, and Cauchy–Schwarz shows A =Σ −1 has the best signal to noise for every deviation at once, needing 4 z ²/( D T Σ −1 D ) tasks. An isotropic score has efficiency at least 4κ/(1+κ)² (Kantorovich), attained by a deviation split between the extreme eigendirections: 25× more tasks at condition number 100, and power 0.29 against 0.80 at 48 tasks in simulation. Per-layer normalisation alone barely helps; with Σ estimated from m reference draws, efficiency is 0.61 at m =2 d and 0.95 at m =100. Quadratic scores, trusted reference, finite covariance.

title: How much accuracy can a market buy from contributors who value their privacy?
summary: A market pays each contributor the log-score gain of a public Gaussian belief for releasing a statistic plus Gaussian-mechanism noise, so the expected payment is exactly the information released, ½λln(1+τ/a). The best noise is a closed-form quadratic root, and participation is possible if and only if κa < 1 with κ = cΔ 2 /λ: precision is capped at λ/(cΔ 2 ) however many contributors arrive, approached geometrically at rate 2σ 2 /(2σ 2 +κ), and total payout is at most ½λln(1/(κa 0 )). Early arrivals add too little noise (1.5–5×; 1–22% welfare loss against a planner), and admitting small data holders first lifts final precision from 28.0 to 34.2. Checked against grid search and 10 6 -run Monte Carlo. Stylised.

title: The subsidy cost of privacy in prediction markets
summary: Differentially private LMSR via the binary-tree mechanism: error scales as 1/(bε), tree noise beats per-release noise ~15×, and privacy noise is exploitable so market-maker loss far exceeds b ln 2. Stylised.

title: Property elicitation for verifiable ML training
summary: Quantile, expectile and Bregman scoring rules, a check that variance is not elicitable alone but is jointly, and a study of pricing benign-drift thresholds for replica verification.

title: What does a Kalman filter tuned in an ideal-sensor twin cost on a quantizing real sensor?
summary: A twin whose sensor is ideal ( y = x + v ) tunes the gain for variance R , but the real sensor rounds to a step D . In simulation ( a =0.9, Q =1) the twin’s gain costs +11% at D =4 for R =1, and up to +64% when R =0.01. Retuning on R + D 2 /12 (Sheppard) lands within 1% of the best gain in all 12 configurations, but its closed-form MSE claim under-predicts the real error by 28–43% once D exceeds the state’s scale (1.61 vs 2.82 at D =8, R =0.01). Stylised: scalar linear-Gaussian plant, fixed gain, one seed per cell.

title: How many bits does a probability report need?
summary: Regret of reporting from a finite grid under Brier and log scores: a high-resolution law for the optimal grid (matched to 0.3%), a ln N loss for uniform grids under log score, and a 13× penalty for raw minifloat formats versus symmetrised ones. Stylised.

title: How much load can a shared lab instrument carry when its twin assumes exponential service?
summary: With Poisson arrivals and one server, the mean wait is exactly ρ (1+ c 2 )/(2(1− ρ )) service times (Pollaczek–Khinchine; matched to a 1.5-million-job simulation within one standard error), so a twin with exponential service is off by (1+ c 2 )/2 at every load. At a mean-wait SLA of 2 service times the twin admits ρ =0.667 while the real instrument admits 0.444 ( c 2 =4) or 0.133 ( c 2 =25): real mean waits 2.5× to 13× the SLA, and 11.7× the twin’s tail-exceedance claim at c 2 =4. With a Pareto tail of index below 2 the real mean wait is infinite. A negative repair result: a plug-in c 2 fitted from n logged service times violates the SLA in 70–89% of repeats for n =25–1600, and a 90% bootstrap bound still 46% at n =1600. Stylised (Poisson arrivals, one server, simulated “real” instrument).

title: Who drops out of a race when workers have unequal costs?
summary: If only the first k of n finishers are paid, a slow worker entering at a vanishing rate wins with probability rate × E X ( k ) of the fast workers, which gives an exact exit rule: workers with cost ratio c s / c f ≥ n f /( n f − k ) stay out entirely, and paying k ≥ n f never excludes anyone (checked by best-entry payoffs at thresholds 4/3, 2, 4). At cost ratio 4 with four fast workers, k ≤ 3 shuts the slow ones out and k =4..7 readmits them (share of prizes 0.21→0.46 against a fair 0.5). The note also proves the telescoping identity behind the symmetric race and shows that with convex speed cost, headcount does buy speed. Two cost types, exponential races, grid-checked equilibria.

title: What does a Gaussian-clutter radar simulator do to a CFAR detector's false-alarm rate?
summary: A CA-CFAR threshold set in a Gaussian-clutter twin and deployed in gamma-textured (K-distributed) clutter has an exact false-alarm law, matched to direct simulation to ~1%. At design 10 −4 the real rate is 9× (ν=5) to 30× (ν=2) too high, and 50× to 358× at 10 −6 ; restoring it costs 1.9–3.7 dB of threshold at 10 −4 . If texture is shared across the window CFAR is unaffected, so the twin must model spatial correlation. A moment fit of ν from 1000 real clutter cells brings the median to 1.1× (90th percentile 2×), versus ~10 6 cells to threshold empirically. Stylised: no target, no measured data.

title: What does a Gaussian-clutter radar twin promise about detection, not just false alarms?
summary: With CA- and OS-CFAR thresholds set in a Gaussian twin and deployed in gamma-textured clutter, the exact false-alarm and detection laws (including a new one-dimensional OS-CFAR law) match simulation to ~1%. OS-CFAR is inflated much like CA (design 1e-4, ν=2: 30× vs 35×). Repairing the threshold costs 3.7–4.6 dB, yet the SNR needed for Pd = 0.9 at Pfa = 1e-4 is 6.3 dB above the twin’s promise at ν=2 (2.8 dB at ν=5, 0.8 dB at ν=20), and at the twin’s own threshold and promised SNR real Pd is 0.84 while Pfa is 30× design. Texture does not reverse the CA-beats-OS ranking (a negative result). Stylised: iid gamma texture, constant-SNR target, no interferers, no real radar data.

title: Is a clear-air or mean-rain-rate radar twin right when rain comes in cells?
summary: Radar detection range under intermittent rain attenuation. The power law in rain rate has a Jensen gap (1.52× the mean-rate attenuation), so a mean-rate twin (closed-form Lambert W range, 18.84 km) is reached by only 39% of real storm fields; matching the mean attenuation barely helps (Brier 0.054 vs 0.055). A rain ensemble scores 0.038 vs 0.101 for clear air, and long cells flip the mean-rate twin from optimistic to pessimistic. Stylised: simulated rain, illustrative coefficients, no radar data.

title: How wide should domain randomization be, and what does it buy?
summary: Randomizing the twin's input gain over ±ε trains a more conservative gain (monotone in ε; small-width law k ε − k * = −(ε b ) 2 J kbb /(6 J kk )) at a quartic price when the twin was right, and moves the deployment stability cliff out by about 15%. At 2.3× the twin's gain the nominal controller has regret 84 versus 1.4 at ε=0.9. But uniform-average training is not minimax: its worst-case regret exceeds the nominal gain's for ε ≤ 0.7, and the best width equals the prior's half-width, paying off only when the prior reaches the cliff. Stylised.

title: What does a twin whose sensor reads at any distance get wrong about a loop with a range-limited lidar or radar?
summary: A twin with unlimited sensor range predicts geometric convergence; a real sensor reading clip( x , − R , R ) caps the approach speed at kR . The exact step-count law matches simulation in 108/108 cases; for k =0.25 the twin says 49 steps from 1000 R and the real loop takes 4021 (82×), an error linear in x 0 / R with slope 1/ k . For a PI loop the twin's overshoot is neither a bound nor a lower bound: smaller at 2–5 R , 4.1× larger at 1000 R ; conditional integration repairs overshoot but not settling time. Logs within range fit the gain exactly and cannot reveal R ; from logs uniform on [− L , L ] the fitted gain factor is 1.5 q −0.5 q 3 , q = R / L . Stylised: scalar noiseless loop, hard symmetric clip.

title: What does it cost to pay for a ranking instead of probabilities?
summary: A verifier who reports only the order of K classes can be paid with a score linear in the outcome indicator. It is strictly proper, and swapping two classes at adjacent ranks costs exactly (p i −p j )(w r −w r+1 ), linear in the gap. Per unit of payment range that beats a Brier-derived ranking whenever the gap is below 1/(K−1) (2.5× at gap 0.1, 250× at 0.001, K=5). Equal spacing maximises the smallest incentive, ranking everything costs K−1 times the mode, a top-k set costs the same as the mode, and the sample size to detect a swap is identical to Brier’s.

title: If a twin gives every scene the same inlier fraction, how many RANSAC iterations does it say we need, and is that enough when real scenes vary?
summary: With N = 100 correspondences, minimal sample 2 and 50% mean inliers, the twin's budget for 99% success is 17 iterations. If the real scene inlier count is beta-binomial with concentration κ, the exact failure at 17 iterations is 1.3% (binomial variation only), 7.0% (κ = 10) and 14.1% (κ = 4); restoring 99% takes 19, 58 and 458 iterations, and for κ ≤ 2 no budget exists because scenes with fewer than 2 inliers cannot succeed. Exact values match a sampler, and an end-to-end noisy line fit goes from 0.9% to 12.6% slope failures at κ = 4 (1.8% with the larger budget, still above 1%). Stylised: assumed scene law, line fitting only, no real data.

title: How far over its limit can a rate limiter be pushed in a true rolling window?
summary: A stylised free-choice study of five limiters configured as L requests per window W , by adversarial search on an integer tick clock and a Poisson overload test. Only the sliding log never admits more than L in a rolling window. The sliding-window counter admits up to about 1.4–1.5 L (1.40, 1.45, 1.48 for W = 20, 40, 100), and token and leaky buckets admit 1.90–1.98 L ; fixed window reaches 2 L . At 1.5× offered Poisson load, 47% of rolling windows exceed L for fixed window, 39% for the buckets, 8.8% for the sliding counter and none for the sliding log. The searches give lower bounds, not proofs; one client, no distributed state.

title: Which surrogate should train a verifier that can escalate?
summary: Reject-option surrogates for accept/reject/escalate decisions: the generalised-hinge conditional risk embeds the Bayes action at its kinks, regret transfers linearly with constant exactly 2d (grid-verified), logistic transfer degrades as 2d(1−d)/δ, and a negative result shows logistic-plus-thresholds still learns faster in scalar SGD. Stylised.

title: How often should a mapping team rendezvous when its twin's odometry drift has no bias?
summary: Robots reset their dead-reckoning error at rendezvous; the real error variance is s 2 t + b 2 t 2 (white noise plus a per-run bias rate), but a twin fitted on short-horizon increments sees only the first term, so it plans a rendezvous every 10 and claims a peak error std of 3.16. The real optimum solves a cubic; at a bias/noise ratio ρ = 0.1/0.3/1/3 the twin's interval has 0.19/1.35/8.65/34.6% regret, the real error is exactly √(1+ρ) times the claim, and under an error budget the twin breaches it for 8–55% of every cycle. In the pairwise frame used for map merging a shared bias cancels (twin regret 5.3% → 0.10% at bias correlation 0.9). Repair needs ground-truth error at a long lag as well as a short one and about 5–10 runs to beat the twin reliably. Variance law and pairwise law checked by Monte Carlo. Stylised: one-dimensional Gaussian error, constant per-run bias, perfect reset.

title: When should a continual learner replay an old task, and does a fixed schedule beat random replay?
summary: Replaying a task alongside each fresh one is a joint projection, so the expected loss on a tracked task is an exact product of 2×2 matrices for any schedule (matched to simulation at every step; recovers the no-replay law). One replay is best at the forgetting-peak lag — 5 at d =32, r =4; 89 at d =128, r =1 — yet removes only 25–42% of total forgetting (replaying at step 1 barely helps at small r / d ). A period longer than the peak lag never touches the peak, and a fixed period beats random replay at the same rate only below roughly 1.2–3 peak lags (e.g. 1/8 at d =32, r =4, but random wins at 1/12). Halving forgetting needs a rate 0.25 at d =12, r =3 and 0.015 at d =128, r =1; tasks with 2 r ≥ d are fully recovered by one replay. Stylised: realizable linear regression, exact convergence, one tracked task.

title: How much of an old task must a continual learner store, and is it better to replay a little often or a lot rarely?
summary: If only m of an old task’s r examples are stored, replaying them with a fresh task is “project out the stored subspace, then take a plain step in dimension d − m ”. That gives an exact 2×2 mean-state matrix interpolating no replay ( m =0) and full replay ( m = r , matched to replay-law to 12 digits), agreeing with simulation at every step. One replay at its best step recovers a fraction of the full saving that is nearly linear in m / r (0.23, 0.47, 0.72 at ¼, ½, ¾ for d =12, r =4; within 0.004 of m / r at d =128, r =8). At a fixed rate, half the memory buys 57–65% of the saving. At a fixed budget of examples per step, one large replay beats many small ones, but only by 0.1–2 points of total forgetting in wide models and up to 6 in a tight one ( d =12, r =4), so buffer size matters more than schedule. Stylised: realizable linear regression, exact convergence, one tracked task.

title: One long twin run or many replications when every run starts in the wrong state?
summary: Splitting a fixed budget of N twin draws into r replications, each started at an offset and with d draws deleted, gives iid replication means, but the warm-up bias does not shrink with r . For an AR(1) the MSE and the exact coverage of the Student- t interval are closed-form (0.921 vs 0.921 simulated at r =50): a single run minimises MSE, replication costs at most 1.07× at φ =0.9 but 2.2× at φ =0.99, and the nominal-95% interval covers 92% at the MSE-optimal deletion once replications are short (no deletion reaches 94% at 40 draws each). Single-run batch means were not worse in this model. Preliminary M/M/1 simulation: 30 short replications cover 5.8% of the time, and no setting tried reaches 95%. Stylised: Gaussian AR(1), one start offset, simulated “real” system.

title: What does secret task assignment buy?
summary: Random k-fold replication with slashing against a colluding fraction β of workers: with secret assignment cheating is a coordination game and honesty is the unique equilibrium iff S ≥ Gβ k−1 /(1−β k−1 ), geometric in k; with public assignment colluders cheat only on all-friend jobs, so corruption is β k at any stake; a leak probability λ leaves a λβ k floor, so each order of magnitude of leakage costs about two replicas. Formulas match Monte Carlo. Stylised.

title: Reproducible operators and refereed training
summary: Measured float32 drift across reduction orders (relative drift is Cauchy-tailed, state-level drift is a few ulps), a Merkle-committed training trace with a teacher-forced referee, and the finding that a per-step tolerance is a cumulative hidden-deviation budget while bitwise-reproducible operators remove it.

title: How many retries does a grasp need when the simulator treats attempts as independent?
summary: A pick skill is retried until success. The twin draws attempts independently at p = 0.6; in the “real” system each object has a latent success probability (Beta, same mean), so single-attempt validation cannot tell them apart while attempts on one object are correlated. Real failure after k attempts is exactly ∏( b + j )/( a + b + j ), a power law k − a against the twin’s geometric law (matched to simulation). At the twin’s 6-attempt budget for δ = 0.01 (claimed 0.004) real failure is 0.010, 0.042 or 0.151 at correlation 0.05, 0.2 or 0.5, and the budget actually needed is 7, 13 or 571. The payoff cost of a wrong budget is mostly small (0–6%, 23% in one case) because the optimal give-up rule is closed-form. Two forced attempts per object identify the correlation, but a budget aimed at δ still needs a safety margin (met in 51–79% of repeats). Stylised.

title: What do risk-averse verifiers report under proper scoring?
summary: Proper scoring rules are truthful only for risk-neutral agents. For a CARA verifier the log score yields reported odds exactly equal to true odds^(1/(1+k)), k = αb; the Brier score yields logit p = logit r + k(2r−1), which the principal can invert exactly. Summing reported logits under-extremises (log-loss 0.332 vs 0.214 at k=2); correcting with the mean k under heterogeneous verifiers is worse than not correcting; a log-score report needs true belief 0.964 to clear a 0.9 accept threshold at k=0.5. A binarised lottery rule is truthful for every increasing utility at a 2.6–27% certainty-equivalent cost. Stylised.

title: Does arm torque or jaw friction limit how fast an arm carries a printed part?
summary: A follow-up to robofab-graspmove and robofab-reach : a planar two-link arm with assumed masses carries each of the six free parts of the toy gripper on a min-jerk joint move, as fast as an assumed joint torque limit allows. With 0.12 m links and 5 N m the carries take 0.06 to 0.10 s and the 5.95 g cover needs 1.25 N per jaw, 21× its static force; a jaw force under about 0.5 N makes the grip, not the arm, the limit. A larger arm is slower at a fixed torque. Stylised: assumed masses and torques, and the grip bound, simulated only up to 40 m/s 2 earlier, is applied beyond that range.

title: How much carry time does a time-optimal move save over min-jerk, and what does it cost the jaws?
summary: A follow-up to robofab-armaccel : the same planar two-link arm carries the six free parts of the toy gripper along the same joint-space line, once with min-jerk and once with the time-optimal speed profile under an assumed joint torque limit. Over nine arm and torque cases the six-part total time falls by 21–29%, but the per-jaw force bound rises 1.2–2.4×. Stylised: every parameter except the geometry is assumed, the grip bound is not re-simulated above 40 m/s 2 , and the path is fixed.

title: Does a stiffer friction cone make the held-bar result in robofab-liftload threshold-free?
summary: A follow-up to robofab-sliprate , which traced the bar’s creep to MuJoCo’s contact settings. Raising the impratio option from 1 to 1000 cuts the creep of a 10×10×40 mm bar held at one end from 3.66 to 0.004 deg/s, roughly as 1/ impratio . From impratio 10 the minimum holding forces for 1° and 5° tolerances agree within 26% in all 12 cases, so the answer no longer depends on the threshold. The simulated force is below the uniform-pressure torque bracket in 10 of 12 cases (0.67–1.17× its lower bound) and 1.15–1.67× a point-contact bound built on the five contacts per pad MuJoCo reports. One engine, one bar section, no torsional friction. Stylised and preliminary.

title: Can a printed gripper assemble its own next generation?
summary: A follow-up to the self-parts project: the arm that builds generation k+1 is the printed gripper of generation k, with an assumed jaw opening of 32 s − 2 t mm for fixed-size pads of thickness t . Exhaustive assembly search gives a required opening of exactly 30 s mm, so a gripper can build a copy only at scale s ≥ t (scale 4 for 4 mm pads), and a stroke cap S admits one only if 30 t ≤ S . Seeds of 130 and 140 mm sustain a chain; 60 and 100 mm seeds shrink and stop. Largely algebraic given the assumed opening; one toy design; simulation only.

title: Which resource limits a small robot-printer-inspection cell, and does the busiest one tell you what to upgrade?
summary: A discrete-event twin of one arm, 1–8 printers and one inspection station (30 parts, 200 replications, illustrative times). Printers have the highest utilisation at every size, yet at 6 printers an extra arm saves 10.9 min of makespan against 2.3 for an extra inspection station, because a printer is held while it waits for the arm. Dispatch rules trade makespan for mean flow time as textbook scheduling predicts, and a mean-value twin underestimates the stochastic makespan by 1–133 min. Stylised; parameters are invented, not measured.

title: Can a blocking-aware correction to queueing analysis predict a robot-printer cell across loads?
summary: A follow-up to the held-printer project: held demand plus a fitted stall (printers waiting for the arm to unload them) helps only at saturation (1.4% mean error) and double-counts load and unload time elsewhere (8.5%). A predictor that keeps latency (plain demand plus stall) apart from capacity (held demand plus stall) scores 3.6% against 4.7% for plain MVA on 32 design settings, but ties plain MVA on a held-out job mix (3.4% against 3.5%) and still underestimates by up to 8% at moderate load. Stylised; illustrative times; 20 seeds.

title: Where is the bottleneck of an arm, printer and inspection cell?
summary: A hand-written discrete-event twin of one arm that loads and unloads P 3D printers, plus an inspection station with reprints, against a utilisation bound. The bound names the bottleneck (printers up to 10 printers, the arm from 12, about 12.7 good parts/h) and the simulation reaches it within 1–2% far from the switch but sits 10–11% below it at 10–12 printers. A 25% faster arm lifts throughput from 11.34 to 12.68 parts/h at 12 printers while a second inspector does nothing; arm dispatch rules made no measurable gain, and WIP beyond one job per printer plus one only lengthens flow time. Stylised parameters of my choosing, no travel or breakdowns, 20 seeds.

title: Is the error of queueing analysis of a robot-printer cell from print-time variability or from the cell's structure?
summary: An exact Markov-chain solution of a stylised cell (one arm, 2–6 printers held through load and unload, one inspector; Erlang print time, cv 0.33–1; illustrative times) used as a noise-free reference. It matches a simulation in 10 settings (largest |z| 1.73). Changing the print-time cv from 1 to 0.33 moves the exact throughput by at most 0.71%, so the error of mean value analysis is structural: plain MVA is within 0.6% when work in process equals the printer count but overshoots by up to 20.3% beyond it (mean error 12.8% at twice the printers), and held-demand MVA is 2.8% off at saturation but −5% to −12% off at low load. One job class, exponential load, unload and inspect times. Stylised, simulation-only.

title: Where does exact queueing analysis of a robot-printer cell stop working?
summary: A follow-up to the mean-value-analysis project: a coefficient-of-variation sweep (0–2, lognormal times, 4–16 printers, 20 seeds) and a directly measured printer stall share (finished parts waiting for the arm). At 12 printers the MVA error runs from −6.2% to +8.4% and crosses zero near cv 1, while the utilisation bound stays 8–25% high. Stall is small (about 4.6% at 8 printers), but holding the printer through load and unload plus the stall reproduces the saturated rate at 4 and 8 printers (8.59 against 8.56 ± 0.09). Stylised, illustrative times, simulation only.

title: Where should a print-failure detector's alarm threshold go in a robot-arm 3D-printer cell?
summary: Replaces the monitor project's fixed detection delay with a detector that looks at a print every few minutes and has a Gaussian score (separation d′) and an alarm threshold z, and asks which z maximises good parts per hour, with an exact analytic bound and a 40-seed discrete-event simulation (6 printers, 0.3 failures per printing hour, looks every 2 min). A threshold that sounds strict (z = 2, 2.3% false alarms per look) makes the cell 19–23% worse than blind printing for every detector quality, because a 60 min print is looked at 30 times; the best z is 3–3.5, and the gain over blind printing is +5.8% at d′ = 2, +9.7% at 3 and +11.3% at 4, and within noise below d′ of about 1. Stylised: looks are independent, which real consecutive frames are not.

title: Can a flow-equivalent-server decomposition predict a robot-printer cell's throughput without enumerating its states?
summary: A follow-up to the exact Markov-chain project: Norton’s theorem applied to the same stylised cell (one arm, 2–6 printers held through load and unload, one inspector; Erlang print time; illustrative times). The arm-and-printers subsystem is solved exactly at each population and replaced by one load-dependent server. Over the same 42 settings the mean absolute error against the exact chain is 0.32% (maximum 1.57%), against 6.8% (up to 20.3%) for plain mean value analysis and 4.3% for the held-printer variant; in five cells of 8–12 printers it is 0.09–0.31%. It underestimates in 38 of 42 settings because the cell is not product form. The subsystem chain is about a tenth the size of the full chain, but both solve in under a second here, so no speed claim. Stylised: one job class, exponential load, unload and inspect times.

title: Where does a flow-equivalent-server decomposition of a robot-printer cell go wrong as the inspector speeds up or slows down?
summary: A follow-up to the decomposition project, which reported a 0.32% mean error at one inspection time. Sweeping the inspection time from 0.1 to 100 min in 10 stylised cells (2–6 printers, Erlang-4 print time, illustrative times) against the exact Markov chain, the decomposition’s error is 0.000% for a fast inspector and at most 0.52% for a very slow one, but peaks at −2.2% to −5.0% (mean −3.2%) just below the knee t* = 1/H(N), where the inspector alone matches the subsystem’s rate (0.81–0.99 t*, grid-limited). It is never positive, and smaller cells err more. The explanation (ignored correlation between inspection queue and subsystem state) is untested. Stylised: one job class, exponential load, unload and inspect times.

title: Does holding the printer through load and unload fix queueing analysis of a robot-printer cell?
summary: A follow-up to the variability-sweep project: mean value analysis with the printer demand increased by the arm’s load and unload time, compared with plain MVA and two utilisation bounds against the simulated cell (cv 0.3 and 1.0, 4–16 printers, four loads, 20 seeds, 32 settings; illustrative times). The repair helps only at saturation (mean absolute error 2.9% against 8.2% for plain MVA) and hurts elsewhere (7.3% against 3.6%), so over all settings plain MVA is better (4.7% against 6.2%). A mixed result: no single demand setting is right across loads. Stylised and simulation-only.

title: Is a print-failure camera worth it in a robot-arm 3D-printer cell?
summary: Adds mid-print failures (0.3 per printing hour) to the arm, printers and inspection cell and compares blind printing with a camera that aborts a failing print after a delay, including false stops, against an analytic bound and a 40-seed discrete-event simulation. With a 10 min delay the camera adds 6–10% good parts per hour at 2–10 printers, 4.5% at 12 and 0.8% at 16 where the arm limits the cell; the gain falls with detection delay (11% for an instant camera, about 0.5% at 80 min), vanishes between 0.1 and 0.2 false aborts per printing hour, and grows with the failure rate (28% at 1.0 per hour). Stylised: memoryless failures, a fixed detection delay, no real detector or measured farm.

title: Does exact queueing analysis predict a robot-printer cell's throughput better than a utilisation bound?
summary: Mean value analysis of a closed arm, printers and inspection network, checked against a hand-written discrete-event simulation that adds one departure from product form at a time (illustrative times, 20 seeds). The code matches the exact Markov-chain solution on small networks. With exponential times MVA is within −6% to +4% of simulation; with less variable times it is up to 11% low. With printers held while waiting for the arm, MVA beats the utilisation bound at 4, 8 and 12 printers but not at 16, and it overshoots the saturation plateau at high work in process (9.8 against 8.6 parts/h at 8 printers). Stylised, simulation-only; no physical cell.

title: Does an arm-wait-aware printer demand fix queueing analysis of a robot-printer cell?
summary: A follow-up to the held-printer project: the printer’s demand is increased by the arm’s queueing delay, found as a fixed point from the arm’s own queue with no fitted parameter. Against the simulated cell (cv 0.3 and 1.0, 4–16 printers, four loads, 20 seeds, 32 settings; illustrative times) it underpredicts throughput in every setting and is worse overall: mean absolute error 7.9%, against 6.2% for held-demand MVA and 4.7% for plain MVA. At saturation it ties held demand (3.1% against 2.9%) but on the other 24 settings it is worse (9.5% against 7.3%). A negative result: a demand-side patch to product-form MVA is the wrong tool here. Stylised and simulation-only.

title: Once the solver is converged, is the time-optimal carry's edge over a tuned trapezoid still positive in all twelve speed-limited rows?
summary: A follow-up to robofab-scurvefine (stylised). Re-solving the time-optimal carry at 400, 1600 and 6400 nodes lowers the six-part total by 0.01 to 0.46%, and the edge over a ramp-resolved trapezoid, negative in 7 of 12 rows at 400 nodes, becomes +0.11 to +0.88% in every row at 6400. A one-step extrapolation moves it by at most 0.03 percentage points. The trapezoid's own ramp grid is not re-converged, which can only shrink the edge, and every parameter is assumed.

title: Can friction hold each printed part of a gripper?
summary: A follow-up to robofab-selfparts : for each of the six free parts of the toy gripper and each grasp axis that fits a 30 mm jaw opening, the smallest jaw force that holds the part against gravity by friction, from the bound m g /(2μ) and from a MuJoCo simulation, at μ = 0.3, 0.5 and 0.8. Over 33 cases the two agree to within 5%, and the force needed is at most 0.1 N, so in this model the jaw opening, not friction, is the binding constraint. A check on the simulator set-up rather than a new result. Stylised: static hold only, boxes, assumed density and friction, no tipping or insertion loads.

title: Does the jaw-force bound still hold at arm accelerations of 100 to 800 m/s²?
summary: A follow-up to robofab-graspmove and robofab-armaccel , which applied the bound m √(( g + a up ) 2 + a side 2 )/(2μ) beyond the 40 m/s 2 it had been tested to. Here a MuJoCo jaw assembly with prescribed constant acceleration (40 to 800 m/s 2 ) holds three printed parts of a toy gripper. With a 0.05 ms timestep and 0.1 ms contact time constant the simulated minimum force is 0.89 to 1.02 times the bound over 39 cases (median 1.00); with the earlier settings no force up to 60 N holds a part at 400 or 800 m/s 2 , a contact-lag artefact. Stylised: rigid box pads, one friction coefficient, no arm dynamics or trajectory.

title: How hard must the jaws squeeze while the arm moves?
summary: A follow-up to robofab-grasp : the jaw assembly accelerates upward or sideways at up to 40 m/s 2 and the smallest holding force is compared with the bound m √(( g + a up ) 2 + a side 2 )/(2μ) at μ = 0.5. Over 77 cases the two agree to within 7%, and the heaviest part needs at most 0.3 N, so friction is still not the constraint. A fidelity finding: the contact time constant used for the static test (0.004 s) reports slip at any force once the jaws accelerate; 0.0005 s is needed. Stylised: boxes, rigid pads, assumed density and friction.

title: Does an off-centre centre of mass need a harder grasp?
summary: A follow-up to robofab-liftload , whose torque bracket was inconclusive. A 20 mm cube is pinched with its centre of mass shifted 0 to 20 mm in the pad plane. For ball pads (one point contact, an assumed torsional friction coefficient of 2 mm) the elliptic-cone bound matches MuJoCo within 1.1% and the needed force rises 5× (0.097 to 0.50 N). For flat pads the twist is resisted at the corner contacts: MuJoCo lies between an equal-split upper bound and a best-split lower bound at all eight offsets, and needs 0.39× the ball-pad force at 10 mm. The result is insensitive to the rotation tolerance (1, 3, 10°). Stylised: rigid pads, assumed friction, static hold only.

title: Does an insertion policy tuned in one simulator survive a better one?
summary: Cross-entropy-tuned five-parameter peg-in-hole search policies in MuJoCo, trained on three simulator fidelity levels or with domain randomisation and tested on all three plus a held-out parameter set. Tuned on the simplest level, success is 0.91 there but 0.53 on the stiffer-contact level and 0.26 on the held-out one; training on the stiffer level or with randomisation gives 0.43–0.46 on the held-out set, and with 5 seeds the two cannot be ranked. No seed exceeds 0.61 on the held-out level. Toy planar task; sim-to-sim only.

title: How fast can an arm carry a printed part when the jaw force is capped as well as the joint torque?
summary: A follow-up to robofab-armbang : the time-optimal speed profile along the joint-space line is solved with an added cap on the per-jaw force bound (a quadratic constraint on the path acceleration), at 1.25–10× the static hold force, and compared with the fastest min-jerk move meeting the same two limits. Over nine arm and torque cases the time-optimal six-part total is 17–43% shorter, most when the cap is tightest, and at the tightest cap the torque limit no longer changes the time. Stylised: every parameter except the geometry is assumed, the caps are multiples of a friction hold force, the grip bound is not re-simulated above 40 m/s 2 , profiles overshoot the limits by up to 3%, and the path is fixed.

title: Does a joint-speed limit erase the time-optimal carry's advantage over min-jerk?
summary: A follow-up to robofab-jawcap (stylised, preliminary): a peak joint-speed limit is added to the torque and jaw-force limits of a planar two-link arm carrying printed parts. Over three arm sizes, three jaw caps and speed limits of 6 to 1 rad/s, the time-optimal profile is 28 to 46% shorter than min-jerk meeting the same limits (18 to 34% without a speed limit), and the saving tends to 1 − 1/1.875 = 47%, a property of the min-jerk profile shape, so a trapezoidal baseline would show less.
