All parameters are assumed; the speed limits are round numbers, not an actuator rating.

title: Does the friction-grasp bound survive lift acceleration and an off-centre centre of mass?
summary: A follow-up to robofab-grasp . With a constant lift or sideways acceleration applied as an effective gravity, the simulated minimum jaw force for the six free parts of the toy gripper stays within 6% of the scaled bound m √(( g + a z ) 2 + a t 2 )/(2μ) over 66 cases, at most 0.21 N. These parts are symmetric, so they test no torque. For a 10×10 mm bar held at one end the torque bracket is inconclusive: with a 5° rotation tolerance MuJoCo holds with less force than the lower bound in 11 of 12 cases, and with 1° the longer bars do not hold at 20 N. Stylised: constant load, boxes, assumed density and friction, thresholds chosen by me.

title: Is the motor-line edge of the time-optimal carry converged in solver nodes?
summary: Follow-up to robofab-motorcurve (stylised, preliminary). The same nine rows and five motor no-load speeds are solved at 400, 1600 and 6400 nodes. From 1600 to 6400 nodes the six-part time-optimal total changes by at most 0.29% and the edge over the tuned trapezoid by at most 0.28 points, so the 3.5 to 28.6% range stands. The exception is the 0.08 m, k = 2 row at w 0 = 4, whose edge rises from 4.98% to 5.26%. The cover part that had no profile at w 0 = 4 was a node-count limit: it solves at 6400 nodes. Limits: three node counts only, toy arm, assumed motor line.

title: Does the time-optimal carry's edge over a tuned trapezoid survive a motor torque-speed line?
summary: Follow-up to robofab-torquebound (stylised, preliminary). The same nine torque- and jaw-bound rows are re-solved with each joint's torque limit falling linearly with speed, 5 N m × (1 − |speed|/w 0 ), for no-load speeds w 0 of 20, 10, 6 and 4 rad/s. The time-optimal carry stays faster than the tuned trapezoid in every one of the 45 cells, but its edge is no longer one number: 3.5% to 28.6%, against 9.0% to 22.9% under a constant limit. Where a jaw cap binds on the smaller arms the edge shrinks as w 0 falls (22.9% to 5.0% for the 0.08 m arm, k = 2); where only torque binds it grows (9.0% to 28.6% for the 0.2 m arm). The constant-limit profiles reach joint speeds up to 139 rad/s, which no motor does. One planar arm, assumed parameters, a linear motor model, not checked in MuJoCo; simulated only.

title: Do the robofab carry results survive an independent physics engine?
summary: Follow-up to robofab-torquebound (stylised, preliminary). The two-link arm behind every robofab carry result is rebuilt in MuJoCo and the 108 actual profiles (best trapezoid and time-optimal, nine rows, six parts each) are checked with MuJoCo inverse dynamics. The hand-written joint torques agree to at most 1.8e-5 N m against a 5 N m limit, so the 9 to 23% edge is not an artefact of a dynamics bug. Where only torque binds, MuJoCo puts the trapezoid's peak at up to 5.037 N m (0.73% over) and the time-optimal profile's at up to 5.011 N m (0.21% over). An open-loop replay drifts up to 0.023 rad and 1.4 mm. Joint torques only: the jaw-force bound and motor model are not checked. Planar toy arm, assumed parameters; simulated only.

title: Is the trapezoid's duration in the torque- and jaw-bound rows set by peaks a sparse check never looked at?
summary: Follow-up to robofab-torquebound (stylised, preliminary). The nine torque- and jaw-bound rows are re-solved with a trapezoid check of 10,000 whole-move samples, 1,000 per ramp and both sides of the acceleration corners, against 201 plus 160 per ramp before. The six-part trapezoid totals change by between −0.15% and +0.15%, the time-optimal edge stays 9.5% to 23.0% (9.4% to 23.0% before), and the dense answers hold at ten times the density with an estimated missed peak of at most 0.25% of a limit. The large edge does not rest on unseen trapezoid peaks. One row goes the other way (dense trapezoid 0.15% faster) and its cause is not investigated. Stylised toy arm; no hardware.

title: How much of the gap between “the twin passes” and “it fails for real” does each twin fidelity close?
summary: A kinematic SCARA pick-and-place twin at three checking levels (geometry; plus joint, payload and deadline limits; plus stochastic grasp error, grip build-up and slip) against a held-out reference twin. Of 162 injected-bug mutants of three programs, 69 fail the reference; the levels reject 38, 46 and 60 of them, with no false alarms. The misses are effects the checker does not model, so the rates reflect how the reference was built. Four programs written by the building session: three failed the reference as drafted, and one failure (payload at long reach) was invisible to all three levels. Stylised, kinematic only, no language-model API called.

title: Does tuning the trapezoid's ramp fraction beyond a grid shrink the time-optimal carry's edge, and is it still positive?
summary: A follow-up to robofab-edgeconv (stylised). Golden-section refinement of the trapezoid's ramp fraction lowers its six-part total by 0.00 to 0.60% across the twelve speed-limited rows. With the solver at 6400 nodes the time-optimal edge, +0.11 to +0.88% over the grid-tuned trapezoid, falls to +0.05 to +0.28% over the refined one, still positive in every row. The smallest edges are comparable to the solver's residual discretisation error, so their sign is not firmly established. One planar arm, assumed parameters, no motor dynamics; simulated only.

title: How long an arm does it take to assemble its own toy gripper?
summary: A planar two-link arm on a turntable must reach a pick, place and lift point for each of the six free parts of the seven-part toy gripper from robofab-selfparts . With equal links and a 100 mm shoulder height the shortest arm is 60–140 mm per link as the tray moves from 40 to 400 mm away; an elbow limit of 90° raises it from 80 to 180 mm and 60° admits none up to 600 mm. Stylised: wrist point only, no collisions, payload or wrist orientation; results sit on a 10 mm grid.

title: Does the assembly order change the arm an arm needs to build its own gripper?
summary: Combines the order search of robofab-selfparts (384 valid orders) with the two-link reach model of robofab-reach , letting each part’s lift height clear whatever is already assembled. Negative result: for every valid order the shortest arm is the same (for example 80 mm per link at a 100 mm shoulder and 120 mm tray gap, 120 mm at a 200 mm shoulder), because the cover’s own lift point bounds every order and the tray distance dominates. Stylised: wrist point only, 10 mm link grid, 20 mm base grid.

title: How much of the time-optimal carry's edge survives a jerk-limited (S-curve) profile?
summary: A follow-up to robofab-trapezoid (stylised, preliminary): the trapezoid's acceleration corners are rounded into jerk-limited S-curves (half- and full-jerk ramps) under the same torque, jaw-force and joint-speed limits. In none of 45 speed-limited rows is an S-curve faster than the trapezoid; at speed limits of 2 and 1 rad/s it costs 0.0 to 2.0% (half-jerk) or 0.0 to 7.0% (full-jerk), and the time-optimal profile is 1.3 to 9.2% faster than the full-jerk one. With no speed limit the S-curves cost 1.4 to 33.7% and the time-optimal profile is 22.5 to 36.8% faster than the full-jerk one. Jerk is limited by profile shape, not an absolute bound, and the ramp grid is coarse. Simulated only.

title: At tight joint-speed limits, is the time-optimal carry's edge over a trapezoid real or an artefact of the ramp grid?
summary: A check on robofab-scurve (stylised, negative on its old figure). Refining the ramp-fraction grid alone makes the trapezoid beat the time-optimal solver by up to 1.8%, because the 201-point torque check misses the acceleration peak of a 0.2% ramp. With extra samples inside each ramp the time-optimal edge at 2 and 1 rad/s is −0.3 to +0.9% (old figure 1.3 to 1.5%), and raising the solver from 400 to 6400 nodes moves one row by 0.5%, as large as the whole edge. Jerk-limited profiles are still never faster than the trapezoid. Only the speed-limited rows were re-run, and every parameter is assumed.

title: Can a parallel-jaw arm assemble its own gripper?
summary: Exhaustive search over assembly orders of a seven-part toy gripper (axis-aligned boxes) by a modelled arm with a parallel-jaw grasp check, three approach-direction models and a swept jaw opening. No complete order exists below a 30 mm opening, the width of the widest part; above it, 384 of 720 orderings are valid when parts may be slid sideways and 120 when strictly top-down. Jaw-pad thickness from 2 to 10 mm changes nothing (a negative result for this geometry). Stylised single design, no reach, force or fasteners; simulation only.

title: Which assembly orders survive a better checker?
summary: Exact subset dynamic programming over assembly orders for a twelve-part printed gearbox, checked at three fidelity levels. Collision-only admits 4,227,168 of 39,916,800 orders (10.6%); adding quasi-static support leaves 30,760 (0.077%), and the collision-only optimum is infeasible once support is checked. Greedy disassembly needs 4 insertion-direction changes against an optimum of 1; one order written by the session agent (a single attempt, not a benchmark) passes with 2. Stylised axis-aligned boxes, no physics engine.

title: Does a quasi-static support rule agree with a physics engine?
summary: Validates the support rule of robofab-sequence against MuJoCo settle tests on all 2,048 partial assemblies of the printed gearbox. The rule agrees on 1,957 (95.6%): 81 states it accepts topple because a part can count as resting on a part that rests on it, and 10 it rejects hold because a gear bore captures the shaft. An acyclic-support variant reaches 99.5% (fitted on the same states). The count of valid orders is unchanged at 30,760 for three friction values, so this product's conclusions survive. Stylised boxes, static release, one product.

title: Does a rate-based "holds" criterion make a MuJoCo grasp verdict independent of solver settings?
summary: A follow-up to robofab-sliprate . Judging a bar held at one end by its extrapolated creep over a 3 s hold (under 2 mm) instead of a rotation tolerance does not help: across eight MuJoCo contact settings the minimum holding force varies by 33× to 400× or more, about as much as under a 1° tolerance. Only a loose 5° tolerance is stable, and only for bars up to 40 mm. Negative and preliminary: the settings, not the criterion, drive the verdict. Stylised, one engine, no physical grip.

title: Does the loose 20 mm/s “holds” threshold stay settings-robust at other friction and under lift?
summary: A follow-up to robofab-slipthresh , repeating its 16-threshold sweep at friction 0.3, 0.5 and 0.8, with and without a 5 m/s 2 lift acceleration. The loose 20 mm/s threshold (10 mm in 0.5 s) is the only one with a worst-case spread of the minimum holding force under 5× in all six conditions: 1.6× in four, 2.7× at mu 0.5 with lift and 4.5× at mu 0.3 with lift. Every other threshold is at least 20×. Robustness comes from looseness, and it weakens at low friction under load. Stylised, one engine, no physical grip.

title: Is the off-centre bar result in robofab-liftload a grasp effect or solver creep?
summary: A follow-up to robofab-liftload that replaces its pass/fail threshold with the bar’s rotation rate. A 10×10×40 mm bar held at one end creeps at about 3.7 deg/s from 0.3 to 3 N and still 2.2 deg/s at 20 N, so no force stops it. The rate scales with the contact time constant and drops tenfold when impratio goes from 1 to 10; torsional friction lowers it 2.5–3×. Free drops occur only at 0.1 N. The earlier verdict reflects simulator settings, not the grasp. Stylised: one engine, boxes, assumed density and friction.

title: Is any rate threshold settings-robust for a MuJoCo grasp "holds" verdict?
summary: A follow-up to robofab-slipcrit that sweeps the rate criterion’s task time (0.5–10 s) and tip bound (1–10 mm) over four bars and eight MuJoCo contact settings. The worst-case spread of the minimum holding force falls with the allowed tip speed: 242.7–400× at 2 mm/s or less, 89.4× at 3.3–5 mm/s, 20× at 10 mm/s and 1.6× only at 20 mm/s (0.5 s, 10 mm), a loose threshold; 10 s holds fail at every bound. Robustness comes from a loose threshold, not a better criterion. Stylised and preliminary: one engine, boxes, assumed density and friction.

title: How fine must the MuJoCo contact settings be for a moving grasp?
summary: A follow-up to robofab-graspfast . On all seven printed parts of a toy gripper, a jaw assembly accelerating upward at 100, 400 and 800 m/s 2 needs a simulated minimum force of 0.98–1.04 times the bound at contact time constants of 0.2 ms and below (63 cases). At 0.5 ms the bound is matched at 100 m/s 2 but no force up to 60 N holds any part at 400 or 800. A scan on one part shows the largest adequate time constant falls with acceleration and is not a single threshold on their product. Stylised: upward load only, rigid box pads, one friction value, no arm.

title: Is MuJoCo's refsafe clamp what breaks a moving grasp at a coarse timestep?
summary: A follow-up to robofab-solreftimestep , which only read the documentation on the refsafe flag. The same jaw-force test (cover part, 400 and 800 m/s 2 ) is run over contact time constants of 0.5 to 0.1 ms and timesteps of 0.4 to 0.05 ms with the flag on and off. 11 of 32 cells hold with it on and 10 of 32 with it off, and the two settings disagree in 7 cells. With it off, 10 runs end in a solver instability, so the clamp protects some cells and costs others, and the non-monotone timestep behaviour survives with it off. Stylised: one part, upward acceleration only, rigid box pads, no arm.

title: Is it the contact time constant or the timestep that breaks a moving grasp?
summary: A follow-up to robofab-solrefmap . On the cover part of a toy gripper accelerating upward at 400 and 800 m/s 2 , a MuJoCo jaw-force test holds in only 6 of 24 cells of a grid of contact time constant (0.5, 0.3, 0.2 ms) and timestep (0.4 to 0.05 ms). A coarse timestep always fails, probably because MuJoCo raises the effective constant to twice the timestep. A finer timestep does not rescue a marginal constant (at 800 m/s 2 and 0.2 ms only a 0.1 ms step holds, finer ones fail for an unexplained reason), while a 0.1 ms constant holds at every step of 0.1 ms and below. Stylised: one part, upward acceleration only, rigid box pads, no arm.

title: How much clearance does a printed two-pin cover need to assemble, and how wasteful is worst-case stacking?
summary: Monte Carlo of a printed base with two pins and a cover with two holes, each centre with a Gaussian position error and each diameter a Gaussian size error, translation-only assembly (exact two-disk test). With exact sizes, yield is 1 − exp(−c 2 /(8σ p 2 )) (tested against simulation). For position sd 0.10 mm and size sd 0.05 mm, 99% yield needs 0.62 mm nominal diametral clearance and 99.9% needs 0.77 mm, while a ±3σ worst-case stack asks for 2.0 mm (3.0–3.4× the 99% requirement and 2.5–2.8× the 99.9% one across the six unbiased cases); a 3σ root-sum-square rule lands at 0.9990–0.9998 yield where the holes are unbiased. A hole bias adds to the needed clearance one for one. Assumed process spreads, not measured; two pins, no rotation, stylised.

title: Once the time-optimal solver's node count is converged, how big is its edge over a tuned trapezoid?
summary: Follow-up to robofab-scurvefine : all 12 rows (three arm sizes, jaw cap 5× or none, joint speed limit 2 or 1 rad/s, six printed parts each) are re-solved at 400, 1600, 6400 and 25600 nodes. The totals change by at most 0.02% between 6400 and 25600 nodes, while 400 nodes is up to 0.5% pessimistic, which explains the negative “edges” there (7 of 12 rows). At 25600 nodes the time-optimal profile is faster than the ramp-resolved trapezoid in every row, by 0.11–0.88%. The observed convergence order is noisy (1.1–3.2). Stylised and preliminary; the trapezoid side’s ramp sampling is not varied.

title: Does the time-optimal carry's edge over a tuned trapezoid survive when torque or the jaw cap binds?
summary: Follow-up to robofab-toppconv (stylised, preliminary). The nine no-speed-limit rows of robofab-scurve (three arm sizes, jaw cap 2×, 5× or none, six printed parts each) are recomputed with the time-optimal solver at 400 to 25600 nodes and the trapezoid on a fine ramp grid with 40 and 160 extra samples per ramp. The time-optimal carry is 9.4% to 23.0% faster than the trapezoid in every row; the solver is converged to within 0.004% by 6400 nodes, and denser ramp sampling slows the trapezoid by 0.05% to 0.5%, raising the edge by at most 0.4 points. So, unlike the sub-1% edge under a speed limit, the torque- and jaw-bound gap is not a resolution artefact in this toy. A trapezoid-only comparison on assumed parameters; not a claim about real arms.

title: Is the time-optimal carry's speed-limited advantage just the min-jerk profile's shape?
summary: A follow-up to robofab-jointspeed (stylised, preliminary): the min-jerk comparator is replaced by a trapezoidal-velocity move with a tuned ramp fraction, under the same torque, jaw-force and joint-speed limits. Over three arm sizes, three jaw caps and speed limits of 6 to 1 rad/s, the time-optimal profile beats the best trapezoid by only 0.4 to 2.9% at 2 and 1 rad/s (0.4 to 0.8% at 1 rad/s), against 46% over min-jerk, so the earlier ceiling was mostly the comparator. Without a speed limit it still wins by 8.7 to 22.5%. The smallest ramp fraction tried (0.01) binds in most tight-limit rows, so the small gap is bounded by the grid. All parameters are assumed; the speed limits are round numbers, not an actuator rating.

title: How much can Byzantine verifiers move an aggregate?
summary: Mean, median and trimmed-mean aggregation of verifier reports under a Byzantine fraction β: mean bias βB is unbounded, median bias σΦ −1 (1/(2(1−β))) is independent of B and diverges at β=½, trimmed-mean closed form for τ≥β matches simulation, and trimming below β fails. Stylised.

title: What does a median or trimmed-mean outer step cost local SGD, and what does it buy against Byzantine workers?
summary: Because the median and trimmed mean commute with shifts, the outer loop stays exactly linear: floor α V w v /( s (2−α s )) plus a bias V w m 2 / s 2 , with the same stability limit as averaging. With no attackers the median costs N ·Var = 1.35 to 1.56 (→ π/2). With a fraction ε of attackers its bias is bounded (Φ( z ) = 1/(2(1−ε)): 0.18 noise-sigmas at ε = 1/8) and beats averaging once the attack offset exceeds about 1.4 sigmas; more workers shrink only the variance part (total loss 0.103 → 0.102 from N =8 to 128), while a longer inner loop shrinks the bias (39× from H =1 to 256). Trimming exactly the attacker count is worse than the median. Matched to simulation within 1.3%. Stylised: quadratic, Gaussian noise, shared curvature, constant-offset attackers.

title: Does a bigger swarm learn more from shared rollouts?
summary: Not without incentives. With diminishing returns and a peer-rollout discount θ, symmetric Nash play gives every agent exactly the learning level of a lone agent whatever the swarm size (total effort caps at ( a / c −1)/θ), while the efficient level grows linearly in N : welfare per agent is 4.5× higher at N =256. At θ=1 a single agent generates everything. A Pigouvian matching subsidy covering θ( N −1)/(1+θ( N −1)) of cost implements the optimum exactly, and junk rollouts beat honesty iff c −ε > p (τ+ F ).

title: A zero-wind twin of a UAV out-and-back leg: does a tailwind repay the headwind, and what does a twin calibrated on one leg say about the return?
summary: Real round-trip energy is ( v 4 +1)/( v 2 − w 2 ), so wind does not cancel: real/twin is exactly 1/(1−( w / v ) 2 ), 1.33× at w / v =0.5 and 5.3× at 0.9, the same for either sign, with no return at | w |≥ v . The twin-optimal airspeed is 1 for every wind while the real optimum solves v 2 = w 2 +√( w 4 +1), so flying the twin's optimum costs 1.5%, 9.8%, 52% extra at w =0.4, 0.6, 0.8. A twin calibrated on one leg and assumed to see the same wind back is off by exactly + w / v (headwind leg) or − w / v (tailwind leg): ±33% at w =0.5, v =1.5, with a sign set by which leg was flown. Stylised: steady along-track wind, constant airspeed, two-term power law.

title: When continual-learning tasks conflict, how much does a task-aware router of modules actually buy?
summary: With cluster-structured conflicts, the long-run loss on an old task is exactly (2 r / d )[τ w ² + τ b ²(1 − Purity)], where Purity is one minus the router’s expected Gini impurity (matched to simulation within 0.3–2.3% across six routers). Random routing to any number of modules leaves the whole floor; a perfect router onto m modules removes exactly ( m −1)/( K −1) of the between-cluster floor, so half needs 5 of 8 clusters’ worth of modules; and a routing error q costs 2 q of impurity at first order (10% error returns 36% of the shared-model floor at K =8, 25% returns 59%). Purity is auditable with an unbiased pair-collision estimator. Stylised: realizable linear regression, exact convergence, Gaussian cluster centres, hard routing.

title: How long must a real test run be when its length was sized in a twin with the wrong plant pole?
summary: A gain designed in a twin whose pole is m × the real one is validated on hardware for a run length chosen in the twin. The variance of the time-averaged cost of a Gaussian AR(1) loop is exact and depends on the closed-loop pole through (1+ ρ )/(1− ρ ), ρ = a c 2 , so the twin-sized run is 3.8× too short at m =2, r =0.1 (3,177 vs 12,110 steps; real coverage of a ±5% claim 0.69 vs 0.95 nominal, simulated 0.68) and 2.1× too long at m =1.5, r =5; an oscillating (negative-pole) loop averages as slowly as a sluggish one. Sizing from a real pilot’s lag-one autocorrelation is close to median-unbiased but under-sizes about half the time. Stylised: scalar linear-Gaussian, fixed known gain, normal-approximation interval.

title: How wrong is a safety margin certified in a Gaussian-disturbance simulator when real gusts are heavy-tailed?
summary: A stabilised vehicle must stay in a corridor for T = 200 steps; the twin’s disturbances are Gaussian, the real ones Student- t with the same variance, so a variance fit cannot tell them apart. The twin’s certificate is exact (a union bound over its stationary tail), yet at the margin certified for δ = 0.01 the real failure probability is 0.29 (ν = 3) to 0.052 (ν = 8), and the margin the real system needs at δ = 0.001 is 7.3× to 1.25× the twin’s, a ratio that grows as δ shrinks. Inflating the twin variance to match real failure at δ = 0.05 still misses δ = 0.001 by 24×. A conformal margin from real episodes is valid but needs n ≥ 1/δ of them; a Hill tail fit to cheap one-step disturbances needs no failures and is below target in 93% of repeats at 2,000 samples. Stylised: 1-D linear system, i.i.d. disturbance, a simulated ‘real’ system, no flight data.

title: A battery twin with no internal resistance: how much endurance and how large a burst does the real, sagging cell actually give?
summary: A UAV battery twin that keeps the open-circuit voltage curve but drops the series resistance overstates endurance by exactly 1/η( u ) with η = (1 + √(1− u ))/2 (up to 2× at the maximum-power fold, beyond which the real cell cannot deliver the power at all while the twin still quotes an endurance). With droop and a voltage cutoff, real/twin endurance is 0.86, 0.57, 0.30 at normalised power 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 9%, 37%, 66% of the charge is stranded. The deliverable burst power falls linearly with charge, so a burst of 0.5 fails below 51% charge where the twin's floor is zero, a flat 20% reserve covers only a third of the full-charge limit, and keeping a 0.6 burst deliverable leaves 35% of the twin's cruise time. A constant derate fitted at one power errs by +12% to +473% elsewhere, but the resistance is identified to 1–2% from tens of voltage–current samples, and a full-charge fit misses resistance that grows as the cell empties (endurance +42% to +85% too high). Stylised: simulated cell, linear curves, constant-power load, no polarisation or self-heating.

title: A continuous-time twin certifies PD at every gain: which gains survive a zero-order-hold sampled loop?
summary: Double integrator under PD control computed at period T and held. The twin ( T →0) is stable for every gain; the exact step matrix gives the real stable region k p T /2 < k d < 2/ T , i.e. ω n T < min(4 ζ , 1/ ζ ), matched to bisection and an independent RK4 held-input run ( ζ =0.7 fails at ω n T =1.4286). The twin is accurate for ω n T ≲ 0.2 but at 1.2 the real overshoot is 0.234 against its 0.046, and at fixed T raising ω n past ω n T ≈1 slows settling (0.4 → 5.2) then diverges. Deadbeat gains ( k p T 2 =1, k d T =3/2) settle in 2 samples, the real speed limit. Stylised: noiseless, no computation delay.

title: How long does a simulator without actuator limits say an unstable plant stays in control?
summary: An unstable scalar plant ( a =1.2) with a saturating actuator loses control when | x | exceeds U /( a −1). A twin with an unlimited actuator, running its own LQR gain, overstates the mean time to loss of control by 6,295× at noise sd 1 (1.5×10 6 vs 245 steps), 10 6 × at 0.8, and still 5.7× at 2. ln T is linear in 1/ s 2 with slope ≈3.7 on the real plant against ≈12.7–13.2 for the twin (large-deviation value 12.4), so the gap is exponential, not a constant factor. Both are maximised at the deadbeat gain, but the twin’s time-to-failure varies five orders of magnitude across gains against 2× on the real plant. Exit times solve an integral equation (grid- and Monte-Carlo-checked; twin values above 10 10 unresolved). Stylised: scalar plant, one parameter set; the real exponent is empirical.

title: What does a too-narrow scenario generator do to a digital twin's estimate of a rare failure?
summary: With real scenarios x ~N(0,1), failure iff x > a , and a twin generator of width s , the raw twin claims Q( a / s ) and the reweighted (importance-sampling) estimate has per-sample second moment sτ Q( a /τ), τ 2 = s 2 /(2 s 2 −1), finite only for s 2 >½. In a braking example ( P =1.2×10 −3 ) a generator 0.6× too narrow claims 2.1×10 −7 and reported zero failures in all 4,000 simulated runs of 2,000 scenarios; a wide one over-claims but reweighting repairs it, with optimal width ≈1.05 a needing 2,179 runs for 10% error against 83,459 for plain Monte Carlo. A defensive mixture with the real prior makes a narrow twin's variance finite but no better than plain Monte Carlo. Stylised: one-dimensional Gaussian scenarios, known threshold and density, correct twin failure indicator.

title: Should you pay verifiers for their calibration?
summary: A verifier reporting expit(aL+b) for the true posterior logit L is overpaid-for-error by exactly E[(r−p)²] under Brier and E[KL(p‖r)] under log score. Brier is bounded (a hard 0/1 report still beats the prior at μ=1) but log is not: raw log score ranks a higher-resolution verifier first only for slope a in (0.264, 2.49), so at a=4 a weaker calibrated verifier wins, while recalibrated scores never reverse. Recalibrating on n outcomes costs about tr(HI −1 )/2n excess Brier (0.264/n, simulation within ~10% for n≥100), beating raw pay beyond n≈20–80. Quadrature and seeded simulation. Stylised.

title: How optimistic is the best of K controllers chosen in a noisy digital twin?
summary: Scoring K candidate controllers in a twin and deploying the argmin is a winner’s-curse selection. With score noise τ around true costs N ( m , v 2 ), the winner’s claimed cost is exactly m − √( v 2 +τ 2 ) c K and its deployed cost m − v 2 c K /√( v 2 +τ 2 ), so optimism τ 2 c K /√( v 2 +τ 2 ) grows like √(2 ln K ) (simulation agrees to within 0.03). With a fixed rollout budget the winner’s deployed cost is non-monotone in K (best K = 5, 8, 22 in three regimes; 5,000 candidates gain 5–10× less). In an exact-plant LQ twin (50 gains, 10 rollouts each) the claim is 8% below the deployed cost and below what any gain can achieve, though the Gaussian formula understates the size (optimism 0.0036 vs 0.0017 predicted). Fresh re-scoring fixes the claim but not the choice, empirical-Bayes shrinkage barely helps, and screen-then-verify cuts claim bias 4.5× (Gaussian model: regret 0.73 → 0.34 at K =100). Stylised: i.i.d. Gaussian score noise, one scalar plant, twin equal to the real plant.

title: How stiff a rod does a frequency target need, in aluminium and in wood?
summary: Follow-up to selfrep-alurod and selfrep-rodmodes: rods of the printer redesign are sized to a first-mode frequency target (Rayleigh estimate, assumed 0.3 kg carriage) instead of a sag spec. Aluminium reaches 40 Hz with 10.0 mm, inside the assumed 12 mm holder limit, where hardwood needs 16.0 mm; within 12 mm the highest reachable frequency is 56 Hz for aluminium and 23 Hz for hardwood. Closure by mass rises with the target only because thicker stock counts as makeable, while imported stock grows from 1946 g to 2596 g. Stylised: one mode, assumed carriage mass, moduli and holder limit.

title: How thick must a printer rod be to keep carriage ringing small at a given acceleration?
summary: Follow-up to selfrep-alufreq: the rod diameter is derived from an acceleration and a 50 µm ringing tolerance (one-mode oscillator, assumed 0.3 kg carriage and damping ratio 0.01) instead of a bare frequency target. At 3 m/s² with abrupt steps steel needs 7.3 mm, aluminium 9.6 mm and hardwood 15.5 mm; ramping the force over 20 ms cuts aluminium at 5 m/s² from 10.9 to 8.9 mm. Stylised: one mode, assumed damping, nothing measured.

title: Does an aluminium rod fit the printer where a wooden one cannot?
summary: Follow-up to selfrep-rodbeam that adds aluminium bar, cut to length on the router, as a rod substitution in selfrep-redesign. To match the sag of the 8 mm steel rod (0.19 mm at the assumed 5 N) aluminium needs 10.4 mm, inside the assumed 12 mm holder limit, while hardwood needs 16.9 mm and does not fit. Mass closure of the all-substitutions redesign is 39.5% with aluminium at a 0.2 mm spec, 37.8% with wood and 28.7% with steel rods kept as vitamins; the shop imports about 170 g more stock than with wood. Stylised: moduli, load and limit are assumed, and the surface of cut aluminium bar is taken to be adequate for the bushings.

title: Does an aluminium rod change which printer redesign the penalty-budget search picks?
summary: A stylised, preliminary search over 448 designs: a rod choice (steel, hardwood or aluminium at 8, 10 or 12 mm) times subsets of six other part substitutions, with a rod penalty tied to mid-span sag by an assumed log curve. At every budget from 0.5 up the best mass-closure design uses the 12 mm aluminium rod: 40.0% at budget 2.0 against 33.1% for the wooden-rod search of selfrep-redesign , and 41.4% against 35.8% at full budget. The choice sits at the assumed holder limit because the closure metric counts heavier bar stock as makeable, so it says little about the best rod. The pick held for penalty scales from 0.05 to 1. Computed only; nothing was built.

title: Which process capabilities should a printer-replicating shop learn when one capability unlocks several imported parts?
summary: A stylised, preliminary follow-up to selfrep-learnfirst . Each of the 29 imported printer parts needs a set of assumed process capabilities (lathe, heat treatment, winding, stamping, grinding, ...) with an assumed effort each, paid once however many parts share it; all 512 capability sets are enumerated exactly. A lathe with threading is the best first buy by mass (effort 4, +31 points of mass closure but only +10 of cost); winding plus stamping is best by cost (effort 8, +30). Exact capability sets beat picking parts one at a time by up to 10 points at the same real cost, but with efforts scaled 0.5× to 2× the nominal choice stays affordable and optimal in only 20–28% of draws. The efforts and the part-to-capability map are the project’s own assumptions; the controller electronics stays imported.

title: In what order should a printer-replicating shop learn its process capabilities?
summary: A stylised, preliminary follow-up to selfrep-capability : a shop learns capabilities one at a time, so the choice is an order, scored by closure-weeks (closure held while still learning). With the assumed efforts, all 9! orders are covered exactly. The best order differs from walking the budget frontier, which scores only 54–73% of the optimum over 24 weeks; a gain-per-week bundle rule is within 0–6%, a one-capability-at-a-time rule 69–80%. The optimal order is moderately fragile to the efforts (within 1% of the optimum in 39–88% of draws scaled 0.5×–2×). Efforts and the capability map are assumptions; nothing was built.

title: How much of a RepRap printer can a growing seed shop make itself?
summary: The RepRap Prusa Mendel (iteration 2) bill of materials (51 part lines, from the RepRap wiki) against three seed shops. A printer alone makes 18 of 51 lines (35%); adding a CNC router and laser cutter reaches 43% of lines and, under assumed masses and costs, about 22% of mass and 16% of cost; casting helps only if brass bushings replace LM8UU bearings (45% of lines, 24% of mass). Motors, electronics, rods, bearings and fasteners stay vitamins. Stylised: the wiki gives no masses or prices, so those inputs are assumed and shown with a sensitivity range, process assignments are judgement, and only the printer is decomposed.

title: Does pricing a shop’s imports, instead of weighing them, change when its recycling machines repay themselves?
summary: Builds on selfrep-recyclers with assumed round-number prices for feedstock and for each vitamin of the machines. The plastic shredder and extruder repay in 98–111 printer copies on the shop’s own scrap (median 99, 45–235 over price draws), close to the mass-based 99–116, while the aluminium furnace worsens from 94 to about 203 copies because aluminium is cheap per kilogram. Recycling retired plastic brings the plastic pair to 10–26 copies. Stylised: every price and part list is an assumption, and labour and energy costs are ignored.

title: Does greedy substitution search still work when the printer-redesign list grows past seven items?
summary: A synthetic, preliminary test (100 instances per cell, assumed generator) of budgeted weighted coverage, the shape of the printer-redesign search, for 7 to 24 substitutions with 0 to 0.9 overlap. Greedy gain-per-penalty stays at 96–100% of the exact optimum on average but is exactly optimal in only 33–95 of 100 instances, with a worst case of 49.6%. Local search is best on average (about 99.5%); 64 random evaluations are perfect at 7 items and fall to about 89–90% at 24, so small-list random baselines flatter themselves. Nothing here uses the real bill of materials. Computed only.

title: Is the dynamic-programming table for the replicating shop with a resale value converged, and can its policy be trusted?
summary: Follow-up to selfrep-terminalmarket, which found its DP table up to about 10% below the value of its own policy. This project refines the log-spaced fleet grid from 100 to 1,600 points and tries a second interpolation rule (linear in fleet size instead of in log fleet size), on the same fluid model ( W = 50 h, failure 0, horizon 600 h, all inputs assumed). The simulated value of the DP policy changes by only about 0.15% between 800 and 1,600 points and stays within 0.2% of the best bang-bang switch, while the table value approaches it from below roughly in proportion to 1/(grid points): about 8–13% low at 400 points and 2–3% low at 1,600. The table is therefore a slowly converging lower bound, not a certificate; a first-order extrapolation puts it within about 0.8% of the bang-bang value in the three cases tried, but that rests on two grids. The cause of the bias is not diagnosed. Stylised fluid model, preliminary.

title: How much does a smooth copy-then-sell policy beat a single switch for the replicating shop, certified without interpolation?
summary: Follow-up to selfrep-dpgrid, whose DP table sat 2–13% below the value of its own policy. This project chooses a control set whose steps land exactly on a geometric fleet grid, so no interpolation is needed and the table equals the policy value to 1e-14. On the same fluid model ( W = 50 h, failure 0, horizon 600 h, all inputs assumed) a single copy-then-goods switch is optimal when machines keep a resale value of 50 each. With no resale value and a saturating goods market, a three-phase policy (full copying, an intermediate share, then goods) beats the best switch by 4.7% (capacity 1e4) and 7.1% (capacity 1e3); with a resale value of 12.5 and capacity 1e4 the gain is 6.5%, and only appears once the control set is fine enough. Stylised, with a fixed Euler step and no cash constraint; preliminary.

title: Can an exactly solvable birth-death chain explain why short-lived printer fleets die out?
summary: Follow-up to selfrep-wearout. The fleet is a birth-death chain with an absorbing state at zero, and its mean extinction time is solved exactly and checked against a closed form and Monte Carlo. From one seed machine it grows from 358 h (mean life 100 h) to 3967 h (200 h) to 41,602 h (300 h), but the wear-out simulation dies out 1.8–2.5× sooner. Scaling births by the chance a build outlives its machine brings the two within about 35% for a lone seed (16–18% at 200–300 h), a fit made after seeing the gap; it is 1.7–1.9× too short for four seeds at 300 h. Stylised, with assumed inputs; the 500 h rows are unusable.

title: Is the lone-printer die-out an early birth-death accident?
summary: Tests the extinction explanation left open by selfrep-wearout with an exact continuous-time Markov chain of the same shop (Poisson vitamin kits, exponential builds and lives). With assumed inputs and a budget of 4 units/h, the chain gives a 0.194 chance that a lone seed machine is lost before the fleet reaches 6 machines at 500 h mean life (simulation 0.198 ± 0.006), of which 0.162 is the seed retiring before its first copy; relaxing the Markov assumptions moves this by at most about 0.03. Wear-out lives (Weibull shape 2 or more) cut it to under 3%. Exact mean extinction times for small equilibrium fleets match simulation (1464 h against 1511 ± 50 h at 200 h life), but with regular kits and lognormal builds long times roughly double, so the chain is a lower guide there. Stylised: every input is assumed; simulated only.

title: Can a quasi-stationary approximation predict how long a small printer fleet lasts?
summary: Follow-up to selfrep-extinction-kits. The slowest decay rate of the exact Markov chain gives a quasi-stationary estimate 1/λ 0 of the mean extinction time. Stylised, with assumed inputs, it overshoots a lone seed machine by 1.2 to 1.9 times (2388 h against 1465 h exact at 200 h life), but multiplied by the exact chance the fleet survives its start it lands within 5% in four of seven cases (for example 0.999 at 500 h life) and fails where the fleet rarely survives (ratio 1.4 at 200 h life, 42 at 75 h). Seed fleets help only up to the quasi-stationary time: 1 / 2 / 4 / 8 seeds give 1465 / 1983 / 2388 / 2666 h at 200 h life. The survival correction was chosen after seeing the overshoot, so it is a post-hoc fit. Stylised: every input is assumed; simulated only.

title: How fast does a replicating printer shop grow when its vitamins must be bought?
summary: Builds on the selfrep-closure part model. A discrete-event simulation of a fleet of printers that each build copies of themselves, checked against a closed-form fluid model. With a small import budget the doubling time falls almost in proportion to the budget (about 455 h at 4 units/h, 120 h at 16/h); above a crossover fleet size N* = BW/V machine time binds and doubling flattens near the 50 h build time. Failed builds raise the doubling time by about 1/(1− f ), and raising closure helps most when imports bind. Every input (print rate, assembly time, costs, budget, failure rate) is assumed and the fleet is homogeneous. Stylised. The comparison with Lackner and Wendt’s growth model is not done.

title: How much do the RepRap closure numbers depend on which parts a shop is judged able to make?
summary: Flips the make-or-buy judgements behind selfrep-closure. Buying all five optimistic lines (washers, GT2 pulley, MDF bed, brass bushing) cuts the largest shop to 17% mass and 11% cost closure, the printer-alone level, and no single line moves mass closure by more than 2.4 points. Granting a missing capability matters far more: making the NEMA17 motors in-house would add 22 points of mass closure, the 370 mm threaded rods 10. Monte Carlo (judged lines kept with probability 0.5, arguable vitamins granted with 0.1; arbitrary): mass closure 18–35% (5–95%). Stylised; masses and costs are assumed placeholders.

title: Which imported part should a printer-replicating shop learn to make first?
summary: A stylised, preliminary ranking of the 29 parts the printer + router + laser shop of selfrep-closure still imports, by the closure gained if that one part became makeable (free and certain, so an upper bound). By mass or cost the NEMA17 stepper motor is first (+22 and +26 points) and stays first in 90% and 76% of 2,000 draws with every assumed mass and cost scaled 0.5× to 2×; by unit count the M8 nut leads, and by distinct lines every vitamin ties. Three lines buy +52 points of cost closure but +39 of mass. Masses, costs and makers are assumed; difficulty of learning is not modelled.

title: How much imported material can recycling save a self-replicating printer shop?
summary: Builds on the selfrep-closure part list. A stylised steady-state mass and energy balance for building one more RepRap Prusa Mendel, with shredding and re-extrusion of plastic and remelting of aluminium offcuts. With assumed process parameters, vitamins stay about 75% of imported mass for the largest shop (82% for the printer alone), and recycling the shop’s own scrap cuts imports by a median 3% (5–95% over parameter draws: 1–6%). Only plastic from retired machines changes the filament import much, and then the assumed recycled-share cap decides the result. Limitations: every yield, loss and energy figure is an assumption, recycling machines are not counted, and recycled-plastic quality is not modelled.

title: Which machine should a seed shop add next, and does a greedy rule find it?
summary: Builds on the selfrep-closure part model. Choosing among a CNC router, laser cutter and casting setup under a budget, a greedy closure-per-price rule matches exhaustive search at every tested budget on the real three-machine instance (router first, then casting only if brass bushings replace LM8UU). On 500 random synthetic instances greedy is optimal in 72–94% of cases and loses up to about 38% of the closure gain in the worst case. Stylised: machine prices, masses and costs are assumed placeholders, machines have no bills of materials of their own, and the synthetic instances are random.

title: Does sharing part jobs across printers make a replicating printer shop double faster than one copy per printer?
summary: Tests the explanation given in selfrep-growth for the gap between its fluid (34.7 h) and discrete-event (about 53 h) doubling times. A part-level simulation of the Prusa Mendel's 44 printed parts plus assembly compares one copy per printer with a shared pool of part jobs. With no import limit the pool that always serves the oldest copy doubles in 43.2 h against 51.1 h (15% faster), closing about half of the gap; a pool that advances all copies together equals one-copy-per-printer, and under an import budget all three agree. Stylised: every input is assumed, parts are uniform, no plate packing or failed prints.

title: How many parts should a replicating printer print per plate to double its shop fastest?
summary: Groups the Prusa Mendel's 44 printed parts k to a plate in the selfrep-partpool simulator, with an assumed per-plate changeover of 0 to 1 h. With no changeover one part per plate is best (43.2 h effective doubling for a pooled fleet); at 0.25 h the best plate holds 4 parts (46.4 h), at 0.5 h and 1 h it holds 11 (47.8 h and 49.6 h). Pooling keeps an edge over one copy per printer (7.6–15.5%), and large plates cost it the pooling gain: at one plate per copy both policies coincide. Stylised: every input, including the changeover, is assumed, the BOM has no real part masses and plates are full and identical.

title: Why do two exact extinction chains of the same printer shop disagree?
summary: Two sibling chains of the lone replicating printer shop, one on fleet size and one on machines and vitamin kits, give different mean extinction times for the same inputs. Stylised, with assumed inputs, the fleet-size chain is longer by 1.5 to 7 times because its birth law min(n/W, a) lets machines and kits never wait for each other. A fixed-in-advance repair that adds the two waits matches the kit chain within 5% when the fleet stays at 1 to 3 machines, but falls 24 to 60% below it for larger fleets, where kits pool in stock. No law right in both regimes was derived.

title: How many printer copies does it take for a shop's recycling machines to repay their own imports?
summary: Builds on selfrep-materials. A shredder, a filament extruder and an aluminium furnace are given assumed part lists, split into vitamins and parts the shop can make. With the shop’s own scrap only, the plastic pair needs 99–116 printer copies to avoid as much imported mass as it costs (91–164 over part-mass draws) and the furnace about 94. Plastic from retired machines cuts this to about 12–31 copies, depending on an assumed recycled-share cap. Limitations: part lists and masses are placeholders, mass is the only currency (cost, time and energy are ignored), and retirement is a scenario knob. Stylised.

title: Which part substitutions cut a printer's vitamins most, within a performance budget?
summary: Follow-up to selfrep-closure that changes the machine instead of the shop. Seven assumed substitutions (printed bushings and nuts, wooden rods, a printed drive) are searched exhaustively, greedily and at random under an assumed penalty budget. All seven together take the Prusa Mendel’s vitamin lines from 29 to 19 and closure from 43/22/16% to 60/36/48% (lines/mass/cost) for the printer, router and laser shop; mass closure stays below 36% because motors, electronics and threaded rods remain. Cost closure responds most, and the best set depends on the assumed penalties. Stylised: substitutions, masses and penalties are all assumed and no part was tested.

title: When should a replicating shop stop copying itself and start making goods?
summary: Builds on the selfrep-growth fleet model. A fluid optimal-control model splits machine time between building copies and making goods, scored on the total value of goods over 600 h. Copying flat out and then switching to goods one e-folding time (1/ k = W /(1− f ), 50 h with no failures) before the horizon matches the closed form; the best constant split earns only 9–27% of that value, and smooth ramps are no better than the sharp switch. When imports or goods sales fund vitamins, cash binds throughout and the switch lands about 50 h from the end. Every input is assumed, the fleet is a continuous fluid, goods demand is unlimited and the final fleet is worth nothing. Stylised. Piecewise policies are local search, not a proof of optimality.

title: When is repairing a printer worth more than building a new one?
summary: Follow-up to selfrep-wearout. Machines break down at a constant rate and the shop may spend spare-part vitamins to repair one instead of retiring it. A vitamin-balance formula predicts repair gives a bigger fleet exactly when the repair cost share is below the repair success probability; a discrete-event simulation with assumed inputs puts the crossing at that value, within about 9% of the formula in that sweep, but only when spares are held back from new builds (without a reserve the fleet was 70 against a formula value of 157). Repair also cuts die-out from one seed at short lifetimes (for example 55% against 100% at a mean life of 100 h) but does not remove it. Stylised: assumed inputs, memoryless breakdowns, repair returns the machine to new, no printed spares.

title: What happens to a repairing printer shop when repairs need labour?
summary: Follow-up to selfrep-repair. Repairs need one of K benches; broken machines queue after buying spares. The pre-run prediction that the working fleet is about min(import limit, K·L/h) fails: with B = 40 and one bench the fleet is 414 against a cap of 40, because most breakdowns are never served and the queue (2915 machines) is dead stock. An unbounded queue with one bench is worse than never repairing (414 against 458); retiring a breakdown when 1–20 machines already wait gives 487–492. Stylised: assumed inputs, benches are a count with no wages, no corrected closed form.

title: Does paying for spares late rescue the long repair queue of a printer shop?
summary: Follow-up to selfrep-repairlabour. That project found an unbounded repair queue is dead stock (414 working machines against 458 for never repairing, one bench, B = 40) when spares are bought at breakdown. Buying them when a bench frees up instead reverses it: 488 against 458, and 572 against 504 with four benches. The queue is as long (about 3400 machines) but ties up no vitamins, and capping it no longer helps (caps of 1–200 all give 484–492 at one bench; no standard errors computed, so no optimum cap is claimed). Stylised: assumed inputs, first-come service, a machine unaffordable at its turn is retired.

title: How does a falling resale price for the finished fleet change when the shop stops copying?
summary: Follow-up to selfrep-terminalmarket: the fleet is sold at the horizon for s m (1 − e − N / m ), so the first machine fetches s and the price falls with market depth m ( W = 50 h, failure 0, horizon 600 h, all inputs assumed). With an unsaturated goods market a shallower resale market moves the optimal switch from 574 h (linear) to 549 h ( m = 10 3 ), and a single switch matches the DP. With a saturating goods market ( c = 10 4 ) the DP policy beats the best single switch by up to 14%. The DP table value is not a certificate (it overstates at 400 grid points); simulated policy values are reported. Stylised and preliminary; both market curves are assumed, not fitted.

title: What does a wooden rod cost a printer in stiffness?
summary: Replaces the assumed penalty of selfrep-redesign’s wooden-rod substitution with Euler–Bernoulli beam theory. At 8 mm a hardwood rod sags 20× a steel one (the modulus ratio) and a printed PLA rod 80×; matching steel stiffness needs about 17 mm of hardwood, outside the printer’s 8 mm hardware, while a 1–2 mm sag tolerance needs 9–11 mm. The earlier 30 g per dowel was about twice the geometric 13.8 g, moving mass closure from 35.8% to 34.6%; thicker dowels raise closure again, a quirk of counting imported feedstock as makeable. Stylised: properties and the 5 N load are assumed and no rod was tested.

title: What natural-frequency target does a printer’s rod have to meet, and what does a wooden rod cost?
summary: Follow-up to selfrep-rodbeam that derives the rod spec from a vibration target instead of an assumed sag limit. A carriage mass on a simply supported rod (Rayleigh estimate with the 17/35 effective rod mass) gives a first mode of 42 Hz for 8 mm steel but 10 Hz for hardwood and 5 Hz for printed PLA, for an assumed 0.3 kg carriage. Matching steel’s frequency needs about 16 mm of hardwood, close to the sag-matching 17 mm; at equal frequency the dowel is 1.9–2.1× the steel diameter. Stylised: carriage mass and material constants are assumptions, one mode, no damping or bushing play.

title: When the goods market saturates, does a replicating shop’s bang-bang switch turn smooth?
summary: Builds on the selfrep-reinvest fluid model, with concave goods revenue a c (1 − e − g / c ) and a backward dynamic programme (Bellman) as a check on the local-search policies. With a large market the optimum is still copy-then-switch; once market capacity c is below about 10 4 machine-hours per hour the optimal copy share ramps down over 90–300 h, bang-bang loses 4.5–7% of the optimum and a logistic ramp recovers all but 1–1.5%. Slower growth from failed builds sharpens the switch again. Every input is assumed and the saturation form is a convenient choice; cash never binds. The DP value is the optimum of a discretised problem, within a few tenths of a percent of its simulated policy where it is accurate and several percent in near-linear cases. Stylised.

title: Which assumed input of the replicating-printer growth model does the doubling time depend on most?
summary: Follow-up to selfrep-growth: variance-based (Sobol) sensitivity of the fluid-model doubling time to print rate, assembly time, vitamin cost, import budget and build-failure probability over assumed ranges. Import-limited (4/h): budget and vitamin cost carry about 0.45 and 0.43 of the variance of ln T, failure 0.11, print rate and assembly time none. Time-limited (64/h): budget, vitamin cost, failure and print rate are comparable (0.25–0.28). The fluid model overstates budget sensitivity at 64/h against the discrete-event model (elasticity −0.45 vs −0.02). Stylised, with assumed ranges and inputs.

title: What is the closed form of a replicating shop’s smooth switch from copying to goods, and does it match dynamic programming?
summary: Builds on selfrep-satmarket. With concave revenue a c (1 − e − g / c ), Pontryagin’s principle gives three arcs: copy flat out, a singular arc on which goods output grows linearly at rate kc , then goods only for the last 1/ k hours. The entry time solves one scalar equation. In the Euler model the open-loop policy earns 99.96–100.00% of the dynamic-programming policy’s value over 7 market sizes and 4 failure shares. The conditions are necessary, not a proof of optimality, and depend on the assumed exponential revenue form. Stylised.

title: Does a printer shop lose its printed-bushing gain once a printed spare takes print hours?
summary: Follow-up to selfrep-spares. A repair that needs a printed bushing waits extra print hours (mean-downtime approximation in the unchanged selfrep-repair simulation). At the assumed inputs the working fleet is flat up to about 500 h of wait per repair (62.7 vs 64.2 machines with none) and falls at 1000 h (58.5) to 36.0 at 5000 h, because the fleet is import-limited, not downtime-limited. The bushing’s gain over stock bearings (+1.8) was already inside the run-to-run spread. Stylised, assumed inputs; printing does not compete with building for machine time.

title: How much does making its own spare parts cut the cost of repairing a printer?
summary: Follow-up to selfrep-repair. The spare-part cost share of a repair is derived from the Prusa Mendel’s wear parts (belts, bearings, hot end, switches), each with an assumed life, and from which of them a seed shop can make. The printer alone makes none and adding a router and laser cutter makes only the pulleys, so the share stays near 0.021 and the fleet is unchanged (62.5 vs 63.0 machines, against 7.3 with replacement only). Swapping the linear bearings for a printed bushing lowers the share to 0.019, but if the bushing lasts half as long the fleet falls to 43, so breakdown rate matters more than where the spare comes from. Stylised: every life and cost is assumed.

title: Does the best printer redesign change when imported bar stock counts as an import, not as made?
summary: A stylised, preliminary re-scoring of the 448-design search of selfrep-alusearch : the score is the mass (or cost) the shop must still import per printer copy, vitamins plus raw stock at an assumed 0.8 yield. The import-mass minimiser reaches 5.85 kg against 6.72 kg for the steel-rod baseline, with the light 8 mm hardwood rod; the earlier closure-maximising pick (12 mm aluminium) imports 6.79 kg, no better than baseline. By import cost the 12 mm aluminium rod stays best (147.5 against 173.3). Yield, stock price and penalties are assumed; computed only.

title: How does a resale value for the finished fleet move the switch from copies to goods?
summary: Follow-up to selfrep-reinvest. Giving each machine left at the horizon a value s shortens the goods phase from one e-folding time 1/ k to 1/ k − s / a , so the switch moves later; at s ≥ a / k (50 per machine with no failures, 29% of the assumed vitamin cost) the shop copies to the end. The grid optimum of the Euler simulation agrees with this closed form to within 1 h, and ignoring a terminal value of 12.5–50 per machine costs 3–26% of the optimum. Every input is assumed; cash is free and demand unlimited. Stylised.

title: Does a resale value for the finished fleet still end copying late when the goods market saturates?
summary: Follow-up to selfrep-terminal and selfrep-satmarket: a backward dynamic programme with terminal reward s per machine on the saturating-market fluid model ( W = 50 h, failure 0, horizon 600 h, all inputs assumed). With a linear market the DP reproduces the closed-form switch of selfrep-terminal. As the market capacity c falls, a small s moves the optimum from an early switch to copying until the horizon ( c = 1000: switch near 400 h at s = 0, none at s = 12.5), and a policy tuned for s = 0 earns only 14% of the optimum. Where the final fleet is large the DP is not reliable: a bang-bang switch beats its policy by up to 0.7%, so it is a lower bound there. Stylised and preliminary; the resale value is assumed and does not itself saturate.

title: What fleet can a replicating printer shop sustain when its machines wear out?
summary: Extends the selfrep-growth fleet model with random machine lifetimes (Weibull) and a recovered share of vitamin value at retirement. With assumed inputs and a vitamin budget of 4 units/h, a lone seed machine died out in every run when mean life was 200 h or less (20% of runs at 500 h, 3% at 2000 h), while the fluid model predicted a small stable fleet; survivors held about 10 machines at 500 h. Wear-out lifetimes are safer than constant hazard at the same mean. The fluid equilibrium over-predicts fleet size at high recycling (235 vs 73 simulated at 95% recovery); charging for builds cut short by retirement closes the gap (76), though that correction was added after seeing the discrepancy. Stylised: every input is assumed.

title: How many frames from a small sensor, merged, match one frame from a bigger one?
summary: Synthetic scenes with Poisson shot noise, Gaussian read noise and a full-well clip. A burst of N small-sensor frames (each at the large frame's exposure time) ties a sensor with A × the pixel area at N * = A ²( sx + r ²)/( Asx + r ²): A frames when shot noise dominates, up to A ² in the dark or at high read noise (simulation, A =4: 4.0 frames in bright light, 14.4 in dim light with 8 e − read noise). Splitting the same total exposure into frames never ties: the burst has more variance than the large frame at every N . With hand shake and Fourier-shift registration, shifts are recovered to 0.09–0.8 px RMS in good light but fail in the dimmest case tested (3.1 px), and the registration blur means A =4 needs about 21 frames in bright light. A bracketed burst recovers clipped highlights (42 dB against 22 dB for one frame). Stylised: synthetic images, global translation only, no real raw files.

title: How many cheap gyros, fused, match one better gyro at the same cost?
summary: Single-axis gyro model with angle random walk and rate random walk (Allan-variance terms) and a fraction ρ of each shared between units. With independent errors an array of n cheap units ties a unit k times quieter only when the price ratio exceeds k 2 (9 for k = 3, 100 for k = 10); shared error above 1/ k 2 means no array size ties ( k = 10, ρ ≥ 0.01). If the better unit improves white noise 10× but bias walk only 3×, the number of units needed falls from 100 at 1 s to 10 beyond 300 s, so the answer depends on integration time. Monte Carlo matches the closed form within 0.03. Stylised: illustrative grades, not datasheets; no real IMU data; no prices claimed.

title: How many photos does a usable 3-D reconstruction need?
summary: Synthetic bumpy-ellipsoid object, 800 features, pinhole cameras on an orbit with known poses and linear (DLT) triangulation. On a full orbit 12 views reconstruct every feature, 8 views 89%, 6 views 59% and 4 or fewer at most 13%, because a point must be seen by two cameras. Once triangulated, error is about 0.0028 object radii per pixel of image noise, a 1° pose error does the damage of about 2 px, and a narrow baseline (5° span) raises error about 7× against a 40° span. Triangulation stage only: matches and poses are given, there is no occlusion, mesh or splat, and no real images.

title: How accurate must a scan be to rebuild a part as parametric CAD?
summary: Synthetic point-cloud scans of an 80×40×10 mm plate with two 8 mm holes, fitted by RANSAC planes and circle fits. With scan noise of 0.2 mm or less every scan gives all five dimensions within 0.2 mm at 2 000 points or more (worst RMS 0.09 mm). At 0.5 mm noise only 0–50% of scans are usable at any point count because the error is a bias: thickness reads 0.20 mm low and the bias grows with the inlier band (−0.07 to −0.38 mm for 1.5σ to 4σ). A scale error of 0.5% from a reconstruction with no scale reference already moves an 80 mm length by 0.40 mm. Stylised: one shape, assumed Gaussian noise, pre-registered scan, generated CadQuery script not run.

title: Does a low-resolution thermal camera find people in darkness and smoke, and what does misalignment cost?
summary: Synthetic 64×64 scenes with people, cold clutter and warm non-person decoys, seen by a grey RGB camera (shot and read noise, smoke airlight) and a 16×16 thermal camera (0.3 K noise, 10% of the visible smoke extinction assumed). At 10% false alarms per image, RGB alone finds 36% of people in bright clear light, 13% at smoke transmittance 0.4 and none in the dark or dense smoke; thermal alone finds 65% in every condition, capped by the decoys; fusing them gives 94% in bright light and falls back to the thermal level otherwise. A thermal camera displaced by 2 px costs the fused detector 7 points, 4 px (one thermal pixel) 19, and 6 px leaves it below RGB alone (0.12 vs 0.37); training with displacement jitter keeps 0.54 at 6 px but loses 9 points when aligned. Stylised: synthetic scenes, logistic-regression detectors on local contrast, sideways shift only, no real data.

title: How many milliseconds of camera-to-gyro time offset double a fused attitude error, and can online calibration recover it?
summary: Single-axis simulation: a 200 Hz biased gyro and a 30 Hz camera whose timestamps are late by t d , fused by a complementary filter. At 30 deg/s motion the error doubles at 12–14 ms; the doubling offset is 32–34 ms at 10 deg/s and 8–10 ms at 90 deg/s, and grows with camera noise. A gyro-integral alignment fit recovers the offset to about 1 ms rms and restores the zero-offset error, but fails on a nearly still platform. Stylised: one axis, constant offset, angle measurements only, synthetic noise.

title: Can you slash while watching the data stream?
summary: Anytime-valid slashing of miscalibrated verifiers with e-processes: repeatedly re-running a z-test falsely slashes 37% of honest verifiers at nominal 5%, the likelihood-ratio e-process stays under α by Ville’s inequality, detection delay tracks ln(1/α)/KL within 12% (logarithmic in 1/α), and not knowing the cheating rate costs a factor 1.36. Stylised.

title: Can an input shaper make a liquid-carrying cart’s move robust to a stale slosh-frequency calibration, and how fast can it be?
summary: Follow-up to slosh-twin. Convolving the twin’s bang-bang acceleration with a ZV or ZVD shaper multiplies the undamped residual exactly by V ( ε ) = |sin( πε /2)| or sin 2 ( πε /2), ε the frequency error (verified against exact propagation to 10 digits), while distance and the acceleration cap are preserved. Designed at a full tank, both shapers keep the 1 cm tolerance at every fill from 100% to 10% ( ε down to −9.5%; worst residual 4.8 mm ZV, 0.6 mm ZVD) in 5.90 s and 6.90 s, where the null-tuned move needs 8 s at half fill and 28 s at 25% and below. Closed forms give the largest tolerated | ε | (e.g. 10.7% for ZV at half fill). Searching the design frequency for a fill band [0.1, 1] yields a 5.85 s ZV move, but only by detuning to spend the whole tolerance (worst residual 9.88 mm, no margin). Stylised: one linear slosh mode, ideal actuator, no nonlinear slosh.

title: How should Shapley payments be sampled and audited?
summary: In a saturating contribution game v(S)=1−exp(−Σw i ) every estimator variance is exact. Permutation sampling always pays out exactly v(N) but is noisy; size-stratified sampling has 6–8× lower variance (exactly zero for equal contributors) yet misses the pot by up to 7% in a run; reversing each permutation cuts RMSE 1.6× at no cost; Hoeffding sample counts are 4–5× larger than needed, and stratification finds the top-3 payees with about 4× fewer samples. Stylised, n≤10.

title: A constant-variance Gaussian camera twin of Poisson photon counting: which dark/bright decision rule does it teach, and what does that cost on the real sensor?
summary: For Poisson counts the Bayes dark/bright threshold is the logarithmic mean (λ 1 −λ 0 )/ln(λ 1 /λ 0 ); a Gaussian twin with one matched variance puts it at the arithmetic mean (7.28 vs 8.00 for 4 vs 12), and a square-root twin lands in between at (A+G)/2. A detector tuned in the arithmetic twin has 1.25× the optimal real error at (4,12), 1.83× at (10,30) and 1.74× at (50,100), and with λ 1 =2λ 0 the penalty grows to 23× at λ 0 =200, while the twin’s own predicted error stays within 1.8× of the optimum; the square-root rule recovers the optimal integer rule in 8 of 9 pairs. Stylised: ideal Poisson counts, no read noise, no camera data.

title: A global-shutter twin of a rolling-shutter camera ignores target motion: how biased is a twin-trained orientation estimate, and what does the same frame reveal?
summary: Row r is exposed at t = rτ / H , so a moving rectangle is imaged sheared and stretched; closed-form edge normals match a row-by-row simulation. At 1000 px/s horizontal speed the vertical edges tilt 3.58° and the horizontal ones 0, so averaging the two edge families (what a global-shutter twin certifies) is biased 1.79°; 1000 px/s vertical speed makes the target 6.7% taller. One frame of a known-size rectangle identifies orientation and both velocities in closed form: with 0.25 px edge noise orientation error falls from 0.24–0.97° to 0.027° and speeds are recovered to 16 and 4.8 px/s, but vertical speed is very sensitive to the assumed size (a 5% height error moves it by about 800 px/s). Stylised: straight edges, constant velocity, known size, no real footage.

title: A radar twin whose targets occupy a single range cell: how far around a strong target does the real matched filter ghost, and does tapering fix it?
summary: A lone strong target through a matched filter alarms at neighbouring cells with an exact Rician probability where the point-response twin says P fa0 =10 −6 : at the rect peak sidelobe (−13.3 dB) it is 0.020 at 20 dB SNR and 1.0 at 30 dB, and the ghost zone radius grows √10 per 10 dB (3 to 331 cells for 20–60 dB). Tapers raise the ghost-free SNR by exactly the sidelobe-level difference plus the ENBW loss (20.0 dB Hann, 30.8 dB Hamming) at 1.5–1.6× mainlobe width, but ordering by peak sidelobe misleads at very strong targets: Hamming’s 1/ x far sidelobes give a 42-cell zone against Hann’s 7 at 60 dB. A weak target beside a 40 dB one is ‘detected’ with P d =1.0 where the empty cell alarms with probability 1.0. Stylised: white output noise, no CFAR or clutter, no radar data.

title: Can a parametric L-bracket be sized by finite elements for minimum mass and come out printable?
summary: A 2D plane-stress scikit-fem model of an L-bracket with a filleted inner corner (arm width, fillet radius, depth) under a 100 N tip load. Differential evolution reaches 19.6 g against 25.6 g for random search and 31.4 g for a grid at 144–150 evaluations each, under a 20 MPa stress and 4 mm deflection limit. The design is exported as a binary STL and checked for minimum wall and overhang. Stylised: material properties and limits are assumed, the optimum stress rises about 7% on mesh refinement (just over the limit), the sharp-corner stress diverges, and the thin optimum was not checked for out-of-plane buckling.

title: Does the lightest 1.5 mm bracket design clear buckling in a converged 3D eigenbuckling model?
summary: A small finite-element check (stylised, preliminary; ideal elastic clamped arms, one design). Meshing the 1.5 mm, w = 18.4 mm design from simdesign-bucklebound with hexahedra at three resolutions, including two layers through the thickness, the governing vertical-arm buckling factor is 3.49 against 3.47 from the closed form (ratio 1.020 → 1.007 on refinement), so the design clears the floor of 3. The horizontal-arm formula is about 18% conservative. Nothing was made or tested.

title: What changes when the w/b ≤ 8 slenderness ceiling of the laser-cut bracket is replaced by a buckling-factor floor?
summary: A small optimiser study (stylised, preliminary; the buckling factor is an unvalidated closed form). Minimising mass over web width and fillet radius at four sheet gauges with differential evolution (three seeds, mesh 1.5 mm): the old ceiling makes the 1.5 mm gauge infeasible, while a buckling-factor floor of 1 or 3 yields a 31.0 g design (w ≈ 18.4 mm, factor 3.5), about 13% lighter than the best 2 mm design (35.8 g). At 2 and 3 mm the three guards agree to 0.1%. At 1 mm no design is feasible under any guard because the 1.2 mm minimum-wall rule, not buckling, rejects it. Mass is the only objective; nothing was made or tested.

title: What does it cost to replace the w/b ≤ 8 rule of the laser-cut bracket with a buckling-factor guard?
summary: A stylised, preliminary optimisation study (closed-form buckling check, assumed rules, material and load). Replacing the w/b ≤ 8 slenderness rule with a lateral-torsional safety factor of at least 3 lets the differential-evolution optimiser use the 1.5 mm gauge at w ≈ 18.7 mm: 31.1–31.4 g against 35.8–36.0 g under the old rule, about 12% lighter (three seeds each). The guard does not bind at that optimum; the stress limit does. The result depends on the assumed factor: no feasible 1.5 mm design was found for a factor of 5 or more. Simulated only; edge crippling, imperfections and cutting stress are not modelled.

title: How short can SIMP penalty continuation be and still remove the dependence on the starting density field?
summary: Follow-up to simdesign-starts . Half-MBB, volume 0.5, final p = 3, exactly 150 OC iterations, random starts (noise ±0.3; 20 on 60×20, 12 on 90×30), with the penalty ramped 1 → 3 over 0, 6, 12, 25, 50, 75 or 112 iterations. Ramps of 25 iterations or fewer leave most of the start dependence of a fixed penalty (worst start differs from the uniform-start design in 31% and 27% of elements on the two meshes): for ramps of 6–25 it is still 17–23% (60×20) and 16–20% (90×30), and compliance spreads 0.5–1.3%. At 50 iterations the spread falls to 0.01% (60×20) and 0.23% (90×30); at 75 the median disagreement is 0.0–0.3%. A 112-iteration ramp is the most repeatable but gives a worse final compliance (203.55 against 203.08 on 60×20; 197.3 against 196.6 on 90×30), because few iterations remain at full penalty. Stylised: 2D, one problem, two meshes, 150 iterations, not run to convergence.

title: Does weighting parts by mass change which shop process, and which machine, matters?
summary: Follow-up to simdesign-processcover : coverage of a sampled bracket family by FDM, CNC, laser and casting, with each part weighted by arm volume (a same-material mass proxy) instead of counted equally. With a tip load, FDM alone covers 0.30 of parts by count and 0.58 by mass, casting 0.22 and 0.46, laser 0.18 either way, and the laser-versus-CNC order flips. At budgets 600–800 on one seed, exhaustive search picks the laser cutter by count but the casting setup by mass; for the large-part family at 800 it picks the CNC router by count and casting by mass. Stylised: assumed rules and prices, one density, single-seed machine choice. Simulated only.

title: What do manufacturing rules cost a sized bracket on FDM, CNC routing, laser cutting and casting?
summary: The L-bracket of simdesign-bracket is sized for minimum mass under a stress and a deflection limit with and without each process’s rules (tool radius, plate or sheet gauges, minimum walls, draft, an even-section rule), in the same material, so the ratio isolates the rules. Sand casting pays +43% (best of three seeds), driven by its wall-ratio rule rather than draft; CNC routing +24%, from the thinnest plate on the stock list; laser cutting and FDM about nothing, within optimiser noise (three seeds spread over 20%). Re-solved on a fine mesh, every chosen design exceeds its stress limit by 17–26%. Stylised: rule values and materials are assumed, the model is 2D, nothing was built. Exports an STL and DXF profiles.

title: How sharp is the feasible edge of the 2 mm laser-cut bracket web at 0.1 mm resolution, and is it mesh noise?
summary: A small scan (stylised, preliminary). Re-scanning web width w in 0.1 mm steps (15.5–17.5 mm) at three radii and three meshes, the peak von Mises stress is not monotone in w in any of the nine series. Its residual jitter about a quadratic trend is 0.9–2.4 MPa, shrinking with refinement, and the stress just below each feasible edge is only 0.1–1.7 MPa over the 100 MPa limit, so the edge is a band of about 0.5 mm and the refinement shift reported in simdesign-widerweb is not separated from mesh noise. The source of the jitter is not identified. Simulated only.

title: When does a cheaper beam model pick the same design as 3D finite elements?
summary: A rectangular cantilever is sized for minimum mass under a tip-deflection and a top-fibre stress limit with Euler–Bernoulli and Timoshenko beam theory, 2D plane-stress and 3D finite elements (scikit-fem), and each design is judged by the 3D model. Stress read away from the clamp agrees across models; deflection does not. Over 12 length–width cases the cheap models choose a depth within about 5% of the 3D optimum: Euler–Bernoulli is unsafe for narrow, stubby beams (up to 1.05× the deflection limit), while Timoshenko and plane stress are up to about 5% too heavy for wide ones, where plane strain stiffens the beam. Stylised: assumed material, a coarse 3D reference whose deflection still moves about 0.4% under refinement, no stress concentrations, nothing measured.

title: Is the shrinking laser-cutting price scatter under the patch stress caused by the near-sharp fillet floor?
summary: A negative result (stylised). Raising the laser-cutting inner-fillet floor from 0.2 to 1 and 3.175 mm over five seeds does not explain the scatter in the mass price of the rules: the peak-stress designs already use fillets of 7.6–14.3 mm, so the 0.2 and 1 mm floors give identical designs (sd of the price 0.063), and under a 3 mm patch average the price is steady (sd 0.006–0.011) at every floor. The cause of the peak-stress scatter is not identified. Limits: five seeds, one process and load, uncalibrated limit, assumed values, 2D plane stress.

title: Do the mass-weighting machine-choice flips of simdesign-coverweight survive across seeds?
summary: Follow-up to simdesign-coverweight , whose machine-choice flips between count and mass weighting came from one seed. Over 20 fresh seeds of 20 000 sampled brackets and three assumed machines, family log picks the laser cutter by count but the casting setup (or, in 2 seeds at 800, the CNC router) by mass in 20 of 20 seeds at budgets 600 to 800 (95% Wilson interval 0.84 to 1.00; about 2.1 points of mass-weighted coverage given up), family large flips only at budget 800 (20 of 20), and small never flips. The log flips at 1100 and 1400 split 10 of 20 but lose at most 0.26 points, a near-tie. The intervals cover sampling noise only; rules, prices and the volume mass proxy are assumptions. Stylised; simulated only.

title: Do the reversed-load buckling-limited L-bracket designs also pass the forward-load buckling, stress and deflection checks?
summary: A small finite-element check (stylised, preliminary; ideal elastic steel, sharp inner corner, assumed limits). Under the forward 100 N load the four lightest designs that clear the reversed-load buckling floor (1.5 to 3.0 mm sheet) all have forward buckling factors of 4.7 to 5.6, so buckling does not bind. But only the 1.5 mm, 22.5 mm design meets the 100 MPa stress and 4 mm deflection limits; the 2.5 and 3.0 mm designs exceed them by 2 to 8 times, and the 2.0 mm design passes only on the coarse mesh (95.7 MPa against 144.9 MPa on a finer one). The thicker sheet's mass saving is therefore not feasible under these limits.

title: Are the two mass groups of the 2 mm laser-cut bracket search two separate basins?
summary: A small diagnostic (stylised, preliminary). The lighter and heavier groups of gauge-2 search results differ in web width (about 14.3–14.9 against 15.2–15.6 mm), not in fillet radius. A coarse grid shows one connected feasible region, but a 0.1 mm scan shows the feasible set is ragged in width: isolated feasible pockets lie below a contiguous region, and the lighter group matches those pockets. This is consistent with a coarse-mesh stress artefact rather than two broad basins, a mechanism not tested here. Twenty seeds, one process, one mesh; nothing was built.

title: Where does the peak-stress price scatter of laser-cutting rules come from?
summary: A stylised follow-up to the fillet-floor negative result. Keeping the best mass of each of the ten stock-gauge sub-searches shows that the scatter in the rules mass (price 0.990–1.145 over five seeds) sits in the 2 mm gauge: in one seed that sub-search found nothing feasible and the 3 mm gauge won, giving the 1.145 outlier, while gauges of 3 mm and above agree across seeds to within 0.05 g at four times the budget. Quadrupling the search budget cuts the price sd from 0.063 to 0.025, but not monotonically, the no-rules twin moves too, and the 2 mm gauge still spreads over 2 g, so the data are consistent with several nearby optima there, not proof of it. Five seeds, one process and load case, 2D plane stress, assumed rules. Simulated only. Produced with AI assistance.

title: Is the least-mass laser-cut bracket the same on coarse and fine meshes under a patch-averaged stress rule?
summary: Preliminary, stylised 2D plane stress. On a 20×20 grid over arm width and fillet radius, the least mass of a feasible laser-cut bracket under a 3 mm patch-averaged stress rule is the same on a 2.5 mm and a 1.0 mm mesh (2 mm sheet: 32.31 vs 32.33 g; 3 mm: 40.81 vs 40.81 g). Under the element-centroid peak rule the 2 mm sheet has no feasible design on the fine mesh and the 3 mm sheet needs 10.8% more mass. The catch: the patch value hardly depends on the fillet radius (94–102 MPa for r from 0 to 15 mm against a peak of 126–264 MPa), so the rule cannot tell a sharp corner from a generous fillet. Two meshes only; one load case; nothing built or tested.
