title: Do the reversed-load buckling widths of the L-bracket change with more element layers through the thickness?
summary: A small finite-element check (stylised, preliminary; ideal elastic sheet, sharp inner corner, coarse in-plane mesh). Raising the number of hexahedral layers through the sheet from one to four moves the whole-L reversed-load buckling factor at the simdesign-revgauge root widths by at most 1.2% (3.0 mm gauge; under 0.7% at 1.5 to 2.5 mm) and the width needed for a factor of 3 by 0.07 mm or less (2.0 mm: 11.84 to 11.77 mm, 27.4 g). The thicker-sheet mass ranking of that project is not an artefact of a single through-thickness layer; its other doubt, a web barely wider than the sheet is thick, stands.

title: Is the narrow 2 mm laser-cut bracket region a mesh artefact?
summary: A negative result for the search mesh (stylised). All 39 gauge-2 bracket designs that were feasible on the 2.5 mm search mesh (19 under laser rules, 20 for the no-rules twin) are infeasible on finer meshes (1.5, 1.0, 0.75 mm): the peak von Mises stress is 1.09–1.27× higher at 0.75 mm and is still rising, at the point where the fillet meets the arm. Tip deflection is unchanged and the fillet facet count is not the cause. Earlier mass prices in the bracket chain are therefore conditional on the coarse mesh; no fine-mesh optimum was searched.

title: Does a patch-averaged stress make the 2 mm laser-cut bracket region mesh-independent?
summary: Preliminary, stylised 2D plane stress. On the 39 gauge-2 bracket designs that fail the stress limit on fine meshes under the element-centroid peak, a 3 mm patch-averaged stress changes by at most 2.2% between 1.0 and 0.75 mm meshes (the centroid peak rises up to 9.7%), and all 39 stay feasible at every mesh size, with a median of 84–86 MPa on the finest mesh. The verdict flips because the criterion is less strict, not because the model changed; whether a patch average is an adequate design rule was not shown, and no fine-mesh design search was run.

title: Do the isolated feasible pockets of the 2 mm laser-cut bracket survive mesh refinement?
summary: A small mesh-refinement scan (stylised, preliminary). The isolated feasible web widths below 15 mm that appear at 2.5 mm element size vanish at 2.0 and 1.5 mm, and the smallest feasible width moves up (14.4 to 15.6 mm at fillet radius 14 mm). Mesh convergence was not reached, and a stress peak at a corner is itself mesh-sensitive, so the least-mass design on the search mesh is optimistic.

title: Do search restarts remove the missed 2 mm sub-search in the laser-cut bracket problem?
summary: A small search-effort experiment (stylised). At the 2 mm sheet gauge, one differential-evolution run missed the narrow feasible region in 1 of 20 seeds; a second independent run or a doubled population missed in 0 of 40 runs each, at about twice the finite-element solves. Results also shift from an even split towards the lighter of two mass groups (to 70–75% with a restart, 85–95% with the larger population), consistent with the heavier group being a local optimum of the search. Zero misses in 20 does not prove a zero miss rate, and the 2 mm region is itself a coarse-mesh effect, so the lower masses are not better physical designs.

title: What causes the peak-stress price scatter of laser-cutting rules in the bracket search?
summary: A diagnostic with a negative-for-the-rules answer (stylised). The high price in one of five seeds (1.15 vs 1.00–1.01 in the others) is a missed search, not a cost of the laser rules: the 2 mm sheet gauge, which wins, has a feasible region of only 13 of 900 grid cells, and the rules sub-search missed it in 1 of 20 seeds (the rule-free twin in 0 of 20). Feasible 2 mm results fall in two mass groups (33.3–34.0 g and 35.3–35.6 g) whose cause is not identified. Mesh effects were not tested. Stylised 2D plane stress; assumed rules and loads.

title: Does the peak stress at the fillet tangent point of the L-bracket converge under graded mesh refinement?
summary: Preliminary, stylised 2D plane stress. Uniform meshes left the element-centroid peak stress of the 2 mm laser-cut bracket still rising. Refining only around the fillet tangent point, down to 0.025 mm elements, the peak of four designs flattens at 1.09–1.14× its 1.5 mm value (0.0–1.1% change over the last 4× refinement), so it has a finite limit and the earlier mesh dependence was a resolution effect. The converged plateau shifts about 2% with the grading rate; the 16/15/2 design sits marginally above the 100 MPa limit (101.9 MPa). No independent reference solution was compared; nothing was optimised.

title: Does a density filter with Heaviside projection close the gap between a topology-optimised density field and the black-and-white part?
summary: Adds a density filter, a tanh Heaviside projection and β continuation to the SIMP code of simdesign-topopt . On a 90×30 half-MBB beam the sensitivity and density filters leave 26–34% grey elements and a model compliance 10–15% above the thresholded part’s; with projection the two agree to 0.1% (192.1 vs 192.0). The thresholded parts are equally stiff within 0.9% (190.3–192.0), so the gain is an honest model, not a stiffer part. Starting at β = 64 without continuation gives 344.8 against 192.1. A minimum-length-scale check did not separate the formulations (negative): a single projection does not by itself fix a physical minimum feature. Stylised: 2D dimensionless compliance, one problem, one run per setting.

title: Does a patch-averaged stress give a mesh-converged stress concentration for a bolt hole?
summary: A strip in tension with a central circular hole is solved by finite elements on meshes of 48 to 768 points around the hole, and the pointwise peak of σ xx is compared with its average over a disc of 0.1 to 0.5 hole radii, for d/W from 0.05 to 0.4, and with Kirsch’s analytic field. The peak is already nearly settled for a smooth hole (0.3% change over the last refinement; the patch measures 0.0–0.1%), and at d/W = 0.05 the patch values match Kirsch’s disc averages to within 0.4%. The patch reads 65–91% of the peak, so it needs its own limit. One coarse mesh (d/W = 0.4, 96 points) is an unexplained outlier for every measure. Stylised; linear plane stress, no allowable calibrated.

title: How much does a bolt hole cost a tension plate, and which rule sets its width?
summary: A flat plate carrying one required hole is sized for minimum mass under a working-stress limit with three stress models (net section, a fixed Kt = 3, and 2D finite elements over d/W ) and with per-process hole rules (minimum hole, centre-to-edge distance, ligament, stock thickness). FE reproduces the large-plate limit of Kt = 3 as the hole shrinks. Ignoring the concentration gives plates 1.9–2.7× overstressed where stress binds; Kt = 3 is safe but 8–26% heavier for FDM. Where an edge-distance rule binds (CNC routing, laser from 8 mm, casting from 8 mm) the stress model is irrelevant and the plate is 2–4× stronger than needed. Stylised: rule values, load and materials are assumed, 2D plane stress, no bolt contact or fatigue, mesh not fully converged (about 1% low), nothing built.

title: How far below the exact stress concentration does a finite-element peak stress sit, and how fast does it close?
summary: A plate with a circular hole under tension has an exact peak stress of 3× the remote stress (Kirsch). On a graded quarter-plate mesh with exact-solution tractions (48 384 elements at the finest), the usual element-centroid peak sits 27% below it on the coarsest mesh and 1.1% below on the finest, closing only at first order, while the field itself converges at second order: the shortfall is sampling position, not solver error. Reading the stress at the hole-edge vertices instead is within 1% on every mesh. Stylised 2D plane stress, one geometry, regular mesh; the numbers do not transfer to other fillets.

title: Does the 1.5 mm bracket clear buckling when the whole L is one 3D body with a flexible corner?
summary: A small finite-element check (stylised, preliminary; ideal elastic sheet, sharp inner corner, one design). Meshing the whole L of the 1.5 mm, w = 18.4 mm design from simdesign-bucklebound as one hexahedral body, the lowest buckling factor under the design load (vertical arm in tension) is 4.01, above the closed-form 3.47 and the floor of 3. With the load reversed (arm in compression) it falls to 2.25, below the floor, a case the moment-only formula cannot see. Refinement moved the factors by under 2%. No fillet, no imperfections.

title: How do design proposals from a language-model agent compare with CMA-ES, Bayesian optimisation and random search at an equal simulation budget?
summary: The finite-element bracket of simdesign-bracket, with tighter limits (15 MPa, 2.5 mm), is sized for minimum mass with 40 simulator calls per method. The proposer is the session agent itself, writing four rounds of ten designs by hand from the scores (no API key; not a reproducible LLM benchmark). It reaches 23.0 g against medians of 32.2 g (Bayesian optimisation), 33.3 g (CMA-ES) and 39.0 g (random) over 20 seeds, with 22.4 g best known from 1,845 evaluations; no baseline seed beat it. Stylised and weak evidence: n = 1, the agent used mechanics and the sibling project’s results as a prior, baselines were untuned, the stress constraint is mesh-sensitive, assumed material.

title: When does the buckling guard of the laser-cut bracket start to bind as load and arm length change?
summary: A stylised, preliminary sweep (closed-form buckling check, assumed rules, material and loads; two seeds). Over tip loads of 50–400 N and arms of 60–120 mm, a lateral-torsional factor ≥ 3 guard binds in only one of six cases: 120 mm arms, where the unguarded optimum has a factor of 1.9 and the guard costs 16% in mass (69 g vs 59 g). The old w/b ≤ 8 rule was 14–25% heavier than the buckling guard in five of six cases. Gauge steps make mass non-smooth in load; the result moves with the assumed factor.

title: How much stiffness does a topology-optimised cantilever lose when the real load points a different way than the model assumed?
summary: Optimises a 48×24 cantilever (volume fraction 0.4) for a straight-down tip load and for weighted sums over several load directions, then analyses each design under load angles from −90° to 90° against the design optimised for that angle alone. The nominal design is within 5% for tilts up to 30°, but 1.57× off at 60° and 2.58× at horizontal. A {0, ±60°} multi-load design cuts the worst case to 2.00× for 0.6% on the nominal load, and {0, ±90°} to 1.88× for 2.9%; no single topology is stiff in every direction. Stylised 2D, one mesh, one run per design; preliminary.

title: Does the feasible boundary of the 2 mm laser-cut bracket converge when the mesh is refined to 0.5 mm?
summary: A negative result (stylised, preliminary). Scanning web width from 15.0 to 16.0 mm (the slenderness rule forbids wider) at four fillet radii on 1.5, 1.0, 0.75 and 0.5 mm meshes, the feasible widths found at 1.5 mm are all infeasible at 1.0 and 0.5 mm under the 100 MPa peak-stress limit, with a single feasible point at 0.75 mm. The lowest peak stress rises 11–14% from 1.5 to 0.5 mm and is still creeping up, so convergence is not shown. One gauge, one load, a peak measure at a near-sharp fillet floor; no search was run on the fine meshes.

title: Does a mesh-aware stress margin change what manufacturing rules cost a sized bracket?
summary: The process-rule search of simdesign-dfm is repeated with a coarse mesh, a coarse mesh with the stress limit divided by 1.3, and a finer mesh, and every design is re-solved on a finer check mesh. The ordering of the mass prices survives: casting about 1.4, CNC routing about 1.23, FDM 1.0 by construction. The laser-cutting price does not (1.01 to 1.22 across settings, with only two seeds). A margin of 1.3 leaves the designs at 0.88 to 1.02 of the limit on the check mesh, at a 17at a 20–35% mass costndash;35% mass cost. Stylised: the peak stress is not converged even on the check mesh, rule values are assumed, and nothing was made.

title: Does relaxing the 1.2 mm minimum-wall rule open thinner sheet gauges for the laser-cut bracket, or is the buckling floor what binds?
summary: A small optimiser study (stylised, preliminary; the buckling factor is an unvalidated ideal-bar closed form). Relaxing the minimum wall from 1.2 to 1.0 or 0.8 mm changes nothing at 1.5 mm (31.0 g in every cell) and does not by itself open 1.0 mm sheet: with a buckling-factor floor of 3 no design exists at 0.8 or 1.0 mm (the widest allowed web reaches a factor of only 1.5 at 1.0 mm). With a floor of 1 and a minimum wall of 1.0 mm or less, a 1.0 mm design appears at 24.8 g (w = 22.7 mm, factor 1.33, 2 of 3 seeds), 20% under the 1.5 mm optimum, but a factor of 1.33 from an ideal-bar formula is no margin. Simulated results only.

title: Does a patch-averaged stress change what manufacturing rules cost a sized bracket?
summary: The minimum-mass bracket search under FDM, CNC-routing, laser-cutting and casting rules is repeated with a 3 mm patch-averaged stress in place of the peak element stress, using the same numeric limit, then every design is re-solved on a fine check mesh (h = 0.55 mm). The ordering of the mass prices survives (casting 1.35, CNC 1.23–1.27, laser 1.03–1.05, FDM 1.0), and the laser-cutting price, which varied from 0.99 to 1.15 across three seeds under the peak measure, varies by under 0.005. Patch-searched designs exceed the limit by 2–12% on the fine mesh, against 19–34% for peak-searched designs, but they are lighter only because the same numeric limit is a looser test; the patch limit is uncalibrated. Three seeds, assumed rules and material, stylised 2D.

title: Does a patch-averaged stress converge under mesh refinement where the peak element stress does not?
summary: On four L-bracket designs solved on five meshes (h = 2.5 to 0.55 mm), the peak von Mises stress rises by 18–41% while a 3 mm patch average moves by 1–6%. The peak is not monotone along the sequence, so a two-mesh check can mislead. The patch average is not conservative: it reads 0.45–0.69 of the fine-mesh peak and would need its own calibrated limit. Stylised: 2D plane stress, one load case, a non-nested mesh family, assumed material, nothing made.

title: Do the isolated feasible pockets of the 2 mm laser-cut bracket survive mesh refinement?
summary: A small mesh-refinement scan (stylised, preliminary). Scanning web width in 0.1 mm steps at four fillet radii on 2.5, 2.0 and 1.5 mm meshes, the isolated feasible widths below 15.4 mm seen on the 2.5 mm mesh are absent at 1.5 mm, and the smallest feasible width rises from about 14.4–14.8 to 15.6–15.7 mm. This is consistent with the lighter search group being a coarse-mesh artefact, but the boundary was still moving, so convergence is not shown. No search was rerun on the finer meshes. Simulated only.

title: How wide are the budget bands where mass weighting changes the machine choice when prices are uncertain?
summary: Follow-up to simdesign-flipseeds , whose count-vs-mass machine-choice flips sat exactly on thresholds set by assumed round prices. Machine prices (800, 600, 300) are scaled by independent U(1−s, 1+s) factors, 400 draws over 8 samples of 20 000 sampled brackets. For family log the flip band widens from budgets 600–800 to 500–1000, but its edges soften to about one half; large 's single nominal flip at 800 appears in 44% of draws at s = 0.2 and spills to 700 and 900; small never flips. Near-tie flips never lose more than 0.5 points. Stylised: assumed prices and rules, uniform independent noise, arbitrary 0.5-point materiality threshold.

title: Which share of a bracket family can each shop process make, and which machine should a shop add next?
summary: Using the assumed rules of simdesign-dfm (FDM, CNC routing, laser cutting, casting) as feasibility checks on 20 000 sampled bracket feature sets, geometry alone gives a degenerate answer: FDM covers 89% and no other process covers anything FDM cannot, so no machine adds coverage (a negative result). With a tip-load requirement of 1–1000 N and closed-form beam checks the processes separate: FDM alone covers 30%, adding casting and a laser cutter 41%, and the best next machine depends on the budget and on the part sizes. Greedy selection from selfrep-nextmachine is sometimes 1–2 coverage points below exhaustive search. Stylised: all rule values, working stresses and prices are assumed, the beam check ignores fillet stress concentration, and nothing was made.

title: Do cheap beam and 2D models rank candidate cantilever designs like 3D finite elements?
summary: Stylised. 80 random cantilever designs per seed (3 seeds) are ranked by stiffness per mass with Euler–Bernoulli and Timoshenko beam theory and 2D plane-stress FE, and compared with a 3D finite-element reference (scikit-fem). Single-design merit is off by up to 14% (Euler–Bernoulli, stubby sections), yet every cheap model ranks the designs almost identically: Kendall τ 0.987–0.996 with 3D, 3D’s best design always ranked first, top-8 overlap 7 or 8 of 8. Stubby designs agree least (τ 0.96–0.99). Limits: one load case, assumed material, a coarse 3D reference, no stress or constraints in the ranking.

title: Does rolling back a robust topology-optimisation step that spikes compliance, and redoing it at half the move, beat shrinking the move afterwards?
summary: Follow-up to simdesign-robustadapt . The same nine robust half-MBB cases are run with five move-limit rules (45 deterministic runs): fixed 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, the earlier adaptive rule, and reject-and-retry, which discards a step whose worst-case compliance jumps more than 3× and redoes it at half the move. Blueprint failures: fixed 0.2, 5 of 9; adaptive, 2; retry, 1; fixed 0.1 and 0.05, none. Retry costs at most 2% more evaluations but never beat fixed 0.05, and on eroded-design quality it is 1.22× the best on average (fixed 0.1 hides one eroded design 25× worse that the blueprint test passes). Stylised: 2D dimensionless, one problem, one run per cell.

title: Is a thicker sheet lighter than a wider 1.5 mm web for clearing the reversed-load buckling floor?
summary: A small finite-element sweep (stylised, preliminary; ideal elastic sheet, sharp inner corner, buckling only, one element layer through the thickness). Reusing the whole-L 3D eigenbuckling model of simdesign-lbuckle , the smallest web width that lifts the reversed-load factor to 3 falls from 22.6 mm at 1.5 mm sheet to 11.8 mm at 2 mm and 6.8 mm at 2.5 mm, so the plate mass at the floor falls from 36.6 g to 27.5 g (−25%) and 20.5 g (−44%). Thick, narrow webs are where the model is weakest, and forward load, stress and minimum-wall rules were not rechecked, so this is an indication, not a design.

title: How wide must the 1.5 mm L-bracket be to clear the buckling floor when the load is reversed?
summary: A small finite-element sweep (stylised, preliminary; ideal elastic sheet, sharp inner corner, buckling only). Reusing the whole-L 3D eigenbuckling model of simdesign-lbuckle , the reversed-load factor of the 1.5 mm bracket rises from 2.27 at w = 18.4 mm to 3.0 at w ≈ 22.5–22.6 mm (coarse root 22.47, finer-mesh bracket 22.54–22.62), about 0.22 per extra millimetre. The plate mass rises from 30.7 to 36.6 g (+19%). Stress, slenderness and minimum-wall limits were not rechecked at the wider web, the floor of 3 is an assumption, and the corner is sharp.

title: Does a topology-optimised beam survive a 0.2 threshold error, and what does the robust formulation cost?
summary: Adds the eroded / blueprint / dilated robust projection formulation to the SIMP code of simdesign-heaviside and tests both on a half-MBB beam at three mesh sizes, each design judged at projection thresholds 0.7, 0.5 and 0.3. The plain Heaviside design fails when eroded on every mesh (a member disconnects; compliance 10 5 –10 9 against about 190), while the robust design stays at 224–226 eroded, 14–16% above its nominal value. The nominal compliance costs 0.8–3.4% more and the run about 2.5× the time. A minimum-length-scale gain was not shown (negative): feature sizes match Heaviside’s to within a pixel. Stylised: 2D dimensionless compliance, one problem, one run per setting, a density threshold standing in for etch error.

title: Can an adaptive move limit that shrinks after a compliance spike rescue a robust topology optimisation as well as a fixed small one?
summary: Follow-up to simdesign-robustmove . The same nine robust half-MBB cases are run with three move-limit rules (27 deterministic runs): fixed 0.2, fixed 0.05, and an adaptive rule that starts at 0.2 and halves after any iteration whose worst-case compliance jumps more than 3×. Fixed 0.2 fails (blueprint compliance > 1.5× the best of the three) in 5 of 9 cases, fixed 0.05 in none, adaptive in 2 of 9. The rule reacts only after the damaging step, so it rescues some cases and not others; in one 120×40 case its blueprint is fine but its eroded compliance is 2 839 against 284 for the fixed small move. Stylised: 2D, one problem, one run per cell.

title: Does the minimum feature of a robust topology-optimised beam follow the filter radius when the mesh is refined?
summary: Repeats the simdesign-robustradius sweep on 60×20 and 180×60 meshes with the filter radius held at 1/30, 1/20 and 1/15 of the beam length, plain Heaviside against the robust eroded / blueprint / dilated design (12 runs, one each). On the 180×60 mesh the minimum solid feature is 5 pixels (2.8% of the beam) at all three radii, 6, 9 and 12 elements; on 60×20 it is 1–3 pixels. With the earlier 120×40 runs the feature in pixels grows with the mesh (1, 3, 5) and not with the radius, so it is set by the grid here, not by the filter (negative for radius control; one problem, coarse integer measure). Two robust runs on the 60×20 mesh ended at poor blueprints (compliance about 740 against about 195), reported as such. Stylised: 2D, dimensionless.

title: Does the optimality-criteria move limit decide whether a robust topology optimisation survives its beta steps?
summary: Diagnoses two unexplained poor runs from simdesign-robustmesh . The robust eroded / blueprint / dilated half-MBB design is rerun at move limits 0.2, 0.1 and 0.05 over nine mesh-and-radius cases (27 deterministic runs). At 0.2, the value every earlier project used, five of nine blueprint compliances are more than 1.5× the best (e.g. 742 against about 200 on 60×20); at 0.1 and 0.05 none are. The failing runs show worst-case compliance jumping up to 400× in one iteration after β reaches 32–64. The mechanism (a thin member breaking when the eroded field sharpens) is a hypothesis, not tested. Stylised: 2D, dimensionless, one problem.

title: Does the filter radius or the threshold gap set the minimum feature size of a robust topology-optimised beam?
summary: Sweeps filter radius (2, 4, 6 elements) against threshold gap Δη (0, 0.1, 0.2) on a half-MBB beam, 120×40 elements, nine designs each judged at thresholds 0.7, 0.5 and 0.3. A gap of 0.1 already stops the erosion failure: eroded compliance 255–276 against 187–200 nominal, where the plain Heaviside design disconnects (10 7 –10 9 ). The radius does not give a clean length-scale control by the opening-rule measure: solid feature size is 3 px at both radius 4 and 6. Stylised: one problem, one mesh, one run per cell, integer-pixel measure.

title: At what bar slenderness does the 3D eigenbuckling model agree with the slender-beam closed form?
summary: A stylised, preliminary scan of one steel bar cross-section (8×2 mm, tip shear, clamped end) at l/w = 3, 6, 12 and 24 on a fixed element size. The finite-element critical load sits 14.5%, 7.4%, 3.8% and 2.1% above the Timoshenko–Gere closed form, so the gap shrinks roughly in proportion to w/l and is consistent with a short-bar effect rather than mesh error. One cross-section and one cross-section mesh; no refinement at the longer lengths.

title: Does refining the mesh of the 3D eigenbuckling check change how the closed-form bracket-arm buckling factors compare?
summary: A stylised, preliminary mesh study of the model in simdesign-webshell . Refining the quadratic-hexahedron mesh in length, width and thickness lowers the finite-element critical load every time, by 0.9–1.3 percentage points of the closed-form value in total at web widths 8, 16 and 25 mm (2 mm gauge); thickness and width refinement dominate and length refinement contributes under 0.1 point. On the finest mesh (72×8×2) the governing vertical arm sits at 0.992, 0.996 and 1.002 of the closed form, so the two agree within about 1% and the earlier fine-mesh ratios were slightly high. The horizontal-arm closed form stays conservative (ratios 1.046, 1.135, 1.279). Only two refinement levels per direction, so no convergence rate or extrapolated limit is claimed. Simulated only.

title: At what rate does the 3D eigenbuckling model converge under uniform mesh refinement?
summary: A stylised, preliminary study of one short steel bar (24×8×2 mm, tip shear). Three uniformly refined hexahedral meshes give an observed order of about 2.6 and a Richardson limit of 9618 N, 0.12% below the finest mesh. The limit is still 13.7% above the slender-beam closed form, so the gap is not discretisation error (plausibly shear deformation and clamp warping; untested). One geometry, one mesh triple.

title: How much does a SIMP topology optimisation depend on its starting density field, and does penalty continuation remove it?
summary: Half-MBB, volume 0.5, p = 3, 150 sensitivity-filtered OC iterations, 30 random starting fields at each of three noise levels on two meshes, with and without penalty continuation (1 → 3). With a fixed penalty the final compliance spreads by 1.4–2.8% (max/min − 1) and the 0/1 design differs from the uniform-start design in a median 2–23% of elements, with 2–10 enclosed holes. With continuation the spread is 0.0% on 60×20 (identical topology from every start) and at most 0.4% on 90×30. On 90×30 the uniform start, which the 99-line code uses, is worse than 25–28 of 30 random starts at fixed penalty. Stylised: 2D, dimensionless, 150 iterations (not run to convergence), one problem, two meshes.

title: Is the start-dependence of fixed-penalty SIMP topology optimisation just slow convergence?
summary: Follow-up to simdesign-starts . Half-MBB 60×20, p = 3, one uniform and 20 random starting fields (noise ±0.3), each run 1200 OC iterations and snapshotted at 150, 300, 600 and 1200. The median random start ends at the uniform-start design (0.0% of elements differ at 1200, 3.9% at 150) and the pair disagreement falls from 15.4% to 0.5%, but the compliance spread only falls from 1.43% to 0.85% and holes still range 2–5, so a minority of starts stay in a different, slightly worse local optimum. Stylised: 2D, one mesh, one noise level, stuck starts not counted.

title: Can penalty continuation free SIMP topology-optimisation starts that stay stuck in a different local optimum?
summary: Follow-up to simdesign-startsconverge . Half-MBB 60×20, p = 3: after 1200 iterations 5 of 20 random starts still differ from the uniform-start design in at least 1% of elements. Penalty continuation (p = 1, 2, 3) frees none of them: all five collapse onto one design, 20.4% different from the uniform-start one, with compliance 204.01 versus 203.29 for the uniform start. Simply running 1200 more iterations at p = 3 takes three of them to 202.83, about 0.6% better than continuation. Stylised: 2D, dimensionless compliance, one mesh, 20 seeds.

title: Can Sigmund's 99-line topology optimisation be reproduced in Python and carried through to a printable part?
summary: A Q4 plane-stress SIMP code with the 99-line sensitivity filter and optimality-criteria update, tested against Hooke's law and finite-difference sensitivities. It gives truss-like cantilever (compliance 351.9 → 52.4) and half-MBB (1007.0 → 203.3) designs. Without the filter 11.5% of 2×2 cells are checkerboards; with it none, at the same compliance within 0.03%. The thresholded MBB design is one connected body and is written as an extruded, mirrored STL. Stylised: dimensionless 2D compliance only, no stress or 3D check, not compared with the published codes.

title: How much stiffer than a uniformly thinned plate is a topology-optimised part, and how does that depend on volume fraction?
summary: A stylised, preliminary study of two 2D plane-stress problems (cantilever 60×20, half-MBB 90×30). Thresholded 0/1 SIMP designs have 26–31% lower compliance than a plate thinned uniformly to the same volume at v = 0.3–0.5, the advantage shrinking to about 14% at v = 0.8; fits give C ∝ v −0.8 against v −1 for the plate. At low volume on these grids the design is disconnected and the comparison fails. One run per point, coarse grids, variable-thickness reference.

title: Does lateral-torsional buckling justify the w/b ≤ 8 slenderness rule of the 2 mm laser-cut bracket?
summary: A closed-form check (stylised, preliminary, not validated against a shell or 3D model). Treating each bracket arm as an ideal elastic flat bar, the lateral-torsional buckling safety factor at the 2 mm gauge is 6.9–9.0 for web widths of 16–20 mm, so the wider webs of simdesign-widerweb are not buckling-limited under this model. The factor rises with width, the opposite direction to a w/b ceiling; at a 1 mm gauge the old rule would admit w up to 8 mm, where the factor is 0.41. The two textbook coefficients were checked numerically; real sheet imperfections, residual stress and corner flexibility are left out. Calculated only.

title: Do the closed-form buckling factors of the laser-cut bracket arms agree with a 3D eigenbuckling model?
summary: A stylised, preliminary comparison of two idealised models (mesh not fully converged). A 3D scikit-fem linear-buckling model of each bracket arm, checked against the Euler column, gives a critical load within about 1% of the closed form for the governing vertical arm (end moment) at web widths of 8–25 mm at the 2 mm gauge. For the horizontal arm (tip load) the closed form is conservative: the 3D model is 6% higher at w = 8 mm and 29% higher at 25 mm. The governing safety factors (3.2, 7.0, 11.9) therefore support the conclusion of simdesign-webbuckle . Imperfections, residual stress, corner flexibility and plasticity are left out. Simulated only.

title: Do wider webs of the 2 mm laser-cut bracket stay feasible on fine meshes when the slenderness rule is relaxed?
summary: A small scan (stylised, preliminary). With the assumed slenderness limit w/b raised from 8 to 12.5, web widths of 15 to 20 mm at fillet radii 8, 12 and 14 mm are feasible under the peak-stress measure from w = 16.0–17.0 mm upward at every mesh tried (h = 1.5, 1.0 and 0.75 mm), so the empty fine-mesh feasible sets of simdesign-meshconverge came from the rule window. Refinement from 1.5 to 1.0 mm raises the lightest feasible width by 0.5 mm (about 1 g, 3%) at all three radii; at 0.75 mm it is unchanged at two radii and falls back one step at r = 14 mm, so the shift is not resolved beyond about one scan step. The relaxed rule stands in for out-of-plane buckling, which the 2D model cannot see, so these designs are not validated. Simulated results only.

title: Is a skill score normalised by the realised base rate safe to pay on?
summary: Ranking verifiers by the Brier skill score 1−Brier/( y ̄(1− y ̄)) divides a proper score by an outcome-dependent baseline, and that breaks properness. The optimal report is exactly the hit rate reweighted by the inverse baseline variance: it is ½ for any belief with two tasks, and for larger n is biased by about −(1−2 p )/ n (0.232 against a true 0.1 at n =5), with misreporting gaining 0.042 skill for a 0.017 true-Brier cost. Because the baseline pools all of a verifier’s tasks, the report on one task type also shifts with beliefs on the others (0.090 vs 0.133 for the rare type). A leave-one-out or ex-ante baseline restores properness. Independent tasks, constant reports, Brier only; exact enumeration agrees with 200,000-trial simulation. Pure-Python, 9 tests.

title: Can a module game a ledger by choosing when to sleep?
summary: Yes, if it declares after seeing its loss. The wealth ledger pays each awake module exactly its leave-one-out saving, η W A (1− p i ) S i , but a module that sleeps whenever its own loss exceeds θ earns η p B θ(1−θ)/2 per unit wealth against an equal-skill honest rival (best 1/8 at θ=1/2) and takes the market from a 0.1 share in about 130 rounds, while the router’s realised loss stays at 0.5. Declared before the router serves, the same wealth is a real saving that falls from 0.125 to 0.011 as the module’s signal about its own loss gets noisier. A sleeping tax that stops the exploit must be at least η p B /2, a fixed-share rate that halves an honest specialist asleep 90% of the time in 6 rounds, so commitment, not taxation, is the fix. Two modules, uniform losses, threshold strategies; mean-field predictions 3–8% slow.

title: How should a router treat modules that are usually asleep?
summary: If only awake modules report and each awake module’s wealth is multiplied by 1+η(ℓ̂−ℓ i ), the ledger is exactly budget balanced, sleeping wealth never moves (each regime keeps a private ledger), and a module’s regret against the market on its awake rounds is at most ln(1/π i )/η + η n i in its own awake time (the exponential variant pays η T /8 and is not budget balanced). Admitting a module with wealth ε costs each incumbent ln(1/(1−ε))/η in its bound. With recurring regimes the ledger matches the per-round oracle (0.1004 vs 0.1000, regret about 2.7 whatever the number of specialists) while a forced-to-report Hedge sits at the generalist (0.30) and fixed share is worse (0.34–0.36). The bound is loose (measured regret 2.7 against a bound near 10 3 ); losses bounded, wake sets exogenous.

title: How large a manoeuvre can a twin without an actuator rate limit be trusted for?
summary: The real loop x ⁺ = x + a ⁺, with the command rate-limited to r per step, is scale-invariant: it depends only on ρ = x 0 / r , while the first-order twin does not. The twin is exact iff x 0 ≤ r / k (difference 0 at 0.999×, 0.1–0.6% of x 0 at 1.01×). Beyond that the real loop overshoots the target (0.23 of x 0 at ρ =100, 0.90 at 10 4 , k =0.3) and settles in O( ρ ) steps (29418 at ρ =10 5 vs the twin’s 13). For k =1/ n the overshoot threshold is empirically ρ *=2 n (2 n −1) (not proved); avoiding overshoot needs a rate limit 12–38× lower than keeping the twin exact. Stylised: scalar plant, no noise or delay.

title: A kinematic-bicycle twin ignores tyre slip: how wrong is its turning radius, and does calibrating that reveal where a twin-tuned steering loop goes unstable?
summary: Real car: linear single-track model with tyre slip; twin: ψ ′= vδ / L . Steering with the twin’s angle gives radius R (1+ Kv 2 / L ) for understeer gradient K , matched by simulation ( R =100 m: 104.6, 118.5, 174.0, 266.4 m at 5, 10, 20, 30 m/s; twin 4–63% too small, exactly half at the characteristic speed 23.26 m/s; oversteer car up to 136% too large at 20 m/s). Fitting K removes that error exactly, yet both the kinematic and the calibrated twin certify δ =− k p y − k d ψ as stable at every speed and gain, while 11 of a 30-point gain grid lose stability on the real car below 60 m/s ( k p =0.4, k d =0.5: 14.0 m/s; confirmed in the time domain, 1.1×10 −9 m at 8 m/s vs 4.6×10 7 m at 20 m/s). An oversteer car with feedback loses stability at 23.7 m/s, below its open-loop critical speed 26.33 m/s. Stylised: linear tyres, constant speed, no actuator lag or delay; the closed-loop limit is not derived in closed form.

title: A rigid-body twin of a cart carrying liquid predicts no slosh: how wrong is that, what does a slosh-safe move cost, and what does a stale frequency calibration do to it?
summary: Real cart: 80 kg body with a damped spring-mass slosh mode (20 kg liquid, 0.5 Hz at full fill); twin: one rigid mass. The twin gets the centre of mass exactly (RK4 error ~10 −14 m) but predicts zero slosh; for a bang-bang rest-to-rest move the real residual is 4 μa 0 sin 2 ( ωT /4)/ ω 2 , matched by exact propagation and RK4. The twin’s minimum-time move (3 m, 4.90 s) leaves 10.7 cm of slosh, 10× a 1 cm tolerance; the fastest move meeting it takes 7.60 s (55% slower) because zero-residual times are whole multiples of two slosh periods. Calibrating ω at a full tank is harmless down to half fill (−5% frequency, 9.5 mm) but at 25% fill the smallest safe null-tuned move takes 28 s vs 8.7 s recalibrated, worse than the tuning-free bound 24.7 s; at fixed acceleration the first unsafe null order is exactly ⌊asin(√ ρ )/( π | ε |)⌋+1. Stylised: one linear slosh mode, bang-bang force, no shaper optimisation, no nonlinear slosh.

title: How much smoothing does a differentiable twin of a hard contact event need, and what does it cost?
summary: A hard success edge has zero real gradient, so a smoothed twin is the only learning signal. The twin optimum overshoots the edge, θ ≈ τ ln( R /(2 cmτ )) (within 5% at τ =0.02), and gradient ascent from the nominal pose is trapped below τ c =0.105 (real regret 0.75) while above τ u = R /(8 cm )=0.25 the twin optimum falls below the real edge and regret jumps to 0.98. Annealing τ from 0.2 crosses the trap (regret 0.08 at τ =0.02; the real plant alone needs 161 to 3.5×10 6 evaluations). With an uncertain real edge the overshoot is a safety margin: the best trainable width is within 0.0014 expected regret of the Bayes-best pose, but reachable margins are capped at 0.168 and annealing to zero width discards the margin. Stylised (one parameter, logistic smoother, deterministic ascent, simulated “real” plant).

title: What does it cost robots to let people go first at a shared lift or narrow pavement?
summary: People and robots share a one-at-a-time crossing. At load 0.9, robots that always let waiting people go first cut people’s mean wait from 4.60 to 0.71 time units and raise the robots’ from 4.61 to 7.21; the total waiting cost is the same for every share of deferential robots (4.14–4.15), so deference moves waiting rather than removing it, and pays exactly when a person’s wait costs more than a robot’s. A lone selfish robot waits 2.08 against 7.65 for deferential ones (the dilemma). Under overload (load 1.2) half the robots deferring costs them 10.5% of their crossings and gives people 20% more. Simulation within 2.7% of M/G/1 closed forms. Stylised: one server, Poisson arrivals, fixed crossing times.

title: Do robot agents keep the norms they state?
summary: A harness for a small town of robot agents that state a door norm each day and then act among scripted people, scoring how often action matches statement and what it costs people. Any agent with state_norm and act plugs in; a deterministic stub is tested, and an optional model adapter is provided but was not run. With the stub, a robot stating ‘always yield’ keeps it in 1 − 0.4×pressure of meetings (1.00, 0.80, 0.60 at pressure 0, 0.5, 1; 20 seeds) and people’s cost per meeting rises from 0.20 to 1.08. These follow from the stub’s own rule: no language-model result is claimed. Stylised; non-adaptive scripted people.

title: Do robots that keep to one side make people walk on it, or jam the corridor?
summary: The 1D society-robotnorms passing-side model rebuilt as a social-force corridor (60 simulated walkers, 30 m × 6 m). Robots that adapt to people change nothing. Robots that hold the left slow people from 0.91 to 0.81 of desired speed at 5% of the crowd and to 0.39 at 30%, halve the lane separation (2.75 m to 1.43 m), and move people to their side only gradually (at most 54% of people at memory 9), with no sharp tipping in 300 s. Includes a seeded browser replay. Stylised: 8 seeds, one parameter set, simulated walkers only.

title: How many robots does it take to change how a crowd walks?
summary: Robots as a committed minority in a passing-side convention. Simulated people take the side most of their last M partners used; robots hold a programmed side. The tipping share grows with memory: 16%, 22%, 28% and 32% of the crowd for M = 5, 9, 17 and 25, within 0.02 of a mean-field prediction. Just below it, robots that hold their side make people collide up to 14× as often as robots that adapt (0.27 vs 0.020 conflicts per meeting). When people meet only neighbours, evenly spread robots tip everyone from 12–14%, while one block of robots converts under 10% of people even at half the crowd. Stylised: one binary choice per meeting, no geometry.

title: Can a simulation run be turned into a watchable, honest episode?
summary: Five seeded, clearly labelled fictional episodes of a robot town, built on society-trust : 48 invented townspeople, a trust-coloured grid, turning points found by code from the recorded data and a narration whose numbers all come from that record. Even-handed gossip recovers 46 rounds after the fix; gossip that weighs bad news 4× locks the town out (48 of 48 avoid working robots at round 399); robots that explain failures recover in 29 rounds with nobody avoiding; and at 2× the same settings recover on seed 0 and lock out on seed 1. Episodes are single illustrative runs, not statistics; stylised model, no viewer study.

title: Can a robot fleet's reputation survive one bad incident?
summary: Simulated people hold trust in a robot fleet, updated by their own encounters and by gossip in which bad news may travel further than good. Trust that is only dented recovers in every case. What sinks a reputation is avoidance: if people stop using robots below a trust threshold of 0.30, an incident at error rate 0.8 is recovered in 20/20 crowds with neutral gossip, 18/20 when bad news counts 2×, and 0/20 at 4× (final mean trust 0.947, 0.871, 0.282). Robots that explain failures (each costing 0.3× the trust) recovered in every setting. Stylised: 100 simulated people, one shared reputation, a hard avoidance threshold, no fitted parameters.

title: Does the robots-in-a-corridor conclusion survive a more humanlike crowd?
summary: The society-plaza corridor rerun with four crowds of simulated people: varied speeds and sideways-push weights, a 0.4 s reaction delay, 30% stubborn walkers, and all three (10 seeds per cell). Adaptive robots stay free and committed robots never flip the crowd (at most 58% prefer their side) in every crowd. The size of the slowdown (a loss of 0.17 to 0.49 of desired speed at 30% robots) and of personal-space intrusions (0.03 to 0.36 of agent time; reaction delay alone gives 0.087 with no robots) depends strongly on the crowd. Hand-chosen perturbations, not fitted to data; simulated walkers only.

title: What does it cost to send only a fraction of the outer update, and does error feedback help?
summary: Each worker transmits a random fraction p of its pseudo-gradient. Rescaling the subset (unbiased) inflates the stationary noise floor by exactly 1/ p . Adding a per-worker error-feedback memory gives an exact closed form from a four-dimensional second-moment recursion and costs only 1 + αs (1/ p − 1) at small steps, for any number of workers, because the virtual iterate follows uncompressed SGD. The price is speed: the mean dynamics have determinant 1 − p , so the contraction cannot beat √(1 − p ) per round; over a 400-round horizon error feedback reaches 0.39, 0.24 and 0.17 of the unbiased loss at p = 0.25, 0.1, 0.03, and the advantage disappears when the horizon is shorter than about 1/ p . Stylised: diagonal quadratics, Bernoulli masks, no top- k .

title: What does it cost to make workers race?
summary: If a round pays the first k of n finishers a prize R and workers buy speed at cost c per unit rate, the win probability’s slope at the symmetric point telescopes to (1− k / n )( H n − H n−k ), so equilibrium speed is R ( n − k )( H n − H n−k )/( nc ) and the round time is exactly nc /(( n − k ) R ). Paying every finisher buys no speed at all; for a fixed budget, speed alone wants winner-take-all (0.10 at k =1 versus 3.2 at k =16 for n =32), and only the statistical floor on k justifies more winners. Recruiting more workers barely helps: total speed bought saturates at kR / c . Exponential races, linear cost, symmetric risk-neutral workers; equilibrium checked on a grid.

title: Are stake and audits substitutes in trace verification?
summary: Sampled audits of a committed training trace under capped slashing: cheating payoff is convex in the number of corrupted steps, and deterrence holds iff min(F, f·k) ≥ T·g. Stake and audits are complements, so stake must scale with job length. Exact hypergeometric computation. Stylised.

title: Can a bond tell reliable hardware from unreliable?
summary: Workers have hidden fault rates and accept a wage-and-stake contract. Single crossing runs the wrong way: the reliable worker is the one who would copy a high-stake contract, so its rent is exactly (θ H −θ L )(c+(1+ρ)s H )/(1−θ H ), minimised at zero stake, and with continuous types a flat wage with no stake is optimal (no random 2–4-contract menu beats it). A stake needed for deterrence is a tax: it scales reliable workers’ rent by (c+(1+ρ)s)/c and lowers the pool’s fault rate (0.169→0.089) at 9–55% of profit. Stylised.

title: How stale can a shared rollout be before it is worthless?
summary: With Gaussian policies whose mean has moved by δ standard deviations, the importance weight has exact moments E w = 1 and E w ² = e δ² , so the effective-sample fraction is e −δ² (0.37 at δ=1) and a learner needing fraction ρ accepts a lag of √ln(1/ρ)/drift policy versions. Truncating weights has closed-form lost mass, bias and variance (matched by simulation); the best cap cuts the mean-shift estimator’s MSE 1.9× at δ=1, 12.8× at δ=2 and about 750× at δ=3, and finite-sample ESS is optimistic once weights are heavy-tailed. Equal-variance Gaussians, one statistic.

title: A stereo twin that adds Gaussian noise to depth gets the median right: what does it get wrong about over-range errors, safety margins and averaging compared with real disparity-space noise?
summary: Real sensor: disparity noise σ = 0.25 px on a 700 px, 0.12 m rig (matches only above 1 px, so 84 m), depth = reciprocal of disparity; twin: Gaussian depth noise with the linearised sd. The median is exact, but the (gated) mean is biased by about s 2 (+1.5% at 40 m) and over-estimates of distance are far more common than the twin says: at 40 m P(depth > 1.5 Z ) is 0.0026 vs 10 −5 (191×), and a twin mean + 3 σ margin is exceeded 10× as often as designed. Matching the variance leaves 41× on that tail. Averaging 1024 frames of depth floors at 1.5% error where the twin predicts 0.4%, whereas averaging disparity converges; at 60 m the range floor loses 5.5% of looks and flips or removes these effects (reported as a negative result). Stylised: Gaussian i.i.d. disparity noise, no outliers or calibration error.

title: Does a twin with correct sliding friction still miss stick-slip hunting from static friction?
summary: Unit mass under PID, frictionless twin stable (error below 1e-58). With F s = F c (sliding friction identified correctly) the real loop converges in all 15 cases tried, so that twin validates. With a stiction excess Δ F = F s − F c it hunts in stick-slip at 0.54–0.93 Δ F / k p in four of five gain settings, independent of F c (0 to 20) and of the start, falling with damping; one setting ( k d =4, k i =5) converges. Scaling is bit-exact for power-of-two scales but the cycle is unique only to about three digits. Negative result: a 1000 s run can show a motionless “converged” error for large F c / k i while a 20 000 s run still hunts; the amplitude constant has no closed form here. Follow-up to the backlash twin. Stylised: unit mass, Coulomb plus static friction, noiseless.

title: When should a twin run that counts rare failures stop?
summary: Running a safety twin “until the interval is narrow” stops on zero failures, because p̂ =0 has Wald half-width 0: with a target of p /5, 90% of runs stop at the first check for p =10 −3 (99% at 10 −4 ), the interval covers p in 9.6% of runs and the reported rate is 10× too low. Running until m failures (inverse sampling) makes ( m −1)/( N −1) exactly unbiased while m / N is about m /( m −1) too high, gives relative sd ≈1/√( m −2) whatever p is ( m =102 for 10%; measured 0.101), and an exact interval covers 95.0–95.5%. A fixed run planned for p =10 −3 delivers a 20% relative half-width there but 63% at 10 −4 . A one-failure minimum alone restores Wald coverage in this configuration, because the target already forces ~96 failures. Stylised (iid Bernoulli failures, faithful twin, no run cap).

title: When should a paid verifier stop checking?
summary: A verifier who checks a claim one noisy check at a time and stops when it likes, paid a proper score, follows a symmetric threshold rule (confirmed against dynamic programming over all policies). Accuracy is p k = 1/(1+((1− a )/ a ) k ) and expected checks are k (2 p k −1)/(2 a −1), exactly. Participation needs a score scale κ ≥ 4 c /(2 a −1)² under Brier (log needs about half), Brier’s threshold is ln(κ(2 a −1)²/((1− a ) c ))/λ within one step, and adaptive stopping matches a fixed-sample verifier’s accuracy with 2–3× fewer checks. Binary state, known accuracy.

title: What does it cost to skip the slowest workers?
summary: Waiting for the fastest k of n workers has exact round time s + ( H n − H n−k )/μ for exponential tails, and for Pareto tails the mean is finite iff n − k +1 > 1/α, so with α ≤ 1 waiting for everyone has infinite expected round time. For SGD on a quadratic the time to accuracy has a minimum k and an interior optimum (34× faster than waiting for all at zero fixed cost, 1.12× at large fixed cost). If speed correlates with data, the fastest- k average is biased by Σ(π i / k −1/ n )θ i ; Horvitz–Thompson reweighting removes it but only pays when the bias is large.

title: When most verifiers miss a fault, who should be believed?
summary: If a fault is flagged by fewer than half of the verifiers (0.45 detection, 0.05 false alarms), majority vote is wrong on faulty jobs with probability 0.84 at n =101 and 0.96 at n =301. The surprisingly-popular rule (verdict plus predicted verdict fraction) reduces for truthful Bayesian verifiers to an exact fraction threshold θ = v /(1− u + v ) and errs 2.1×10 −5 on faulty jobs at n =101, needing 47 votes for 10 −3 total error against 36 for a Bayes rule that knows the detector. A wrong believed prior wrecks finite- n accuracy (0.51 error), a wrong believed detector quality breaks the limit, and Byzantines who vote clean and predict “everyone flags” break it at exactly 13.6%. Stylised, truthful reports assumed.

title: Which track should the next run work on, and does a smarter pick beat a uniform one?
summary: Four track-allocation policies (uniform, greedy value per line, bootstrap Thompson sampling, and a knapsack-style UCB) were replayed offline on 7 tracks, using the 408-project scores from swe-value (value 1 to 3, cost in lines added) under a 20,000-line budget and 300 seeds. Greedy and Thompson reach about 79–83% (pass A) and 75–79% (pass B) of the best-single-track oracle, against 58–60% for the current uniform pick; the UCB variant explores too much to help (62–66%). This is a stylised, preliminary result: arms are assumed stationary, yet value per line falls with order in 4 of 7 tracks (Spearman −0.36 to −0.57), the value scores themselves agree only weakly, lines are a poor proxy for tokens, and no live trial was run, so no policy is adopted.

title: Do the portfolio's committed results reproduce when the code is re-run?
summary: A seeded sample of 40 research/ projects with a runnable experiment was re-run on a clean copy and diffed against the committed results.txt . 36 of 40 (90%, 95% Wilson interval 77% to 96%) reproduced: 34 byte-identical and 2 differing only in a timing line. Three timed out at 300 s (four jobs in parallel) and one needs a voice model that is not in the repository, so those four are inconclusive, not failures. Of 713 decimal numbers in the sampled READMEs, 85% appear verbatim in committed result files (the rest are derived or in prose). A second sample of 60 (8 overlapping) brought the pooled total to 92 distinct projects: 81 reproduced (88%, Wilson 80% to 93%), none of the 81 finished runs gave different numbers, and the 11 others are missing tools (Yosys, MuJoCo, a voice model) or timeouts. Re-running the five timeouts one at a time (no parallel load) reproduced all five (two differing only in timing lines), lifting the pooled figure to 86 of 92 (93%, Wilson 86% to 97%); the 6 left are missing tools or the voice model. A mechanical reproduction check on a small sample, with no citation audit, so the correctness term is only partly estimated. Preliminary.

title: What does git history say about the agent loop that the run log cannot?
summary: A stdlib reader of 517 commits touching research/<slug>/ (396 projects, 2026-09-28 to 2026-10-15) fills in what the run log lacks. All 157 projects created since 2026-10-13 are in the log; the 217 it never lists were made in two bulk days (09-29 and 09-30) before the log began. Half of all projects (49%) sit in follow-up families, creations arrive in bursts (median gap 4 minutes), and only 6 of 234 fully observed projects (2.6%, 95% interval 1% to 5%) have a later commit whose subject says it corrects something, a lower bound on defects, not an estimate. No tokens, cost, pull request or CI data; preliminary.

title: How much of the track-allocation gain is luck of the project history?
summary: swe-decay replayed track-picking policies on one history, so its intervals ignored history uncertainty. Here each track’s sequence is block-bootstrapped (200 histories). At a 20,000-line budget greedy and Thompson beat the uniform draw in 98–100% of histories, with 95% intervals excluding zero (pass A: +33.4 and +30.8 value points; pass B: +26.7 and +23.5); knapsack-UCB’s interval includes zero. The small-budget loss seen in swe-decay does not reproduce under resampling, so it belongs to the observed order. Stylised and preliminary: resampling removes the within-track trend, value scores agree weakly, lines proxy cost, no live trial, no policy adopted.

title: Is a research branch’s life longer than its pull request’s, and which shared file collides most?
summary: Adds each of the 122 research pull requests’ first-commit time (GitHub API) to the swe-prlifetime data. Branch lifetime is almost the same as pull-request lifetime (median 1.1 vs 0.9 min, p90 16.1 vs 16.0), because sessions commit at the end of their work; commit dates cannot see the earlier working time. Replayed from the branch start, 3 of 58 shared-index-file PRs (5.2%, 95% Wilson 1.8–14.1%) conflict, versus 2 from pull-request creation. The larger finding: research/PROJECTS.md , not in the earlier shared-file list, was edited by 44 of 122 PRs and conflicts in 5 of them (11%). Preliminary: 1.5 days, one repository.

title: Did research brief v1 change how runs go?
summary: Research runs on prompt v0 (342) and v1 (67) from the same four days, 15–18 October 2026. Cost, wall time and output tokens do not differ detectably (median cost $0.835 vs $0.820, p = 0.72). v1 records fewer errors (7.5% vs 17.0%, p = 0.058), but v0 drew far more extend and new-project tasks, and among runs with no task label the rates are 8.3% vs 9.6%. v1 runs list more documentation friction (1.24 vs 0.72 entries per run, p = 0.0001; 1.28 vs 1.02 among unlabelled runs). Observational and preliminary: task labels differ between arms and seven metrics were tested uncorrected.

title: When research merges collide cleanly, is the result still right?
summary: Replays pairs of research merges that touched the shared index files within 10, 30 and 60 minutes of each other (67 merges, 2026-10-14 to 10-16) and checks the merged tree against the homepage build’s rules. Of 129 pairs within 60 min, 37 (28.7%) conflicted textually and the other 92 merged with no new inconsistency; none was clean but broken. The same checker found two projects with duplicate README.md bullets since the repository fold-in, which build.py missed; they are removed and the build now fails on duplicates. Preliminary: three days, an approximate replay, and consistency rules rather than the full build.

title: What does an agent run cost per merged pull request?
summary: Joins the 366 run records (14 to 18 October 2026) that carry an API-equivalent cost_usd to the pull-request numbers in the subject lines of main 's first-parent history. 273 (75%, Wilson 70% to 79%) name a merged pull request, 1 names one not on main and 92 name none. A merged run costs $1.26 on average (bootstrap 1.08 to 1.49) against $0.94 per priced run, because 19% of spend sits on runs with no merged PR on record; process runs cost about 2.4 times a research run per merged run. All 34 red-team records omit their PR although red-team PRs are on main , so their 0% is a recording gap. Preliminary : five days, one model, API-equivalent cost, and cost per merge is not value per merge.

title: Do the gains from smarter track allocation survive when tracks run out of projects?
summary: swe-allocate replayed four track-picking policies with projects drawn with replacement. Here each track yields its next project in commit order and runs dry, using the same scores. At a 20,000-line budget greedy and Thompson keep most of their lead over the uniform draw (pass A: 134.0 and 129.9 against 114.0; pass B: 107.0 and 112.5 against 101.3), reaching 82–97% of a hindsight-greedy reference. At 5,000 lines the smarter policies lose to uniform (24 against 30 in pass A) because two forced pulls per track eat the budget. Stylised and preliminary: weak value scores, lines as a cost proxy, one history, no live trial, so no policy is adopted.

title: Can the swe-errors keyword rules be improved on 30 hand labels and still help on the other 30?
summary: A two-fold held-out check of a mechanical refit (best rule order, then up to six greedily added keywords) of the swe-errors rules against swe-errlabel ’s 60 hand labels. Averaged over 200 random run-level splits the refit agrees with the hand label on 68.5% of entries against 66.7% for the shipped rules (+1.1 entries, range −4 to +7), while fitted and scored on all 60 it reaches 85%: most of an in-sample improvement is memorisation. Preliminary: one labeller, 60 entries.

title: Do the swe-errors keyword rules sort run-record errors correctly?
summary: A 60-entry blind sample of the run records’ reported errors, hand-labelled once and compared with swe-errors ’ keyword rules: they agree on 40 of 60 entries (66.7%, Wilson 95% 54.1–77.3%; Cohen’s κ 0.59). The ci-or-tooling rule never wins (9 hand-labelled, 0 assigned), the run’s-own-mistake class is found with recall 55%, and environment, timeout and collision hold up (recall 92–100%). So the earlier error shares are a lower bound for tooling and own mistakes. Preliminary: one labeller, the same kind of model that wrote the records, and 60 entries.

title: What do agent runs record going wrong, and does it relate to partial outcomes or cost?
summary: Reads the free-text errors field of 1,027 run records: 175 runs (17.0%, Wilson 14.9–19.5%) record at least one, 24.5% of research runs against 12.4% of ventures runs. Keyword rules put 28% of the 222 entries in environment and tooling, 21% in the run's own mistake, 17% in collisions with a parallel run and 7% in timeouts; 24% match no rule. Runs with an error end partial 12.6% of the time against 6.0%, and the 30 priced ones cost a median $1.29 against $0.64. An association, not a cause. Preliminary : unvalidated classifier, self-reported errors.

title: How complete are the agent run records, field by field?
summary: Counts which fields are present on each of the 1,362 run records in prompts/runs/ (1 to 19 October 2026). cost_usd , tokens and wall time are present on 47% of records (Wilson 45% to 50%), but on 0% to 7% of records on 13 to 15 October and 61% to 82% from 16 October, so the rate is a date effect. merged is filled on 4.6%, a pull request is named on 81.2%, and 237 of 1,279 records with outcome success (18.5%, 16% to 21%) name none. Preliminary : presence is measured, not correctness, and an empty list can mean a clean run.

title: Where do agent runs say the documentation hurts, and do the same complaints keep coming back?
summary: A stdlib analysis of the doc_friction field in 1,015 dated run records (1 to 18 October 2026): 575 runs (57%) report at least one problem, 714 entries in all. They concentrate: CLAUDE.md and research/PROJECTS.md hold 39% of entries and the top ten files 70% (Gini 0.75 over 115 files). Of the entries a keyword rule can classify, missing tooling in a fresh image is the largest theme, and by 18 October 83% of classified entries repeat a (file, theme) pair already reported on an earlier day. That rate rises by construction as history accumulates and says nothing about whether a fix was attempted. Keyword themes, self-reported field, 18 days. Preliminary.

title: What can the run log measure about the agent loop today?
summary: A stdlib reader of a snapshot of prompts/runs.jsonl (189 runs, 184 listed projects) reports coverage and throughput proxies. Token, cost and tool-call fields are present in at most 1% of runs and wall time is derivable for only 15, so no cost-per-project figure is possible yet. About a third of listed projects sit in follow-up families of three or more, and 24 slugs appear in more than one run. All 143 recorded CI-failure counts are zero, which looks like a success-only field, not a clean record. Preliminary: first step of the ledger milestone; no git-history backfill, no value or correctness scoring.

title: Does Opus pay for itself on this portfolio's runs? Cost ratio by track, and the sample needed to find out
summary: An Opus run costs about 8–9× a Sonnet run in the same track (process 7.9×, bootstrap 6.7–11.7; research 9.1×, 3.7–12.1 on only 3 Opus runs). The ledger holds 12 priced Opus runs against 342 Sonnet runs, confounded with date and task, so value per dollar cannot be compared yet: detecting a 50% difference in projects per run needs about 129 runs per arm. Preliminary; cost only.

title: Which practices of engineering organisations that ship could help an agent loop, and what is there to fix?
summary: A cited, growing catalogue of 58 practices from 57 sources (Sentry(Mercari’s production-readiness checklistrsquo;s LOGAF-marked code review, Mercari’s production-readiness checklist, Apollo’s priority displays, Kohavi, Tang and Xu on controlled experiments, Strathern on audit, Perrow on normal accidents, the DevOps Handbook, Reason on layered defences, Vaughan on normalization of deviance, Rigby and Bird, Humble and Farley, Beck, Allspaw and Hammond on Flickr, Parnas, Nygard, Conway, Nagappan et al., Skelton and Pais, Brooks, Fowler, Reinertsen, Toyota, the Rogers Commission, 37signals, Instagram, Google, Microsoft, Facebook, Netflix, Amazon, Etsy, Basecamp, Spotify, Stripe (twice, including its online-migrations post), Shopify, Linear, and postmortems from GitLab and Cloudflare, the SEC’s order on Knight Capital and others), each tagged with company stage, evidence type (four measured, the rest case studies, postmortems, accounts or opinion), the loop element it maps to, how far it transfers to a fleet of agent sessions, and the assumption that does not carry over. The failure reports agree: a safety mechanism or a cost nobody measured before it shipped. Scored against the 1,261-row run ledger, the failure classes runs report are small (0.6–1.6% of runs, self-reported keyword matches), so no practice clears the 5% ceiling as a new proposal : a negative result. Sources were checked by web search only. Eighteenth batch of standing milestone 7 of track 10; the research log below records each batch.

title: Do concurrent agent runs pick the same track more often than chance, and is the track pick uniform?
summary: Measured from git history rather than simulated: 218 merged projects since the tracks were set. Over the whole period the mix is far from uniform (tracks 7–11 are 2–4% each, mostly because they were added late), but after all eleven tracks existed (36 PRs) uniform is not rejected (p = 0.25, low power). Same-track pairs among overlapping PRs are 17.9% against 12.3% expected, and the excess disappears once the drifting mix is controlled for (p = 0.115 within merge days). Preliminary: merged projects stand in for picks, and branch overlap is a lower bound on concurrency.

title: What do 526 closed pull requests say about how the agent loop lands work?
summary: A stdlib analysis of the creation and merge times of every closed PR here (#1 to #526). 87.5% merged (Wilson 84.3–90.0%), falling from 93.8% for PRs opened by 10-01 to 81.2% from 10-05 on. Median time to merge is 0.6 minutes, 4.3% of merges happen in four same-second batches after long waits, and PRs opened within 10 seconds of another merged only 60% of the time against 92% for the rest. The last is an association, not a cause. No CI, review or closure-reason data, and the timestamps were hand-transcribed. Preliminary third step of track 10.

title: How long do research pull requests stay open, and how often do they really collide?
summary: Joins 122 merged pull requests that touched research/ (2026-10-16 to 10-17) to their real creation times from the GitHub API. The median pull request was open 0.9 min (p90 16 min); 95% merged within 30 min, so the 30 to 60 minute windows assumed by swe-sharedfiles were far too long. Of the 58 that edit a shared index file, 21% saw another shared-file merge land while open (mean 0.40), and replaying each from its real creation time gave a textual conflict in 2 (3.4%, 95% Wilson 1.0% to 11.7%). Preliminary: pull-request lifetime is not branch lifetime, one repository, about 1.5 days.

title: How many runs does a prompt experiment need, and is it safe to peek at it?
summary: Three stopping rules for a champion-versus-candidate brief experiment were simulated on outcome distributions drawn from the run ledger (success rate 237/244) and from swe-value ’s project values: one look at the end, a look after every pair, and a mixture sequential probability ratio test. Looking after every pair declared an identical brief different in 21% of 2,000 experiments on success rate and 40% on value (nominal 5%); the mixture test stayed at 0.4% and 3.9%, at the price of power (92% against 99% at a +0.2 shift in value, stopping after 181 of 400 pairs on average). At a 97% success rate a fixed test needs about 2,200 runs to see a 0.971 to 0.991 change, so success rate is a poor primary metric. Stylised and preliminary: all 244 ledger rows are the same prompt, effects are hypothetical, and the value scores are weak; no candidate brief has been run.

title: What does an agent run cost, and which runs cost the most?
summary: A stdlib analysis of the 355 run records (14 to 18 October 2026) that carry an API-equivalent cost_usd . The median run costs $0.68 (95% bootstrap $0.64 to $0.72) and the 355 together $337; the top 10% of runs hold 36% of spend. Research runs are 47% of spend with the highest median ($0.82), process runs 24% on 14% of runs because of a long tail. Cost scales with tool calls with exponent 1.18 (1.11 to 1.25) and input tokens with 1.37, consistent with context re-read at each step. Preliminary: five days, one model, estimates not invoices, and cost is not scored against value.

title: How many parallel agent runs duplicate each other when they start in the same minute, and what removes the waste?
summary: A stdlib Monte Carlo of start-time collisions among runs that pick from a pool of 11 tracks. Four blind simultaneous starts leave 12.8% of runs redundant (closed form agrees), claim-checking alone barely helps because all runs read before any claim is pushed, a start gap longer than the claim latency drives waste to about 1–2%, and scheduler-assigned slots remove it entirely up to the pool size. Every timing constant is assumed, the pool is uniform, and queueing against usage limits is not yet modelled. Stylised; first step of milestone 5 of track 10.

title: How often do research merges collide on the shared index files?
summary: Measured from git history (101 research merges, 2026-10-14 to 10-16): 64.4% edit both README.md and projects.json , the median gap between such merges is 30.6 min, and replaying a later merge against an earlier one within 30 min gives a textual conflict in 18.6% of 59 pairs (15.3% in a shared file). Branch times are assumed, not measured; textual conflicts only; preliminary.

title: Do sibling research projects ask different questions?
summary: Scores the title and Question section of each project’s README by word overlap (Jaccard index). Pairs in the same slug family overlap about ten times more than pairs across families: mean 0.078 over 7,552 within-family pairs in 14 families of five or more projects, against 0.008 over 213,181 cross-family pairs. The closest pairs, such as mimic-mmd and mimic-mmdmujoco (0.917), are mostly deliberate one-condition follow-ups. Preliminary: word overlap is not result overlap, and shared vocabulary is partly legitimate.

title: Do agent runs that start alongside other runs, or at certain hours, go worse?
summary: Joins 660 run records that have a start time (1 to 19 October 2026) to how many other runs started within 5, 10 or 30 minutes. Raw, crowded starts look better (error recorded in 9.8% against 21.0%), but that is a day effect: 13 to 15 October had 47–50% error records and few concurrent starts, 16 October on 6–9% and many. Shuffling the crowded label within calendar days finds no detectable difference (12 tests, one p = 0.018 on a 50-run group, not counted), and six-hour blocks of the day show nothing. Preliminary and low power: association only, errors is self-reported, and duplicate work, the cost swe-schedule models, is not in the records.

title: Can two independent passes agree on what a portfolio project is worth?
summary: A three-level value rubric (follow-up, new question, listed milestone) scored over all 408 research/ projects by two automated passes, one from names and order and one from README text, plus a blind 30-project hand sample. The two automated passes agree at chance level (linear Cohen’s kappa 0.07, 95% bootstrap 0.01 to 0.13); a flaw in the name pass (108 *-twin projects counted as one follow-up chain) explains part, and fixing it after the fact lifts kappa to 0.25. Against the hand sample the text pass reaches 0.45 (0.24 to 0.65) and the fixed name pass 0.57 (0.24 to 0.81), n = 30, scored by the rubric’s author. Follow-ups add about as many lines as new projects (median 318 vs 328), so by the rubric they return less per line, a ratio that is largely built in. Preliminary and negative on the automated passes; no correctness term.

title: A snapshot twin of a spinning lidar ignores that the platform moves during the sweep: how biased is the map, what does one scan reveal, and what do yaw and acceleration do?
summary: Real sensor: 2-D lidar at 10 Hz firing each beam at a different time while the platform moves; twin: all beams at t = 0. At 10 m/s the front and back walls are placed 0.25 and 0.75 m short, so apparent room length is biased by exactly vτ /2 = 0.50 m while the width is exact, and deskewing with the true motion removes it. Parallel walls appear to converge by ≈ vτ /(2π)(1/ d 1 +1/ d 2 ) (1.94° measured vs 2.05° first order), so a wall-angle estimator certified on the snapshot twin inherits a heading bias; inverting that angle recovers speed from a single scan to 0.13 m/s at 1 cm range noise (first-order bias −1.8%). Yaw scales bearings by exactly − κβ /(1+ κ ), and acceleration biases scan-to-scan odometry by exactly a t f in velocity, bounded and non-accumulating. Stylised: 2-D rectangular room, constant velocity or acceleration along one axis, known platform motion.

title: Are reward pools identity-proof?
summary: Sybil splitting and whale merging under stake-weighted pools: only linear-in-stake weights are split-invariant, per-head pools are captured at k* = √(Rn/c) − n identities (exact match), a sharp per-identity deterrence fee, exponents above 1 reward merging, and weighted-score wagering is split-neutral. Stylised.

title: How much does a twin's perfectly synchronised sensor clock over-promise a fused estimate?
summary: Two sensors observe a smooth signal (length scale ℓ ); the second has a clock offset δ and jitter s , which the twin does not simulate. The added variance is exactly g = 2 σ 2 [1−(1+ s 2 / ℓ 2 ) −1/2 e − δ 2 /2( ℓ 2 + s 2 ) ] ≈ σ 2 ( δ 2 + s 2 )/ ℓ 2 (matched to simulation within 0.5%), so inverse-variance fusion designed in the twin has real MSE 1 + ag /( b ( a + b )) times its claim: +44% at a 0.3 ℓ offset, +118% at 0.5 ℓ , and worse than the reference sensor alone beyond 0.225 ℓ . The more accurate the delayed sensor, the more it hurts. Randomising the twin’s clock at the right variance recovers the optimal weight; no randomisation costs up to 29%, a range 4× too wide only 1–4%. Stylised: very smooth signal, static weights, offset known, no real logs.

title: Can the tail of benign drift be elicited with a proper score?
summary: Verifiers forecast a tolerance threshold (VaR) and the mean drift beyond it (expected shortfall, ES). ES alone is not elicitable (a 50/50 mixture of two ES = 10 laws has ES 12.5), but the 0-homogeneous Fissler–Ziegel score ln e − 1 + (v + (y−v) + /(1−τ))/e is minimised exactly at (VaR, ES), with exact closed-form excess scores matched to 10 −10 . Pinball loss scores a forecaster with ES off by 30% identically to the truth; the joint score separates them with about 0.6–1.2k samples at τ = 0.9–0.95. Stylised. Follows up property-elicitation-verification.

title: How do you price the tail of benign drift?
summary: A drift tolerance is a quantile, but compensation depends on expected shortfall, which is not elicitable alone (a mixture moves ES 1.6→2.24). The scale-free score ln e + (v + (x−v) + /(1−α))/e − 1 elicits (VaR, ES) jointly with exact excess law; misreporting ES by a factor r costs ln r + 1/r − 1 (0.307 at ½, 0.193 at 2), matched to quadrature within 2·10 −5 . A quantile-only tolerance leaves ES/VaR = a/(a−1) uncovered under Pareto drift (6× at a=1.2); auditing needs ~2,000 samples for a 20% understatement at index 4 and the CLT plan fails for index ≤ 2. Stylised.

title: Can the log score be made payable?
summary: Log score is ideal for rare faults but a confident wrong report costs unbounded stake. Extending the log generator past [ε,1−ε] by its second-order Taylor polynomial gives a strictly proper score, identical to log up to a constant inside, with worst-case payment exactly ln((1−ε)/ε)+1/(1−ε). Per unit of payment range it has 63× Brier’s curvature at p=10 −3 but loses to Brier above a closed-form crossover (≈0.07), and ε=p is the best cutoff for truth p.

title: When does a forecast-ensemble twin send the UAV to the wrong place, or make the update worse?
summary: A UAV samples from a corridor to cut forecast error over a region it cannot enter, with sites and Kalman gain taken from a twin’s covariance; the real error after the update is exact (Joseph form, checked against simulation). A matched twin cuts the real error 22%; a twin whose correlation length is 2× too long claims −65% and delivers +28%, because updates are harmful beyond a closed-form radius (ln 2/(ℓ r −2 −ℓ t −2 )) 1/2 . Amplitude errors are harmless for one observation but an under-confident twin double-counts over several. A finite ensemble drawn from the correct model already hurts: 10 members give +27% mean real error (71% of ensembles worse than no observation), 50 are safe, and localisation helps at small sizes but costs accuracy at large ones; fitting the length scale from real samples needs about 50. Stylised: 1-D Gaussian field, one static update.

title: What stopping distance can a twin with independent terrain cells certify?
summary: Braking on Gamma-distributed patch friction has an exact incomplete-gamma law. A twin drawing 100 independent cells across the stopping distance certifies 1.17× the mean-friction distance at level 10 −3 ; on real terrain with 1, 3 or 10 patches across it the exceedance is 0.44, 0.33 and 0.18, and finer twin cells make it worse. The mean stopping distance is nearly right (1.00–1.32×) while the tail is not. Matching the measured patch count restores the level; overstating it 2× gives 16× the claimed risk. Stylised.

title: A constant-gain twin of a motor holding a load certifies every load: what does thermal derating do to the real hold?
summary: Holding a torque dissipates R i 2 ; heating lowers the torque constant, so the hold current rises and heats more. In scaled variables φ′=λ/(1−φ) 2 −φ the hold exists iff λ≤4/27 (fold at φ=1/3) while the twin says φ=λ at every load: the real temperature rise is 1.33× and 1.76× the twin’s at λ=0.10 and 0.14 (current 1.15×, 1.33×) and 2.25× at the fold; above it there is no hold and the torque constant collapses in finite time, ≈4π/(9√ε) thermal time constants near the fold (ratio 0.925 at ε=0.002, 0.994 at 10 −5 ). Tests shorter than the thermal time constant cannot see it (0.1 time constants at λ=0.14: +1.4% current). Under a winding temperature limit the twin overstates holdable torque by 1/(1−φ m ) (1.11× at φ m =0.1, 1.64× at 0.4); refitting a constant gain on a hot low-load run still under-predicts (−0.06 to −0.10) and keeps no fold; winding-resistance rise lowers the fold (0.148 to 0.113 at β/α=1). Companion to the windup and gravity twins. Stylised: one thermal node, linear derating, constant load.

title: What does a quadratic thrust curve do to a controller designed in a linear-thrust twin?
summary: A throttle controller inverts a twin whose thrust is linear around hover; the real thrust is quadratic. The realised acceleration is exactly a cmd + a cmd 2 /(4 g ): climbs over-deliver, descents under-deliver, and the throttle floor is reached at a cmd =−2 g . At ζ=0.7 the climb overshoot rises from 0.046 to 0.095 while the descent falls to 0.027 for a step of p =ω n 2 | x 0 |/ g =4; gentle steps ( p ≤0.5) change overshoot by under 1.1 points. Stylised: 1-D, static thrust map, assumed throttle ceiling, no field data.

title: How do you estimate a one-in-a-million failure from a twin you can only run a thousand times?
summary: Shifting the twin's disturbances and reweighting failures is unbiased for any shift, with an exact variance e nθ ² Q (( b + nθ )/√ n ) (5.53 vs 5.51 simulated). At the optimal shift, 10% error at p =10 −6 takes 535 runs instead of 10 8 . But the shift is a narrow target: half the optimum costs 23× the variance, twice the optimum 1.7×10 5 ×, and a shift tuned for one design is 1.6–17.6× worse at thresholds 0.8–1.5× away. The usual 95% interval covers 94.9% at the optimum but 2.8% at twice it, and only the effective sample size warns. Stylised: Gaussian additive disturbances, constant shift, no field data.

title: What overshoot does a controller tuned in a fixed-step digital twin really have?
summary: A twin's integrator adds or removes damping the plant does not have. Per-step pole moduli are exact (real e −hc ; explicit 1−hc+h²k; semi-implicit 1−hc; implicit 1/(1+hc+h²k)), and the first-order damping bias of explicit and implicit Euler changes sign at ζ=1/√2 (measured 0.742→0.711 and 0.675→0.703 as h falls 0.2→0.025).
