Tuned to 10% overshoot in the twin, the real plant overshoots 0.105–0.192 (semi-implicit and implicit, h=0.05–0.4) while forward Euler is conservative (0.091–0.036); at a 1% target the semi-implicit twin under-claims by up to 4.9×. The excess halves with h (first order); Richardson extrapolation of the twin’s overshoot at fixed gain recovers the real value to 0.0003–0.0012, and re-tuning with substeps costs ×4 to ×32. Stylised: one linear oscillator, textbook integrators (not any engine’s scheme), overshoot read from samples, no robot data.

title: How should a router pick k distinct experts?
summary: Sparse mixture-of-experts routing as a capped Hedge market: expert prices are min(1, λ w i ) with a single shadow price λ and an exact KL projection. Regret against the best fixed k -set stayed within k ln( N / k )/η + η Tk /2 in every run (41–58% of it, not proved here); plain normalisation prices an expert above 1 in 282 of 300 rounds and understates loss 3.2×; systematic sampling realises exactly k distinct experts with 8–14× lower loss variance. Oblivious losses only.

title: How long can a digital twin be wrong before you can prove it, and what does waiting cost?
summary: A Gaussian-mixture e-process on the closed-loop residual audits a deployed twin continuously: it false-alarms 2.4% of the time against 58% for a z-test checked every step. Detection delay follows ≈ 2[ln(1/α)+½ln(1+τ 2 nU )]/(Δ 2 U ) with U the controller’s own excitation (simulation 0–18% earlier); expected regret accumulated before detection is nearly independent of the gap (8–10 while per-step regret spans 38×); an expensive-control operator needs 11× longer to catch the same gap; and added probing pays only for gross errors (true gain above 2.25× or below 0.35× the twin’s), with the rule failing at the near-cliff edge. Stylised.

title: Can a digital twin shorten a real-world safety certification?
summary: Certifying a failure rate p < ε from n real trials with a twin-derived prior. The worst-case false-certification probability of any ‘certify iff k ≤ c ’ rule is exactly P(Bin( n ,ε) ≤ c ), so by Karlin–Rubin the twin cannot cut real trials at a fixed level: at ε=0.01, δ=0.05 the exact test needs 299 zero-failure trials, a twin prior reaches 133 only at worst-case size 0.26, and the exact test held to the same size needs the same n (1057 vs 1057 for 90% power at p =ε/3). A weakly informative Jeffreys bound is already anti-conservative (size 0.147 at 191 trials). Optimistic twins inflate size, pessimistic ones (claim 2ε) block certification entirely, and the largest safe twin weight is about 90 twin-trial equivalents at n =299. Stylised: one Bernoulli failure rate, no continuous margins.

title: How many real rollouts does a biased digital twin save when certifying a policy?
summary: A twin evaluated alone is biased however many rollouts you run (nominal 95% intervals cover the truth 0–0.4% of the time at a 12% bias, 20% gain error); used as a control variate it removes variance without bias. In scalar LQ the rollout cost is a Gaussian quadratic form, so the twin/plant correlation ρ = λ tr( GG′ )/√(tr G 2 tr G′ 2 ) is exact, the optimal twin-to-real ratio is ρ /√((1− ρ 2 ) w ) and the speed-up 1/(√(1− ρ 2 )+ ρ √ w ) 2 , matched by simulation to a few percent. Twin gain error is first order in the bias (5% error → 2.7%) but second order in 1− ρ , so the twin’s value is capped by the fraction λ of the real disturbance it can replay: a 5% certificate costs 168 real-only, 28 with λ = 0.95 and 163 with λ = 0.3. Twin-only beats real-only only below σ 2 /bias 2 real rollouts (35 at 10% error). Stylised.

title: What does a too-clean digital twin do to a student cloned from a privileged teacher?
summary: A teacher that sees the true state is trained in a twin and cloned into a student that sees only a noisy sensor. Least-squares cloning attenuates the gain to gP /( P + s ), where P is the demonstration state variance, so the student depends on the twin only through its process-noise-to-sensor-noise ratio. A twin with a quarter of the real process noise yields a lazy student with excess cost 0.36 ( s =0.5) to 1.11 ( s =2) against 0.005 to 0.10 from an exact twin, 2.8–3.6× worse than on-policy DAgger in the same twin. On-policy imitation of an exact teacher is within 3.5% of the best memoryless student over 252 cases; cloning can cancel an actuator error, but the cancellation point moves with sensor noise. Injecting demonstration noise in the twin, set from one real scalar (Var z − s ), recovers the on-policy gain in two rounds (regret 0.357 → 0.0035 → 0.00003). Stylised: scalar linear–quadratic, no robot data.

title: What should you pay a digital-twin provider for?
summary: A provider paid Brier score on the twin’s parameter reports its posterior mean; one paid the deployed control cost reports the Bayes gain, which is more conservative (0.778 vs 0.823 at posterior sd 0.3, mean 1) and equals domain randomization under the provider’s own uncertainty. Certainty equivalence costs a quartic in spread (16× per doubling); reports with equal squared error have regret ratios of 1.3–24×; a payment cap makes the elicited gain jump at a closed-form threshold M * (19.3 in the example) that decides whether rare catastrophic plants are priced in; and Brier under- or over-pays probing by a 15× spread in decision value per unit variance. Stylised.

title: How many real rollouts does a biased digital twin save when evaluating a robot policy?
summary: Using the twin as a control variate keeps the estimate unbiased whatever the twin's bias (twin-only error +0.700 vs +0.001) with exact variance σ R ²((1−ρ²)/n + ρ²/N). Real and twin cannot share execution noise, so ρ is set by the observed scenario context: a faithful twin gets ρ=η but a noise-free twin gets ρ=√η (1.33× vs 2.0× real-sample equivalent at η=0.5). A twin is worth its compute only if c T /c R < (1−√(1−ρ²))²/ρ² (0.072 at ρ=0.5), and where twin bias favours the wrong policy, twin-only ranking is wrong while 86–125 real episodes per policy give a 90% correct order against 164 real-only. Stylised: Gaussian returns, exact context replay, no robot data.

title: Which rungs of a ladder of digital twins are worth running?
summary: For twins of decreasing cost and fidelity used as nested control variates the variance is exact, σ 2 Σ(ρ i 2 −ρ i+1 2 )/m i , and a cheaper rung pays below a twin already in use iff ρ 2 /ρ 1 > 2√r/(1+r) (0.943 for halved cost, 0.575 for a 10× drop), the single-twin threshold applied to the step correlation. Using every rung is not best (q=0.99, r=0.5, six rungs: 0.284 of real-only variance vs 0.196 for the best two; q=0.9 makes all rungs 1.41× worse than real-only while the best subset gets 0.83), and 10 of 336 paying grid points are infeasible. On a saturated PD mass-spring timestep ladder the best ladder reaches 0.156 of real-only variance (0.204 for the best single twin), collapsing to the cheapest twin at 90%/70% disturbance replay (0.52/0.89 simulated); a coarser rung diverged in 2 of 20,000 contexts. Stylised: one plant, known correlations, step-count costs.

title: How fast can a deployed digital twin be caught going stale, and when is it invisible?
summary: An e-process on the twin's closed-loop prediction residuals is valid however often it is checked (2.3% false alarms versus 51.6% for a repeatedly refit χ 2 test at nominal 5%). Its detection rate is exactly the twin-transfer score gap, affine in the exploration variance v ; a mixture-delay formula matches simulated medians within 10–20% (leading order L /rate is 40–55% too fast). Twins on the line Δa = k Δ b are invisible under the deployed policy (rate exactly 0) and detectable at rate Δ b 2 v /2σ 2 with dither; most of them cost almost nothing (regret 6·10 −4 ) so dither does not pay, but the one that thinks the actuator is nearly dead (regret 0.23) is worth a v ≈0.006 dither that cuts expected cost 12×. Stylised.

title: How do you estimate a controller's real-world cost with a biased digital twin?
summary: A twin-only cost estimate is biased by the twin’s error, a real-only one is noisy; as a control variate the twin keeps the estimate unbiased and is worth its correlation with real rollouts, not its accuracy. Under common disturbances the cost correlation has a closed form and decays as (1+ c 4 )/(1− c 4 ) 2 ( kδ ) 2 in the twin’s gain error (0.985, 0.941, 0.782, 0.472 for gains 1.15, 1.3, 1.6, 2.0 while the twin-only bias grows 0.004 to 1.34); replaying only a fraction λ of the real disturbance multiplies it by exactly λ 2 . The optimal twin-to-real rollout ratio is √( c r ρ 2 /( c t (1−ρ 2 ))), the twin pays only below price (1−√(1−ρ 2 )) 2 /ρ 2 , and a simulated estimator cut variance to 0.228 of real-only against 0.225 predicted. Twin-only wins at tiny budgets or tiny bias; the control variate is best elsewhere. Stylised.

title: How big a pilot decides whether a biased digital twin is worth using?
summary: The twin pays iff its correlation with the real return exceeds ρ*=2√r/(1+r) (0.426 at cost ratio r=0.05), and the gain is linear in ρ−ρ* there, so a small pilot's wrong calls are frequent but cheap (probability 0.36–0.11 at ρ=0.5 for m=10–160 pairs, regret 0.004–0.016 of real-only variance). Decision regret follows f·slope·(1−ρ* 2 ) 2 /(2m) (simulated/law 0.63 at m=10, 1.00 at 160) and plug-in allocation costs ≈0.27–0.30/m extra variance. The adaptive two-stage design (pilot reused) stays unbiased (|bias| ≤ 0.002 against twin bias 0.7) with 95% intervals covering 0.946–0.955. Stylised: Gaussian returns, exact context replay, asymptotic law, no robot data.

title: How often, and how long, should a digital twin be re-identified as the plant drifts?
summary: For a twin refitted from dedicated experiments rather than filtered from operating data, the second-order-optimal schedule is closed-form: interval T * = (4 c σ 2 /( v ρ q d 2 )) 1/3 , with experiment downtime, estimation noise and drift regret exactly equal at the optimum, so excess cost scales as q d 1/3 (fitted slope 0.333) and 10× cheaper experiments lower it only 2.2×. Misjudging the drift rate by 4× costs at most 26%. But the second-order optimum is unsafe: 0.7–15% of its cycles destabilise the loop, and a schedule with failure probability ≤ 10 −3 costs 1.2–16× more and is 37–200× worse than an always-on Kalman twin. Stylised.

title: How many designs should a digital twin shortlist for real-plant verification?
summary: A twin ranks K =50 designs and a fixed budget of 20 noisy real trials verifies only the top m . The twin alone is worth exactly ρc K ( c K =2.249), and the best shortlist shrinks as the twin improves ( m =8 at ρ =0.6, 2 at 0.95), reaching 1.87 and 2.17 sd against 1.20 for real-only testing and an oracle 2.25. A useless twin still gains 0.12 by concentrating the budget on fewer designs, so that part is not the twin's. Stylised Gaussian model, even budget split, Monte Carlo.

title: How far should a real-plant estimate be pulled toward its digital twin?
summary: Shrinking a real estimate of d plant parameters toward the twin's prediction (James–Stein) has an exact risk d−(d−2) 2 E[1/(d−2+2K)], K~Poisson(λ/2): it never raises total error for d≥3, a perfect twin gives risk 2 at any d (saving 33% at d=3, 80% at d=10), and a twin as noisy as the data (λ/d=1) still saves 14–49% while using it alone saves nothing. At large d the twin is worth n+σ 2 /τ 2 real samples (exact values 0.72–0.998 of that at d=5–100). The guarantee is aggregate only: one badly mismatched parameter among d takes about d/4 noise variances of damage (measured 2.9 at d=10, 25.5 at d=100 against 1), and blocks of 5 cap that at 1.65 (d=30) while keeping 72% of the perfect-twin saving. Stylised: Gaussian noise, orthogonal design, no robot data.

title: What is a digital twin worth for training a controller?
summary: In a scalar linear-quadratic plant the twin-trained gain has exact deployment regret, asymmetric with a stability cliff: underestimating actuation to 0.21× is infinitely costly while 2× over costs 0.22. A twin can score perfectly on passive logs (log-score gap exactly 0) yet mistrain the controller, and closed-loop logs are blind along Δa = kΔb, so validation needs designed probing. Used as a ridge prior, a twin with bias δ is worth exactly σ 2 /( v δ 2 ) real probe steps at every accuracy target (22 steps at δ=0.3), and removes small-sample divergence (3.1% to 0 at n =10). Matched to simulation within 1–4%. Stylised.

title: What does it cost to keep a digital twin in sync with a drifting plant, and is probing worth it?
summary: A Kalman twin tracks a drifting actuator gain from the closed-loop data the controller already produces. Its steady-state predictive variance is a closed-form quadratic root ( m = q /2 + √( q 2 /4 + q σ 2 / v ) for a random walk), matching closed-loop simulation to 1–3%, and control regret is ½ J kk (d k */d b ) 2 m (0.00447 predicted vs 0.00466 simulated). A calibrate-and-freeze twin loses half its edge over the population mean after ln 2/(2(1−ρ)) = 34.5 steps. For one drifting parameter a dedicated probing budget never pays (information price 0.70 vs marginal value ≤ 0.04); for two, the closed-loop blind direction makes a fixed-gain twin unobservable and the mean-field optimal dither scales exactly as q 1/6 , yet simulation shows the controller’s own gain jitter supplies most of that excitation, so the mean-field law is an upper bound. Stylised.

title: How much battery should a UAV carry when its twin has a constant wind?
summary: A leg flown at airspeed v against a headwind that is uniform across flights costs P ( v )/( v − w ) in energy per distance; a constant-wind twin has no spread. Its cruise speed is nearly right (1.100 vs the real optimum 1.123, regret 0.10%), but its energy claim is low by exactly artanh( x )/ x with x = a /( v −μ) (3.5% here), and a battery sized to that claim runs out in 50% of real flights (42% with a 5% margin). A 5% depletion target needs a 39% margin and 1% needs 44%, in closed form, and the real-optimal speed trims only 39.2% to 37.6%. The speed error itself grows to 6.4% of the optimum at wind half-width 0.6, and the twin speed meets a stalling wind (infinite energy) once the half-width exceeds v −μ = 0.80. Refitting the twin to n = 50 logged winds beats the constant-wind speed in 97% of fits. Stylised: one leg, constant airspeed, wind fixed within a flight, chosen parameters, no gusts or turn-back.

title: How many real trials before “the twin passed validation” means anything for a rare failure?
summary: A twin states a failure probability q ; the real rate is c q . An exact two-sided binomial difference test “passes” a twin that is 3× wrong with probability 0.81 at 500 trials ( q = 10 −3 ), and rejecting a 2× error with 80% power needs about 11 real failures , independent of q (normal approximation 9.9). Passing barely moves the odds that a twin is off by 2× (0.325 prior, 0.31 after passing at 0.3 expected failures). An equivalence test (TOST) caps false validation at 5% but needs about 20, 58 and 178 real failures for margins 2, 1.5 and 1.25, so certifying a rare-failure twin within 2× takes about 20/ q real trials. Stylised: one Bernoulli failure, known q , no scenario shift, illustrative prior.

title: Can a verifier be paid for reporting drift variance?
summary: Not from one re-execution (variance’s level sets are not convex), but two independent ones suffice: D=(y 1 −y 2 )²/2 is unbiased with variance σ 4 (κ+1)/2. Brier excess is exactly (r−σ²)²; the scale-free loss D/r+ln r has excess 1/λ+ln λ−1, so halving the report costs 0.307 and doubling 0.193. Catching a 10% misreport at 95% takes about 2–4 thousand tasks (2z²(κ+1)/(λ−1)², simulated 0.93–0.97); disjoint pairs are 1.8× worse than the sample variance at n=10; with Pareto tail index 3 the error decays like m −1/3 , not m −1/2 . Stylised.

title: Economics of refereed verification
summary: Inspection-game equilibrium for optimistic verification: stake substitutes for re-execution, extra verifiers dilute rewards (free-riding saturates), and joint tolerance/stake design under floating-point drift. Stylised model.

title: Bribing the verifiers
summary: Closed-form bribe floor for buying verifier silence in refereed verification: a sharp collusion-proof stake (falls as 1/m verifiers), and planted-fault jackpots that lift the floor. Verified against brute force and Monte Carlo. Stylised model.

title: Why should the first verifiers be sealed?
summary: Verifiers who are paid for being right and see earlier verdicts herd: once two more revealed signals point one way than the other, everyone copies. With signal accuracy a the cascade is wrong with probability exactly (1− a )²/( a ²+(1− a )²) (0.155 at a =0.7) and forms after 2/( a ²+(1− a )²) revealed signals (3.4), so accuracy is capped at 0.845 however many verifiers join, versus ≈1 for an independent majority of 101. A sealed first batch of m ≥ 3 lifts the cap (0.875 at m =3, 0.949 at 11) and beats a majority of the same paid size. Recursion checked against fully Bayesian simulated agents. Stylised, symmetric signals.

title: When do verifiers complement rather than substitute?
summary: Exact value of verifier committees for an accept/slash decision: value is zero below a closed-form minimum committee size (4 at π=0.05, q=0.7) even though mutual information is submodular, 24–34% of triples violate diminishing returns, myopic marginal-value hiring buys nothing (ratio 0 to the optimum) and leave-one-out pay is a parity sawtooth that falls 7× below average value at 40 verifiers. Stylised.

title: Which of n verifiers is best, decided at any time?
summary: Under Brier loss the best verifier is the one whose report is closest to the outcome frequency q, and each pair has an anytime-valid betting e-process growing at KL(q‖midpoint). Certifying the leader means beating every rival, so the delay is ln(1/α) over the smallest such rate, which belongs to the rival whose midpoint with the leader is nearest q: the best rival on the opposite side of q, not the runner-up (rate 0.0026 against 0.0086 in a six-verifier league). A bet mixture certifies within 1.35–1.60× of the oracle prediction; successive elimination cuts verifier evaluations 4cuts evaluation cost 2–4× at n=8–12ndash;5× at n=8–12; a peeking z-test declares a false strict best in 59% of exact-tie runs against 1.6% for the e-process. Stylised: fixed reports, i.i.d. tasks.

title: Wagering mechanisms as routers for modular, continually learning experts
summary: Weighted-score wagering (Lambert et al.) as a budget-balanced, replayable mixture-of-experts gate under recurring regime drift: plain wagering locks in, fixed-share wealth tax repairs it but subsidises free-riders.

title: How biased is a short digital-twin run that starts from a default state?
summary: A twin reset to an empty queue and averaged over n steps is biased toward that start. For AR(1) output the bias, variance and best warm-up deletion are exact (bias/sd 1.88 to 0.12 for n =20 to 2500 at φ =0.9). For the M/M/1 wait the summed empty-start bias is ρ /(1− ρ ) 3 (verified numerically against an exact series and coupled simulation), so it equals one standard deviation only at 23 jobs at ρ =0.9: at run lengths that give a valid interval it costs 1–3 coverage points. Short runs are different: 50 jobs from an empty start read 5.6 below the true mean wait of 9; starting at the mean reduces bias but not reliably RMSE; a noisy real-state start is unbiased with 3.6× the sd; MSER-5 truncation made bias and coverage worse here. Stylised (AR(1) and M/M/1, simulated “real” system).

title: How much of a digital-twin run should be thrown away because it started in the wrong state?
summary: A twin started from an empty queue or a nominal sensor value is biased at first. For AR(1) output the bias and variance of the run mean are exact (0.300 vs 0.300 simulated at φ =0.9, n =100), and the MSE-optimal warm-up is about one relaxation time 1/(1− φ ) with a gain of at most 1.5× and 1.03× once n is about a hundred relaxation times. An M/M/1 instrument started empty underestimates the mean wait by 21%, 6% and 1.2% at ρ =0.9 with 500, 2000 and 10 4 jobs, but at 5000 jobs the bias (−0.14) is far below the run-to-run RMSE (2.4). Negative result: fixed deletion does not lower RMSE, and MSER-5 truncation leaves a larger bias (−0.77), covers 61% against 72% for no truncation, and passes a violating system 28% of the time against 18%. Stylised (Gaussian AR(1), M/M/1, simulated “real” system).

title: A heartbeat twin that drops packets independently: how often does the real bursty link trip a missed-beat watchdog, and what timeout is safe?
summary: At 5% mean loss a watchdog that e-stops after m = 5 missed heartbeats false-trips once in 3.4×10 6 ticks (18.7 h at 50 Hz) in the i.i.d.-loss twin but every 235–990 ticks (5–20 s) on a two-state bursty link with mean burst 2–50, from an exact recursion checked against enumeration and Monte Carlo. The error is not monotone in burst length: it is worst at L ≈ m , where the mean time to trip is only ≈ e m / p . For a 10 6 -tick target the twin picks m = 5 (0.10 s to detect a dead link) while the real link needs 16–154 (0.3–3.1 s) growing linearly in L , and with L unknown no affordable timeout guarantees it. Stylised: Gilbert channel, plain miss counter, no link traces.

title: A twin with an unlimited actuator says a PI step response ignores step size: what does the real loop with a command limit do?
summary: Integrator plant under PI control, real actuator limited to |u|≤ U with constant load d ; the twin has neither. The twin is exact iff k p x 0 ≤ U (zero deviation up to x 0 =0.714), so gentle step tests certify it. Beyond that the integrator winds up to exactly x 0 2 /(2 U ): overshoot rises from the twin’s 21% to 74%, 93%, 97% and the settling time from 4.9 to 17, 165, 944 ( x 0 / U =5, 20, 50); a load d ≥ U is never rejected and settling blows up as d → U . “Faster is better” fails: the twin’s settling time falls 32× over ω n =0.25–8 while the real one is best near ω n =1 and rises to 77; conditional integration recovers most of it. Companion to the lag and slew twins. Stylised: one integrator, static limit, noiseless.

title: What does a deterministic-duration twin of a lab workcell promise, and how many stations does it buy?
summary: A batch is split over k parallel stations with a serial arm handover; a twin running every step at its mean picks k = √( W / a ) = 8 and promises 16 min. The real makespan uses the exact expected maximum of gamma branches (checked against harmonic numbers and simulation): with exponential branches it averages 1.86× the promise, only 2.6% of runs finish every branch within its mean, and the 95% quantile is 3.03× the promise. Whether the twin also buys the wrong layout depends on how variability scales with splitting: task-level variability makes it under-buy (optimum 12, 24.7% regret on the 95% quantile), while a chain of random unit steps cancels the effect so k = 8 stays optimal yet the real makespan is still 6–59% above the promise. Fitting the branch-time shape needs about 5 real durations to fix the decision and about 50 to make the predicted makespan accurate to 1%. Stylised: one fork-join stage, i.i.d. gamma branches.
